Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿With you, listening﴾ is a figure of speech; he means: I am for you both and against your enemy like a supporting helper, who is present and listens to what passes between you and him, then He makes you victorious, overcomes him for you, breaks his power against you, and reverses him. End. It is permissible that "ma'akum" be connected to "musta'miʿun", and that it be a predicate, with "musta'miʿun" as a second predicate. The "being with" here is metaphorical, and likewise the listening, because it means attentiveness, and listening does not necessarily entail hearing. You say: "asma'a ilayhi" (he listened to him), but "fa-ma sami'a" (he did not hear), while "istama'a ilayhi" (he listened to him) "fa-sami'a" (and heard), as He said: ﴿A group of the jinn listened and said: Indeed we heard﴾ [al-Jinn: 1]. He used the singular "rasul" here without the dual, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed we are two messengers of your Lord﴾ [Taha: 47], either because it is a verbal noun meaning the message, so it is permissible for it to occur in singular as a predicate for singular or more, or because the two of them have one law, so they are as one messenger. And by His saying "Anna" (I) or "each one of us is a messenger" is intended.

And ﴿the messenger of the Lord of the worlds﴾ contains a refutation of him, and that he is a subject of Allah, exalted is He. He confronted him with the abolition of what he had established of the claim of divinity, and for this reason he denied and said: ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ The meaning is "to you". ("And that send") may be explanatory of what is in "rasul" of the meaning of speech, and it may be a verbal (masdariyya) clause. "Arsala" here means (p-9) to release and set free, as you say: "I released the stone from my hand" and "I released the falcon". Moses was sent to Pharaoh with two matters: sending the Children of Israel so that servitude and the worship of other than Allah would be removed from them, and the faith in Allah; and he was sent with the acts of worship and the law to the Children of Israel, and their being sent with the two of them was to Palestine, and it was the dwelling of Moses and Harun.

﴿He said: Did We not rear you among us as a child, and you remained among us for some years of your life?﴾ ﴿And you did your deed that you did, and you were among the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿He said: I did it then, and I was among the astray.﴾ ﴿So I fled from you when I feared you, then my Lord granted me wisdom and made me among the messengers.﴾ ﴿And this is a favor you bestow upon me, that you enslaved the Children of Israel.﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 22] ﴿Pharaoh said: And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 23] ﴿He said: Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, if you were certain.﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 24] ﴿He said to those around him: Do you not listen?﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 25] ﴿He said: Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest.﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 26] ﴿He said: Indeed your messenger who has been sent to you is mad.﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 27] ﴿He said: Lord of the east and the west and what is between them, if you were reasoning.﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 28] ﴿He said: If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned.﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 29] ﴿He said: Even if I bring you something clear?﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 30] ﴿He said: Bring it, if you are among the truthful.﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 31] ﴿So he threw his staff, and behold, it was a clear serpent.﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 32] ﴿And he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white to the observers.﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 33]

(p-10) It is narrated that they went to the gate of Pharaoh, and were not admitted for a year, until the doorkeeper said: Here is a man who claims that he is a messenger of the Lord of the worlds. Pharaoh said to him: Admit him, perhaps we will laugh at him. They conveyed the message to him, and Moses recognized him, and he said to him: ﴿Did We not rear you among us as a child?﴾ In the speech there is an ellipsis that the meaning indicates, its estimate being: So they came to Pharaoh, and said to him that. When Moses confronted him by saying that he was a messenger of the Lord of the worlds, and commanded him to send the Children of Israel with him, he began to belittle him, strike at the sender and at what he brought from Allah, and remind him of his state of youth and the favor upon him by rearing. "Al-walid" is the child, and it is a form (fa'il) in the sense of (maf'ul), applied to him because of his nearness to birth. Abu 'Amr in one narration read "min 'umrika" with the sukun on the mim, and the disagreement about the number of these years was mentioned in Taha. The majority read "fa'latakа" with a fatha on the fa, since it was a single blow; al-Sha'bi read it with a kasra on the fa, meaning the form, because the blow is a type of killing. He enumerated upon him the favor of rearing and its extent in his estimation, the extent of men, since he used to kill his peers among the Children of Israel, and reminded him of what happened at his hand of the killing of the Copt, and magnified that by His saying: ﴿And you did your deed that you did﴾, because this vagueness, in not stating explicitly that it was killing, is an amplification of the event and a magnification of its matter.

﴿And you were among the disbelievers﴾ may be a circumstantial clause, meaning: you killed him while you were then among the disbelievers, so Pharaoh falsely attributed this state to him at that time, while the prophets, peace be upon them, are protected from sin. It may also be a new statement from Pharaoh, judging him to be among the disbelievers in the favor that I have upon you of rearing and kindness, as said by Ibn Zayd; or among the disbelievers in me in that I am your god, as said by al-Hasan; or among the disbelievers in Allah, because you were with us upon this religion of ours which you now criticize, as said by al-Suddi.

﴿He said: I did it then﴾ is Moses' answer to his last statement, which included the killing, since the excuse in it was more important than the answer regarding the mention of the favor of rearing, because it involved taking a soul. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Idhan" is a connective in the speech, and it is as if it means "then" (hinaʾidh). End. But it is not a connective; rather it is a particle of meaning. His saying "and it is as if it means then" should be taken as an explanation of meaning, since no one holds that "idhan" is synonymous with "hinaʾidh" in terms of grammatical function. Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you say): "idhan" is both a response and a condition at once, and the speech came as a response to Pharaoh, so how did it come as a condition? (I say): Pharaoh's saying: ﴿And you did your deed﴾ carries the meaning: you have repaid my favor by what you did; so Moses said to him: Yes, I did it, (p-11) repaying you, accepting his words, as if his favor was deserving in his estimation of being repaid with such a recompense. End. What he mentioned, that "idhan" is both response and condition, is the view of Sibawayh, but the commentators understood that it may be both response and condition, and it may be response alone without condition. The necessary meaning of it is the response, and it may with that also be a condition. They took His saying: ﴿I did it then﴾ as among the places where it came as response only, though some of our imams strained here to make it both condition and response; all of this is set out in what we wrote on "idhan" in the explanation of al-Tashil, and we only wished to mention that what al-Zamakhshari said is not the correct view, nor the view of most scholars.

﴿And I was among the astray﴾. Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is "among the ignorant", in that my striking him would come upon his own soul. Abu 'Ubayda said: "among the forgetful", and he drew this from His saying: ﴿lest one of them should err﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282]. In the reading of Abdullah and Ibn 'Abbas: "wa-ana min al-jahilin" (and I was among the ignorant), and it appears that this is an explanation of "al-dallin", not a reading transmitted from the Messenger ﷺ. Al-Zamakhshari said: among the doers of the deeds of the people of ignorance, as Joseph said to his brothers: ﴿when you were ignorant﴾ [Yusuf: 89]; or among the sincere ones, like one who kills by mistake without intending to kill; or among those who have gone away from that attribute. End. It was said: "among the astray", meaning from prophethood, and no word from Allah had come to me concerning it, so there is no blame upon me for what I did in that state. Among the strange interpretations of it is that the meaning of "and I was among the astray" is: among the lovers of Allah, and I did not kill the Copt except out of zeal for Allah. It was said: "dalal" is used and meant as love, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed you are in your old error﴾ [Yusuf: 95], meaning in your old love.

The pronoun of address in "minkum" and "khiftukum" is plural, though it had been singular in "tamunnuha" and "abbadta", because the fear and the flight were not from him alone, but from him and from his community mentioned before ﴿that you go to the wrongdoing people, the people of Pharaoh﴾, and they were a people who were conspiring to kill him. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Indeed the chiefs are conspiring against you to kill you, so leave﴾ [al-Qasas: 20].

The majority read "lamma" as a particle of obligation for obligation, according to Sibawayh, and as an adverb meaning "when", according to the view of al-Farisi. Hamzah in one narration read "lima" with a kasra on the lam and lightening of the mim, meaning: because of your fear. Isa read "hukuman" with a damma on the kaf; the majority with sukun. The "hukm" is prophethood.

﴿And He made me among the messengers﴾ is a second rank beyond prophethood, for many a prophet is not a messenger. It was said: "al-hukm" is knowledge and understanding.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 26, verse 1–21 (part 1 of 3):

(p-٢) (Surat ash-Shu'ara' has two hundred and twenty-seven verses, and it is Meccan.)
(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.) ﴿Ta, Sin, Mim.﴾ ﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book.﴾ ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not become believers.﴾ ﴿If We willed, We could send down upon them from the sky a sign, and their necks would remain humbled before it.﴾ ﴿Never does there come to them any new reminder from the Most Gracious except that they turn away from it.﴾ ﴿Indeed they have denied, so there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock.﴾ ﴿Have they not seen the earth, how many noble kinds of every pair We have caused to grow therein?﴾ ﴿Indeed in that is a sign, yet most of them are not believers.﴾ ﴿And indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿And when your Lord called Moses, [saying]: "Go to the wrongdoing people,﴾ ﴿the people of Pharaoh. Will they not fear Allah?"﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, I fear that they will deny me,﴾ ﴿and my breast will be constricted and my tongue will not be eloquent, so send for Aaron.﴾ ﴿And they have a charge against me, so I fear that they will kill me."﴾ ﴿He said: "No! Go, both of you, with Our signs. Indeed We are with you, listening.﴾ ﴿So go to Pharaoh and say: 'Indeed we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds,﴾ ﴿that you send with us the Children of Israel.'"﴾ .
(p-٣) Ash-shirdhimah: a small, despised group; the base remnant of everything. Abu 'Ubayda recited:
"in the shardhimah of mules"
Another said:
"Winter has come and my shirt is worn, tatters (sharadhim) at which he laughs."
Al-Jawhari said: ash-shirdhimah is a group of people, a piece of something; a garment that is shara[dh]im means pieces. End of quote. It is also said: the lowly of people. Kabkabahu: he turned some of it over upon other parts. Its letters are all original (radicals) according to the majority of the Basran grammarians. Al-Zamakhshari said: kabkabah is the repetition of kabb, the repetition being placed in the wording as evidence of repetition in meaning. Ibn 'Atiyya said: kabkaba is a doubled form of kabb; this is the view of the majority and is the correct one, because their meaning is one, and doubling in the verb is like sarra and sarsara. End of quote. The view of al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya is that of al-Zajjaj, who claims that words like kabkabahu, whose meaning is understood by dropping the third letter, are of the kind in which the letter ba' is doubled. The Kufans went (p-٤) to the view that the third letter is a substitute for a letter like the second, so its original form was kabbaba, and the second ba' was replaced by a kaf. Al-hamim: the close and near friend; hammat al-rajul: his intimate circle. Al-Zamakhshari said: al-hamim derives from al-ihtimam, which is concern, and it is one who is concerned with what concerns you; or from al-hamma in the sense of the inner circle, and it is the sincere friend.
﴿Ta, Sin, Mim.﴾ ﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book.﴾ ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not become believers.﴾ ﴿If We willed, We could send down upon them from the sky a sign, and their necks would remain humbled before it.﴾ ﴿Never does there come to them any new reminder from the Most Gracious except that they turn away from it.﴾ ﴿Indeed they have denied, so there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock.﴾ ﴿Have they not seen the earth, how many noble kinds of every pair We have caused to grow therein?﴾ ﴿Indeed in that is a sign, yet most of them are not believers.﴾ ﴿And indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿And when your Lord called Moses, [saying]: "Go to the wrongdoing people,﴾ ﴿the people of Pharaoh. Will they not fear Allah?"﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, I fear that they will deny me,﴾ ﴿and my breast will be constricted and my tongue will not be eloquent, so send for Aaron.﴾ ﴿And they have a charge against me, so I fear that they will kill me."﴾ ﴿He said: "No! Go, both of you, with Our signs. Indeed We are with you, listening.﴾ ﴿So go to Pharaoh and say: 'Indeed we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds,﴾ ﴿that you send with us the Children of Israel.'"﴾ .
(p-٥) This entire surah is Meccan according to the majority, except four verses, from ﴿And the poets, the misguided follow them﴾ [26:224] to the end of the surah; this is related from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata' and Qatada. Muqatil said: ﴿Is it not a sign for them﴾ [26:197] and what follows is Medinan. The connection of its beginning to the end of what precedes it is that He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So you have denied, and it will be inevitable﴾ [25:77], mentioning the anguish of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ over their not believing, and their denying the truth when it came to them. When He threatened them at the end of the surah with His words ﴿so it will be inevitable﴾ [25:77], He threatened them at the beginning of this one, saying after informing of their denial: ﴿so there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock﴾ [6:5]. "Those" refers to the verses of the surah or the verses of the Qur'an. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr, imala the fatha of the ta'; the rest of the seven read it with fatha. Hamzah shows the nun of "sin" clearly, while the rest of the seven assimilate it. 'Isa read the mim of "ta sin mim" with kasra here and in al-Qasas, and this is also reported from Nafi'. In the Mushaf of 'Abdullah it is "ta sin mim" separated; this is the reading of Abu Ja'far. They spoke about these letters in a manner resembling riddles and puzzles, and I have left out their discussion, since there is no evidence for anything they said.
(And the Clear Book) is the Qur'an; it is clear in itself and makes clear other rulings, laws, and everything it contains; or its miraculousness is clear, and the soundness of its being from Allah. The explanation of ﴿perhaps you would kill yourself﴾ was given earlier, at the beginning of al-Kahf. (Alla yakunu) means lest they believe, or for fear that they would not believe. Qatada and Zayd ibn 'Ali read "bakhi'u nafsika" with the idafa construction.
﴿If We willed﴾: "in" entered upon "nasha'" and "in" is for the possible, or for what is certain but whose time is unspecified. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the conditional's indefiniteness is here within our scope; as for Allah, exalted is He, it is known that He will not send down upon them a sign of compulsion; rather, Allah placed the signs of the prophets and the signs indicating Him open to observation and thought, so that whoever His knowledge has preceded for guidance may be guided, and whoever His knowledge has preceded for misguidance may go astray, and so that there may be an acquisition through the looking by which reward and punishment are connected; a sign of compulsion would negate all of this, were it to exist. End of quote. The meaning of "a sign" is: one compelling them to belief, forcing them to it. Abu 'Amr, in the narration of Harun from him, read "in yasha' yunazzal" in the third person, meaning if Allah wills He sends down; and in the mushafs it is "law nasha'na la-anzalna" (if We willed, We would have sent down). The majority read "fa-zallat" in the past form with future meaning, since it is conjoined to "nunazzil". Talha read "fa-tuzallal" and "a'naquhum". Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you say): how is it correct for "khadi'in" to come as a predicate of "a'naq"? I say: the original sentence is "fa-zallu lahā khādi'in", so "a'naq" was inserted to show the place of humility, and the sentence was left in its original form, like their saying: "dhahabtu ahl al-Yamama", where "the people" is not mentioned. End of quote. Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and al-Akhfash said: "a'naq" means their groups; it is said: "a neck of people came to me", meaning a group; and from it is the poet's saying:
"Indeed Iraq and its people are a neck toward you, so hayta hayta."
It is also said: the "necks" of people are their chiefs and leaders (p-٦), who are likened to necks, just as it is said: "for them are the heads, the forelocks, and the chests."
The poet said:
"In an assembly of forelocks of horses, witnessed."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 26, verses 1–21 (part 2 of 3):

It was also said: what is meant is the body part (al-jarihah). Ibn 'Isa said: it is by omission of a modifier (hadhf mudaf), meaning "the owners of the necks" (ashab al-a'naq). This omitted noun is taken into account in His words, ﴿khadi'in﴾ (humbled), where it came in the plural masculine rational form. Or there is no omission, but the word acquired the attribute of its annexation to a masculine rational noun, so it was described as such, just as a masculine noun acquires the feminine through being annexed to a feminine noun, as in the verse:

"Just as the shaft of the spear was stained with blood."

Or there is no omission, but since it was applied to an action that can only be intended by a rational being, which is submission (al-khudu'), it was made plural in the way that action is, as in His words: ﴿We came willingly (ta'i'in)﴾ [Fussilat: 11]. 'Isa and Ibn Abi 'Abla read khadi'ah (in the feminine singular). It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: this verse was revealed concerning us and the Banu Umayyah. "Dominion will be ours over them, and their necks will be humbled after Mu'awiyah, and disgrace will befall them after honour."

﴿And there does not come to them any reminder from the Most Merciful, newly revealed﴾. Its explanation has already been given in al-Anbiya'. (Illa kanu) is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah), meaning: except that they are turning away from it. This indicates that their habit and custom is turning away from the remembrance of Allah. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, how did the expressions differ while the purpose is one, namely turning away? I say: before a time they turned away from the reminder, then they denied it, and when they denied it, its worth became light to them and it became a target of mockery and ridicule. For whoever is receptive to the truth and turns towards it will undoubtedly believe in it, and he will not be suspected of denial. And whoever believes in it will revere it. End of quote.

(Fa-sa-ya'tihim) is a threat of the punishment of this world, such as the day of Badr, and the punishment of the Hereafter. Since their turning away from reflecting on the Creator of existence, and their denial of what His messengers brought, is among the greatest disbelief, and since they were making idols into gods, Exalted is He, drew attention to His power and that He is the Creator, the Originator, who deserves worship, by His words: ﴿Have they not looked at the earth...?﴾. The word (zawj) means kind (naw'). It was also said: a thing and its like. It was also said: white, black, red, yellow, sweet, and sour. Al-Farra' said: zawj means colour. Al-Karim means good (al-hasan), as said by Mujahid and Qatadah. It was also said: what people and animals eat. It was also said: what is abundant in benefit. It was also said: al-karim is an attribute of everything that is pleasing and praised. A karim face is one that is pleasing in its beauty and loveliness; a karim book is one that is pleasing in its meanings and benefits. And [the poet] said: "Until he splits the ranks by his nobility," meaning by his being pleasing in his courage and might. What is intended is the things by which the affairs are sustained: foods and plants, and this includes animals, since it is from two (sexes). Exalted is He said: ﴿And Allah has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth﴾ [Nuh: 17]. Al-Sha'bi said: people are from the growth of the earth. Whoever goes to Paradise is karim, and whoever goes to the Fire is the opposite of that.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, what is the meaning of combining "kam" and "kull"? If it were said: "We caused to grow in it from every karim pair," [would it not suffice]? I say: "kull" indicates encompassing all pairs of plants in detail, and "kam" indicates that this encompassing is abundant and extremely numerous. This is the meaning of the combination, and by it He drew attention to the perfection of His power. End of quote. He used the singular (la-ayah) even though what indicates multiplicity in the pairs, namely "kam," and what indicates encompassing generality in the pairs, has preceded it. This is because the thing referred to is one, namely the causing to grow, even if its objects differ. Or it is intended that in each one of those pairs there is a sign (ayah).

﴿And most of them were not believers﴾: this is a recording against most of them with disbelief.

﴿And indeed your Lord is the Almighty, the Most Merciful﴾, i.e., the Dominant, the Subduer. Since the context is one of demonstrating power, He placed the attribute of might before the attribute of mercy. When mercy comes from power, its effect is greater. The meaning is: He is mighty in His vengeance against the disbelievers, and He shows mercy to the believers of every nation.

When He mentioned the denial of Quraysh of the truth that came to them and their turning away from it, He mentioned the story of Musa, peace be upon him, and what he endured with Pharaoh and his people, so that this would be a consolation for what the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was suffering from the disbelievers of Quraysh. Since Quraysh had taken gods besides Allah, and the people of Pharaoh had taken him as a god, and the followers of the creed of Musa, peace be upon him, were the neighbours of those who believed in the Messenger, He began with the story of Musa, then mentioned after that the stories that are yet to be mentioned.

The governing element (al-'amil) in (idh) [when]: al-Zajjaj said: it is "recite" (utlu), implied, meaning: recite this story in what you recite, when he called out. The evidence for this is: ﴿And recite to them the news of Ibrahim﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 69], idh. It was also said: the governing element is "remember" (udhkur), which is like "recite," and the meaning of "called out" (nada) is "called" (da'a). It was also said: it is a command. "An" (that) may be a verbal particle (masdariyyah), and it may be explanatory (tafsiriyyah). He recorded their wrongdoing: the wrong they did to themselves by disbelief, and the wrong to the Children of Israel by enslavement and the slaughter of their sons. ﴿The people of Pharaoh﴾: it was said it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿the wrongdoing people﴾, but the better view is that it is an explicative apposition ('atf bayan), since the two expressions are synonymous referring to one meaning, for each of them, being an explicative apposition and justified by it, is independently a predicate. Since ﴿the wrongdoing people﴾ might give the impression of being shared with others, the explicative apposition came to remove that, since it is more well known. Al-Jumhur read: ﴿Will they not fear (Allah)?﴾ with the yā' (third person, the third person plural). 'Abd Allah ibn Muslim ibn Yasar, Shaqiq ibn Salamah, Hammad ibn Salamah and Abu Qilabah read it with the tā' of address, in the manner of iltifat (turning) towards them, expressing disapproval and anger against them, even though they were not present, because he is conveying that message to them and confronting them with it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: its meaning is "say to them," so this expression gathers the meanings of negating piety from them and commanding them to be pious.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, with what is His saying ﴿Will they not fear?﴾ connected? I say: it is a new (independent) statement that He, Exalted and Mighty, followed with His sending of him to them, as a warning and a recording against them of wrongdoing, and as an expression of wonder to Musa, peace be upon him, at their state, which strove in oppression and tyranny, and at their sense of security regarding consequences, and their lack of fear and caution regarding the days of Allah. It is possible that ﴿Will they not fear?﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿the wrongdoers﴾, meaning: they wrong while not fearing Allah and His punishment, so the interrogative hamzah of denial was introduced into the circumstantial clause. End of quote. This possibility he raised is a grave error, because he made it a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "the wrongdoers," while he himself parsed ﴿the people of Pharaoh﴾ as an explicative apposition, so there came to be a separation between the governing element and the governed by a foreign element between them, because "the people of Pharaoh" is governed by his saying "come" (i'ti). And what he claimed to be a circumstantial clause is governed by "the wrongdoers." This is also not permissible even if he had not separated them with "the people of Pharaoh": the clause cannot be a circumstantial clause, because what follows the hamzah cannot be governed by what precedes it. Your saying: "Did you come hastening (amusri'an)?" with "hastening" as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "you came" is not permitted. If you were to supply a governing element after the hamzah, it would be permitted. It was read with the nun both open and with kasrah, the estimated form being: "Will they not fear Me?" So the nun of the nominative was deleted to avoid two consecutive unvowelled letters, and the yā' of the speaker was deleted, sufficing with the kasrah. Al-Zamakhshari said: in ﴿ya-tanuna﴾ with the yā' and the kasrah of the nun there is another possibility, which is that the meaning is: "Ah, O people, fear Me," like His saying: ﴿Ah, [that] they should not prostrate﴾ [al-Naml: 25]. End of quote. He means: the alif of "ya" is deleted both in writing and in pronunciation, to avoid two consecutive unvowelled letters. This is a far-fetched derivation. The apparent meaning is that "ala" (ah) is for the expression of urging (al-'ard al-mudammin al-hadd), urging towards piety, and the saying of whoever says that it is for alerting (tanbih) is not correct, and likewise the saying of al-Zamakhshari that it is for negation, to which the hamzah of denial has been added.

Since Pharaoh was greatly arrogant to the point that he claimed divinity, and held great awe, and hearts were steeped in fear of him, especially those who were from the Children of Israel, Musa, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Indeed I fear that they will deny me﴾. Al-Jumhur read: ﴿wa-yadiqu﴾ (and my breast tightens) and ﴿wa-la yantaliqu﴾ (and my tongue does not speak freely), with the raf' (nominative) in both, in coordination with "I fear" (akhafu). The meaning is that it implies three causes: the fear of denial, the tightness of the chest, and the impediment of the speech of the tongue. Al-A'raj, Talhah, 'Isa, Zayd ibn 'Ali, Abu Hayawah, Za'idah from al-A'mash, and Ya'qub read both with the nasb (accusative), in coordination with "they deny me," so that the denial and what follows it are linked to the fear. Abu 'Amr al-Dani narrated from al-A'raj that he read "wa-yadiqa" with the accusative and "wa-la yantaliqu" with the nominative. The non-release of the tongue is by what results from fear and tightness of the chest, because the tongue at that time stammers and hardly makes clear the intended meaning of the person. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the tongue may not release speech due to the obscurity of the meanings that are sought to be expressed in precise words, so when this happens at a time of tightness of the chest, the tongue will not flow.

﴿So send (word) to Harun﴾: its meaning is "let him help me and support me." Harun, peace be upon him, was eloquent and broad of chest. So some of the intended meaning of the speech is omitted, since the remainder indicates it. End of quote. Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning of ﴿So send to Harun﴾ is: send Jibril, peace be upon him, to him, and make him a prophet, and support me through him, and strengthen my arm through him. This is a concise statement, and he has excelled in brevity when he said: ﴿So send to Harun﴾, bringing what contains the meaning of an exception. And his saying ﴿Indeed I fear﴾ to the end, after Allah had commanded him to go to the wrongdoing people, is not a hesitation regarding what Allah, Exalted, had commanded him with, but it is a request from Allah that He strengthen him with his brother, so that the two of them may cooperate in carrying out His command, Exalted, and conveying His message. Before requesting that, he set out his excuse and then made the request. Requesting help is a sign of acceptance, not of hesitation or making excuses. The object of "send" (arsil) is omitted. It was said: it is Jibril, as already mentioned. In a report it is said that Allah sent Musa to Harun, and Harun was in Egypt when Allah sent Musa as a prophet in al-Sham. Al-Suddi said: He travelled with his family to Egypt, and he met Harun, who did not recognise him, so he said: I am Musa. They recognised each other, and he commanded them both to go to Pharaoh to deliver the message. Their mother cried out in fear for them both, so they went to him.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 26, verse 1–21 (part 3 of 3):

﴿And they have a crime against me﴾, meaning: a retribution (qawad) for a crime, or a punishment is owed by me, namely his killing of the Coptic disbeliever, the baker of Pharaoh, with the blow (wakza) that he struck. Or he called the consequence of the sin a sin, just as he called the recompense of an evil deed an evil deed. Moses' statement is not a hesitation in carrying out the message; rather he said this seeking to ward off what he expected from them of killing, and he feared that he would be killed before conveying the message. This is indicated by his saying: ﴿Nay﴾ (kalla), which is the word of restraint. Then Allah, exalted is He, promised him protection and defense.

"Kalla" is a rejection of his saying: ﴿I fear﴾, meaning: do not fear that, for I have decreed your victory and triumph. His saying "fa-dhhaba" (so go) is a command addressed to Moses alone, since Harun is not spoken to by consensus; rather He said to Moses: ﴿Go, you and your brother﴾ [Taha: 42]. Al-Zamakhshari said: Allah combined both responses in His saying: ﴿Nay, so go﴾, because he (Moses) sought protection from their calamity, so He promised him protection by restraining him from fear, and he asked for support through his brother, so He answered him with His saying: "Go", meaning: go, you and the one you requested, Harun. (If you say): To what did He conjoin His saying "fa-dhhaba"? (I say): To the action indicated by "kalla", as if it were said: Desist, O Moses, from what you suppose, so go, you and Harun, with Our signs, which encompasses all that Allah sent them with, and the greatest of that is the staff, and by it the incapacity occurred. Ibn 'Atiyya said: There is no disagreement that Moses is the one whom Allah charged with the matter of prophethood and entrusted with it, and that Harun was a prophet, a messenger, a helper and a minister to him. End.

"Ma'akum" (with you): it was said that it is the placing of the plural in place of the dual, meaning "ma'akuma" (with you two). And it was said that it is on its literal plural sense, and what is intended is Moses, Harun and those to whom they were sent. Our shaykh, the teacher Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, preferred that the plural form was intended to mean the dual, and the address is to Moses and Harun only. He said: Because the word "with" (ma'a) with the distinction of who would be a disbeliever, it is not said that Allah is "with" him. And on the basis that the plural was intended as the dual, Sibawayh, may Allah have mercy on him, adopted this; and it is as if they, because of their nobility before Allah, were treated in address as a plural, since it is permissible for a single person to be addressed in this manner because of his nobility and greatness.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Musta'miʿun" (listening) is an expression of attentiveness (ihtibal); it is not in the form of "sami'un" (hearing), for otherwise Allah, exalted is He, is not described as seeking to listen. Rather the intent is to show concern, so that Moses' sense of intimacy is magnified, or the angels are listening by Allah's command to them. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿With you, listening﴾ is a figure of speech; he means: I am for you both and against your enemy like a supporting helper, who is present and listens to what passes between you and him, then He makes you victorious, overcomes him for you, breaks his power against you, and reverses him. End. It is permissible that "ma'akum" be connected to "musta'miʿun", and that it be a predicate, with "musta'miʿun" as a second predicate. The "being with" here is metaphorical, and likewise the listening, because it means attentiveness, and listening does not necessarily entail hearing. You say: "asma'a ilayhi" (he listened to him), but "fa-ma sami'a" (he did not hear), while "istama'a ilayhi" (he listened to him) "fa-sami'a" (and heard), as He said: ﴿A group of the jinn listened and said: Indeed we heard﴾ [al-Jinn: 1]. He used the singular "rasul" here without the dual, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed we are two messengers of your Lord﴾ [Taha: 47], either because it is a verbal noun meaning the message, so it is permissible for it to occur in singular as a predicate for singular or more, or because the two of them have one law, so they are as one messenger. And by His saying "Anna" (I) or "each one of us is a messenger" is intended.

And ﴿the messenger of the Lord of the worlds﴾ contains a refutation of him, and that he is a subject of Allah, exalted is He. He confronted him with the abolition of what he had established of the claim of divinity, and for this reason he denied and said: ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ The meaning is "to you". ("And that send") may be explanatory of what is in "rasul" of the meaning of speech, and it may be a verbal (masdariyya) clause. "Arsala" here means (p-9) to release and set free, as you say: "I released the stone from my hand" and "I released the falcon". Moses was sent to Pharaoh with two matters: sending the Children of Israel so that servitude and the worship of other than Allah would be removed from them, and the faith in Allah; and he was sent with the acts of worship and the law to the Children of Israel, and their being sent with the two of them was to Palestine, and it was the dwelling of Moses and Harun.

﴿He said: Did We not rear you among us as a child, and you remained among us for some years of your life?﴾ ﴿And you did your deed that you did, and you were among the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿He said: I did it then, and I was among the astray.﴾ ﴿So I fled from you when I feared you, then my Lord granted me wisdom and made me among the messengers.﴾ ﴿And this is a favor you bestow upon me, that you enslaved the Children of Israel.﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 22] ﴿Pharaoh said: And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 23] ﴿He said: Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, if you were certain.﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 24] ﴿He said to those around him: Do you not listen?﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 25] ﴿He said: Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest.﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 26] ﴿He said: Indeed your messenger who has been sent to you is mad.﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 27] ﴿He said: Lord of the east and the west and what is between them, if you were reasoning.﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 28] ﴿He said: If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned.﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 29] ﴿He said: Even if I bring you something clear?﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 30] ﴿He said: Bring it, if you are among the truthful.﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 31] ﴿So he threw his staff, and behold, it was a clear serpent.﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 32] ﴿And he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white to the observers.﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 33]

(p-10) It is narrated that they went to the gate of Pharaoh, and were not admitted for a year, until the doorkeeper said: Here is a man who claims that he is a messenger of the Lord of the worlds. Pharaoh said to him: Admit him, perhaps we will laugh at him. They conveyed the message to him, and Moses recognized him, and he said to him: ﴿Did We not rear you among us as a child?﴾ In the speech there is an ellipsis that the meaning indicates, its estimate being: So they came to Pharaoh, and said to him that. When Moses confronted him by saying that he was a messenger of the Lord of the worlds, and commanded him to send the Children of Israel with him, he began to belittle him, strike at the sender and at what he brought from Allah, and remind him of his state of youth and the favor upon him by rearing. "Al-walid" is the child, and it is a form (fa'il) in the sense of (maf'ul), applied to him because of his nearness to birth. Abu 'Amr in one narration read "min 'umrika" with the sukun on the mim, and the disagreement about the number of these years was mentioned in Taha. The majority read "fa'latakа" with a fatha on the fa, since it was a single blow; al-Sha'bi read it with a kasra on the fa, meaning the form, because the blow is a type of killing. He enumerated upon him the favor of rearing and its extent in his estimation, the extent of men, since he used to kill his peers among the Children of Israel, and reminded him of what happened at his hand of the killing of the Copt, and magnified that by His saying: ﴿And you did your deed that you did﴾, because this vagueness, in not stating explicitly that it was killing, is an amplification of the event and a magnification of its matter.

﴿And you were among the disbelievers﴾ may be a circumstantial clause, meaning: you killed him while you were then among the disbelievers, so Pharaoh falsely attributed this state to him at that time, while the prophets, peace be upon them, are protected from sin. It may also be a new statement from Pharaoh, judging him to be among the disbelievers in the favor that I have upon you of rearing and kindness, as said by Ibn Zayd; or among the disbelievers in me in that I am your god, as said by al-Hasan; or among the disbelievers in Allah, because you were with us upon this religion of ours which you now criticize, as said by al-Suddi.

﴿He said: I did it then﴾ is Moses' answer to his last statement, which included the killing, since the excuse in it was more important than the answer regarding the mention of the favor of rearing, because it involved taking a soul. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Idhan" is a connective in the speech, and it is as if it means "then" (hinaʾidh). End. But it is not a connective; rather it is a particle of meaning. His saying "and it is as if it means then" should be taken as an explanation of meaning, since no one holds that "idhan" is synonymous with "hinaʾidh" in terms of grammatical function. Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you say): "idhan" is both a response and a condition at once, and the speech came as a response to Pharaoh, so how did it come as a condition? (I say): Pharaoh's saying: ﴿And you did your deed﴾ carries the meaning: you have repaid my favor by what you did; so Moses said to him: Yes, I did it, (p-11) repaying you, accepting his words, as if his favor was deserving in his estimation of being repaid with such a recompense. End. What he mentioned, that "idhan" is both response and condition, is the view of Sibawayh, but the commentators understood that it may be both response and condition, and it may be response alone without condition. The necessary meaning of it is the response, and it may with that also be a condition. They took His saying: ﴿I did it then﴾ as among the places where it came as response only, though some of our imams strained here to make it both condition and response; all of this is set out in what we wrote on "idhan" in the explanation of al-Tashil, and we only wished to mention that what al-Zamakhshari said is not the correct view, nor the view of most scholars.

﴿And I was among the astray﴾. Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is "among the ignorant", in that my striking him would come upon his own soul. Abu 'Ubayda said: "among the forgetful", and he drew this from His saying: ﴿lest one of them should err﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282]. In the reading of Abdullah and Ibn 'Abbas: "wa-ana min al-jahilin" (and I was among the ignorant), and it appears that this is an explanation of "al-dallin", not a reading transmitted from the Messenger ﷺ. Al-Zamakhshari said: among the doers of the deeds of the people of ignorance, as Joseph said to his brothers: ﴿when you were ignorant﴾ [Yusuf: 89]; or among the sincere ones, like one who kills by mistake without intending to kill; or among those who have gone away from that attribute. End. It was said: "among the astray", meaning from prophethood, and no word from Allah had come to me concerning it, so there is no blame upon me for what I did in that state. Among the strange interpretations of it is that the meaning of "and I was among the astray" is: among the lovers of Allah, and I did not kill the Copt except out of zeal for Allah. It was said: "dalal" is used and meant as love, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed you are in your old error﴾ [Yusuf: 95], meaning in your old love.

The pronoun of address in "minkum" and "khiftukum" is plural, though it had been singular in "tamunnuha" and "abbadta", because the fear and the flight were not from him alone, but from him and from his community mentioned before ﴿that you go to the wrongdoing people, the people of Pharaoh﴾, and they were a people who were conspiring to kill him. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Indeed the chiefs are conspiring against you to kill you, so leave﴾ [al-Qasas: 20].

The majority read "lamma" as a particle of obligation for obligation, according to Sibawayh, and as an adverb meaning "when", according to the view of al-Farisi. Hamzah in one narration read "lima" with a kasra on the lam and lightening of the mim, meaning: because of your fear. Isa read "hukuman" with a damma on the kaf; the majority with sukun. The "hukm" is prophethood.

﴿And He made me among the messengers﴾ is a second rank beyond prophethood, for many a prophet is not a messenger. It was said: "al-hukm" is knowledge and understanding.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 26, verse 1–21 (part 1 of 3):

(p-٢) (Surat ash-Shu'ara' has two hundred and twenty-seven verses, and it is Meccan.)
(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.) ﴿Ta, Sin, Mim.﴾ ﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book.﴾ ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not become believers.﴾ ﴿If We willed, We could send down upon them from the sky a sign, and their necks would remain humbled before it.﴾ ﴿Never does there come to them any new reminder from the Most Gracious except that they turn away from it.﴾ ﴿Indeed they have denied, so there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock.﴾ ﴿Have they not seen the earth, how many noble kinds of every pair We have caused to grow therein?﴾ ﴿Indeed in that is a sign, yet most of them are not believers.﴾ ﴿And indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿And when your Lord called Moses, [saying]: "Go to the wrongdoing people,﴾ ﴿the people of Pharaoh. Will they not fear Allah?"﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, I fear that they will deny me,﴾ ﴿and my breast will be constricted and my tongue will not be eloquent, so send for Aaron.﴾ ﴿And they have a charge against me, so I fear that they will kill me."﴾ ﴿He said: "No! Go, both of you, with Our signs. Indeed We are with you, listening.﴾ ﴿So go to Pharaoh and say: 'Indeed we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds,﴾ ﴿that you send with us the Children of Israel.'"﴾ .
(p-٣) Ash-shirdhimah: a small, despised group; the base remnant of everything. Abu 'Ubayda recited:
"in the shardhimah of mules"
Another said:
"Winter has come and my shirt is worn, tatters (sharadhim) at which he laughs."
Al-Jawhari said: ash-shirdhimah is a group of people, a piece of something; a garment that is shara[dh]im means pieces. End of quote. It is also said: the lowly of people. Kabkabahu: he turned some of it over upon other parts. Its letters are all original (radicals) according to the majority of the Basran grammarians. Al-Zamakhshari said: kabkabah is the repetition of kabb, the repetition being placed in the wording as evidence of repetition in meaning. Ibn 'Atiyya said: kabkaba is a doubled form of kabb; this is the view of the majority and is the correct one, because their meaning is one, and doubling in the verb is like sarra and sarsara. End of quote. The view of al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya is that of al-Zajjaj, who claims that words like kabkabahu, whose meaning is understood by dropping the third letter, are of the kind in which the letter ba' is doubled. The Kufans went (p-٤) to the view that the third letter is a substitute for a letter like the second, so its original form was kabbaba, and the second ba' was replaced by a kaf. Al-hamim: the close and near friend; hammat al-rajul: his intimate circle. Al-Zamakhshari said: al-hamim derives from al-ihtimam, which is concern, and it is one who is concerned with what concerns you; or from al-hamma in the sense of the inner circle, and it is the sincere friend.
﴿Ta, Sin, Mim.﴾ ﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book.﴾ ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not become believers.﴾ ﴿If We willed, We could send down upon them from the sky a sign, and their necks would remain humbled before it.﴾ ﴿Never does there come to them any new reminder from the Most Gracious except that they turn away from it.﴾ ﴿Indeed they have denied, so there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock.﴾ ﴿Have they not seen the earth, how many noble kinds of every pair We have caused to grow therein?﴾ ﴿Indeed in that is a sign, yet most of them are not believers.﴾ ﴿And indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿And when your Lord called Moses, [saying]: "Go to the wrongdoing people,﴾ ﴿the people of Pharaoh. Will they not fear Allah?"﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, I fear that they will deny me,﴾ ﴿and my breast will be constricted and my tongue will not be eloquent, so send for Aaron.﴾ ﴿And they have a charge against me, so I fear that they will kill me."﴾ ﴿He said: "No! Go, both of you, with Our signs. Indeed We are with you, listening.﴾ ﴿So go to Pharaoh and say: 'Indeed we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds,﴾ ﴿that you send with us the Children of Israel.'"﴾ .
(p-٥) This entire surah is Meccan according to the majority, except four verses, from ﴿And the poets, the misguided follow them﴾ [26:224] to the end of the surah; this is related from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata' and Qatada. Muqatil said: ﴿Is it not a sign for them﴾ [26:197] and what follows is Medinan. The connection of its beginning to the end of what precedes it is that He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So you have denied, and it will be inevitable﴾ [25:77], mentioning the anguish of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ over their not believing, and their denying the truth when it came to them. When He threatened them at the end of the surah with His words ﴿so it will be inevitable﴾ [25:77], He threatened them at the beginning of this one, saying after informing of their denial: ﴿so there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock﴾ [6:5]. "Those" refers to the verses of the surah or the verses of the Qur'an. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr, imala the fatha of the ta'; the rest of the seven read it with fatha. Hamzah shows the nun of "sin" clearly, while the rest of the seven assimilate it. 'Isa read the mim of "ta sin mim" with kasra here and in al-Qasas, and this is also reported from Nafi'. In the Mushaf of 'Abdullah it is "ta sin mim" separated; this is the reading of Abu Ja'far. They spoke about these letters in a manner resembling riddles and puzzles, and I have left out their discussion, since there is no evidence for anything they said.
(And the Clear Book) is the Qur'an; it is clear in itself and makes clear other rulings, laws, and everything it contains; or its miraculousness is clear, and the soundness of its being from Allah. The explanation of ﴿perhaps you would kill yourself﴾ was given earlier, at the beginning of al-Kahf. (Alla yakunu) means lest they believe, or for fear that they would not believe. Qatada and Zayd ibn 'Ali read "bakhi'u nafsika" with the idafa construction.
﴿If We willed﴾: "in" entered upon "nasha'" and "in" is for the possible, or for what is certain but whose time is unspecified. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the conditional's indefiniteness is here within our scope; as for Allah, exalted is He, it is known that He will not send down upon them a sign of compulsion; rather, Allah placed the signs of the prophets and the signs indicating Him open to observation and thought, so that whoever His knowledge has preceded for guidance may be guided, and whoever His knowledge has preceded for misguidance may go astray, and so that there may be an acquisition through the looking by which reward and punishment are connected; a sign of compulsion would negate all of this, were it to exist. End of quote. The meaning of "a sign" is: one compelling them to belief, forcing them to it. Abu 'Amr, in the narration of Harun from him, read "in yasha' yunazzal" in the third person, meaning if Allah wills He sends down; and in the mushafs it is "law nasha'na la-anzalna" (if We willed, We would have sent down). The majority read "fa-zallat" in the past form with future meaning, since it is conjoined to "nunazzil". Talha read "fa-tuzallal" and "a'naquhum". Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you say): how is it correct for "khadi'in" to come as a predicate of "a'naq"? I say: the original sentence is "fa-zallu lahā khādi'in", so "a'naq" was inserted to show the place of humility, and the sentence was left in its original form, like their saying: "dhahabtu ahl al-Yamama", where "the people" is not mentioned. End of quote. Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and al-Akhfash said: "a'naq" means their groups; it is said: "a neck of people came to me", meaning a group; and from it is the poet's saying:
"Indeed Iraq and its people are a neck toward you, so hayta hayta."
It is also said: the "necks" of people are their chiefs and leaders (p-٦), who are likened to necks, just as it is said: "for them are the heads, the forelocks, and the chests."
The poet said:
"In an assembly of forelocks of horses, witnessed."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 26, verses 1–21 (part 2 of 3):

It was also said: what is meant is the body part (al-jarihah). Ibn 'Isa said: it is by omission of a modifier (hadhf mudaf), meaning "the owners of the necks" (ashab al-a'naq). This omitted noun is taken into account in His words, ﴿khadi'in﴾ (humbled), where it came in the plural masculine rational form. Or there is no omission, but the word acquired the attribute of its annexation to a masculine rational noun, so it was described as such, just as a masculine noun acquires the feminine through being annexed to a feminine noun, as in the verse:

"Just as the shaft of the spear was stained with blood."

Or there is no omission, but since it was applied to an action that can only be intended by a rational being, which is submission (al-khudu'), it was made plural in the way that action is, as in His words: ﴿We came willingly (ta'i'in)﴾ [Fussilat: 11]. 'Isa and Ibn Abi 'Abla read khadi'ah (in the feminine singular). It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: this verse was revealed concerning us and the Banu Umayyah. "Dominion will be ours over them, and their necks will be humbled after Mu'awiyah, and disgrace will befall them after honour."

﴿And there does not come to them any reminder from the Most Merciful, newly revealed﴾. Its explanation has already been given in al-Anbiya'. (Illa kanu) is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah), meaning: except that they are turning away from it. This indicates that their habit and custom is turning away from the remembrance of Allah. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, how did the expressions differ while the purpose is one, namely turning away? I say: before a time they turned away from the reminder, then they denied it, and when they denied it, its worth became light to them and it became a target of mockery and ridicule. For whoever is receptive to the truth and turns towards it will undoubtedly believe in it, and he will not be suspected of denial. And whoever believes in it will revere it. End of quote.

(Fa-sa-ya'tihim) is a threat of the punishment of this world, such as the day of Badr, and the punishment of the Hereafter. Since their turning away from reflecting on the Creator of existence, and their denial of what His messengers brought, is among the greatest disbelief, and since they were making idols into gods, Exalted is He, drew attention to His power and that He is the Creator, the Originator, who deserves worship, by His words: ﴿Have they not looked at the earth...?﴾. The word (zawj) means kind (naw'). It was also said: a thing and its like. It was also said: white, black, red, yellow, sweet, and sour. Al-Farra' said: zawj means colour. Al-Karim means good (al-hasan), as said by Mujahid and Qatadah. It was also said: what people and animals eat. It was also said: what is abundant in benefit. It was also said: al-karim is an attribute of everything that is pleasing and praised. A karim face is one that is pleasing in its beauty and loveliness; a karim book is one that is pleasing in its meanings and benefits. And [the poet] said: "Until he splits the ranks by his nobility," meaning by his being pleasing in his courage and might. What is intended is the things by which the affairs are sustained: foods and plants, and this includes animals, since it is from two (sexes). Exalted is He said: ﴿And Allah has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth﴾ [Nuh: 17]. Al-Sha'bi said: people are from the growth of the earth. Whoever goes to Paradise is karim, and whoever goes to the Fire is the opposite of that.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, what is the meaning of combining "kam" and "kull"? If it were said: "We caused to grow in it from every karim pair," [would it not suffice]? I say: "kull" indicates encompassing all pairs of plants in detail, and "kam" indicates that this encompassing is abundant and extremely numerous. This is the meaning of the combination, and by it He drew attention to the perfection of His power. End of quote. He used the singular (la-ayah) even though what indicates multiplicity in the pairs, namely "kam," and what indicates encompassing generality in the pairs, has preceded it. This is because the thing referred to is one, namely the causing to grow, even if its objects differ. Or it is intended that in each one of those pairs there is a sign (ayah).

﴿And most of them were not believers﴾: this is a recording against most of them with disbelief.

﴿And indeed your Lord is the Almighty, the Most Merciful﴾, i.e., the Dominant, the Subduer. Since the context is one of demonstrating power, He placed the attribute of might before the attribute of mercy. When mercy comes from power, its effect is greater. The meaning is: He is mighty in His vengeance against the disbelievers, and He shows mercy to the believers of every nation.

When He mentioned the denial of Quraysh of the truth that came to them and their turning away from it, He mentioned the story of Musa, peace be upon him, and what he endured with Pharaoh and his people, so that this would be a consolation for what the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was suffering from the disbelievers of Quraysh. Since Quraysh had taken gods besides Allah, and the people of Pharaoh had taken him as a god, and the followers of the creed of Musa, peace be upon him, were the neighbours of those who believed in the Messenger, He began with the story of Musa, then mentioned after that the stories that are yet to be mentioned.

The governing element (al-'amil) in (idh) [when]: al-Zajjaj said: it is "recite" (utlu), implied, meaning: recite this story in what you recite, when he called out. The evidence for this is: ﴿And recite to them the news of Ibrahim﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 69], idh. It was also said: the governing element is "remember" (udhkur), which is like "recite," and the meaning of "called out" (nada) is "called" (da'a). It was also said: it is a command. "An" (that) may be a verbal particle (masdariyyah), and it may be explanatory (tafsiriyyah). He recorded their wrongdoing: the wrong they did to themselves by disbelief, and the wrong to the Children of Israel by enslavement and the slaughter of their sons. ﴿The people of Pharaoh﴾: it was said it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿the wrongdoing people﴾, but the better view is that it is an explicative apposition ('atf bayan), since the two expressions are synonymous referring to one meaning, for each of them, being an explicative apposition and justified by it, is independently a predicate. Since ﴿the wrongdoing people﴾ might give the impression of being shared with others, the explicative apposition came to remove that, since it is more well known. Al-Jumhur read: ﴿Will they not fear (Allah)?﴾ with the yā' (third person, the third person plural). 'Abd Allah ibn Muslim ibn Yasar, Shaqiq ibn Salamah, Hammad ibn Salamah and Abu Qilabah read it with the tā' of address, in the manner of iltifat (turning) towards them, expressing disapproval and anger against them, even though they were not present, because he is conveying that message to them and confronting them with it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: its meaning is "say to them," so this expression gathers the meanings of negating piety from them and commanding them to be pious.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, with what is His saying ﴿Will they not fear?﴾ connected? I say: it is a new (independent) statement that He, Exalted and Mighty, followed with His sending of him to them, as a warning and a recording against them of wrongdoing, and as an expression of wonder to Musa, peace be upon him, at their state, which strove in oppression and tyranny, and at their sense of security regarding consequences, and their lack of fear and caution regarding the days of Allah. It is possible that ﴿Will they not fear?﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿the wrongdoers﴾, meaning: they wrong while not fearing Allah and His punishment, so the interrogative hamzah of denial was introduced into the circumstantial clause. End of quote. This possibility he raised is a grave error, because he made it a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "the wrongdoers," while he himself parsed ﴿the people of Pharaoh﴾ as an explicative apposition, so there came to be a separation between the governing element and the governed by a foreign element between them, because "the people of Pharaoh" is governed by his saying "come" (i'ti). And what he claimed to be a circumstantial clause is governed by "the wrongdoers." This is also not permissible even if he had not separated them with "the people of Pharaoh": the clause cannot be a circumstantial clause, because what follows the hamzah cannot be governed by what precedes it. Your saying: "Did you come hastening (amusri'an)?" with "hastening" as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "you came" is not permitted. If you were to supply a governing element after the hamzah, it would be permitted. It was read with the nun both open and with kasrah, the estimated form being: "Will they not fear Me?" So the nun of the nominative was deleted to avoid two consecutive unvowelled letters, and the yā' of the speaker was deleted, sufficing with the kasrah. Al-Zamakhshari said: in ﴿ya-tanuna﴾ with the yā' and the kasrah of the nun there is another possibility, which is that the meaning is: "Ah, O people, fear Me," like His saying: ﴿Ah, [that] they should not prostrate﴾ [al-Naml: 25]. End of quote. He means: the alif of "ya" is deleted both in writing and in pronunciation, to avoid two consecutive unvowelled letters. This is a far-fetched derivation. The apparent meaning is that "ala" (ah) is for the expression of urging (al-'ard al-mudammin al-hadd), urging towards piety, and the saying of whoever says that it is for alerting (tanbih) is not correct, and likewise the saying of al-Zamakhshari that it is for negation, to which the hamzah of denial has been added.

Since Pharaoh was greatly arrogant to the point that he claimed divinity, and held great awe, and hearts were steeped in fear of him, especially those who were from the Children of Israel, Musa, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Indeed I fear that they will deny me﴾. Al-Jumhur read: ﴿wa-yadiqu﴾ (and my breast tightens) and ﴿wa-la yantaliqu﴾ (and my tongue does not speak freely), with the raf' (nominative) in both, in coordination with "I fear" (akhafu). The meaning is that it implies three causes: the fear of denial, the tightness of the chest, and the impediment of the speech of the tongue. Al-A'raj, Talhah, 'Isa, Zayd ibn 'Ali, Abu Hayawah, Za'idah from al-A'mash, and Ya'qub read both with the nasb (accusative), in coordination with "they deny me," so that the denial and what follows it are linked to the fear. Abu 'Amr al-Dani narrated from al-A'raj that he read "wa-yadiqa" with the accusative and "wa-la yantaliqu" with the nominative. The non-release of the tongue is by what results from fear and tightness of the chest, because the tongue at that time stammers and hardly makes clear the intended meaning of the person. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the tongue may not release speech due to the obscurity of the meanings that are sought to be expressed in precise words, so when this happens at a time of tightness of the chest, the tongue will not flow.

﴿So send (word) to Harun﴾: its meaning is "let him help me and support me." Harun, peace be upon him, was eloquent and broad of chest. So some of the intended meaning of the speech is omitted, since the remainder indicates it. End of quote. Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning of ﴿So send to Harun﴾ is: send Jibril, peace be upon him, to him, and make him a prophet, and support me through him, and strengthen my arm through him. This is a concise statement, and he has excelled in brevity when he said: ﴿So send to Harun﴾, bringing what contains the meaning of an exception. And his saying ﴿Indeed I fear﴾ to the end, after Allah had commanded him to go to the wrongdoing people, is not a hesitation regarding what Allah, Exalted, had commanded him with, but it is a request from Allah that He strengthen him with his brother, so that the two of them may cooperate in carrying out His command, Exalted, and conveying His message. Before requesting that, he set out his excuse and then made the request. Requesting help is a sign of acceptance, not of hesitation or making excuses. The object of "send" (arsil) is omitted. It was said: it is Jibril, as already mentioned. In a report it is said that Allah sent Musa to Harun, and Harun was in Egypt when Allah sent Musa as a prophet in al-Sham. Al-Suddi said: He travelled with his family to Egypt, and he met Harun, who did not recognise him, so he said: I am Musa. They recognised each other, and he commanded them both to go to Pharaoh to deliver the message. Their mother cried out in fear for them both, so they went to him.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 26, verse 1–21 (part 3 of 3):

﴿And they have a crime against me﴾, meaning: a retribution (qawad) for a crime, or a punishment is owed by me, namely his killing of the Coptic disbeliever, the baker of Pharaoh, with the blow (wakza) that he struck. Or he called the consequence of the sin a sin, just as he called the recompense of an evil deed an evil deed. Moses' statement is not a hesitation in carrying out the message; rather he said this seeking to ward off what he expected from them of killing, and he feared that he would be killed before conveying the message. This is indicated by his saying: ﴿Nay﴾ (kalla), which is the word of restraint. Then Allah, exalted is He, promised him protection and defense.

"Kalla" is a rejection of his saying: ﴿I fear﴾, meaning: do not fear that, for I have decreed your victory and triumph. His saying "fa-dhhaba" (so go) is a command addressed to Moses alone, since Harun is not spoken to by consensus; rather He said to Moses: ﴿Go, you and your brother﴾ [Taha: 42]. Al-Zamakhshari said: Allah combined both responses in His saying: ﴿Nay, so go﴾, because he (Moses) sought protection from their calamity, so He promised him protection by restraining him from fear, and he asked for support through his brother, so He answered him with His saying: "Go", meaning: go, you and the one you requested, Harun. (If you say): To what did He conjoin His saying "fa-dhhaba"? (I say): To the action indicated by "kalla", as if it were said: Desist, O Moses, from what you suppose, so go, you and Harun, with Our signs, which encompasses all that Allah sent them with, and the greatest of that is the staff, and by it the incapacity occurred. Ibn 'Atiyya said: There is no disagreement that Moses is the one whom Allah charged with the matter of prophethood and entrusted with it, and that Harun was a prophet, a messenger, a helper and a minister to him. End.

"Ma'akum" (with you): it was said that it is the placing of the plural in place of the dual, meaning "ma'akuma" (with you two). And it was said that it is on its literal plural sense, and what is intended is Moses, Harun and those to whom they were sent. Our shaykh, the teacher Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, preferred that the plural form was intended to mean the dual, and the address is to Moses and Harun only. He said: Because the word "with" (ma'a) with the distinction of who would be a disbeliever, it is not said that Allah is "with" him. And on the basis that the plural was intended as the dual, Sibawayh, may Allah have mercy on him, adopted this; and it is as if they, because of their nobility before Allah, were treated in address as a plural, since it is permissible for a single person to be addressed in this manner because of his nobility and greatness.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Musta'miʿun" (listening) is an expression of attentiveness (ihtibal); it is not in the form of "sami'un" (hearing), for otherwise Allah, exalted is He, is not described as seeking to listen. Rather the intent is to show concern, so that Moses' sense of intimacy is magnified, or the angels are listening by Allah's command to them. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿With you, listening﴾ is a figure of speech; he means: I am for you both and against your enemy like a supporting helper, who is present and listens to what passes between you and him, then He makes you victorious, overcomes him for you, breaks his power against you, and reverses him. End. It is permissible that "ma'akum" be connected to "musta'miʿun", and that it be a predicate, with "musta'miʿun" as a second predicate. The "being with" here is metaphorical, and likewise the listening, because it means attentiveness, and listening does not necessarily entail hearing. You say: "asma'a ilayhi" (he listened to him), but "fa-ma sami'a" (he did not hear), while "istama'a ilayhi" (he listened to him) "fa-sami'a" (and heard), as He said: ﴿A group of the jinn listened and said: Indeed we heard﴾ [al-Jinn: 1]. He used the singular "rasul" here without the dual, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed we are two messengers of your Lord﴾ [Taha: 47], either because it is a verbal noun meaning the message, so it is permissible for it to occur in singular as a predicate for singular or more, or because the two of them have one law, so they are as one messenger. And by His saying "Anna" (I) or "each one of us is a messenger" is intended.

And ﴿the messenger of the Lord of the worlds﴾ contains a refutation of him, and that he is a subject of Allah, exalted is He. He confronted him with the abolition of what he had established of the claim of divinity, and for this reason he denied and said: ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ The meaning is "to you". ("And that send") may be explanatory of what is in "rasul" of the meaning of speech, and it may be a verbal (masdariyya) clause. "Arsala" here means (p-9) to release and set free, as you say: "I released the stone from my hand" and "I released the falcon". Moses was sent to Pharaoh with two matters: sending the Children of Israel so that servitude and the worship of other than Allah would be removed from them, and the faith in Allah; and he was sent with the acts of worship and the law to the Children of Israel, and their being sent with the two of them was to Palestine, and it was the dwelling of Moses and Harun.

﴿He said: Did We not rear you among us as a child, and you remained among us for some years of your life?﴾ ﴿And you did your deed that you did, and you were among the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿He said: I did it then, and I was among the astray.﴾ ﴿So I fled from you when I feared you, then my Lord granted me wisdom and made me among the messengers.﴾ ﴿And this is a favor you bestow upon me, that you enslaved the Children of Israel.﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 22] ﴿Pharaoh said: And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 23] ﴿He said: Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, if you were certain.﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 24] ﴿He said to those around him: Do you not listen?﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 25] ﴿He said: Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest.﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 26] ﴿He said: Indeed your messenger who has been sent to you is mad.﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 27] ﴿He said: Lord of the east and the west and what is between them, if you were reasoning.﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 28] ﴿He said: If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned.﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 29] ﴿He said: Even if I bring you something clear?﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 30] ﴿He said: Bring it, if you are among the truthful.﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 31] ﴿So he threw his staff, and behold, it was a clear serpent.﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 32] ﴿And he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white to the observers.﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 33]

(p-10) It is narrated that they went to the gate of Pharaoh, and were not admitted for a year, until the doorkeeper said: Here is a man who claims that he is a messenger of the Lord of the worlds. Pharaoh said to him: Admit him, perhaps we will laugh at him. They conveyed the message to him, and Moses recognized him, and he said to him: ﴿Did We not rear you among us as a child?﴾ In the speech there is an ellipsis that the meaning indicates, its estimate being: So they came to Pharaoh, and said to him that. When Moses confronted him by saying that he was a messenger of the Lord of the worlds, and commanded him to send the Children of Israel with him, he began to belittle him, strike at the sender and at what he brought from Allah, and remind him of his state of youth and the favor upon him by rearing. "Al-walid" is the child, and it is a form (fa'il) in the sense of (maf'ul), applied to him because of his nearness to birth. Abu 'Amr in one narration read "min 'umrika" with the sukun on the mim, and the disagreement about the number of these years was mentioned in Taha. The majority read "fa'latakа" with a fatha on the fa, since it was a single blow; al-Sha'bi read it with a kasra on the fa, meaning the form, because the blow is a type of killing. He enumerated upon him the favor of rearing and its extent in his estimation, the extent of men, since he used to kill his peers among the Children of Israel, and reminded him of what happened at his hand of the killing of the Copt, and magnified that by His saying: ﴿And you did your deed that you did﴾, because this vagueness, in not stating explicitly that it was killing, is an amplification of the event and a magnification of its matter.

﴿And you were among the disbelievers﴾ may be a circumstantial clause, meaning: you killed him while you were then among the disbelievers, so Pharaoh falsely attributed this state to him at that time, while the prophets, peace be upon them, are protected from sin. It may also be a new statement from Pharaoh, judging him to be among the disbelievers in the favor that I have upon you of rearing and kindness, as said by Ibn Zayd; or among the disbelievers in me in that I am your god, as said by al-Hasan; or among the disbelievers in Allah, because you were with us upon this religion of ours which you now criticize, as said by al-Suddi.

﴿He said: I did it then﴾ is Moses' answer to his last statement, which included the killing, since the excuse in it was more important than the answer regarding the mention of the favor of rearing, because it involved taking a soul. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Idhan" is a connective in the speech, and it is as if it means "then" (hinaʾidh). End. But it is not a connective; rather it is a particle of meaning. His saying "and it is as if it means then" should be taken as an explanation of meaning, since no one holds that "idhan" is synonymous with "hinaʾidh" in terms of grammatical function. Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you say): "idhan" is both a response and a condition at once, and the speech came as a response to Pharaoh, so how did it come as a condition? (I say): Pharaoh's saying: ﴿And you did your deed﴾ carries the meaning: you have repaid my favor by what you did; so Moses said to him: Yes, I did it, (p-11) repaying you, accepting his words, as if his favor was deserving in his estimation of being repaid with such a recompense. End. What he mentioned, that "idhan" is both response and condition, is the view of Sibawayh, but the commentators understood that it may be both response and condition, and it may be response alone without condition. The necessary meaning of it is the response, and it may with that also be a condition. They took His saying: ﴿I did it then﴾ as among the places where it came as response only, though some of our imams strained here to make it both condition and response; all of this is set out in what we wrote on "idhan" in the explanation of al-Tashil, and we only wished to mention that what al-Zamakhshari said is not the correct view, nor the view of most scholars.

﴿And I was among the astray﴾. Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is "among the ignorant", in that my striking him would come upon his own soul. Abu 'Ubayda said: "among the forgetful", and he drew this from His saying: ﴿lest one of them should err﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282]. In the reading of Abdullah and Ibn 'Abbas: "wa-ana min al-jahilin" (and I was among the ignorant), and it appears that this is an explanation of "al-dallin", not a reading transmitted from the Messenger ﷺ. Al-Zamakhshari said: among the doers of the deeds of the people of ignorance, as Joseph said to his brothers: ﴿when you were ignorant﴾ [Yusuf: 89]; or among the sincere ones, like one who kills by mistake without intending to kill; or among those who have gone away from that attribute. End. It was said: "among the astray", meaning from prophethood, and no word from Allah had come to me concerning it, so there is no blame upon me for what I did in that state. Among the strange interpretations of it is that the meaning of "and I was among the astray" is: among the lovers of Allah, and I did not kill the Copt except out of zeal for Allah. It was said: "dalal" is used and meant as love, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed you are in your old error﴾ [Yusuf: 95], meaning in your old love.

The pronoun of address in "minkum" and "khiftukum" is plural, though it had been singular in "tamunnuha" and "abbadta", because the fear and the flight were not from him alone, but from him and from his community mentioned before ﴿that you go to the wrongdoing people, the people of Pharaoh﴾, and they were a people who were conspiring to kill him. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Indeed the chiefs are conspiring against you to kill you, so leave﴾ [al-Qasas: 20].

The majority read "lamma" as a particle of obligation for obligation, according to Sibawayh, and as an adverb meaning "when", according to the view of al-Farisi. Hamzah in one narration read "lima" with a kasra on the lam and lightening of the mim, meaning: because of your fear. Isa read "hukuman" with a damma on the kaf; the majority with sukun. The "hukm" is prophethood.

﴿And He made me among the messengers﴾ is a second rank beyond prophethood, for many a prophet is not a messenger. It was said: "al-hukm" is knowledge and understanding.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 26, verse 1–21 (part 1 of 3):

(p-٢) (Surat ash-Shu'ara' has two hundred and twenty-seven verses, and it is Meccan.)
(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.) ﴿Ta, Sin, Mim.﴾ ﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book.﴾ ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not become believers.﴾ ﴿If We willed, We could send down upon them from the sky a sign, and their necks would remain humbled before it.﴾ ﴿Never does there come to them any new reminder from the Most Gracious except that they turn away from it.﴾ ﴿Indeed they have denied, so there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock.﴾ ﴿Have they not seen the earth, how many noble kinds of every pair We have caused to grow therein?﴾ ﴿Indeed in that is a sign, yet most of them are not believers.﴾ ﴿And indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿And when your Lord called Moses, [saying]: "Go to the wrongdoing people,﴾ ﴿the people of Pharaoh. Will they not fear Allah?"﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, I fear that they will deny me,﴾ ﴿and my breast will be constricted and my tongue will not be eloquent, so send for Aaron.﴾ ﴿And they have a charge against me, so I fear that they will kill me."﴾ ﴿He said: "No! Go, both of you, with Our signs. Indeed We are with you, listening.﴾ ﴿So go to Pharaoh and say: 'Indeed we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds,﴾ ﴿that you send with us the Children of Israel.'"﴾ .
(p-٣) Ash-shirdhimah: a small, despised group; the base remnant of everything. Abu 'Ubayda recited:
"in the shardhimah of mules"
Another said:
"Winter has come and my shirt is worn, tatters (sharadhim) at which he laughs."
