Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn al-Ustadh Abi al-Hasan ʿAli ibn Ahmad ibn Khalaf al-Ansari, who is Ibn al-Baadhish, said in his book al-Iqnāʿ: تَرَاءَى الْجَمْعَانِ in al-Shuʿarāʾ, when Hamzah and al-Kisa'i pause upon it, they incline the alif that has changed from the weak lām of the verb; Hamzah also inclines the alif of tafā'ala, both in connection and in pause, for the sake of inclining the alif that has changed. Thus in his reading there is imālat al-imāla (inclination of an inclination). In this verb, and in rāʾā when followed by an alif of connection, for one who inclines in this manner, there is the omission of the cause while retaining the effect, as they said ṣaʿqī in the nisba to al-ṣaʿq. The majority read لَمُدْرَكُونَ with the dāl unvocalized (sukūn). al-A'raj and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read it with the dāl vowelled with a fatḥah and doubled, and the rāʾ with a kasrah, on the pattern of mufta'iluna, which is intransitive and means perishing and vanishing. It is said from it: adraka al-shay' bi-nafsihi, when it perishes gradually; and for this reason the rāʾ is kasrah in this reading. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi explicitly stated the kasrah in Kitāb al-Lawāmiḥ, as did al-Zamakhshari in his Kashshāf and others. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: adraka may also be iftaʿala in the sense of afʿala transitively; if the reading were of that form, the rāʾ would have to be fatḥah, but this has not reached me from them, meaning from al-A'raj and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr. al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is "we are indeed being destroyed one after another at their hands until none of us remains." From it is the line of the Ḥamāsa:

After the sons of my mother who died one after another,
Do I hope for life, or am I more afraid of death?

﴿قَالَ كَلَّا إِنَّ مَعِيَ رَبِّي سَيَهْدِينِ﴾ ("He said: 'Never! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me.'") He rebuked and repelled them with the particle of repulsion (ḥarf al-radʿ), which is kallā. The meaning: they will not overtake you, because Allah has promised you victory and deliverance from them. ﴿إِنَّ مَعِيَ رَبِّي سَيَهْدِينِ﴾, "indeed my Lord is with me; He will guide me," soon, to the path of salvation and make it known to me. It was also said: He will suffice me against their affair. When Moses reached the sea, a believer from the family of Pharaoh, who was in front of Moses, said to him: "Where were you commanded to go? This sea is in front of you, and the family of Pharaoh has overtaken you?" He said: "I was commanded to go by the sea," and Moses did not know what to do. This statement was also related from Yūshaʿ, who said it to Moses, peace be upon him. Then Allah revealed to him ﴿أَنِ اضْرِب بِّعَصَاكَ الْبَحْرَ﴾ ("Strike the sea with your staff"), so Yūshaʿ plunged into the water, and Moses struck with his staff, and in it appeared twelve paths, one for each tribe. He, exalted is He, intended to make this sign connected to Moses and related to an action he performed, but it was by the power of Allah, since striking the sea with a staff does not by itself necessitate the splitting of the sea. Had He, exalted is He, willed, He would have split it without striking it with the staff. The disagreement about the location of this sea has already been mentioned.

﴿فَانفَلَقَ﴾ ("so it split"). There is an omitted element here, its estimate being: "so he struck, and it split." Ibn ʿUṣfūr claimed in such a construction that the omitted element is ḍaraba (struck), and the fā' of infalaqa is the fā' of ḍaraba. Thus from each of them is retained what indicates the omitted part: the fā' from fa-ḍaraba is retained and joined to infalaqa to indicate the omitted ḍaraba, and infalaqa is retained to indicate the omitted fā' from it. This is a view resembling the statement of the one afflicted with brain fever (ṣāḥib al-birsām), and it would require a revelation to clarify this view. When you examine the Qur'an, you find many omitted clauses in which there is a fā', such as His saying ﴿فَأَرْسِلُونِ﴾ ("so send me") [Yusuf: 45], ﴿يُوسُفُ أَيُّهَا الصِّدِّيقُ﴾ ("Yusuf, O truthful one") [Yusuf: 46], meaning: so they sent him, and he said, "Yusuf, O truthful one." The farq (divided part) is the separated portion. ﴿الطَّوْدُ﴾ ("the mountain") means the great mountain that rises high in the sky. Ya'qub related from some reciters that he read كُلُّ فَلْقٍ with the lām in place of the rā'.

(﴿وَأَزْلَفْنَا﴾ ("And We brought near"), meaning: We drew near; (﴿ثَمَّ﴾ ("there"), meaning: there, and thamma is an adverb of place used for distance; (﴿الْآخَرِينَ﴾ ("the others"), meaning: the people of Pharaoh, i.e., We brought them near. He did not mention from whom they were brought near, so it may mean: We brought them near at the place where the sea split for the Children of Israel, or We brought some of them near to others until none escaped, or We brought them near to the sea. al-Hasan and Abu Ḥaywah read وَزَلَّفْنَا without an alif. Ubayy, Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Ḥārith read وَأَزْلَقْنَا with qāf in place of fā', meaning "We caused to slip," as stated by the author of al-Lawāmiḥ. It was said: whoever reads with qāf makes al-ākhirīn refer to Pharaoh and his people, and whoever reads with the common reading, meaning the widely known reading, then al-ākhirūn are Moses and his companions, meaning: We gathered their scattered forces and brought them near to deliverance. End of quote. There is an omission in the statement, its estimate being: and Moses and the Children of Israel entered the sea, and We delivered them. It was said: they entered the sea by its length and came out on the bank they had entered from after a distance, and between the place of entry and the place of exit were rough terrain and mountains that cannot be traversed.)

﴿إِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ لَآيَةً﴾ ("Indeed in that is a sign"), meaning: an evident sign which people witnessed and whose matter became widely known. al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿وَمَا كَانَ أَكْثَرُهُم مُّؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("yet most of them were not believers") means: most of them did not take heed of it, nor did they believe. The Children of Israel, who were the companions of Moses specially singled out for deliverance, had asked him for a cow to worship, took the calf, and demanded to see Allah openly. End of quote. What appears clear is that His saying ﴿وَمَا كَانَ أَكْثَرُهُم مُّؤْمِنِينَ﴾ refers to most of the people of Pharaoh, who were the Copts, since the sorcerers believed, Asiya the wife of Pharaoh believed, the believer from the family of Pharaoh believed, and an old woman named Maryam believed; she guided Moses to the grave of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and they exhumed it and carried it with them when they left Egypt.

﴿وَاتْلُ عَلَيْهِمْ نَبَأَ إِبْرَاهِيمَ﴾ ("And recite to them the story of Ibrahim"), ﴿إِذْ قَالَ لِأَبِيهِ وَقَوْمِهِ مَا تَعْبُدُونَ﴾ ("when he said to his father and his people, 'What do you worship?'"), ﴿قَالُوا نَعْبُدُ أَصْنَامًا فَنَظَلُّ لَهَا عَاكِفِينَ﴾ ("They said: 'We worship idols and remain devoted to them.'"), ﴿قَالَ هَلْ يَسْمَعُونَكُمْ إِذْ تَدْعُونَ﴾ ("He said: 'Do they hear you when you call?'"), ﴿أَوْ يَنفَعُونَكُمْ أَوْ يَضُرُّونَ﴾ ("'Or do they benefit you or harm you?'"), ﴿قَالُوا بَلْ وَجَدْنَا آبَاءَنَا كَذَلِكَ يَفْعَلُونَ﴾ ("They said: 'Rather, we found our fathers doing so.'"), ﴿قَالَ أَفَرَأَيْتُم مَّا كُنتُمْ تَعْبُدُونَ﴾ ("He said: 'Have you considered what you have been worshipping,'"), ﴿أَنتُمْ وَآبَاؤُكُمُ الْأَقْدَمُونَ﴾ ("'you and your forefathers?'") [al-Shu'ara': 76], ﴿فَإِنَّهُمْ عَدُوٌّ لِّي إِلَّا رَبَّ الْعَالَمِينَ﴾ ("'Indeed they are enemies to me, except the Lord of the worlds,'") [al-Shu'ara': 77], ﴿الَّذِي خَلَقَنِي فَهُوَ يَهْدِينِ﴾ ("'Who created me, and it is He who guides me,'") [al-Shu'ara': 78], ﴿وَالَّذِي هُوَ يُطْعِمُنِي وَيَسْقِينِ﴾ ("'And who feeds me and gives me drink,'") [al-Shu'ara': 79], ﴿وَإِذَا مَرِضْتُ فَهُوَ يَشْفِينِ﴾ ("'And when I am ill, it is He who cures me,'") [al-Shu'ara': 80], ﴿وَالَّذِي يُمِيتُنِي ثُمَّ يُحْيِينِ﴾ ("'And who causes me to die and then gives me life,'") [al-Shu'ara': 81], ﴿وَالَّذِي أَطْمَعُ أَن يَغْفِرَ لِي خَطِيئَتِي يَوْمَ الدِّينِ﴾ ("'And who I hope will forgive my sin on the Day of Recompense,'") [al-Shu'ara': 82], ﴿رَبِّ هَبْ لِي حُكْمًا وَأَلْحِقْنِي بِالصَّالِحِينَ﴾ ("'My Lord, grant me wisdom and join me with the righteous,'") [al-Shu'ara': 83], ﴿وَاجْعَل لِّي لِسَانَ صِدْقٍ فِي الْآخِرِينَ﴾ ("'And make for me a tongue of truthfulness among the later generations,'") [al-Shu'ara': 84], ﴿وَاجْعَلْنِي مِن وَرَثَةِ جَنَّةِ النَّعِيمِ﴾ ("'And make me among the inheritors of the Garden of bliss,'") [al-Shu'ara': 85], ﴿وَاغْفِرْ لِأَبِي إِنَّهُ كَانَ مِنَ الضَّالِّينَ﴾ ("'And forgive my father; indeed he was among the misguided,'") [al-Shu'ara': 86], ﴿وَلَا تُخْزِنِي يَوْمَ يُبْعَثُونَ﴾ ("'And do not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected,'") [al-Shu'ara': 87], ﴿يَوْمَ لَا يَنفَعُ مَالٌ وَلَا بَنُونَ﴾ ("'The Day when wealth will not benefit, nor children,'") [al-Shu'ara': 88], ﴿إِلَّا مَنْ أَتَى اللَّهَ بِقَلْبٍ سَلِيمٍ﴾ ("'Except one who comes to Allah with a sound heart.'") [al-Shu'ara': 89], ﴿وَأُزْلِفَتِ الْجَنَّةُ لِلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾ ("'And Paradise will be brought near to the righteous,'") [al-Shu'ara': 90], ﴿وَبُرِّزَتِ الْجَحِيمُ لِلْغَاوِينَ﴾ ("'And Hellfire will be made apparent to the deviators,'") [al-Shu'ara': 91], ﴿وَقِيلَ لَهُمْ أَيْنَ مَا كُنتُمْ تَعْبُدُونَ﴾ ("'And it will be said to them: Where is what you used to worship,'") [al-Shu'ara': 92], ﴿مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ هَلْ يَنصُرُونَكُمْ أَوْ يَنتَصِرُونَ﴾ ("'Besides Allah? Can they help you or defend themselves?'") [al-Shu'ara': 93], ﴿فَكُبْكِبُوا فِيهَا هُمْ وَالْغَاوُونَ﴾ ("'So they will be thrown into it, they and the deviators,'") [al-Shu'ara': 94], ﴿وَجُنُودُ إِبْلِيسَ أَجْمَعُونَ﴾ ("'And the soldiers of Iblis, all of them.'") [al-Shu'ara': 95], ﴿قَالُوا وَهُمْ فِيهَا يَخْتَصِمُونَ﴾ ("They will say, while they dispute therein:") [al-Shu'ara': 96], ﴿تَاللَّهِ إِن كُنَّا لَفِي ضَلَالٍ مُّبِينٍ﴾ ("'By Allah, we were indeed in clear error,'") [al-Shu'ara': 97], ﴿إِذْ نُسَوِّيكُم بِرَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ﴾ ("'When we equated you with the Lord of the worlds.'") [al-Shu'ara': 98], ﴿وَمَا أَضَلَّنَا إِلَّا الْمُجْرِمُونَ﴾ ("'And none misled us except the criminals.'") [al-Shu'ara': 99], ﴿فَمَا لَنَا مِن شَافِعِينَ﴾ ("'So we have no intercessors,'") [al-Shu'ara': 100], ﴿وَلَا صَدِيقٍ حَمِيمٍ﴾ ("'Nor a devoted friend.'") [al-Shu'ara': 101], ﴿فَلَوْ أَنَّ لَنَا كَرَّةً فَنَكُونَ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("'If only we had a return, that we might be among the believers!'") [al-Shu'ara': 102], ﴿إِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ لَآيَةً وَمَا كَانَ أَكْثَرُهُم مُّؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("'Indeed in that is a sign, yet most of them were not believers.'") [al-Shu'ara': 103], ﴿وَإِنَّ رَبَّكَ لَهُوَ الْعَزِيزُ الرَّحِيمُ﴾ ("'And indeed your Lord is the Exalted in Might, the Most Merciful.'") [al-Shu'ara': 104].

The commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 26, verses 27–75 (part 4 of 4):

Since the Arabs had a particular connection to Ibrahim (ʿalayhi al-salam), Allah commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to recite to them his story and what happened to him with his people. In none of the stories of this surah is there a command to the Prophet (ﷺ) to recite a story except in this one. As for the governing element (al-ʿamil) in it: al-Hawfi said, "Recite (utlu)." What he said cannot be conceived except by removing it from the sense of a time adverb (ẓarf) and making it a substitute (badal) for "naba'" (news), while believing that the governing element for the substitute and the item substituted is one and the same. Abu al-Baqa' said: the governing element in idh is "naba'" (news).

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (wa-qawmihi) (and his people) refers to Ibrahim. It was also said that it refers to his father, meaning "and the people of his father," as in Allah's words: ﴿Indeed, I see you and your people in manifest error﴾ [al-An'am: 74].

Ma (what) is an interrogative with the meaning of belittling and affirmation (taqrir). Ibrahim (ʿalayhi al-salam) knew that they were worshippers of idols, but he asked them in order to show them that what they worshipped did not deserve to be worshipped, because of what followed from their answer of the attributes of their objects of worship, which are incompatible with worship. And when he asked them about what they worshipped, they did not limit themselves to mentioning it alone; rather they answered with the verb, its object, and what was joined to it, which are all part of the full description of them together with their deity. They said: ﴿We worship idols, and we remain devoted to them﴾ (p-23), out of pride and boasting. Thus they gave their whole account of themselves, and did not limit themselves to answering with their words, "Idols," as in the verse: ﴿What has your Lord sent down?" They say, "Good"﴾ [al-Nahl: 30], and ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say, "The surplus"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219]. For this reason they joined to that verb their words (fa-nazallu, "so we remain"). It was said: it is like when you say to a leader, "What do you wear?" and he replies, "I wear a fine silk garment, and I trail its skirts," intending in the answer: his condition together with what he wears. They said "fa-nazallu" because they used to worship them by day and not by night.

When they answered Ibrahim, he began to make them stand before the weakness of their intellects, by asking them about attributes that are removed from them, whose existence belongs only to Allah, exalted is He.

Al-Jumhur recited (yasmaʿunakum) from sami'a (to hear). If sami'a is followed by something heard, it takes one object, as in: "I heard the speech of Zayd." If it is followed by something not heard, al-Farisi held that it takes two objects, and the condition for the second of them is that it be something that can be heard, as in: "I heard Zayd reciting." The correct view is that it takes one object, and that verb is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). The preference between the two views is mentioned in grammar. Here it is followed by only one object, but that object is not something heard, so they interpreted it by means of an elided noun (hadhf mudaf), the intended sense being: "Do they hear you, when you call (tadʿunaʿ)?" It was also said that ﴿Do they hear you?﴾ means: "Do they answer you?"

Qatadah and Yahya ibn Yaʿmur recited (yusmiʿunakum) with a damma on the yaʾ and a kasra on the mim, from asmaʿa (to make hear), and the second object is elided, its intended sense being: "the answer" or "the speech."

Idh (when) is a time adverb for what has passed. It may either be extended to mean idha (whenever), or the present tense may be extended to occupy the position of the past, so that the sense is: "Did they hear you when you called (idh daʿawtum)?" Our companions mentioned that among the indicators for turning the present tense into the past is the addition of idh to a clause beginning with the present tense, and they gave as an example His words: ﴿And when you were saying to the one on whom Allah had bestowed favour﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37], meaning: "And when you said." Al-Zamakhshari said: The present tense occurs with idh in order to depict the past situation in which you used to claim it. And say: "Did they hear, or did they ever make [anything] hear?" This is more forceful in rebuke. End of quote.

It was recited with the dhal of idh made clear, and also with its assimilation (idgham) into the taʾ of tadʿunaʿ. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "It is permissible in it, by analogy, to use a masculine form, though no one has recited it that way; the analogical form would be to pronounce it as idh tadʿunaʿ. What prevented this wording is the joining of the original dal in the verb, so there is an abundance of identical letters." End of quote.

What he mentioned as permissible by analogy in this case is not permissible, because that substitution, namely the changing of the taʾ into a dal, occurs only in the form (iftaʿala) when its first radical is a dhal, a zay, or a dal, as in idhdakara, izdajara, and iddahana, whose original forms were idhtakara, iztajara, and idtahana. Or it occurs with a jim as an irregularity, as they said ijdamaʿa for ijtamaʿa. It also occurs with the taʾ of the pronoun after a zay or a dal, and they illustrated this with the taʾ of the pronoun for the first person: in fuztu they said fuzdu, and in jaladtu they said jalladu. It also occurs irregularly with the taʾ of tuwlij, where they said dulij. The taʾ of the present-tense prefix (taʾ al-mudari') is none of the things we have mentioned, so its taʾ is not changed.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah's words "And what prevented this wording..." to the end indicate that, were it not for that, it would be permissible to change the taʾ of the present-tense prefix into a dal and assimilate the dhal into it, so that one would say: idhtakhraja becomes iddakhraja. But no one says this. Rather, when a form like this is assimilated, the dhal is changed into a taʾ and assimilated into the taʾ, so one says: ittakhraja.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 26, verse 27–75 (part 1 of 4):

﴿He said: Indeed your messenger who has been sent to you is surely a madman.﴾ Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: The introduction through this report is more evident, and therefore Musa (peace be upon him) shifted from the first speech to it, since a sensible person cannot believe that he and his fathers are necessarily existent in their own essences, because observation shows their existence after their non-existence and their non-existence after their existence. At that point Pharaoh said: "What is" — meaning that the purpose of asking "what is" is the quiddity (al-mahiyyah) and the particular reality. The introduction through these external effects does not convey that particularity. So this one who claims to be a messenger is a madman who does not understand the question, let alone answer it. Then Musa (peace be upon him) said: ﴿Lord of the East and the West and what is between them, if you were to understand.﴾ He thus shifted to a clearer method than the second. He meant by the East the rising of the sun and the appearance of day, and by the West the setting of the sun and the passing of day.

This continuous arrangement in a wondrous manner is not complete except by the arrangement of an arranger, and this is precisely the method of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) with Nimrod. He first argued by giving life and causing death, which is what Musa (peace be upon him) mentioned here by saying: ﴿Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest ones.﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 26] Nimrod replied to him with: ﴿I give life and cause death.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258] Ibrahim then said: ﴿Indeed Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west,﴾ and ﴿the one who disbelieved was confounded.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258] This is what Musa (peace be upon him) mentioned here by saying: ﴿Lord of the East and the West and what is between them, if you were to understand﴾, meaning: if you are among the intelligent, you would know that there is no answer to the question except what I have mentioned. End of quotation, with some abridgement.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: Musa (peace be upon him) added to it the attributes that reveal Pharaoh's deficiency and show that he is far from being capable of them, namely the lordship of the East and the West. Pharaoh had no dominion except the kingdom of Egypt from the sea to Aswan and the land of Alexandria.

Mujahid, Humayd and al-Aʿraj read ﴿Ursila ilaykum﴾ in the active form, meaning: his Lord sent him to you. ʿAbd Allah and his companions and al-Aʿmash read ﴿Lord of the easts and the wests﴾ in the plural in both.

When Pharaoh was cut off in the domain of argument, he returned to domination and force, and this is the clearest sign of being cut off. So when Musa's discourse wearied him, he threatened Musa with prison: ﴿He said: If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned.﴾

Al-Zamakhshari said: When Musa answered with what he answered, his people were astonished at his answer, since he attributed lordship to other than him. When he repeated the affirmation of his statement, they considered him mad and suspected him, since he called him their messenger. When he repeated it a third time, he became violently angry and said: ﴿If you take a god other than me.﴾

(If you say): How did he say first ﴿if you are certain﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 24] and last ﴿if you were to understand﴾? (I say): At first he was gentle, but when he saw the stubbornness in obstinacy and little readiness to listen to the presentation of proofs, he became harsh and opposed the statement "your messenger is surely a madman" with ﴿if you were to understand﴾.

(If you say): Would "I will imprison you" not have been shorter than ﴿I will surely make you among the imprisoned﴾ and performed the same function? (I say): As for shorter, yes; as for performing the same function, no, because its meaning is: I will make you one of those whose condition you know in my prisons. It was his custom to take the one he wanted to imprison and throw him into a pit going deep into the earth, very deep, alone, where he neither sees nor hears, and this was worse than killing. End of quotation.

When Musa (peace be upon him) had regarding Pharaoh's affair what would not alarm him with Pharaoh's threat, he said to him, out of gentleness toward him and hope for his faith: ﴿Even if I bring you something clear?﴾ meaning: which makes clear to you my truthfulness. "Would you imprison me?" Al-Zamakhshari said: "Even if I bring you" — the waw is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), into which the interrogative hamzah entered, meaning: will you do that to me even if I bring you something clear? End of quotation. We have already discussed this waw and what enters upon "law" in such a context in His words: ﴿Even though their fathers did not understand anything and were not guided?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 170], so there is no need to repeat it. Al-Hawfi said: the waw of coordination entered upon it with the interrogative hamzah for affirmation, and the meaning is: will you imprison me even in this state, which does not suit my being imprisoned while I am clothed in it?

When Pharaoh heard this from Musa, he hoped to find a point of opposition, so he said to him: ﴿Then bring it, if you are among the truthful﴾, that you have a Lord who sent you as a messenger to us. Al-Zamakhshari said: In His words ﴿if you are among the truthful﴾ is evidence that one who brings a miracle is only a truthful claimant in his claim, because a miracle is a confirmation from Allah of the one who claims prophethood, and the Wise does not confirm a liar. It is strange that someone like Pharaoh was not hidden from him such a thing, while it was hidden from some people of the qibla, who permitted what is abhorrent to Allah, to the point that they were obliged to affirm liars through miracles. End of quotation.

Its estimate: "if you are among the truthful, then bring it"; the response is omitted, since the command to bring it indicates it. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it: "If you are among the truthful in your claim, you have brought it." He made the omitted response a past verb, and it is only estimated from the kind of the evidence, with his saying: "You are a wrongdoer if you do it," its estimate being: "You are a wrongdoer if you do it, then you are a wrongdoer." Al-Hawfi said: "in" is a conditional particle, and what precedes it may be its response, and the response may be placed first, because the omission of the condition did not affect the wording at all. It is also possible that the response is omitted, its estimate being "then bring it." Al-Zamakhshari's saying: "until they were obliged to affirm liars through miracles" is an allusion to denying the karamat (marvels of saints) which the People of the Sunnah went to affirm. For them, the miracle (mu'jiz) is what is outside custom, and it is not except for a prophet or in the time of a prophet; if it occurs at the hand of another, it is a miracle for that prophet, or in the way of a preliminary sign (irhas) for a prophet.

﴿So he threw his staff﴾ he cast it from his hand, and the discussion of Musa's staff has already been treated. The thu'ban (serpent) is the largest of what snakes can be. The meaning of ﴿clear﴾ (mubin) is: manifestly a serpent, not one of the things that are faked by sleight of hand and magic.

﴿And he drew out his hand﴾ from his collar, and behold, it shone like a piece of the sun. The meaning of ﴿to the onlookers﴾ is: its whiteness, so that the spectators gathered to look at it because it went out of custom, and it was a luminous whiteness. It is related that when he saw the affair of the staff, he said: "Is there anything other than it?" So he brought out his hand, and he said: "What is this?" He said: "Your hand." So he put it into his armpit, then drew it out, and it had a ray that nearly blinded the eyes and filled the horizon.

﴿He said to the chiefs around him: Indeed this is a knowing sorcerer. He wants to drive you out of your land by his magic, so what do you advise?﴾ They said: ﴿Put him off, and his brother, and send into the cities gatherers, to bring you every knowing sorcerer.﴾ ﴿So the sorcerers were gathered for the appointment of a known day.﴾ ﴿And it was said to the people: Will you gather?﴾ ﴿Perhaps we will follow the sorcerers if they are the victors.﴾ ﴿When the sorcerers came, they said to Pharaoh: Shall we indeed have a reward if we are the victors?﴾ ﴿He said: Yes, and you will then indeed be among those brought near.﴾ ﴿Musa said to them: Throw what you are going to throw.﴾ ﴿So they threw their ropes and their staffs, and said: By the might of Pharaoh, we are surely the victors.﴾ ﴿Then Musa threw his staff, and behold, it swallowed what they were faking.﴾ ﴿So the sorcerers were thrown down prostrate.﴾ ﴿They said: We believe in the Lord of the worlds,﴾ ﴿the Lord of Musa and Harun.﴾ ﴿He said: Do you believe in Him before I give you permission? Indeed he is your chief who taught you magic. You will surely know. I will surely cut off your hands and feet on opposite sides, and I will surely crucify you all.﴾ ﴿They said: No harm; indeed we are returning to our Lord.﴾ ﴿Indeed we hope that our Lord will forgive us our sins, because we were the first of the believers.﴾

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "Around him" (hawlahu) is in the accusative as an adverb of place, and it is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal), meaning: being around him. The governing element is therefore omitted, and the true governing element is the circumstantial phrase itself, and what governs it, he said, is the one who governs the possessor of the state through the particle of genitive (lam al-jarr), like: "I passed by Hind laughing." The Kufans make al-mala' a relative noun, as if it were said: "He said to those who are around him," so there is no position for the governing element in the adverb, because it occurs as a relative clause. Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you say): What governs "hawlahu"? (I say): It is in the accusative in two respects: an accusative in wording and an accusative in position. The governing element for the verbal accusative is what is estimated in the adverb, namely "they settled around him," and this is estimated in all adverbs; and the governing element for the positional accusative is the accusative as a circumstantial phrase. End of quotation. This is bombast and a heap of words on a matter clear from the early principles of the science of Arabic.

When Pharaoh saw the affair of the staff and the hand, and the signs that appeared in them, it alarmed him, and he had no means of repelling it, so he resorted to accusing him of sorcery. He hoped, because of the prevalence of the science of magic in that era, that there would be someone who could contend with him, or he had known the truth of the miracle. He obscured that proof for his people by accusing him of sorcery, and that he ﴿wants to drive you out of your land by his magic,﴾ so that their aversion from him would grow strong, and their seeking of ruin for him, and so that they would not accept his word. For among the hardest things for souls is parting from the homeland in which they grew up. Then he consulted them about what he should do with him, and that was because of the bewilderment and astonishment that had befallen him and his decline from the rank of his divinity, to the point that he began to consult them about his affair, and they commanded him in what appeared to them, so he became one commanded after being a commander. The discussion of ﴿What do you advise?﴾ and of the words that agreed with what is in Surah al-A'raf has already been treated, so there is no need to repeat it. When he said ﴿Indeed this is a knowing sorcerer﴾, they countered with ﴿every sorcerer﴾, bringing the word of totality and the form that serves emphasis, so as to relieve him of some of the distress that had reached him. Al-A'mash and ʿAsim in one narration read "bi-kulli sahirin" (every magician). The known day is the day of adornment, and its discussion has already been given in Surah Ta-Ha. His words ﴿Will you gather?﴾ are an urging on them to gather, and what is meant is hastening them, as a man says to his servant: "Are you going?" when he wants to move him and urge him to depart, as it appears to him that the people have departed while he is standing still. From this is the verse of Ta'abbata Sharran:

Will you send a dinar for our need, or a slave of the Lord, brother of ʿAwn ibn Mikhraq?

He wants: send for him to us quickly, and do not delay him. "Perhaps we shall follow the sorcerers" means following them in their religion, if they prevail over Musa (peace be upon him), and not following Musa in his religion. The speech is phrased as a *kinaya* (indirect expression, implying a meaning without stating it), because if they followed the sorcerers, they would not be following Musa (peace be upon him). Here *idha* falls between the subject of *inna* and its predicate, and it serves as a response and a condition. "By the might of Pharaoh": the apparent reading is that the *ba'* is for an oath, and the thing it is attached to is omitted. They shifted from direct address to the third person out of reverence, as one says of kings, "May Allah be pleased with them, they ordered such-and-such," reporting about him as one reports about an absent person. This is a kind of the oaths of the Jahiliyya (pre-Islamic period). Many Muslims have adopted in their oaths something more objectionable than the oaths of the Jahiliyya: they are not content with swearing by Allah and do not regard an oath as binding unless one swears by the favor of the ruler or by the head of the one who requires the oath, and only then is he considered reliable.

Ibn 'Atiyya said, after mentioning that it is an oath: "The best interpretation is that it is for the sake of glorification and seeking blessing through His name, since they used to worship him, just as you say when you begin some work, 'In the name of Allah' and 'with the blessing of Allah,' and the like."

Between His words ﴿He said to them, Musa﴾ and His words ﴿Indeed, you will be among those brought near﴾ there is an omitted statement, which is what is established in *al-A'raf* regarding their giving him the choice of who would throw first. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, 'Who is the agent of the throwing, if it were stated explicitly?' I answer: it is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, through what He granted them of success and faith, or through the clear miracle they witnessed. You may also not posit an agent, because *alqaw* means 'they fell down and collapsed.'" End of quote. This other view is not correct. A verb cannot be put in the passive form without the agent being omitted and something taking its place, and to say that no agent is posited is a view far from the truth.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "al-Bazzi and Ibn Fulayh, from Ibn Kathir, read it with a doubled *ta'*, a *fatha* on the *lam*, and a doubled *qaf*." According to this reading, when one begins, one must drop the connecting hamza (*hamzat al-wasl*, the hamza used to begin a word), and the connecting hamza does not enter imperfect verbs (*mudari'*), just as it does not enter active participles (*ism al-fa'il*). End of quote. It seems that he imagines that one cannot begin with the word except by bringing in a connecting hamza, but that is not necessary. Often the connected form differs from the pause form, and the pause form differs from the connected form, and whoever has practiced the readings (*qira'at*) knows this.

﴿They said, No harm﴾: that is, there is no harm for us in the occurrence of what you have promised us of cutting off hands and feet and crucifixion; rather, for us in it there is complete benefit through patience with it. It is said: *darahu* yadiruhu *dayran*, and *darahu* yadhuruhu *dawran* (both meaning "to harm him"). ﴿Indeed, to our Lord we are returning﴾: that is, to His great reward; or, "there is no harm upon us, since our return to Allah is through one of the causes of death, and killing is the least of its causes." Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: "When they all believed together, Pharaoh was not safe from his people saying that the sorcerers, despite their great number, had believed only through knowledge of the truth of Musa's matter, so they would believe too. Therefore he exaggerated in warning them through his words, ﴿Did you believe in him before I gave you permission?﴾, implying that their hastening to faith was evidence of their earlier inclination toward him. By his words, ﴿Indeed, he is your chief﴾, he stated explicitly what he had hinted at earlier concerning their collusion and their failings, so that the matter of their chief would be made clear. By his words, ﴿So you will surely come to know﴾, in which he threatened them with a general threat, and by his explicit statement of what he had threatened them with of punishment, they replied that if that occurs, it will not harm them. In their words, ﴿Indeed, to our Lord we are returning﴾ there is a noble point: they believed neither out of desire nor out of fear; they only intended pure arrival at the pleasure of Allah and immersion in the lights of His knowledge." End of summary.

Their words ﴿Indeed, we hope﴾ to the end refute this last point, for that would not be said except out of fear of the consequences of sins. The apparent meaning is that *tama'* (hope/desire) remains in its proper sense, as in His words, ﴿and we hope that our Lord will admit us along with the righteous people﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 84]. It has also been said that certainty may be intended, as in the saying of Ibrahim (peace be upon him): ﴿And the One from whom I hope﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 82].

The majority read *an kunna* with a *fatha* on the hamza, and this carries an affirmation of their faith. Aban ibn Taghlib and Abu Mu'adh read *in kunna* with a *kasra* on the hamza. The author of *al-Lawami* said: "It is conditional. The omission of the *fa'* from the response is permitted because the response precedes, and its estimated form is: 'If we are the first of the believers, then we hope.' The conditional form is appropriate because they had not confirmed what they would have with Allah regarding the acceptance of their faith." End of quote. This explanation follows the view of the Kufans, Abu Zayd, and al-Mubarrad, who permit placing the response of the condition before it, whereas the majority of the Basran grammarians hold that this is not permitted, and the response to such a condition is omitted because what precedes it indicates it. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is of the type of conditional which brings a matter already known and certain in its validity, since they were certain that they were the first of the believers. A parallel is the words of a worker to someone who delays his wage: 'If I have worked, then pay me my due.'" From this is His words, ﴿If you have come out in struggle in My cause and seeking My pleasure﴾ [al-Mumtahana: 1], although He knows that they had come out only for that. Ibn 'Atiyya said, with a similar meaning: "Their hope is only through this condition." End of quote. It is also possible that *in* here is the lightened form of the heavy *inna*, and the *lam* of distinction was omitted because the context indicates that they are believers, so negation is not intended. The estimated form is: "Indeed we are the first of the believers." In a hadith it is said: "*In kana Rasul Allah* (ﷺ) *yuhibbu al-'asal*," meaning: "Indeed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) loved honey." The poet said:

*We are the men who refuse oppression, of the family of Malik,*
*And indeed the family of Malik were noble in origin.*

That is: "and indeed the family of Malik were noble in origin." *Awwal* means "first of the believers" either from among the Copts, or the first of the believers among those present at that assembly. Al-Zamakhshari said: "They were the first group of believers in their time," and this is not correct, because the Children of Israel were believers before the sorcerers believed.

﴿And We revealed to Musa: Travel by night with My servants, for you will be pursued﴾. ﴿Then Pharaoh sent into the cities gatherers﴾. ﴿Indeed, these are a small band﴾. ﴿And indeed, they are enraging us﴾. ﴿And indeed, we are a vigilant host﴾. ﴿So We expelled them from gardens and springs﴾. ﴿And treasures and a noble station﴾. ﴿Thus, and We caused the Children of Israel to inherit them﴾. ﴿So they pursued them at sunrise﴾. ﴿And when the two groups saw each other, the companions of Musa said: Indeed, we are overtaken﴾. ﴿He said: No! Indeed, my Lord is with me; He will guide me﴾. ﴿So We revealed to Musa: Strike the sea with your staff, and it split, and each part was like a great mountain﴾. ﴿And We brought near there the others﴾. ﴿Then We drowned the others﴾. ﴿Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers﴾. ﴿And indeed your Lord, He is the Mighty, the Merciful﴾.

The disagreement over *asri* was mentioned earlier, and that it was read with a connecting hamza and with a cut hamza in Surat Hud. Al-Yamani read *an sir*, as an imperative from *sara yasiru*. Allah commanded Musa (peace be upon him) to set out with the Children of Israel by night from Egypt toward the direction of the sea, and informed him that they would be pursued. So he set out at dawn, with the Syrian road on his left, and headed toward the sea. It was said to him, when he left the road, "Why?" and he replied, "This is what I was commanded." When morning came, Pharaoh learned of Musa's night journey with the Children of Israel, so he went out after them and sent to the cities of Egypt so that the armies would catch up with him. They mentioned numbers for Pharaoh's followers and for the Children of Israel, and Allah knows best the accuracy of that.

﴿Indeed, these are a small band﴾: that is, he said, "Indeed, these..." He described them as few, then used the plural for the small number, making each party a small group, using the sound plural that is for the paucity of number (*jam' al-salama*). The small number may also be pluralized as *aqillah* and *qilal*, and the apparent meaning is the reduction of their number. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is possible that by *qilla* he meant lowliness and insignificance, not small numbers. The meaning is: because of their small number, they are not heeded, nor is their negligence expected, but they do acts that enrage us and constrict our hearts. We are a people whose custom is vigilance, caution, and the use of firmness in affairs. So when someone comes out against us, we hasten to cut off his flank." These were excuses he offered to the people of the cities, lest it be assumed of him anything that would break his dominance and authority. End of quote.

Abu Hatim said: "Someone not relied upon in transmission read: *la-shirdhimatun qalilun*, and it is not established as transmitted from anyone." He means that this reading is not attributed to anyone who narrated it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It was also said: ﴿they are enraging us﴾ means by their opposition, and by their taking the wealth when they had borrowed it and did not return it, and by their going out in flight.

The Kufans, Ibn Dhakwan, and Zayd ibn 'Ali read ﴿hadhirun﴾ with an *alif*, which is the one who has begun to be cautious and renews his caution; *hadhara* is transitive, as in His words: ﴿He fears the Hereafter﴾ [al-Zumar: 9]. Al-'Abbas ibn Mirdas said:

*And indeed I am cautious, I sharpen my weapon,*
*Toward the joints of a deceitful, treacherous man.*

The remaining of the seven read it without the *alif*, meaning the one who is alert. Al-Zajjaj said: *mu'addun*, meaning those who possess tools and weapons, that is, armed. It was also said: *hadhirun* in the present, and *hadhirun* in the future. Al-Farra' said: *al-hadhir* is the one afraid of what he sees, and *al-hadhar* is the one created with caution. Abu 'Ubayda said: "A man who is *hadhir*, *hadhur*, and *hadhir* have one meaning." Sibawayh held that *hadhir* is used for emphasis, and that it governs the object as *hadhir* does, and he cited:

*Cautious of matters that cannot be harmful, and secure*
*Against what will not save him from destiny.*

This has been disputed on grounds mentioned in the books of grammar. Also from al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i: a man is *hadhir* when caution is part of his nature, so he is alert and watchful. Sumayt ibn 'Ajlan, Ibn Abi 'Ammar, and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read *hadirun* with an unpointed *dal*, from their saying "a large eye" (*'ayn hadirah*), meaning great. *Al-hadir* is one who is swollen. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The meaning is: filled with rage and pride." Ibn Khalawayh said: *al-hadir* is the fat, strong, and powerful; one says a boy is *hadir badir*. The author of *al-Lawami* said: "*Hadira al-rajul*: his might became strong; from it one says a man is *hadir badir* if he is fierce in battle; and one says *hadur*, with a *damma* on the *dal*, for emphasis, like *yaqur*." The poet said:

*I love the wicked boy for the sake of his mother,*
*And I hate him for the sake of her hatred, and he is hadir.*

That is, fat and strong. It was also said: they are fully armored in weapons.

﴿So We expelled them﴾: the pronoun refers to the Copts.

﴿From gardens and springs﴾: on the two banks of the Nile from Aswan to Rashid, as Ibn 'Umar and others said. The majority hold that they are springs of water. Ibn Jubayr said: the meaning is springs of gold. ﴿And treasures﴾ are the wealth they had laid waste. Mujahid said: "He called them treasures because he never spent it in obedience to Allah." Al-Dahhak said: "The treasures are the rivers." The author of *al-Tahbir* said: "This needs consideration, because the springs include both." It was also said: they are the treasures of al-Muqattam and its hills. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "They remain to this day."

Egyptians in our own time are extremely eager for these treasures that they claim are buried in al-Muqattam. They spend large sums on digging these spots in al-Muqattam and go to the greatest depths, yet they see nothing but dirt or the kaddan stone from which al-Muqattam is formed. Whenever a Maghribi (North African) comes to them, they ask him about the knowledge of treasure-seeking. Many of them write papers for this purpose in order to devour the wealth of the Egyptians unjustly. A man among them keeps losing his money in this pursuit until he becomes poor, and he only grows more eager for it until he dies. I stayed among them until the time of writing these lines, about forty-five years, and I never knew anyone among them to obtain anything except poverty. Their view on the draining of water is similar. They claim that there are wells, and that names are written on a potsherd which is thrown into the well, whereupon the water recedes and descends to a door in the well, through which one enters a chamber filled with gold, silver, jewels and rubies. They constantly ask whoever comes from the Maghribis about who memorizes those names written on the potsherd. The devils among the Maghribis then take large sums of money from them and make them their food, and they gain nothing but the loss of their wealth. They have other things of this kind of superstition, which they rely upon, speak of, and assert. I have only elaborated on this as a warning to whoever has understanding.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وَمَقَامٍ كَرِيمٍ﴾ ("and a noble station"). Ibn Lahi'ah said: it is al-Fayyum. Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him), Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: it is the pulpits of the preachers. It was also said: the thrones in the pavilions. It was said: the councils of the rulers, the nobles and the judges. al-Naqqash said: the fine dwellings. It was said: the stables for horses, related by al-Mawardi. Qatadah and al-A'raj read ﴿وَمُقَامٍ﴾ with a ḍammah on the mīm, from aqāma (to dwell). al-Zamakhshari said: it may have three grammatical readings: the accusative, on the basis of "We made them leave in that manner which We have described"; the genitive, as a description of maqām, meaning "and a noble station like that station which they had"; and the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "the matter is so." End of quote. The first reading is not permissible, because it leads to comparing a thing with itself, and likewise the second, because the station they had is the noble station, and a thing is not likened to itself.

The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿وَأَوْرَثْنَاهَا بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ﴾ ("and We caused the Children of Israel to inherit it") is that they took possession of the lands of Egypt after the drowning of Pharaoh and his people, because His saying ﴿وَأَوْرَثْنَاهَا﴾ follows His saying "and We made them leave." This was also said by al-Hasan, who said: when they crossed the river, they returned and inherited their dwellings and their wealth. It was also said that they went to Syria and took possession of Egypt during the time of Solomon. The majority read ﴿فَأَتْبَعُوهُمْ﴾, meaning "they overtook them." al-Hasan and al-Dhimari read فَاتَّبَعُوهُم, with the alif connected and the tā' doubled.

﴿مُشْرِقِينَ﴾ ("at sunrise") means entering the time of sunrise, from "the sun rose" (sharqat al-shams shurūqan), meaning it came up. Like aṣbaḥa, meaning he entered the time of morning, and amsā, meaning he entered the time of evening. Abu ʿUbaydah said: they followed them toward the east, like anjada, meaning he headed toward Najd. The apparent view is that ﴿مُشْرِقِينَ﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of the verb. It was also said: ﴿مُشْرِقِينَ﴾ means "in light," whereas Pharaoh and his people were in haze and darkness, and they were confused in it until the Children of Israel had crossed the sea. Accordingly, ﴿مُشْرِقِينَ﴾ would be a circumstantial clause from the object.

﴿فَلَمَّا تَرَاءَى الْجَمْعَانِ﴾ ("then when the two hosts saw each other"), meaning one of them saw the other. The companions of Moses said ﴿إِنَّا لَمُدْرَكُونَ﴾ ("Indeed we are overtaken"), meaning: we will be caught up with. They said this when they saw the powerful enemy behind them and the sea before them, and their thoughts became evil. al-A'mash and Ibn Wathhab read تَرَايَ الْجَمْعَانِ without a hamzah, following the method of easing it bayn bayn (between the hamzah and its vowel-sound). The conversion of the hamzah into a long vowel is not valid, since the hamzah falls between two alifs: one is the alif of tafā'ala, which comes after the fā', and the second is the weak lām of the verb. If it were eased by conversion, three consecutive alifs would gather, and this never occurs. So said Abu al-Fadl al-Razi. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: Hamzah read تَرِيءَ with a kasrah on the rā', with madd and then a hamzah; the same was related from ʿĀṣim, and it was also related from him with a fatḥah and madd. The majority read it like تَرَاعَى, and this is the correct reading, because it is of the pattern tafā'ala. Abu Hatim said: Hamzah's reading of this word is impossible, and he was influenced by it. He said: what was related from Ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash is an error. End of quote. Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn al-Ustadh Abi al-Hasan ʿAli ibn Ahmad ibn Khalaf al-Ansari, who is Ibn al-Baadhish, said in his book al-Iqnāʿ: تَرَاءَى الْجَمْعَانِ in al-Shuʿarāʾ, when Hamzah and al-Kisa'i pause upon it, they incline the alif that has changed from the weak lām of the verb; Hamzah also inclines the alif of tafā'ala, both in connection and in pause, for the sake of inclining the alif that has changed. Thus in his reading there is imālat al-imāla (inclination of an inclination). In this verb, and in rāʾā when followed by an alif of connection, for one who inclines in this manner, there is the omission of the cause while retaining the effect, as they said ṣaʿqī in the nisba to al-ṣaʿq. The majority read لَمُدْرَكُونَ with the dāl unvocalized (sukūn). al-A'raj and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read it with the dāl vowelled with a fatḥah and doubled, and the rāʾ with a kasrah, on the pattern of mufta'iluna, which is intransitive and means perishing and vanishing. It is said from it: adraka al-shay' bi-nafsihi, when it perishes gradually; and for this reason the rāʾ is kasrah in this reading. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi explicitly stated the kasrah in Kitāb al-Lawāmiḥ, as did al-Zamakhshari in his Kashshāf and others. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: adraka may also be iftaʿala in the sense of afʿala transitively; if the reading were of that form, the rāʾ would have to be fatḥah, but this has not reached me from them, meaning from al-A'raj and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr. al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is "we are indeed being destroyed one after another at their hands until none of us remains." From it is the line of the Ḥamāsa:

After the sons of my mother who died one after another,
Do I hope for life, or am I more afraid of death?

﴿قَالَ كَلَّا إِنَّ مَعِيَ رَبِّي سَيَهْدِينِ﴾ ("He said: 'Never! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me.'") He rebuked and repelled them with the particle of repulsion (ḥarf al-radʿ), which is kallā. The meaning: they will not overtake you, because Allah has promised you victory and deliverance from them. ﴿إِنَّ مَعِيَ رَبِّي سَيَهْدِينِ﴾, "indeed my Lord is with me; He will guide me," soon, to the path of salvation and make it known to me. It was also said: He will suffice me against their affair. When Moses reached the sea, a believer from the family of Pharaoh, who was in front of Moses, said to him: "Where were you commanded to go? This sea is in front of you, and the family of Pharaoh has overtaken you?" He said: "I was commanded to go by the sea," and Moses did not know what to do. This statement was also related from Yūshaʿ, who said it to Moses, peace be upon him. Then Allah revealed to him ﴿أَنِ اضْرِب بِّعَصَاكَ الْبَحْرَ﴾ ("Strike the sea with your staff"), so Yūshaʿ plunged into the water, and Moses struck with his staff, and in it appeared twelve paths, one for each tribe. He, exalted is He, intended to make this sign connected to Moses and related to an action he performed, but it was by the power of Allah, since striking the sea with a staff does not by itself necessitate the splitting of the sea. Had He, exalted is He, willed, He would have split it without striking it with the staff. The disagreement about the location of this sea has already been mentioned.

﴿فَانفَلَقَ﴾ ("so it split"). There is an omitted element here, its estimate being: "so he struck, and it split." Ibn ʿUṣfūr claimed in such a construction that the omitted element is ḍaraba (struck), and the fā' of infalaqa is the fā' of ḍaraba. Thus from each of them is retained what indicates the omitted part: the fā' from fa-ḍaraba is retained and joined to infalaqa to indicate the omitted ḍaraba, and infalaqa is retained to indicate the omitted fā' from it. This is a view resembling the statement of the one afflicted with brain fever (ṣāḥib al-birsām), and it would require a revelation to clarify this view. When you examine the Qur'an, you find many omitted clauses in which there is a fā', such as His saying ﴿فَأَرْسِلُونِ﴾ ("so send me") [Yusuf: 45], ﴿يُوسُفُ أَيُّهَا الصِّدِّيقُ﴾ ("Yusuf, O truthful one") [Yusuf: 46], meaning: so they sent him, and he said, "Yusuf, O truthful one." The farq (divided part) is the separated portion. ﴿الطَّوْدُ﴾ ("the mountain") means the great mountain that rises high in the sky. Ya'qub related from some reciters that he read كُلُّ فَلْقٍ with the lām in place of the rā'.

(﴿وَأَزْلَفْنَا﴾ ("And We brought near"), meaning: We drew near; (﴿ثَمَّ﴾ ("there"), meaning: there, and thamma is an adverb of place used for distance; (﴿الْآخَرِينَ﴾ ("the others"), meaning: the people of Pharaoh, i.e., We brought them near. He did not mention from whom they were brought near, so it may mean: We brought them near at the place where the sea split for the Children of Israel, or We brought some of them near to others until none escaped, or We brought them near to the sea. al-Hasan and Abu Ḥaywah read وَزَلَّفْنَا without an alif. Ubayy, Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Ḥārith read وَأَزْلَقْنَا with qāf in place of fā', meaning "We caused to slip," as stated by the author of al-Lawāmiḥ. It was said: whoever reads with qāf makes al-ākhirīn refer to Pharaoh and his people, and whoever reads with the common reading, meaning the widely known reading, then al-ākhirūn are Moses and his companions, meaning: We gathered their scattered forces and brought them near to deliverance. End of quote. There is an omission in the statement, its estimate being: and Moses and the Children of Israel entered the sea, and We delivered them. It was said: they entered the sea by its length and came out on the bank they had entered from after a distance, and between the place of entry and the place of exit were rough terrain and mountains that cannot be traversed.)

﴿إِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ لَآيَةً﴾ ("Indeed in that is a sign"), meaning: an evident sign which people witnessed and whose matter became widely known. al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿وَمَا كَانَ أَكْثَرُهُم مُّؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("yet most of them were not believers") means: most of them did not take heed of it, nor did they believe. The Children of Israel, who were the companions of Moses specially singled out for deliverance, had asked him for a cow to worship, took the calf, and demanded to see Allah openly. End of quote. What appears clear is that His saying ﴿وَمَا كَانَ أَكْثَرُهُم مُّؤْمِنِينَ﴾ refers to most of the people of Pharaoh, who were the Copts, since the sorcerers believed, Asiya the wife of Pharaoh believed, the believer from the family of Pharaoh believed, and an old woman named Maryam believed; she guided Moses to the grave of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and they exhumed it and carried it with them when they left Egypt.

﴿وَاتْلُ عَلَيْهِمْ نَبَأَ إِبْرَاهِيمَ﴾ ("And recite to them the story of Ibrahim"), ﴿إِذْ قَالَ لِأَبِيهِ وَقَوْمِهِ مَا تَعْبُدُونَ﴾ ("when he said to his father and his people, 'What do you worship?'"), ﴿قَالُوا نَعْبُدُ أَصْنَامًا فَنَظَلُّ لَهَا عَاكِفِينَ﴾ ("They said: 'We worship idols and remain devoted to them.'"), ﴿قَالَ هَلْ يَسْمَعُونَكُمْ إِذْ تَدْعُونَ﴾ ("He said: 'Do they hear you when you call?'"), ﴿أَوْ يَنفَعُونَكُمْ أَوْ يَضُرُّونَ﴾ ("'Or do they benefit you or harm you?'"), ﴿قَالُوا بَلْ وَجَدْنَا آبَاءَنَا كَذَلِكَ يَفْعَلُونَ﴾ ("They said: 'Rather, we found our fathers doing so.'"), ﴿قَالَ أَفَرَأَيْتُم مَّا كُنتُمْ تَعْبُدُونَ﴾ ("He said: 'Have you considered what you have been worshipping,'"), ﴿أَنتُمْ وَآبَاؤُكُمُ الْأَقْدَمُونَ﴾ ("'you and your forefathers?'") [al-Shu'ara': 76], ﴿فَإِنَّهُمْ عَدُوٌّ لِّي إِلَّا رَبَّ الْعَالَمِينَ﴾ ("'Indeed they are enemies to me, except the Lord of the worlds,'") [al-Shu'ara': 77], ﴿الَّذِي خَلَقَنِي فَهُوَ يَهْدِينِ﴾ ("'Who created me, and it is He who guides me,'") [al-Shu'ara': 78], ﴿وَالَّذِي هُوَ يُطْعِمُنِي وَيَسْقِينِ﴾ ("'And who feeds me and gives me drink,'") [al-Shu'ara': 79], ﴿وَإِذَا مَرِضْتُ فَهُوَ يَشْفِينِ﴾ ("'And when I am ill, it is He who cures me,'") [al-Shu'ara': 80], ﴿وَالَّذِي يُمِيتُنِي ثُمَّ يُحْيِينِ﴾ ("'And who causes me to die and then gives me life,'") [al-Shu'ara': 81], ﴿وَالَّذِي أَطْمَعُ أَن يَغْفِرَ لِي خَطِيئَتِي يَوْمَ الدِّينِ﴾ ("'And who I hope will forgive my sin on the Day of Recompense,'") [al-Shu'ara': 82], ﴿رَبِّ هَبْ لِي حُكْمًا وَأَلْحِقْنِي بِالصَّالِحِينَ﴾ ("'My Lord, grant me wisdom and join me with the righteous,'") [al-Shu'ara': 83], ﴿وَاجْعَل لِّي لِسَانَ صِدْقٍ فِي الْآخِرِينَ﴾ ("'And make for me a tongue of truthfulness among the later generations,'") [al-Shu'ara': 84], ﴿وَاجْعَلْنِي مِن وَرَثَةِ جَنَّةِ النَّعِيمِ﴾ ("'And make me among the inheritors of the Garden of bliss,'") [al-Shu'ara': 85], ﴿وَاغْفِرْ لِأَبِي إِنَّهُ كَانَ مِنَ الضَّالِّينَ﴾ ("'And forgive my father; indeed he was among the misguided,'") [al-Shu'ara': 86], ﴿وَلَا تُخْزِنِي يَوْمَ يُبْعَثُونَ﴾ ("'And do not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected,'") [al-Shu'ara': 87], ﴿يَوْمَ لَا يَنفَعُ مَالٌ وَلَا بَنُونَ﴾ ("'The Day when wealth will not benefit, nor children,'") [al-Shu'ara': 88], ﴿إِلَّا مَنْ أَتَى اللَّهَ بِقَلْبٍ سَلِيمٍ﴾ ("'Except one who comes to Allah with a sound heart.'") [al-Shu'ara': 89], ﴿وَأُزْلِفَتِ الْجَنَّةُ لِلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾ ("'And Paradise will be brought near to the righteous,'") [al-Shu'ara': 90], ﴿وَبُرِّزَتِ الْجَحِيمُ لِلْغَاوِينَ﴾ ("'And Hellfire will be made apparent to the deviators,'") [al-Shu'ara': 91], ﴿وَقِيلَ لَهُمْ أَيْنَ مَا كُنتُمْ تَعْبُدُونَ﴾ ("'And it will be said to them: Where is what you used to worship,'") [al-Shu'ara': 92], ﴿مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ هَلْ يَنصُرُونَكُمْ أَوْ يَنتَصِرُونَ﴾ ("'Besides Allah? Can they help you or defend themselves?'") [al-Shu'ara': 93], ﴿فَكُبْكِبُوا فِيهَا هُمْ وَالْغَاوُونَ﴾ ("'So they will be thrown into it, they and the deviators,'") [al-Shu'ara': 94], ﴿وَجُنُودُ إِبْلِيسَ أَجْمَعُونَ﴾ ("'And the soldiers of Iblis, all of them.'") [al-Shu'ara': 95], ﴿قَالُوا وَهُمْ فِيهَا يَخْتَصِمُونَ﴾ ("They will say, while they dispute therein:") [al-Shu'ara': 96], ﴿تَاللَّهِ إِن كُنَّا لَفِي ضَلَالٍ مُّبِينٍ﴾ ("'By Allah, we were indeed in clear error,'") [al-Shu'ara': 97], ﴿إِذْ نُسَوِّيكُم بِرَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ﴾ ("'When we equated you with the Lord of the worlds.'") [al-Shu'ara': 98], ﴿وَمَا أَضَلَّنَا إِلَّا الْمُجْرِمُونَ﴾ ("'And none misled us except the criminals.'") [al-Shu'ara': 99], ﴿فَمَا لَنَا مِن شَافِعِينَ﴾ ("'So we have no intercessors,'") [al-Shu'ara': 100], ﴿وَلَا صَدِيقٍ حَمِيمٍ﴾ ("'Nor a devoted friend.'") [al-Shu'ara': 101], ﴿فَلَوْ أَنَّ لَنَا كَرَّةً فَنَكُونَ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("'If only we had a return, that we might be among the believers!'") [al-Shu'ara': 102], ﴿إِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ لَآيَةً وَمَا كَانَ أَكْثَرُهُم مُّؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("'Indeed in that is a sign, yet most of them were not believers.'") [al-Shu'ara': 103], ﴿وَإِنَّ رَبَّكَ لَهُوَ الْعَزِيزُ الرَّحِيمُ﴾ ("'And indeed your Lord is the Exalted in Might, the Most Merciful.'") [al-Shu'ara': 104].

The commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 26, verses 27–75 (part 4 of 4):

Since the Arabs had a particular connection to Ibrahim (ʿalayhi al-salam), Allah commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to recite to them his story and what happened to him with his people. In none of the stories of this surah is there a command to the Prophet (ﷺ) to recite a story except in this one. As for the governing element (al-ʿamil) in it: al-Hawfi said, "Recite (utlu)." What he said cannot be conceived except by removing it from the sense of a time adverb (ẓarf) and making it a substitute (badal) for "naba'" (news), while believing that the governing element for the substitute and the item substituted is one and the same. Abu al-Baqa' said: the governing element in idh is "naba'" (news).

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (wa-qawmihi) (and his people) refers to Ibrahim. It was also said that it refers to his father, meaning "and the people of his father," as in Allah's words: ﴿Indeed, I see you and your people in manifest error﴾ [al-An'am: 74].

Ma (what) is an interrogative with the meaning of belittling and affirmation (taqrir). Ibrahim (ʿalayhi al-salam) knew that they were worshippers of idols, but he asked them in order to show them that what they worshipped did not deserve to be worshipped, because of what followed from their answer of the attributes of their objects of worship, which are incompatible with worship. And when he asked them about what they worshipped, they did not limit themselves to mentioning it alone; rather they answered with the verb, its object, and what was joined to it, which are all part of the full description of them together with their deity. They said: ﴿We worship idols, and we remain devoted to them﴾ (p-23), out of pride and boasting. Thus they gave their whole account of themselves, and did not limit themselves to answering with their words, "Idols," as in the verse: ﴿What has your Lord sent down?" They say, "Good"﴾ [al-Nahl: 30], and ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say, "The surplus"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219]. For this reason they joined to that verb their words (fa-nazallu, "so we remain"). It was said: it is like when you say to a leader, "What do you wear?" and he replies, "I wear a fine silk garment, and I trail its skirts," intending in the answer: his condition together with what he wears. They said "fa-nazallu" because they used to worship them by day and not by night.

When they answered Ibrahim, he began to make them stand before the weakness of their intellects, by asking them about attributes that are removed from them, whose existence belongs only to Allah, exalted is He.

Al-Jumhur recited (yasmaʿunakum) from sami'a (to hear). If sami'a is followed by something heard, it takes one object, as in: "I heard the speech of Zayd." If it is followed by something not heard, al-Farisi held that it takes two objects, and the condition for the second of them is that it be something that can be heard, as in: "I heard Zayd reciting." The correct view is that it takes one object, and that verb is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). The preference between the two views is mentioned in grammar. Here it is followed by only one object, but that object is not something heard, so they interpreted it by means of an elided noun (hadhf mudaf), the intended sense being: "Do they hear you, when you call (tadʿunaʿ)?" It was also said that ﴿Do they hear you?﴾ means: "Do they answer you?"

Qatadah and Yahya ibn Yaʿmur recited (yusmiʿunakum) with a damma on the yaʾ and a kasra on the mim, from asmaʿa (to make hear), and the second object is elided, its intended sense being: "the answer" or "the speech."

Idh (when) is a time adverb for what has passed. It may either be extended to mean idha (whenever), or the present tense may be extended to occupy the position of the past, so that the sense is: "Did they hear you when you called (idh daʿawtum)?" Our companions mentioned that among the indicators for turning the present tense into the past is the addition of idh to a clause beginning with the present tense, and they gave as an example His words: ﴿And when you were saying to the one on whom Allah had bestowed favour﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37], meaning: "And when you said." Al-Zamakhshari said: The present tense occurs with idh in order to depict the past situation in which you used to claim it. And say: "Did they hear, or did they ever make [anything] hear?" This is more forceful in rebuke. End of quote.

It was recited with the dhal of idh made clear, and also with its assimilation (idgham) into the taʾ of tadʿunaʿ. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "It is permissible in it, by analogy, to use a masculine form, though no one has recited it that way; the analogical form would be to pronounce it as idh tadʿunaʿ. What prevented this wording is the joining of the original dal in the verb, so there is an abundance of identical letters." End of quote.

What he mentioned as permissible by analogy in this case is not permissible, because that substitution, namely the changing of the taʾ into a dal, occurs only in the form (iftaʿala) when its first radical is a dhal, a zay, or a dal, as in idhdakara, izdajara, and iddahana, whose original forms were idhtakara, iztajara, and idtahana. Or it occurs with a jim as an irregularity, as they said ijdamaʿa for ijtamaʿa. It also occurs with the taʾ of the pronoun after a zay or a dal, and they illustrated this with the taʾ of the pronoun for the first person: in fuztu they said fuzdu, and in jaladtu they said jalladu. It also occurs irregularly with the taʾ of tuwlij, where they said dulij. The taʾ of the present-tense prefix (taʾ al-mudari') is none of the things we have mentioned, so its taʾ is not changed.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah's words "And what prevented this wording..." to the end indicate that, were it not for that, it would be permissible to change the taʾ of the present-tense prefix into a dal and assimilate the dhal into it, so that one would say: idhtakhraja becomes iddakhraja. But no one says this. Rather, when a form like this is assimilated, the dhal is changed into a taʾ and assimilated into the taʾ, so one says: ittakhraja.

Ibn Abi Hayyan's *al-Bahr al-Muhit* (commentary) on surah 26, verses 76–89 (part 1 of 2):

(Or do they benefit you by your drawing near to them and calling upon them, or do they harm you) by your abandoning their worship? If they neither benefit nor harm, then what is the meaning of your worshipping them? ﴿They said: Rather, we found our fathers doing so﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:74]. This is an evasion (*haydah*) from answering the question. For if they had said, "They hear us, benefit us and harm us," they would have exposed themselves through a lie that cannot be disputed. And if they had said, "They hear us but do not harm us," they would have recorded against themselves a plain error. So they resorted to blind imitation (*taqlid*) of their fathers in worshipping them, without any proof or argument. The *kaf* (in *kadhalika*, "like that") is in the accusative position, governed by *yaf'alun* ("they do"). That is, they do in their worship of those idols a deed like that which they do, namely, their worship. Evasion from the answer is one of the signs of the failure of the argument. Here *bal* ("rather") marks a turning away (*idrab*) from its answer: when he asked the question and then took up another matter that he had not asked them about, this signified their helplessness and their admission of incapacity.

﴿And your forefathers of old﴾. He described them as "of old" to indicate the antiquity of idol-worship among them. Since they had worshipped them in the time of Noah, peace be upon him, what then was the time of those after him? *'Aduwwun* ("enemy") can be used for the singular and the plural, as in His saying: ﴿They are the enemy, so beware of them﴾ [al-Munafiqun 63:4]. It has been said that it is patterned on the verbal noun (*masdar*), like *qabul* and *walu'*. Al-Zamakhshari said: He said "an enemy to me" in order to present the matter as it was in his own mind, meaning: I considered my affair, and I saw that my worship of them was worship of an enemy, so I shunned them and preferred the worship of Him from whom all good comes. By this he showed them that it was advice which he gave to himself first, and on which he based the management of his own affair, so that they might consider and say: "Ibrahim gave us no advice except what he gave to himself, and he wanted for us only what he wanted for his own soul," so that this would make them more inclined to accept and more prompted to listen to him. Had he said, "Indeed they are an enemy to you," it would not have had that effect. Moreover, he entered upon a mode of allusion (*ta'rid*, indirect speech), and allusion may reach the one advised in a way that explicit statement does not, because he may reflect upon it, and reflection may lead him to acceptance. From this is what is related of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him: a man confronted him with something, and he said, "If I were in your position I would need discipline." And a man heard people talking about al-Hijr and said, "It is neither my house nor yours." End of quotation. This is a statement with some exaggeration, in keeping with his habit. As for those who held that His saying, ﴿for they are an enemy to me﴾, is inverted, the original being "for I am an enemy to them," because idols cannot be enemies, being inanimate, and his being their enemy is nothing (of significance), with no necessity for that: do you not see His saying: ﴿Nay, they will deny their worship and become opposed to them﴾ [Maryam 19:82]? This is the meaning of enmity. Also, the one who incites enmity toward them is the enemy of man, namely Satan. It has been said: it is because He, exalted is He, will bring to life the idols that they worshipped, so that they will disown their worshippers and rebuke them. It has also been said: this is with an elision, meaning: for the worshippers of them are an enemy to me. The apparent reading is to keep the exception in its place without any advancing or delaying. Al-Jurjani said: its implied sense is: "Have you considered what you used to worship, you and your forefathers of old, except the Lord of the worlds? For they are an enemy to me," and *illa* ("except") here means "other than" and "besides." End of quotation. So he made it an exception from what follows "you used to worship." But there is no need for this elision, since it is valid for the exception to be from His saying: ﴿for they are an enemy to me﴾. A group, among them al-Farra' (whom al-Zamakhshari followed), made it a *munqati'* (disjunctive) exception, meaning: "but the Lord of the worlds," because they understood from His saying "what you used to worship" that they were the idols. Al-Zajjaj permitted that it be a *muttasil* (connected) exception, on the basis that they used to worship Allah and worship idols alongside Him; so He informed them that he disavowed what they worshipped, except Allah. They also permitted in ﴿Who created me﴾ the accusative, as a qualifier of "Lord of the worlds," or by supposing an implied "I mean" (*a'ni*). The nominative is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "He is the One who." Al-Hawfi said: It is also permissible that ﴿Who created me﴾ be nominative, as the subject, with ﴿so He guides me﴾ being a complete subject-and-predicate clause in the place of the predicate of "the One who," and the *fa'* has entered because of the meaning of a conditional in the speech. End of quotation. But "the One who" here does not carry the sense of a conditional noun, since it is specific and there is no room for generality in it, so it is not like "the one who comes to me, to him is a dirham." Also, the verb *khalaqa* ("created") does not admit of being restricted with respect to Ibrahim.

Abu al-Baqa' followed al-Hawfi in this parsing, but he did not say: "and the *fa'* entered because of the conditional meaning in the speech." If he meant that, it is not sound for the reasons we have mentioned. If he did not mean it, then this is not permissible except on the basis of the *fa'* being extra, according to the view of al-Akhfash in such a construction as: "Zayd, so strike him." "The One who created me by His power, so He guides me to His obedience." It has been said: to His Paradise. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿so He guides me﴾, meaning that when He perfected his creation and breathed the spirit into him, He followed that with continuous guidance which never ceases, to what would set him right and assist him. Otherwise, who guided him to feed upon the blood in the womb by sucking? Who guided him to recognize the breast at birth, and to know its place? Who guided him to the manner of suckling? And other guidances for livelihood and for the hereafter. End of quotation. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿and He feeds me and gives me drink﴾ is ordinary food and ordinary drink, and in it is an enumeration of the blessing of provision. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: "He feeds me without food, and gives me drink without drink," as has come in the report: "Indeed I spend the night and my Lord feeds me and gives me drink." Since creation cannot be claimed by anyone, it was not emphasized with *huwa* ("He"), so the construction of ﴿who created me﴾ (did not require it). Guidance, however, can be claimed, and likewise feeding and giving drink, so he emphasized with *huwa* in His saying ﴿so He guides me﴾ and ﴿and the One who feeds me and gives me drink﴾. After the blessings of creation and guidance, he mentioned that by which life continues and by which the order of creation is sustained, namely nourishment and drink. Since that is a cause of one of the qualities (of the body) dominating the others, through increase or decrease of food, from which sickness arises, he mentioned His blessing in removing the sickness that occurred. He attributed the sickness to himself and did not say, "and when He makes me ill," although Allah, exalted is He, is the agent of that. Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was enumerating Allah's blessings upon him, and cure is beloved while sickness is hated. Since sickness was not from those (blessings), he did not attribute it to Allah. It is reported from Ja'far al-Sadiq (though it is perhaps not authentic): "When I fall ill through sins, He cures me with repentance." Al-Zamakhshari said: He said "I fell ill" rather than "He made me ill," because many causes of sickness arise through a person's negligence in his food, drink, and other matters. For this reason the wise said: If most of the dead were asked, "What is the cause of your deaths?" they would say, "Overeating." Since cure may be ascribed to the physician and to the medicine by way of metaphor, as in His saying: ﴿In it is healing for mankind﴾ [al-Nahl 16:69], he emphasized with His saying ﴿so He cures me﴾, meaning: the One who guides me, feeds me and gives me drink, is Allah and no other.

Since death after resurrection cannot be ascribed except to Allah, no emphasis was needed for it. The claim of Numruz to giving life and death is, from him, a matter of fabrication (*makhrafa*) and insolence. Likewise, no emphasis was needed in ﴿and the One whom I hope﴾. Ibn Abi Ishaq affirmed the first-person *ya'* in *yahdini* and what follows it, and this is a transmission from Nafi'. "Hope" (*tam'*) is an expression for expectation, and Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was certain of forgiveness. Al-Zamakhshari said: He did not state definitively that He would forgive, and in this there is instruction for his people, and a means of gentleness toward them, so that they would avoid sins, guard against them, and seek forgiveness for what they commit. End of quotation. Al-Razi refuted this, saying: "For its outcome returns to the point that he . . . ," and he uttered a word which I will not mention, and after it: "upon himself for the sake of teaching the community," and this is certainly false. Al-Jubba'i said: he meant by it all the believers, for they are the ones who hope and do not despair. Al-Razi refuted him by making the speech of one person the speech of another, which destroys the structure of the speech. Al-Hasan said: the intended meaning of *tam'* is certainty. Al-Razi said: This is not correct except according to our school, where we say that nothing is obligatory upon Allah, that everything is good from Him, and that no one may object to His action. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: He made himself stand upon hope of forgiveness, and this is evidence of the intensity of his fear, together with his high station and intimacy with Allah.

The majority read ﴿my sin﴾ (*khati'ati*) in the singular, and al-Hasan read *khata'ay* in the plural. Most scholars held that the "sins" are His saying ﴿I am sick﴾ [al-Saffat 37:89], ﴿Rather, the greatest of them did it﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:63], and "She is my sister" concerning Sarah. A group said: by *khati'ah* he meant the generic noun, estimating it in all his affairs without specification. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is more evident to me, because many scholars have interpreted those three (statements) as allusions (*ma'arid*). Al-Zamakhshari said: What is meant is what occurs from him in some minor matters, because the prophets, peace be upon them, are protected, chosen above the worlds, and it is His saying . . . He mentioned the three, then said: "They are nothing but allusions, words and imaginings directed at the disbelievers, and they are not sins for which forgiveness is sought." End of quotation. (If you say): If only minor sins occur from them, and these are expiated, why then did he affirm for himself a sin or sins, and hope that He would forgive him? (I say): The answer is what has preceded: the prophets' seeking forgiveness is humility before their Lord and self-abasement, and this is indicated by his saying "I hope," and he did not state it definitively. End of quotation. ﴿The Day of Judgment﴾ (*yawm al-din*) is an adverbial object of time, and the governing verb is *yaghfir* ("forgive"). Forgiveness, though it occurs in this world, its effect is not made manifest except on the Day of Recompense, and in this world it is known only through Allah's informing.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi weakened the interpretation of "sin" as those three, because attributing to Ibrahim what does not conform (to the truth) is impermissible. He interpreted it as a way of humility, saying: For if it conforms in this place, the difficulty disappears; and if it does not conform, the answer returns to attributing disobedience to him, in order to exonerate him from disobedience. He said: The correct answer is that this is interpreted as leaving what is better (*tark al-awla*), which may be called "error" (*khata'*). For whoever sells a jewel worth a thousand for a dinar is said to have erred, and leaving what is better is permissible for prophets. End of quotation. In this there is some abridgement and alteration of wording for courtesy, in a manner suited to the station of prophethood.

Ibrahim, peace be upon him, put praise of Allah, exalted is He, first, and mentioned Him with fine attributes before his request and petition, then he asked Him, exalted is He, saying: ﴿My Lord, grant me judgment﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:83]. This shows that placing praise before the request is among the important matters. (The apparent meaning is that *hukm* is the judging between people with truth. It has been said: *hukm* means wisdom and prophethood, because these are what follow on the request for prophethood, since the prophet possesses wisdom and possesses judgment among people.) Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: It is not permissible to interpret *hukm* as prophethood, because it is already attained; if he sought prophethood, it would be sought, either as the very thing already attained, or as something other. The first is impossible, since obtaining what is already obtained is impossible; the second is impossible, since it is inadmissible that one person be a prophet twice. Rather, what is meant by *hukm* is the perfection of practical prophethood, which is that one should know the good in order to act upon it. End of quotation. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: *Hukm* has been interpreted as wisdom and prophethood. He said: His supplication, peace be upon him, in such a matter concerns steadfastness and permanence. And his being joined with the righteous means: Allah's granting him success in a deed that places him among them, or that brings him and them together in Paradise. Allah has answered him, exalted is He, when He said: ﴿And indeed he in the Hereafter is among the righteous﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:130].
