Abu al-Baqa' followed al-Hawfi in this parsing, but he did not say: "and the *fa'* entered because of the conditional meaning in the speech." If he meant that, it is not sound for the reasons we have mentioned. If he did not mean it, then this is not permissible except on the basis of the *fa'* being extra, according to the view of al-Akhfash in such a construction as: "Zayd, so strike him." "The One who created me by His power, so He guides me to His obedience." It has been said: to His Paradise. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿so He guides me﴾, meaning that when He perfected his creation and breathed the spirit into him, He followed that with continuous guidance which never ceases, to what would set him right and assist him. Otherwise, who guided him to feed upon the blood in the womb by sucking? Who guided him to recognize the breast at birth, and to know its place? Who guided him to the manner of suckling? And other guidances for livelihood and for the hereafter. End of quotation. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿and He feeds me and gives me drink﴾ is ordinary food and ordinary drink, and in it is an enumeration of the blessing of provision. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: "He feeds me without food, and gives me drink without drink," as has come in the report: "Indeed I spend the night and my Lord feeds me and gives me drink." Since creation cannot be claimed by anyone, it was not emphasized with *huwa* ("He"), so the construction of ﴿who created me﴾ (did not require it). Guidance, however, can be claimed, and likewise feeding and giving drink, so he emphasized with *huwa* in His saying ﴿so He guides me﴾ and ﴿and the One who feeds me and gives me drink﴾. After the blessings of creation and guidance, he mentioned that by which life continues and by which the order of creation is sustained, namely nourishment and drink. Since that is a cause of one of the qualities (of the body) dominating the others, through increase or decrease of food, from which sickness arises, he mentioned His blessing in removing the sickness that occurred. He attributed the sickness to himself and did not say, "and when He makes me ill," although Allah, exalted is He, is the agent of that. Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was enumerating Allah's blessings upon him, and cure is beloved while sickness is hated. Since sickness was not from those (blessings), he did not attribute it to Allah. It is reported from Ja'far al-Sadiq (though it is perhaps not authentic): "When I fall ill through sins, He cures me with repentance." Al-Zamakhshari said: He said "I fell ill" rather than "He made me ill," because many causes of sickness arise through a person's negligence in his food, drink, and other matters. For this reason the wise said: If most of the dead were asked, "What is the cause of your deaths?" they would say, "Overeating." Since cure may be ascribed to the physician and to the medicine by way of metaphor, as in His saying: ﴿In it is healing for mankind﴾ [al-Nahl 16:69], he emphasized with His saying ﴿so He cures me﴾, meaning: the One who guides me, feeds me and gives me drink, is Allah and no other.

Since death after resurrection cannot be ascribed except to Allah, no emphasis was needed for it. The claim of Numruz to giving life and death is, from him, a matter of fabrication (*makhrafa*) and insolence. Likewise, no emphasis was needed in ﴿and the One whom I hope﴾. Ibn Abi Ishaq affirmed the first-person *ya'* in *yahdini* and what follows it, and this is a transmission from Nafi'. "Hope" (*tam'*) is an expression for expectation, and Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was certain of forgiveness. Al-Zamakhshari said: He did not state definitively that He would forgive, and in this there is instruction for his people, and a means of gentleness toward them, so that they would avoid sins, guard against them, and seek forgiveness for what they commit. End of quotation. Al-Razi refuted this, saying: "For its outcome returns to the point that he . . . ," and he uttered a word which I will not mention, and after it: "upon himself for the sake of teaching the community," and this is certainly false. Al-Jubba'i said: he meant by it all the believers, for they are the ones who hope and do not despair. Al-Razi refuted him by making the speech of one person the speech of another, which destroys the structure of the speech. Al-Hasan said: the intended meaning of *tam'* is certainty. Al-Razi said: This is not correct except according to our school, where we say that nothing is obligatory upon Allah, that everything is good from Him, and that no one may object to His action. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: He made himself stand upon hope of forgiveness, and this is evidence of the intensity of his fear, together with his high station and intimacy with Allah.

The majority read ﴿my sin﴾ (*khati'ati*) in the singular, and al-Hasan read *khata'ay* in the plural. Most scholars held that the "sins" are His saying ﴿I am sick﴾ [al-Saffat 37:89], ﴿Rather, the greatest of them did it﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:63], and "She is my sister" concerning Sarah. A group said: by *khati'ah* he meant the generic noun, estimating it in all his affairs without specification. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is more evident to me, because many scholars have interpreted those three (statements) as allusions (*ma'arid*). Al-Zamakhshari said: What is meant is what occurs from him in some minor matters, because the prophets, peace be upon them, are protected, chosen above the worlds, and it is His saying . . . He mentioned the three, then said: "They are nothing but allusions, words and imaginings directed at the disbelievers, and they are not sins for which forgiveness is sought." End of quotation. (If you say): If only minor sins occur from them, and these are expiated, why then did he affirm for himself a sin or sins, and hope that He would forgive him? (I say): The answer is what has preceded: the prophets' seeking forgiveness is humility before their Lord and self-abasement, and this is indicated by his saying "I hope," and he did not state it definitively. End of quotation. ﴿The Day of Judgment﴾ (*yawm al-din*) is an adverbial object of time, and the governing verb is *yaghfir* ("forgive"). Forgiveness, though it occurs in this world, its effect is not made manifest except on the Day of Recompense, and in this world it is known only through Allah's informing.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi weakened the interpretation of "sin" as those three, because attributing to Ibrahim what does not conform (to the truth) is impermissible. He interpreted it as a way of humility, saying: For if it conforms in this place, the difficulty disappears; and if it does not conform, the answer returns to attributing disobedience to him, in order to exonerate him from disobedience. He said: The correct answer is that this is interpreted as leaving what is better (*tark al-awla*), which may be called "error" (*khata'*). For whoever sells a jewel worth a thousand for a dinar is said to have erred, and leaving what is better is permissible for prophets. End of quotation. In this there is some abridgement and alteration of wording for courtesy, in a manner suited to the station of prophethood.

Ibrahim, peace be upon him, put praise of Allah, exalted is He, first, and mentioned Him with fine attributes before his request and petition, then he asked Him, exalted is He, saying: ﴿My Lord, grant me judgment﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:83]. This shows that placing praise before the request is among the important matters. (The apparent meaning is that *hukm* is the judging between people with truth. It has been said: *hukm* means wisdom and prophethood, because these are what follow on the request for prophethood, since the prophet possesses wisdom and possesses judgment among people.) Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: It is not permissible to interpret *hukm* as prophethood, because it is already attained; if he sought prophethood, it would be sought, either as the very thing already attained, or as something other. The first is impossible, since obtaining what is already obtained is impossible; the second is impossible, since it is inadmissible that one person be a prophet twice. Rather, what is meant by *hukm* is the perfection of practical prophethood, which is that one should know the good in order to act upon it. End of quotation. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: *Hukm* has been interpreted as wisdom and prophethood. He said: His supplication, peace be upon him, in such a matter concerns steadfastness and permanence. And his being joined with the righteous means: Allah's granting him success in a deed that places him among them, or that brings him and them together in Paradise. Allah has answered him, exalted is He, when He said: ﴿And indeed he in the Hereafter is among the righteous﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:130].

Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: He placed His words, "Grant me wisdom (ḥukm)," before His words, "and join me with the righteous," because the theoretical faculty (al-quwwa al-nazariyya) precedes the practical faculty (al-quwwa al-amaliyya). This is because a person can know the truth even if he does not act upon it, whereas the reverse is not possible. Knowledge is an attribute of the soul (al-rūḥ), and action is an attribute of the body (al-badan). Just as the soul is nobler than the body, so knowledge is more excellent than reformation. End of quote.

"A tongue of truth" (lisān al-ṣidq): Ibn 'Atiyya said: It means praise and the perpetuation of a lofty standing, by the consensus of the exegetes. Likewise, God answered his supplication, so every religious community holds fast to him and venerates him, and he [Abraham] is upon the ḥanīfiyya (the pure monotheistic faith) with which Muhammad ﷺ came.

Makki said: It has also been said that the meaning of his request was that among his descendants at the end of time there would be one who stands up for the truth, and his supplication was answered in Muhammad, peace be upon him. This is a good meaning, except that the wording of the verse does not yield it except by forcing the sense upon the wording. End of quote.

When he asked for the happiness of this world, he asked for the happiness of the Hereafter, which is the Garden of Bliss (jannat al-na'īm), and he likened it to an inheritance (yūrath), because the inheritance is what is divided in this world. He likened the spoils of this world to the spoils of the Hereafter. God the Exalted said: ﴿That is the Garden which We shall give as an inheritance to those of Our servants who were God-fearing﴾ [Maryam: 63].

When he had finished with the aims of this world and the Hereafter for himself, he asked on behalf of the person most closely attached to him, namely his origin from whom he had sprung, which is his father. So he said: ﴿And forgive my father﴾. His request for forgiveness is conditional upon Islam, and requesting a conditional thing includes requesting the condition, so its sum is that he was praying for him to embrace Islam. His promise of this is clarified by His words: ﴿And Abraham's plea for forgiveness for his father was only due to a promise he had made to him. But when it became clear to him that he was an enemy to God, he disowned him﴾ [al-Tawba: 114], that is, when he died upon disbelief, he disowned him. It has also been said that he [the father] had told him that he was upon his religion inwardly and upon the religion of Nimrod outwardly, out of dissimulation (taqiyya) and fear, so he prayed for him because he believed the matter was so. When the opposite became clear to him, he disowned him. This is why he said in his supplication: ﴿And forgive my father, for he was among the astray﴾. Had he not believed that he was not, at that moment, astray, he would not have said that.

﴿And do not disgrace me﴾: this is either from al-khizy, which is humiliation, or from al-khazāya, which is shame. The pronoun in (yub'athūn) refers to the servants, since it is known; or it refers to (al-ḍāllīn), and then it is part of the plea for forgiveness, since the meaning would be: "On the day when the astray are resurrected." The phrase (yawma lā yanfa'u) is in apposition to ﴿the day they are resurrected﴾.

﴿Neither wealth nor children﴾: that is, just as they benefit in this world, where one's wealth ransoms him and one's children defend him. It has also been said that by "children" is meant all helpers. It has also been said that the meaning is: the day when attachment to the world and its adornments will not benefit, so he intended by that the great and most inclusive remembrance, because wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world. The apparent view is that the exception is disjunctive (munqaṭi'), that is: "But whoever comes to God with a sound heart, his sound heart will benefit him." Al-Zamakhshari said: You may make the exception disjunctive, and in addition to that you must posit an omitted genitive (muḍāf), namely the state, meant by which is soundness, and it is not of the same kind as wealth and children, so that the meaning would reduce to wealth and children not benefiting, while only soundness of heart benefits. Had the omitted genitive not been posited, the exception would have no meaning. End of quote.

There is no necessity to posit an omitted genitive, as he mentioned, since we have posited it [i.e., the exception as disjunctive]; rather ﴿whoever comes to God with a sound heart﴾ will be benefited by that. Al-Zamakhshari, in his first explanation, treated it as connected through a reinterpretation. He said: "Except whoever comes to God," meaning: except the state of whoever comes to God with a sound heart, and this is from his saying:

*"Their greeting among them is a painful blow,*
*and its reward is nothing but the sword."*

An example of this would be if one were asked: "Does Zayd have wealth and children?" and he replied: "His wealth and children are the soundness of his heart," meaning: the negation of wealth and children from him, and the affirmation of soundness of heart for him instead of that. If you wish, you may take the sentence according to its meaning and treat wealth and children as meaning riches, as if it were said: "On the day when riches will not benefit, except the riches of one who comes to God with a sound heart, because a man's wealth in his religion is in the soundness of his heart, just as his wealth in his worldly life is in his property and children." End of quote.

Some of them made it an exception of the emptied type (istithnā' mufarragh), with "man" as the object, and the sense is: "Neither wealth nor children benefits anyone except whoever comes to God with a sound heart, for his wealth spent in the paths of righteousness will benefit him, and his children, who are righteous, since he spent it in obedience to God, guided his children to the religion, and taught them the laws; and soundness of heart means its freedom from polytheism and sins, and from the attachments of the world that are abandoned, even if they are permissible, such as wealth and children." Sufyan said: It is the one who meets his Lord with nothing in his heart other than Him. This implies that the wording is general, but the one sound from polytheism is the more general. Al-Junayd said: [a heart] stung (ladīgh) by the fear of God, and the sound (salīm) is the stung (ladīgh). Al-Zamakhshari said: This is one of the novel interpretations (bida' al-tafasir), and he spoke the truth.

Ibn Abi Hayyan's *al-Bahr al-Muhit* (commentary) on surah 26, verses 76–89 (part 1 of 2):

(Or do they benefit you by your drawing near to them and calling upon them, or do they harm you) by your abandoning their worship? If they neither benefit nor harm, then what is the meaning of your worshipping them? ﴿They said: Rather, we found our fathers doing so﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:74]. This is an evasion (*haydah*) from answering the question. For if they had said, "They hear us, benefit us and harm us," they would have exposed themselves through a lie that cannot be disputed. And if they had said, "They hear us but do not harm us," they would have recorded against themselves a plain error. So they resorted to blind imitation (*taqlid*) of their fathers in worshipping them, without any proof or argument. The *kaf* (in *kadhalika*, "like that") is in the accusative position, governed by *yaf'alun* ("they do"). That is, they do in their worship of those idols a deed like that which they do, namely, their worship. Evasion from the answer is one of the signs of the failure of the argument. Here *bal* ("rather") marks a turning away (*idrab*) from its answer: when he asked the question and then took up another matter that he had not asked them about, this signified their helplessness and their admission of incapacity.

﴿And your forefathers of old﴾. He described them as "of old" to indicate the antiquity of idol-worship among them. Since they had worshipped them in the time of Noah, peace be upon him, what then was the time of those after him? *'Aduwwun* ("enemy") can be used for the singular and the plural, as in His saying: ﴿They are the enemy, so beware of them﴾ [al-Munafiqun 63:4]. It has been said that it is patterned on the verbal noun (*masdar*), like *qabul* and *walu'*. Al-Zamakhshari said: He said "an enemy to me" in order to present the matter as it was in his own mind, meaning: I considered my affair, and I saw that my worship of them was worship of an enemy, so I shunned them and preferred the worship of Him from whom all good comes. By this he showed them that it was advice which he gave to himself first, and on which he based the management of his own affair, so that they might consider and say: "Ibrahim gave us no advice except what he gave to himself, and he wanted for us only what he wanted for his own soul," so that this would make them more inclined to accept and more prompted to listen to him. Had he said, "Indeed they are an enemy to you," it would not have had that effect. Moreover, he entered upon a mode of allusion (*ta'rid*, indirect speech), and allusion may reach the one advised in a way that explicit statement does not, because he may reflect upon it, and reflection may lead him to acceptance. From this is what is related of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him: a man confronted him with something, and he said, "If I were in your position I would need discipline." And a man heard people talking about al-Hijr and said, "It is neither my house nor yours." End of quotation. This is a statement with some exaggeration, in keeping with his habit. As for those who held that His saying, ﴿for they are an enemy to me﴾, is inverted, the original being "for I am an enemy to them," because idols cannot be enemies, being inanimate, and his being their enemy is nothing (of significance), with no necessity for that: do you not see His saying: ﴿Nay, they will deny their worship and become opposed to them﴾ [Maryam 19:82]? This is the meaning of enmity. Also, the one who incites enmity toward them is the enemy of man, namely Satan. It has been said: it is because He, exalted is He, will bring to life the idols that they worshipped, so that they will disown their worshippers and rebuke them. It has also been said: this is with an elision, meaning: for the worshippers of them are an enemy to me. The apparent reading is to keep the exception in its place without any advancing or delaying. Al-Jurjani said: its implied sense is: "Have you considered what you used to worship, you and your forefathers of old, except the Lord of the worlds? For they are an enemy to me," and *illa* ("except") here means "other than" and "besides." End of quotation. So he made it an exception from what follows "you used to worship." But there is no need for this elision, since it is valid for the exception to be from His saying: ﴿for they are an enemy to me﴾. A group, among them al-Farra' (whom al-Zamakhshari followed), made it a *munqati'* (disjunctive) exception, meaning: "but the Lord of the worlds," because they understood from His saying "what you used to worship" that they were the idols. Al-Zajjaj permitted that it be a *muttasil* (connected) exception, on the basis that they used to worship Allah and worship idols alongside Him; so He informed them that he disavowed what they worshipped, except Allah. They also permitted in ﴿Who created me﴾ the accusative, as a qualifier of "Lord of the worlds," or by supposing an implied "I mean" (*a'ni*). The nominative is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "He is the One who." Al-Hawfi said: It is also permissible that ﴿Who created me﴾ be nominative, as the subject, with ﴿so He guides me﴾ being a complete subject-and-predicate clause in the place of the predicate of "the One who," and the *fa'* has entered because of the meaning of a conditional in the speech. End of quotation. But "the One who" here does not carry the sense of a conditional noun, since it is specific and there is no room for generality in it, so it is not like "the one who comes to me, to him is a dirham." Also, the verb *khalaqa* ("created") does not admit of being restricted with respect to Ibrahim.

Abu al-Baqa' followed al-Hawfi in this parsing, but he did not say: "and the *fa'* entered because of the conditional meaning in the speech." If he meant that, it is not sound for the reasons we have mentioned. If he did not mean it, then this is not permissible except on the basis of the *fa'* being extra, according to the view of al-Akhfash in such a construction as: "Zayd, so strike him." Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿so He guides me﴾, meaning that when He perfected his creation and breathed the spirit into him, He followed that with continuous guidance which never ceases, to what would set him right and assist him. "A tongue of truth" (lisān al-ṣidq): Ibn 'Atiyya said: It means praise and the perpetuation of a lofty standing, by the consensus of the exegetes. Likewise, God answered his supplication, so every religious community holds fast to him and venerates him, and he [Abraham] is upon the ḥanīfiyya (the pure monotheistic faith) with which Muhammad ﷺ came.

Makki said: It has also been said that the meaning of his request was that among his descendants at the end of time there would be one who stands up for the truth, and his supplication was answered in Muhammad, peace be upon him. This is a good meaning, except that the wording of the verse does not yield it except by forcing the sense upon the wording. End of quote.

When he asked for the happiness of this world, he asked for the happiness of the Hereafter, which is the Garden of Bliss (jannat al-na'īm), and he likened it to an inheritance (yūrath), because the inheritance is what is divided in this world. He likened the spoils of this world to the spoils of the Hereafter. God the Exalted said: ﴿That is the Garden which We shall give as an inheritance to those of Our servants who were God-fearing﴾ [Maryam: 63].

When he had finished with the aims of this world and the Hereafter for himself, he asked on behalf of the person most closely attached to him, namely his origin from whom he had sprung, which is his father. So he said: ﴿And forgive my father﴾. His request for forgiveness is conditional upon Islam, and requesting a conditional thing includes requesting the condition, so its sum is that he was praying for him to embrace Islam. His promise of this is clarified by His words: ﴿And Abraham's plea for forgiveness for his father was only due to a promise he had made to him. But when it became clear to him that he was an enemy to God, he disowned him﴾ [al-Tawba: 114], that is, when he died upon disbelief, he disowned him. It has also been said that he [the father] had told him that he was upon his religion inwardly and upon the religion of Nimrod outwardly, out of dissimulation (taqiyya) and fear, so he prayed for him because he believed the matter was so. When the opposite became clear to him, he disowned him. This is why he said in his supplication: ﴿And forgive my father, for he was among the astray﴾. Had he not believed that he was not, at that moment, astray, he would not have said that.

﴿And do not disgrace me﴾: this is either from al-khizy, which is humiliation, or from al-khazāya, which is shame. The pronoun in (yub'athūn) refers to the servants, since it is known; or it refers to (al-ḍāllīn), and then it is part of the plea for forgiveness, since the meaning would be: "On the day when the astray are resurrected." The phrase (yawma lā yanfa'u) is in apposition to ﴿the day they are resurrected﴾.

﴿Neither wealth nor children﴾: that is, just as they benefit in this world, where one's wealth ransoms him and one's children defend him. It has also been said that by "children" is meant all helpers. It has also been said that the meaning is: the day when attachment to the world and its adornments will not benefit, so he intended by that the great and most inclusive remembrance, because wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world. The apparent view is that the exception is disjunctive (munqaṭi'), that is: "But whoever comes to God with a sound heart, his sound heart will benefit him." Al-Zamakhshari said: You may make the exception disjunctive, and in addition to that you must posit an omitted genitive (muḍāf), namely the state, meant by which is soundness, and it is not of the same kind as wealth and children, so that the meaning would reduce to wealth and children not benefiting, while only soundness of heart benefits. Had the omitted genitive not been posited, the exception would have no meaning. End of quote.

There is no necessity to posit an omitted genitive, as he mentioned, since we have posited it [i.e., the exception as disjunctive]; rather ﴿whoever comes to God with a sound heart﴾ will be benefited by that. Al-Zamakhshari, in his first explanation, treated it as connected through a reinterpretation. He said: "Except whoever comes to God," meaning: except the state of whoever comes to God with a sound heart, and this is from his saying:

*"Their greeting among them is a painful blow,*
*and its reward is nothing but the sword."*

An example of this would be if one were asked: "Does Zayd have wealth and children?" and he replied: "His wealth and children are the soundness of his heart," meaning: the negation of wealth and children from him, and the affirmation of soundness of heart for him instead of that. If you wish, you may take the sentence according to its meaning and treat wealth and children as meaning riches, as if it were said: "On the day when riches will not benefit, except the riches of one who comes to God with a sound heart, because a man's wealth in his religion is in the soundness of his heart, just as his wealth in his worldly life is in his property and children." End of quote.

Some of them made it an exception of the emptied type (istithnā' mufarragh), with "man" as the object, and the sense is: "Neither wealth nor children benefits anyone except whoever comes to God with a sound heart, for his wealth spent in the paths of righteousness will benefit him, and his children, who are righteous, since he spent it in obedience to God, guided his children to the religion, and taught them the laws; and soundness of heart means its freedom from polytheism and sins, and from the attachments of the world that are abandoned, even if they are permissible, such as wealth and children." Sufyan said: It is the one who meets his Lord with nothing in his heart other than Him. This implies that the wording is general, but the one sound from polytheism is the more general. Al-Junayd said: [a heart] stung (ladīgh) by the fear of God, and the sound (salīm) is the stung (ladīgh). Al-Zamakhshari said: This is one of the novel interpretations (bida' al-tafasir), and he spoke the truth.

Ibn Abi Hayyan's *al-Bahr al-Muhit* (commentary) on surah 26, verses 76–89 (part 1 of 2):

(Or do they benefit you by your drawing near to them and calling upon them, or do they harm you) by your abandoning their worship? If they neither benefit nor harm, then what is the meaning of your worshipping them? ﴿They said: Rather, we found our fathers doing so﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:74]. This is an evasion (*haydah*) from answering the question. For if they had said, "They hear us, benefit us and harm us," they would have exposed themselves through a lie that cannot be disputed. And if they had said, "They hear us but do not harm us," they would have recorded against themselves a plain error. So they resorted to blind imitation (*taqlid*) of their fathers in worshipping them, without any proof or argument. The *kaf* (in *kadhalika*, "like that") is in the accusative position, governed by *yaf'alun* ("they do"). That is, they do in their worship of those idols a deed like that which they do, namely, their worship. Evasion from the answer is one of the signs of the failure of the argument. Here *bal* ("rather") marks a turning away (*idrab*) from its answer: when he asked the question and then took up another matter that he had not asked them about, this signified their helplessness and their admission of incapacity.

﴿And your forefathers of old﴾. He described them as "of old" to indicate the antiquity of idol-worship among them. Since they had worshipped them in the time of Noah, peace be upon him, what then was the time of those after him? *'Aduwwun* ("enemy") can be used for the singular and the plural, as in His saying: ﴿They are the enemy, so beware of them﴾ [al-Munafiqun 63:4]. It has been said that it is patterned on the verbal noun (*masdar*), like *qabul* and *walu'*. Al-Zamakhshari said: He said "an enemy to me" in order to present the matter as it was in his own mind, meaning: I considered my affair, and I saw that my worship of them was worship of an enemy, so I shunned them and preferred the worship of Him from whom all good comes. By this he showed them that it was advice which he gave to himself first, and on which he based the management of his own affair, so that they might consider and say: "Ibrahim gave us no advice except what he gave to himself, and he wanted for us only what he wanted for his own soul," so that this would make them more inclined to accept and more prompted to listen to him. Had he said, "Indeed they are an enemy to you," it would not have had that effect. Moreover, he entered upon a mode of allusion (*ta'rid*, indirect speech), and allusion may reach the one advised in a way that explicit statement does not, because he may reflect upon it, and reflection may lead him to acceptance. From this is what is related of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him: a man confronted him with something, and he said, "If I were in your position I would need discipline." And a man heard people talking about al-Hijr and said, "It is neither my house nor yours." End of quotation. This is a statement with some exaggeration, in keeping with his habit. As for those who held that His saying, ﴿for they are an enemy to me﴾, is inverted, the original being "for I am an enemy to them," because idols cannot be enemies, being inanimate, and his being their enemy is nothing (of significance), with no necessity for that: do you not see His saying: ﴿Nay, they will deny their worship and become opposed to them﴾ [Maryam 19:82]? This is the meaning of enmity. Also, the one who incites enmity toward them is the enemy of man, namely Satan. It has been said: it is because He, exalted is He, will bring to life the idols that they worshipped, so that they will disown their worshippers and rebuke them. It has also been said: this is with an elision, meaning: for the worshippers of them are an enemy to me. The apparent reading is to keep the exception in its place without any advancing or delaying. Al-Jurjani said: its implied sense is: "Have you considered what you used to worship, you and your forefathers of old, except the Lord of the worlds? For they are an enemy to me," and *illa* ("except") here means "other than" and "besides." End of quotation. So he made it an exception from what follows "you used to worship." But there is no need for this elision, since it is valid for the exception to be from His saying: ﴿for they are an enemy to me﴾. A group, among them al-Farra' (whom al-Zamakhshari followed), made it a *munqati'* (disjunctive) exception, meaning: "but the Lord of the worlds," because they understood from His saying "what you used to worship" that they were the idols. Al-Zajjaj permitted that it be a *muttasil* (connected) exception, on the basis that they used to worship Allah and worship idols alongside Him; so He informed them that he disavowed what they worshipped, except Allah. They also permitted in ﴿Who created me﴾ the accusative, as a qualifier of "Lord of the worlds," or by supposing an implied "I mean" (*a'ni*). The nominative is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "He is the One who." Al-Hawfi said: It is also permissible that ﴿Who created me﴾ be nominative, as the subject, with ﴿so He guides me﴾ being a complete subject-and-predicate clause in the place of the predicate of "the One who," and the *fa'* has entered because of the meaning of a conditional in the speech. End of quotation. But "the One who" here does not carry the sense of a conditional noun, since it is specific and there is no room for generality in it, so it is not like "the one who comes to me, to him is a dirham." Also, the verb *khalaqa* ("created") does not admit of being restricted with respect to Ibrahim.

Abu al-Baqa' followed al-Hawfi in this parsing, but he did not say: "and the *fa'* entered because of the conditional meaning in the speech." If he meant that, it is not sound for the reasons we have mentioned. If he did not mean it, then this is not permissible except on the basis of the *fa'* being extra, according to the view of al-Akhfash in such a construction as: "Zayd, so strike him." "The One who created me by His power, so He guides me to His obedience." It has been said: to His Paradise. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿so He guides me﴾, meaning that when He perfected his creation and breathed the spirit into him, He followed that with continuous guidance which never ceases, to what would set him right and assist him. Otherwise, who guided him to feed upon the blood in the womb by sucking? Who guided him to recognize the breast at birth, and to know its place? Who guided him to the manner of suckling? And other guidances for livelihood and for the hereafter. End of quotation. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿and He feeds me and gives me drink﴾ is ordinary food and ordinary drink, and in it is an enumeration of the blessing of provision. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: "He feeds me without food, and gives me drink without drink," as has come in the report: "Indeed I spend the night and my Lord feeds me and gives me drink." Since creation cannot be claimed by anyone, it was not emphasized with *huwa* ("He"), so the construction of ﴿who created me﴾ (did not require it). Guidance, however, can be claimed, and likewise feeding and giving drink, so he emphasized with *huwa* in His saying ﴿so He guides me﴾ and ﴿and the One who feeds me and gives me drink﴾. After the blessings of creation and guidance, he mentioned that by which life continues and by which the order of creation is sustained, namely nourishment and drink. Since that is a cause of one of the qualities (of the body) dominating the others, through increase or decrease of food, from which sickness arises, he mentioned His blessing in removing the sickness that occurred. He attributed the sickness to himself and did not say, "and when He makes me ill," although Allah, exalted is He, is the agent of that. Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was enumerating Allah's blessings upon him, and cure is beloved while sickness is hated. Since sickness was not from those (blessings), he did not attribute it to Allah. It is reported from Ja'far al-Sadiq (though it is perhaps not authentic): "When I fall ill through sins, He cures me with repentance." Al-Zamakhshari said: He said "I fell ill" rather than "He made me ill," because many causes of sickness arise through a person's negligence in his food, drink, and other matters. For this reason the wise said: If most of the dead were asked, "What is the cause of your deaths?" they would say, "Overeating." Since cure may be ascribed to the physician and to the medicine by way of metaphor, as in His saying: ﴿In it is healing for mankind﴾ [al-Nahl 16:69], he emphasized with His saying ﴿so He cures me﴾, meaning: the One who guides me, feeds me and gives me drink, is Allah and no other.

Since death after resurrection cannot be ascribed except to Allah, no emphasis was needed for it. The claim of Numruz to giving life and death is, from him, a matter of fabrication (*makhrafa*) and insolence. Likewise, no emphasis was needed in ﴿and the One whom I hope﴾. Ibn Abi Ishaq affirmed the first-person *ya'* in *yahdini* and what follows it, and this is a transmission from Nafi'. "Hope" (*tam'*) is an expression for expectation, and Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was certain of forgiveness. Al-Zamakhshari said: He did not state definitively that He would forgive, and in this there is instruction for his people, and a means of gentleness toward them, so that they would avoid sins, guard against them, and seek forgiveness for what they commit. End of quotation. Al-Razi refuted this, saying: "For its outcome returns to the point that he . . . ," and he uttered a word which I will not mention, and after it: "upon himself for the sake of teaching the community," and this is certainly false. Al-Jubba'i said: he meant by it all the believers, for they are the ones who hope and do not despair. Al-Razi refuted him by making the speech of one person the speech of another, which destroys the structure of the speech. Al-Hasan said: the intended meaning of *tam'* is certainty. Al-Razi said: This is not correct except according to our school, where we say that nothing is obligatory upon Allah, that everything is good from Him, and that no one may object to His action. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: He made himself stand upon hope of forgiveness, and this is evidence of the intensity of his fear, together with his high station and intimacy with Allah.

The majority read ﴿my sin﴾ (*khati'ati*) in the singular, and al-Hasan read *khata'ay* in the plural. Most scholars held that the "sins" are His saying ﴿I am sick﴾ [al-Saffat 37:89], ﴿Rather, the greatest of them did it﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:63], and "She is my sister" concerning Sarah. A group said: by *khati'ah* he meant the generic noun, estimating it in all his affairs without specification. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is more evident to me, because many scholars have interpreted those three (statements) as allusions (*ma'arid*). Al-Zamakhshari said: What is meant is what occurs from him in some minor matters, because the prophets, peace be upon them, are protected, chosen above the worlds, and it is His saying . . . He mentioned the three, then said: "They are nothing but allusions, words and imaginings directed at the disbelievers, and they are not sins for which forgiveness is sought." End of quotation. (If you say): If only minor sins occur from them, and these are expiated, why then did he affirm for himself a sin or sins, and hope that He would forgive him? (I say): The answer is what has preceded: the prophets' seeking forgiveness is humility before their Lord and self-abasement, and this is indicated by his saying "I hope," and he did not state it definitively. End of quotation. ﴿The Day of Judgment﴾ (*yawm al-din*) is an adverbial object of time, and the governing verb is *yaghfir* ("forgive"). Forgiveness, though it occurs in this world, its effect is not made manifest except on the Day of Recompense, and in this world it is known only through Allah's informing.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi weakened the interpretation of "sin" as those three, because attributing to Ibrahim what does not conform (to the truth) is impermissible. He interpreted it as a way of humility, saying: For if it conforms in this place, the difficulty disappears; and if it does not conform, the answer returns to attributing disobedience to him, in order to exonerate him from disobedience. He said: The correct answer is that this is interpreted as leaving what is better (*tark al-awla*), which may be called "error" (*khata'*). For whoever sells a jewel worth a thousand for a dinar is said to have erred, and leaving what is better is permissible for prophets. End of quotation. In this there is some abridgement and alteration of wording for courtesy, in a manner suited to the station of prophethood.

Ibrahim, peace be upon him, put praise of Allah, exalted is He, first, and mentioned Him with fine attributes before his request and petition, then he asked Him, exalted is He, saying: ﴿My Lord, grant me judgment﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:83]. This shows that placing praise before the request is among the important matters. (The apparent meaning is that *hukm* is the judging between people with truth. It has been said: *hukm* means wisdom and prophethood, because these are what follow on the request for prophethood, since the prophet possesses wisdom and possesses judgment among people.) Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: It is not permissible to interpret *hukm* as prophethood, because it is already attained; if he sought prophethood, it would be sought, either as the very thing already attained, or as something other. The first is impossible, since obtaining what is already obtained is impossible; the second is impossible, since it is inadmissible that one person be a prophet twice. Rather, what is meant by *hukm* is the perfection of practical prophethood, which is that one should know the good in order to act upon it. End of quotation. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: *Hukm* has been interpreted as wisdom and prophethood. He said: His supplication, peace be upon him, in such a matter concerns steadfastness and permanence. And his being joined with the righteous means: Allah's granting him success in a deed that places him among them, or that brings him and them together in Paradise. Allah has answered him, exalted is He, when He said: ﴿And indeed he in the Hereafter is among the righteous﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:130].

Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: He placed His words, "Grant me wisdom (ḥukm)," before His words, "and join me with the righteous," because the theoretical faculty (al-quwwa al-nazariyya) precedes the practical faculty (al-quwwa al-amaliyya). This is because a person can know the truth even if he does not act upon it, whereas the reverse is not possible. Knowledge is an attribute of the soul (al-rūḥ), and action is an attribute of the body (al-badan). Just as the soul is nobler than the body, so knowledge is more excellent than reformation. End of quote.

"A tongue of truth" (lisān al-ṣidq): Ibn 'Atiyya said: It means praise and the perpetuation of a lofty standing, by the consensus of the exegetes. Likewise, God answered his supplication, so every religious community holds fast to him and venerates him, and he [Abraham] is upon the ḥanīfiyya (the pure monotheistic faith) with which Muhammad ﷺ came.

Makki said: It has also been said that the meaning of his request was that among his descendants at the end of time there would be one who stands up for the truth, and his supplication was answered in Muhammad, peace be upon him. This is a good meaning, except that the wording of the verse does not yield it except by forcing the sense upon the wording. End of quote.

When he asked for the happiness of this world, he asked for the happiness of the Hereafter, which is the Garden of Bliss (jannat al-na'īm), and he likened it to an inheritance (yūrath), because the inheritance is what is divided in this world. He likened the spoils of this world to the spoils of the Hereafter. God the Exalted said: ﴿That is the Garden which We shall give as an inheritance to those of Our servants who were God-fearing﴾ [Maryam: 63].

When he had finished with the aims of this world and the Hereafter for himself, he asked on behalf of the person most closely attached to him, namely his origin from whom he had sprung, which is his father. So he said: ﴿And forgive my father﴾. His request for forgiveness is conditional upon Islam, and requesting a conditional thing includes requesting the condition, so its sum is that he was praying for him to embrace Islam. His promise of this is clarified by His words: ﴿And Abraham's plea for forgiveness for his father was only due to a promise he had made to him. But when it became clear to him that he was an enemy to God, he disowned him﴾ [al-Tawba: 114], that is, when he died upon disbelief, he disowned him. It has also been said that he [the father] had told him that he was upon his religion inwardly and upon the religion of Nimrod outwardly, out of dissimulation (taqiyya) and fear, so he prayed for him because he believed the matter was so. When the opposite became clear to him, he disowned him. This is why he said in his supplication: ﴿And forgive my father, for he was among the astray﴾. Had he not believed that he was not, at that moment, astray, he would not have said that.

﴿And do not disgrace me﴾: this is either from al-khizy, which is humiliation, or from al-khazāya, which is shame. The phrase (yawma lā yanfa'u) is in apposition to ﴿the day they are resurrected﴾.

﴿Neither wealth nor children﴾: that is, just as they benefit in this world, where one's wealth ransoms him and one's children defend him. It has also been said that by "children" is meant all helpers. It has also been said that the meaning is: the day when attachment to the world and its adornments will not benefit, so he intended by that the great and most inclusive remembrance, because wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world. Had the omitted genitive not been posited, the exception would have no meaning. End of quote.

There is no necessity to posit an omitted genitive, as he mentioned, since we have posited it [i.e., the exception as disjunctive]; rather ﴿whoever comes to God with a sound heart﴾ will be benefited by that. If you wish, you may take the sentence according to its meaning and treat wealth and children as meaning riches, as if it were said: "On the day when riches will not benefit, except the riches of one who comes to God with a sound heart, because a man's wealth in his religion is in the soundness of his heart, just as his wealth in his worldly life is in his property and children." End of quote.

Ibn Abi Hayyan's *al-Bahr al-Muhit* (commentary) on surah 26, verses 76–89 (part 1 of 2):

As for those who held that His saying, ﴿for they are an enemy to me﴾, is inverted, the original being "for I am an enemy to them," because idols cannot be enemies, being inanimate, and his being their enemy is nothing (of significance), with no necessity for that: do you not see His saying: ﴿Nay, they will deny their worship and become opposed to them﴾ [Maryam 19:82]? This is the meaning of enmity. Also, the one who incites enmity toward them is the enemy of man, namely Satan. It has been said: it is because He, exalted is He, will bring to life the idols that they worshipped, so that they will disown their worshippers and rebuke them. It has also been said: this is with an elision, meaning: for the worshippers of them are an enemy to me. The apparent reading is to keep the exception in its place without any advancing or delaying. Al-Jurjani said: its implied sense is: "Have you considered what you used to worship, you and your forefathers of old, except the Lord of the worlds? For they are an enemy to me," and *illa* ("except") here means "other than" and "besides." End of quotation. So he made it an exception from what follows "you used to worship." But there is no need for this elision, since it is valid for the exception to be from His saying: ﴿for they are an enemy to me﴾. A group, among them al-Farra' (whom al-Zamakhshari followed), made it a *munqati'* (disjunctive) exception, meaning: "but the Lord of the worlds," because they understood from His saying "what you used to worship" that they were the idols. Al-Zajjaj permitted that it be a *muttasil* (connected) exception, on the basis that they used to worship Allah and worship idols alongside Him; so He informed them that he disavowed what they worshipped, except Allah. They also permitted in ﴿Who created me﴾ the accusative, as a qualifier of "Lord of the worlds," or by supposing an implied "I mean" (*a'ni*). The nominative is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "He is the One who." Al-Hawfi said: It is also permissible that ﴿Who created me﴾ be nominative, as the subject, with ﴿so He guides me﴾ being a complete subject-and-predicate clause in the place of the predicate of "the One who," and the *fa'* has entered because of the meaning of a conditional in the speech. End of quotation. But "the One who" here does not carry the sense of a conditional noun, since it is specific and there is no room for generality in it, so it is not like "the one who comes to me, to him is a dirham." Also, the verb *khalaqa* ("created") does not admit of being restricted with respect to Ibrahim.

Abu al-Baqa' followed al-Hawfi in this parsing, but he did not say: "and the *fa'* entered because of the conditional meaning in the speech." If he meant that, it is not sound for the reasons we have mentioned. If he did not mean it, then this is not permissible except on the basis of the *fa'* being extra, according to the view of al-Akhfash in such a construction as: "Zayd, so strike him." "The One who created me by His power, so He guides me to His obedience." It has been said: to His Paradise. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿so He guides me﴾, meaning that when He perfected his creation and breathed the spirit into him, He followed that with continuous guidance which never ceases, to what would set him right and assist him. Otherwise, who guided him to feed upon the blood in the womb by sucking? Who guided him to recognize the breast at birth, and to know its place? Who guided him to the manner of suckling? And other guidances for livelihood and for the hereafter. End of quotation. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿and He feeds me and gives me drink﴾ is ordinary food and ordinary drink, and in it is an enumeration of the blessing of provision. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: "He feeds me without food, and gives me drink without drink," as has come in the report: "Indeed I spend the night and my Lord feeds me and gives me drink." Since creation cannot be claimed by anyone, it was not emphasized with *huwa* ("He"), so the construction of ﴿who created me﴾ (did not require it). Guidance, however, can be claimed, and likewise feeding and giving drink, so he emphasized with *huwa* in His saying ﴿so He guides me﴾ and ﴿and the One who feeds me and gives me drink﴾. After the blessings of creation and guidance, he mentioned that by which life continues and by which the order of creation is sustained, namely nourishment and drink. Since that is a cause of one of the qualities (of the body) dominating the others, through increase or decrease of food, from which sickness arises, he mentioned His blessing in removing the sickness that occurred. He attributed the sickness to himself and did not say, "and when He makes me ill," although Allah, exalted is He, is the agent of that. Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was enumerating Allah's blessings upon him, and cure is beloved while sickness is hated. Since sickness was not from those (blessings), he did not attribute it to Allah. It is reported from Ja'far al-Sadiq (though it is perhaps not authentic): "When I fall ill through sins, He cures me with repentance." Al-Zamakhshari said: He said "I fell ill" rather than "He made me ill," because many causes of sickness arise through a person's negligence in his food, drink, and other matters. For this reason the wise said: If most of the dead were asked, "What is the cause of your deaths?" they would say, "Overeating." Since cure may be ascribed to the physician and to the medicine by way of metaphor, as in His saying: ﴿In it is healing for mankind﴾ [al-Nahl 16:69], he emphasized with His saying ﴿so He cures me﴾, meaning: the One who guides me, feeds me and gives me drink, is Allah and no other.

Since death after resurrection cannot be ascribed except to Allah, no emphasis was needed for it. The claim of Numruz to giving life and death is, from him, a matter of fabrication (*makhrafa*) and insolence. Likewise, no emphasis was needed in ﴿and the One whom I hope﴾. Ibn Abi Ishaq affirmed the first-person *ya'* in *yahdini* and what follows it, and this is a transmission from Nafi'. "Hope" (*tam'*) is an expression for expectation, and Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was certain of forgiveness. Al-Zamakhshari said: He did not state definitively that He would forgive, and in this there is instruction for his people, and a means of gentleness toward them, so that they would avoid sins, guard against them, and seek forgiveness for what they commit. End of quotation. Al-Razi refuted this, saying: "For its outcome returns to the point that he . . . ," and he uttered a word which I will not mention, and after it: "upon himself for the sake of teaching the community," and this is certainly false. Al-Jubba'i said: he meant by it all the believers, for they are the ones who hope and do not despair. Al-Razi refuted him by making the speech of one person the speech of another, which destroys the structure of the speech. Al-Hasan said: the intended meaning of *tam'* is certainty. Al-Razi said: This is not correct except according to our school, where we say that nothing is obligatory upon Allah, that everything is good from Him, and that no one may object to His action. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: He made himself stand upon hope of forgiveness, and this is evidence of the intensity of his fear, together with his high station and intimacy with Allah.

The majority read ﴿my sin﴾ (*khati'ati*) in the singular, and al-Hasan read *khata'ay* in the plural. Most scholars held that the "sins" are His saying ﴿I am sick﴾ [al-Saffat 37:89], ﴿Rather, the greatest of them did it﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:63], and "She is my sister" concerning Sarah. A group said: by *khati'ah* he meant the generic noun, estimating it in all his affairs without specification. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is more evident to me, because many scholars have interpreted those three (statements) as allusions (*ma'arid*). Al-Zamakhshari said: What is meant is what occurs from him in some minor matters, because the prophets, peace be upon them, are protected, chosen above the worlds, and it is His saying . . . He mentioned the three, then said: "They are nothing but allusions, words and imaginings directed at the disbelievers, and they are not sins for which forgiveness is sought." End of quotation. (If you say): If only minor sins occur from them, and these are expiated, why then did he affirm for himself a sin or sins, and hope that He would forgive him? (I say): The answer is what has preceded: the prophets' seeking forgiveness is humility before their Lord and self-abasement, and this is indicated by his saying "I hope," and he did not state it definitively. End of quotation. ﴿The Day of Judgment﴾ (*yawm al-din*) is an adverbial object of time, and the governing verb is *yaghfir* ("forgive"). Forgiveness, though it occurs in this world, its effect is not made manifest except on the Day of Recompense, and in this world it is known only through Allah's informing.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi weakened the interpretation of "sin" as those three, because attributing to Ibrahim what does not conform (to the truth) is impermissible. He interpreted it as a way of humility, saying: For if it conforms in this place, the difficulty disappears; and if it does not conform, the answer returns to attributing disobedience to him, in order to exonerate him from disobedience. He said: The correct answer is that this is interpreted as leaving what is better (*tark al-awla*), which may be called "error" (*khata'*). For whoever sells a jewel worth a thousand for a dinar is said to have erred, and leaving what is better is permissible for prophets. End of quotation. In this there is some abridgement and alteration of wording for courtesy, in a manner suited to the station of prophethood.

Ibrahim, peace be upon him, put praise of Allah, exalted is He, first, and mentioned Him with fine attributes before his request and petition, then he asked Him, exalted is He, saying: ﴿My Lord, grant me judgment﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:83]. This shows that placing praise before the request is among the important matters. (The apparent meaning is that *hukm* is the judging between people with truth. It has been said: *hukm* means wisdom and prophethood, because these are what follow on the request for prophethood, since the prophet possesses wisdom and possesses judgment among people.) Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: It is not permissible to interpret *hukm* as prophethood, because it is already attained; if he sought prophethood, it would be sought, either as the very thing already attained, or as something other. The first is impossible, since obtaining what is already obtained is impossible; the second is impossible, since it is inadmissible that one person be a prophet twice. Rather, what is meant by *hukm* is the perfection of practical prophethood, which is that one should know the good in order to act upon it. End of quotation. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: *Hukm* has been interpreted as wisdom and prophethood. He said: His supplication, peace be upon him, in such a matter concerns steadfastness and permanence. And his being joined with the righteous means: Allah's granting him success in a deed that places him among them, or that brings him and them together in Paradise. Allah has answered him, exalted is He, when He said: ﴿And indeed he in the Hereafter is among the righteous﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:130].

Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: He placed His words, "Grant me wisdom (ḥukm)," before His words, "and join me with the righteous," because the theoretical faculty (al-quwwa al-nazariyya) precedes the practical faculty (al-quwwa al-amaliyya). This is because a person can know the truth even if he does not act upon it, whereas the reverse is not possible. Knowledge is an attribute of the soul (al-rūḥ), and action is an attribute of the body (al-badan). Just as the soul is nobler than the body, so knowledge is more excellent than reformation. End of quote.

"A tongue of truth" (lisān al-ṣidq): Ibn 'Atiyya said: It means praise and the perpetuation of a lofty standing, by the consensus of the exegetes. Likewise, God answered his supplication, so every religious community holds fast to him and venerates him, and he [Abraham] is upon the ḥanīfiyya (the pure monotheistic faith) with which Muhammad ﷺ came.

Makki said: It has also been said that the meaning of his request was that among his descendants at the end of time there would be one who stands up for the truth, and his supplication was answered in Muhammad, peace be upon him. This is a good meaning, except that the wording of the verse does not yield it except by forcing the sense upon the wording. End of quote.

When he asked for the happiness of this world, he asked for the happiness of the Hereafter, which is the Garden of Bliss (jannat al-na'īm), and he likened it to an inheritance (yūrath), because the inheritance is what is divided in this world. He likened the spoils of this world to the spoils of the Hereafter. God the Exalted said: ﴿That is the Garden which We shall give as an inheritance to those of Our servants who were God-fearing﴾ [Maryam: 63].

When he had finished with the aims of this world and the Hereafter for himself, he asked on behalf of the person most closely attached to him, namely his origin from whom he had sprung, which is his father. So he said: ﴿And forgive my father﴾. His request for forgiveness is conditional upon Islam, and requesting a conditional thing includes requesting the condition, so its sum is that he was praying for him to embrace Islam. His promise of this is clarified by His words: ﴿And Abraham's plea for forgiveness for his father was only due to a promise he had made to him. But when it became clear to him that he was an enemy to God, he disowned him﴾ [al-Tawba: 114], that is, when he died upon disbelief, he disowned him. It has also been said that he [the father] had told him that he was upon his religion inwardly and upon the religion of Nimrod outwardly, out of dissimulation (taqiyya) and fear, so he prayed for him because he believed the matter was so. When the opposite became clear to him, he disowned him. This is why he said in his supplication: ﴿And forgive my father, for he was among the astray﴾. Had he not believed that he was not, at that moment, astray, he would not have said that.

﴿And do not disgrace me﴾: this is either from al-khizy, which is humiliation, or from al-khazāya, which is shame. The pronoun in (yub'athūn) refers to the servants, since it is known; or it refers to (al-ḍāllīn), and then it is part of the plea for forgiveness, since the meaning would be: "On the day when the astray are resurrected." The phrase (yawma lā yanfa'u) is in apposition to ﴿the day they are resurrected﴾.

﴿Neither wealth nor children﴾: that is, just as they benefit in this world, where one's wealth ransoms him and one's children defend him. It has also been said that by "children" is meant all helpers. It has also been said that the meaning is: the day when attachment to the world and its adornments will not benefit, so he intended by that the great and most inclusive remembrance, because wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world. The apparent view is that the exception is disjunctive (munqaṭi'), that is: "But whoever comes to God with a sound heart, his sound heart will benefit him." Al-Zamakhshari said: You may make the exception disjunctive, and in addition to that you must posit an omitted genitive (muḍāf), namely the state, meant by which is soundness, and it is not of the same kind as wealth and children, so that the meaning would reduce to wealth and children not benefiting, while only soundness of heart benefits. Had the omitted genitive not been posited, the exception would have no meaning. End of quote.

There is no necessity to posit an omitted genitive, as he mentioned, since we have posited it [i.e., the exception as disjunctive]; rather ﴿whoever comes to God with a sound heart﴾ will be benefited by that. Al-Zamakhshari, in his first explanation, treated it as connected through a reinterpretation. He said: "Except whoever comes to God," meaning: except the state of whoever comes to God with a sound heart, and this is from his saying:

*"Their greeting among them is a painful blow,*
*and its reward is nothing but the sword."*

An example of this would be if one were asked: "Does Zayd have wealth and children?" and he replied: "His wealth and children are the soundness of his heart," meaning: the negation of wealth and children from him, and the affirmation of soundness of heart for him instead of that. If you wish, you may take the sentence according to its meaning and treat wealth and children as meaning riches, as if it were said: "On the day when riches will not benefit, except the riches of one who comes to God with a sound heart, because a man's wealth in his religion is in the soundness of his heart, just as his wealth in his worldly life is in his property and children." End of quote.

Some of them made it an exception of the emptied type (istithnā' mufarragh), with "man" as the object, and the sense is: "Neither wealth nor children benefits anyone except whoever comes to God with a sound heart, for his wealth spent in the paths of righteousness will benefit him, and his children, who are righteous, since he spent it in obedience to God, guided his children to the religion, and taught them the laws; and soundness of heart means its freedom from polytheism and sins, and from the attachments of the world that are abandoned, even if they are permissible, such as wealth and children." Sufyan said: It is the one who meets his Lord with nothing in his heart other than Him. This implies that the wording is general, but the one sound from polytheism is the more general. Al-Junayd said: [a heart] stung (ladīgh) by the fear of God, and the sound (salīm) is the stung (ladīgh). Al-Zamakhshari said: This is one of the novel interpretations (bida' al-tafasir), and he spoke the truth.

Ibn Abi Hayyan's *al-Bahr al-Muhit* (commentary) on surah 26, verses 76–89 (part 1 of 2):

(Or do they benefit you by your drawing near to them and calling upon them, or do they harm you) by your abandoning their worship? If they neither benefit nor harm, then what is the meaning of your worshipping them? ﴿They said: Rather, we found our fathers doing so﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:74]. This is an evasion (*haydah*) from answering the question. For if they had said, "They hear us, benefit us and harm us," they would have exposed themselves through a lie that cannot be disputed. And if they had said, "They hear us but do not harm us," they would have recorded against themselves a plain error. So they resorted to blind imitation (*taqlid*) of their fathers in worshipping them, without any proof or argument. The *kaf* (in *kadhalika*, "like that") is in the accusative position, governed by *yaf'alun* ("they do"). That is, they do in their worship of those idols a deed like that which they do, namely, their worship. Evasion from the answer is one of the signs of the failure of the argument. Here *bal* ("rather") marks a turning away (*idrab*) from its answer: when he asked the question and then took up another matter that he had not asked them about, this signified their helplessness and their admission of incapacity.

﴿And your forefathers of old﴾. He described them as "of old" to indicate the antiquity of idol-worship among them. Since they had worshipped them in the time of Noah, peace be upon him, what then was the time of those after him? *'Aduwwun* ("enemy") can be used for the singular and the plural, as in His saying: ﴿They are the enemy, so beware of them﴾ [al-Munafiqun 63:4]. It has been said that it is patterned on the verbal noun (*masdar*), like *qabul* and *walu'*. Al-Zamakhshari said: He said "an enemy to me" in order to present the matter as it was in his own mind, meaning: I considered my affair, and I saw that my worship of them was worship of an enemy, so I shunned them and preferred the worship of Him from whom all good comes. By this he showed them that it was advice which he gave to himself first, and on which he based the management of his own affair, so that they might consider and say: "Ibrahim gave us no advice except what he gave to himself, and he wanted for us only what he wanted for his own soul," so that this would make them more inclined to accept and more prompted to listen to him. Had he said, "Indeed they are an enemy to you," it would not have had that effect. Moreover, he entered upon a mode of allusion (*ta'rid*, indirect speech), and allusion may reach the one advised in a way that explicit statement does not, because he may reflect upon it, and reflection may lead him to acceptance. From this is what is related of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him: a man confronted him with something, and he said, "If I were in your position I would need discipline." And a man heard people talking about al-Hijr and said, "It is neither my house nor yours." End of quotation. This is a statement with some exaggeration, in keeping with his habit. For whoever sells a jewel worth a thousand for a dinar is said to have erred, and leaving what is better is permissible for prophets. End of quotation. In this there is some abridgement and alteration of wording for courtesy, in a manner suited to the station of prophethood.

Ibrahim, peace be upon him, put praise of Allah, exalted is He, first, and mentioned Him with fine attributes before his request and petition, then he asked Him, exalted is He, saying: ﴿My Lord, grant me judgment﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:83]. This shows that placing praise before the request is among the important matters. (The apparent meaning is that *hukm* is the judging between people with truth. It has been said: *hukm* means wisdom and prophethood, because these are what follow on the request for prophethood, since the prophet possesses wisdom and possesses judgment among people.) Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: It is not permissible to interpret *hukm* as prophethood, because it is already attained; if he sought prophethood, it would be sought, either as the very thing already attained, or as something other. The first is impossible, since obtaining what is already obtained is impossible; the second is impossible, since it is inadmissible that one person be a prophet twice. Rather, what is meant by *hukm* is the perfection of practical prophethood, which is that one should know the good in order to act upon it. End of quotation. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: *Hukm* has been interpreted as wisdom and prophethood. He said: His supplication, peace be upon him, in such a matter concerns steadfastness and permanence. And his being joined with the righteous means: Allah's granting him success in a deed that places him among them, or that brings him and them together in Paradise. Allah has answered him, exalted is He, when He said: ﴿And indeed he in the Hereafter is among the righteous﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:130].

Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: He placed His words, "Grant me wisdom (ḥukm)," before His words, "and join me with the righteous," because the theoretical faculty (al-quwwa al-nazariyya) precedes the practical faculty (al-quwwa al-amaliyya). This is because a person can know the truth even if he does not act upon it, whereas the reverse is not possible. Knowledge is an attribute of the soul (al-rūḥ), and action is an attribute of the body (al-badan). Just as the soul is nobler than the body, so knowledge is more excellent than reformation. End of quote.

"A tongue of truth" (lisān al-ṣidq): Ibn 'Atiyya said: It means praise and the perpetuation of a lofty standing, by the consensus of the exegetes. Likewise, God answered his supplication, so every religious community holds fast to him and venerates him, and he [Abraham] is upon the ḥanīfiyya (the pure monotheistic faith) with which Muhammad ﷺ came.

Makki said: It has also been said that the meaning of his request was that among his descendants at the end of time there would be one who stands up for the truth, and his supplication was answered in Muhammad, peace be upon him. This is a good meaning, except that the wording of the verse does not yield it except by forcing the sense upon the wording. End of quote.

When he asked for the happiness of this world, he asked for the happiness of the Hereafter, which is the Garden of Bliss (jannat al-na'īm), and he likened it to an inheritance (yūrath), because the inheritance is what is divided in this world. He likened the spoils of this world to the spoils of the Hereafter. God the Exalted said: ﴿That is the Garden which We shall give as an inheritance to those of Our servants who were God-fearing﴾ [Maryam: 63].

When he had finished with the aims of this world and the Hereafter for himself, he asked on behalf of the person most closely attached to him, namely his origin from whom he had sprung, which is his father. So he said: ﴿And forgive my father﴾. His request for forgiveness is conditional upon Islam, and requesting a conditional thing includes requesting the condition, so its sum is that he was praying for him to embrace Islam. His promise of this is clarified by His words: ﴿And Abraham's plea for forgiveness for his father was only due to a promise he had made to him. But when it became clear to him that he was an enemy to God, he disowned him﴾ [al-Tawba: 114], that is, when he died upon disbelief, he disowned him. It has also been said that he [the father] had told him that he was upon his religion inwardly and upon the religion of Nimrod outwardly, out of dissimulation (taqiyya) and fear, so he prayed for him because he believed the matter was so. When the opposite became clear to him, he disowned him. This is why he said in his supplication: ﴿And forgive my father, for he was among the astray﴾. Had he not believed that he was not, at that moment, astray, he would not have said that.

﴿And do not disgrace me﴾: this is either from al-khizy, which is humiliation, or from al-khazāya, which is shame. The pronoun in (yub'athūn) refers to the servants, since it is known; or it refers to (al-ḍāllīn), and then it is part of the plea for forgiveness, since the meaning would be: "On the day when the astray are resurrected." The phrase (yawma lā yanfa'u) is in apposition to ﴿the day they are resurrected﴾.

﴿Neither wealth nor children﴾: that is, just as they benefit in this world, where one's wealth ransoms him and one's children defend him. It has also been said that by "children" is meant all helpers. It has also been said that the meaning is: the day when attachment to the world and its adornments will not benefit, so he intended by that the great and most inclusive remembrance, because wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world. The apparent view is that the exception is disjunctive (munqaṭi'), that is: "But whoever comes to God with a sound heart, his sound heart will benefit him." Al-Zamakhshari said: You may make the exception disjunctive, and in addition to that you must posit an omitted genitive (muḍāf), namely the state, meant by which is soundness, and it is not of the same kind as wealth and children, so that the meaning would reduce to wealth and children not benefiting, while only soundness of heart benefits. Had the omitted genitive not been posited, the exception would have no meaning. End of quote.

There is no necessity to posit an omitted genitive, as he mentioned, since we have posited it [i.e., the exception as disjunctive]; rather ﴿whoever comes to God with a sound heart﴾ will be benefited by that. Al-Zamakhshari, in his first explanation, treated it as connected through a reinterpretation. He said: "Except whoever comes to God," meaning: except the state of whoever comes to God with a sound heart, and this is from his saying:

*"Their greeting among them is a painful blow,*
*and its reward is nothing but the sword."*

An example of this would be if one were asked: "Does Zayd have wealth and children?" and he replied: "His wealth and children are the soundness of his heart," meaning: the negation of wealth and children from him, and the affirmation of soundness of heart for him instead of that. If you wish, you may take the sentence according to its meaning and treat wealth and children as meaning riches, as if it were said: "On the day when riches will not benefit, except the riches of one who comes to God with a sound heart, because a man's wealth in his religion is in the soundness of his heart, just as his wealth in his worldly life is in his property and children." End of quote.

Some of them made it an exception of the emptied type (istithnā' mufarragh), with "man" as the object, and the sense is: "Neither wealth nor children benefits anyone except whoever comes to God with a sound heart, for his wealth spent in the paths of righteousness will benefit him, and his children, who are righteous, since he spent it in obedience to God, guided his children to the religion, and taught them the laws; and soundness of heart means its freedom from polytheism and sins, and from the attachments of the world that are abandoned, even if they are permissible, such as wealth and children." Sufyan said: It is the one who meets his Lord with nothing in his heart other than Him. This implies that the wording is general, but the one sound from polytheism is the more general. Al-Junayd said: [a heart] stung (ladīgh) by the fear of God, and the sound (salīm) is the stung (ladīgh). Al-Zamakhshari said: This is one of the novel interpretations (bida' al-tafasir), and he spoke the truth.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 26, verse 90–98:

﴿And Paradise will be brought near﴾: it will be brought close so that they may look at it and be delighted by their gathering there.

﴿And Hell will be made manifest﴾: it will be revealed and uncovered, such that it is in full view of them, like His saying: ﴿So when they see it approaching, the faces of those who disbelieved will be distressed, and it will be said, "This is what you used to call for."  Say: "Have you considered, if Allah should destroy me and those with me or have mercy upon us, who would protect the disbelievers from a painful punishment?"﴾ [al-Mulk: 27]. This is by way of reproach: ﴿Can they help you, or help themselves?﴾ Since they and you are the fuel of the Fire?

Al-A'mash read: fa-burrizat (with the fa'), making the manifesting of Hell follow after the bringing near of Paradise. This is because the waw denotes mere joining, so it is possible that the manifesting of each of them occurred before the other. And this is the placing of mercy before punishment, which is good, were it not that the Mushaf's orthography is with a waw.

Malik ibn Dinar read: (wa-baraza) with a fatha and without the tashdid; (al-Jahim) in the nominative, attributing the verb to it figuratively.

When He had reproached and rebuked them, He informed about the state of the Day of Resurrection, and in all of that the past tense was used: atā, uzlifat, and burrizat. It has been said: (fa-kubkibu) is for the certainty of the occurrence of that, even though it had not yet occurred. The pronoun in "fa-kubkibu" refers to the idols, which were treated as those who understand. Al-Kirmani said: fa-kubkibu: they were hurled into it. It has been said: they were gathered. It has been said: they were cast down. It has been said: they were thrown upside down on their faces, tumbling over one another. It has been said: they were cast into Hell, toppling over again and again until they settle at its bottom. (Al-ghawun) are the disbelievers whom misguidance encompassed. It has been said: the pronoun refers to the disbelievers, and al-ghawun are the devils. (Wa-junud Iblis) is a host, and everyone who followed him is a soldier and helper for him. Al-Suddi said: they are the polytheists of the Arabs, and al-ghawun are all the other polytheists. It has been said: they are the leaders and the base followers. They said: that is, the worshippers of idols. The clause after it is a circumstantial clause, and what was said is the clause of the oath and its complement. The address in (nusawwikum) is to the idols, by way of acknowledgment and admission of the truth. Ibn 'Atiyya said: they swore by Allah that, if we were not astray, in that we worship you and make you equal with Allah – exalted is He – who is the Lord of the worlds, its Creator and its Owner. End of quotation. As for his statement: "in ṭalālin" ("if we were not astray"), if he intends an explanation of the meaning, it is correct; but if he intends that "in" here is a negation and the lam in "lafī" carries the meaning of "illa" (except), then that is not the position of the Basrans; it is the position of the Kufans. The Basrans' position regarding such a case is that "in" is the lightened form of the heavy "inna," and the lam is the one introduced to distinguish between the negative "in" and the "in" that serves to emphasize the content of the sentence.
