Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 26, verses 116–122:

﴿They said, "If you do not cease, O Noah, you will surely be among those stoned to death"﴾ — that is, for ceasing to denounce what we are upon and your claim to be a messenger from God. "Stoned" means with stones; and it was said: with abuse. He had despaired at that time of their being guided, so he called upon his Lord — and He knows best his state — saying: ﴿My people have denied me﴾. So his supplication was not because they had harmed him, but for the sake of Your religion. (﴿Judge⁠﴾) means: decide [between us]. He supplicated for himself and for those who believed in him, for deliverance, and in that there is an indication that punishment would descend upon his people; that is: (﴿and save me﴾) from what will befall them. It was also said: "save me from their deeds," because these are the cause of punishment.

The word al-fulk (the ship) is both singular and plural, but its usual usage is as a plural, due to His saying: ﴿and you see the ships ploughing through it﴾ [al-Nahl: 14] and ﴿and the ships that run in the sea﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164]. So wherever it occurs in a non-rhyme position it is used as a plural, and wherever it is a rhyme-final (fāṣila), it is used as a singular, in consideration of the rhyme-endings, as in this place. As for the one in Surat Yasin, and the disagreement was already mentioned regarding whether, when its referent is plural, it is a broken plural (jam' taksir) or a collective noun (ism jam'), [that is]...

And al-mashhun (the laden): Ibn ʿAbbas said: "laden" (al-muqawwar, loaded to capacity); ʿAṭāʾ said: "heavily weighted" (al-muthqal).

﴿Then We drowned the rest afterwards﴾ — that is, after the deliverance of Noah and the believers.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 26, verses 116–122:

﴿They said, "If you do not cease, O Noah, you will surely be among those stoned to death"﴾ — that is, for ceasing to denounce what we are upon and your claim to be a messenger from God. "Stoned" means with stones; and it was said: with abuse. He had despaired at that time of their being guided, so he called upon his Lord — and He knows best his state — saying: ﴿My people have denied me﴾. So his supplication was not because they had harmed him, but for the sake of Your religion. (﴿Judge⁠﴾) means: decide [between us]. **Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 26, verses 123–140:**

﴿ʿAd denied the messengers.﴾ ﴿When their brother Hud said to them: "Will you not fear God?"﴾ ﴿Indeed, I am a trustworthy messenger to you.﴾ ﴿So fear God and obey me.﴾ ﴿I ask you for no wage for it; my wage is only from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿Do you build a landmark on every high place, playing?﴾ ﴿And do you take fortresses, perhaps you will live forever?﴾ ﴿And when you seize, you seize as tyrants.﴾ ﴿So fear God and obey me.﴾ ﴿And fear Him who has supplied you with what you know.﴾ ﴿He has supplied you with livestock and sons,﴾ ﴿and gardens and springs.﴾ ﴿Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day.﴾ ﴿They said: "It is all the same to us whether you admonish or are not among the admonishers.﴾ ﴿This is only the custom of the ancients,﴾ ﴿and we will not be punished."﴾ ﴿So they denied him, and We destroyed them. Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.﴾ ﴿And indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful.﴾

He was their brother by lineage, and he was a handsome merchant, the most resembling of creation to Adam (peace be upon him). He lived four hundred and sixty-four years, and between him and Thamud there were one hundred years. The dwellings of ʿAd extended from ʿUman to Hadramawt, the most fertile of lands, but God turned them into deserts and sands. He first commanded them with what Noah had commanded his people, then he reproached them for their evil deeds together with their disbelief, saying: ﴿Do you build on every high place?﴾

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The *rīʿ* is the top of the alley." Mujahid said: "It is a narrow pass between two mountains." ʿAta' said: "It is springs in which there is water." Ibn Bahr said: "It is a mountain." It was also said: "It is a small elevation."

The majority (al-Jumhur, the main body of readers) read *rīʿ* with a kasra on the *rāʾ*, while Ibn Abi ʿAbla read it with a fatha on it.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: *(āyatan)* means "a landmark." Mujahid said: "Dovecotes." Al-Naqqash and others said: "Tall palaces." It was also said: "A house of ʿishār (a kind of pregnant she-camel)." It was also said: "A meeting place for boasting." It was also said: "Tall markers by which they would guide themselves on their journeys; they played with them because they used to guide themselves by the stars." It was also said: "A sign to which whoever wishes to play gathers to annoy those passing along the road."

In His saying, there is a denunciation of building in the form of play, as the affluent do in this world.

*Al-maṣāniʿ* is the plural of *maṣnaʿa*. It was said: "It is building over water." It was said: "It is lofty, firmly constructed palaces." It was said: "It is fortresses." Qatada said: "It is water reservoirs." It was said: "It is dovecotes." It was said: "It is dwellings."

*Ittakhadha* here has the meaning of *ʿamila* (to make/do), i.e., *wa-yaʿmalūna maṣāniʿa* ("and they make cisterns"), that is, you build. Labid said:

*"And mountains will remain after us, and cisterns."*

﴿So that perhaps you will live forever.﴾ The apparent meaning is that *laʿalla* retains its original sense of hope, and it seems to be a justification for the building and the taking (of fortresses): i.e., what moves you to do that is the hope of eternity, but there is no eternity. In the reading of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud): *kay takhludūn* ("in order that you may live forever"). Or the meaning is: your situation resembles the situation of one who lives forever, so for that reason you have built and taken.

Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is interrogative, in the manner of reproach and mockery toward them, i.e., "Are you going to live forever?" The Kufan school holds that *laʿalla* can be interrogative.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: the meaning is "as if you were eternal." In the codex of Ubayy: *kaʾannakum takhludūn* ("as if you were living forever"). It was also read: *kaʾannakum khālidūn* ("as if you were eternal").

Ubayy, ʿAlqama, and Abu al-ʿAliya read it in the passive voice with shadda (*mukhallad*), as the poet said:

*"Will anyone enjoy (life) except a happy one made eternal, / little in cares, who does not pass the night in trouble?"* (p-33)

﴿And when you seize:﴾ i.e., when you intend to seize. It is understood as "intend" so that the condition and its answer do not coincide, as in His saying (the poet):

*"Whenever you rouse her, you rouse her blameworthy."*

i.e., whenever you intend to rouse her.

Al-Hasan said: "They hastened to torment people without deliberation or consideration of the consequences." It was also said: the meaning is that you are angry tyrants, possessing excessive violence and sudden fury. So the building of high edifices indicates love of height, the taking of fortresses in hope of eternity indicates permanence, and tyranny indicates singularity in height; these are attributes of divinity, which cannot be attained by a servant. This indicates that love of the world has taken hold of them to the extent that they have exceeded the limits of servitude, and love of the world is the root of every sin.

When He had warned them and rebuked them for their vile deeds, He commanded them a second time to fear God and obey His prophet. Then He commanded them a third time to fear God, to alert them to His goodness toward them and the abundance of His blessing upon them. He mentioned the relative clause (*alladhī*) connected to their knowledge, to alert them and to urge them toward obedience and piety, since thanking the benefactor is obligatory and obeying him is required; and to indicate to them that whoever supplied them with goodness is capable of withdrawing it and of punishing whoever does not fear Him, since this supply does not come from you but is from His bounty, so that He has followed His goodness to you one thing after another.

When He had mentioned what He supplied them with in general terms, referring to their knowledge, He then mentioned it in detail. He began with livestock, which is what establishes leadership in this world and strength against those who oppose them; wealth is the reason for the acquisition of offspring in most cases. Strength is also attained through sons, which is why He joined them with livestock, and because they help in guarding the livestock and tending to it. He followed that with gardens and flowing waters, since supplying them with these is part of perfecting the blessing.

*(Wa-bi-anʿāmin)*: Some grammarians held that it is a *badal* (substitute/apposition) of His saying *(bi-mā taʿlamūna)*, and the governing word was repeated, as in His saying: ﴿Follow the messengers. Follow one who does not ask you for a wage.﴾ [Yasin: 20]. Most grammarians do not consider such a thing a *badal*; rather, in their view it is a repetition of clauses, even if the meaning is one, and it is called *tatbīʿ* (a follow-up repetition). According to them, the governing word may be repeated only when it is a preposition (*ḥarf jarr*) and not the thing it governs, as in: *marartu bi-Zaydin bi-akhīka* ("I passed by Zayd, by your brother").

Then He warned them of the punishment of God, and presented that in the form of fear, not as a definite judgment, since he hoped for their faith. So their reply was: ﴿It is all the same to us,﴾ whether your admonition or its absence. They regarded his words as admonition, since they did not believe in the truth of what he brought, and that he was lying in what he claimed. Their saying this was in the manner of belittling and not caring about what he frightened them with.

The majority read *waʿaẓta* with the *ẓāʾ* clearly pronounced. It is related from Abu ʿAmr, al-Kisaʾi, and ʿAsim that the *ẓāʾ* is assimilated into the *tāʾ* (*idgham*, assimilation). With assimilation, Ibn Muhaysin and al-Aʿmash read it, except that al-Aʿmash added the object pronoun and read: *awaʿaẓtanā* ("did you admonish us?"). It should be a case of *ikhfāʾ* (partial concealment), because the *ẓāʾ* is voiced and emphatic, while the *tāʾ* is voiceless and open; the *ẓāʾ* is stronger than the *tāʾ*. Assimilation is only good between identical sounds or between close sounds when the first is weaker than the second. As for assimilating the stronger into the weaker, it is not good. Nevertheless, such things have come in the Qur'an by the transmission of reliable authorities, so their acceptance is obligatory, even though other readings are more eloquent and more regular.

The phrase ﴿Did you admonish﴾ is balanced (*ʿādala*) by His saying: ﴿or were not among the admonishers﴾, although it could have been balanced by *am lam taʿiẓ* ("or did you not admonish"). As He said: ﴿It is all the same to us whether we grieve or are patient﴾ [Ibrahim: 21], for the sake of the verse-ending (*fāṣila*), just as it balanced in His saying: ﴿It is all the same to you whether you call them or you are silent﴾ [al-Araf: 193], and the construction "am samattum" (or you are silent) did not come. Often, with verse-endings, something is good that would not be good without them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: there is a difference between them, meaning between what came in the verse, namely *am lam takun min al-wāʿiẓīn*, and *am lam taʿiẓ*. He said: because the intended meaning is "It is all the same to us whether you did this act which is admonition, or you were not at all of its people nor engaged in it." So it is more emphatic in showing their lack of regard for his admonition than your saying "or you did not admonish."

When they did not care about what he commanded them, and what he reminded them of of the blessings of God and his warning them of God's vengeance upon them, they answered him by saying: ﴿This is only the custom of the ancients.﴾

ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud), ʿAlqama, al-Hasan, Abu Jaʿfar, Abu ʿAmr, Ibn Kathir, and al-Kisaʾi read *khalquu* with a fatha on the *khāʾ* and sukun on the *lām* (*khalq*). This may mean: what you say and claim is only the fabrication (*ikhtilāq*) of the ancients among the liars before you, so you are upon their paths. ʿAlqama related from ʿAbd Allah: ﴿This is only the fabrication of the ancients.﴾ It may also mean: this structure in which we are is only the structure upon which the ancients were: life and death, with no resurrection and no punishment.

The remaining seven readers read *khuluqu* with two damma (*khuluq*). Abu Qilaba and al-Asmaʿi, from Nafiʿ, read it with a damma on the *khāʾ* and sukun on the *lām*. This reading admits of the two possible meanings that apply to *khuluqu*.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 26, verses 123–140:**

﴿ʿAd denied the messengers.﴾ ﴿When their brother Hud said to them: "Will you not fear God?"﴾ ﴿Indeed, I am a trustworthy messenger to you.﴾ ﴿So fear God and obey me.﴾ ﴿I ask you for no wage for it; my wage is only from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿Do you build a landmark on every high place, playing?﴾ ﴿And do you take fortresses, perhaps you will live forever?﴾ ﴿And when you seize, you seize as tyrants.﴾ ﴿So fear God and obey me.﴾ ﴿And fear Him who has supplied you with what you know.﴾ ﴿He has supplied you with livestock and sons,﴾ ﴿and gardens and springs.﴾ ﴿Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day.﴾ ﴿They said: "It is all the same to us whether you admonish or are not among the admonishers.﴾ ﴿This is only the custom of the ancients,﴾ ﴿and we will not be punished."﴾ ﴿So they denied him, and We destroyed them. He was their brother by lineage, and he was a handsome merchant, the most resembling of creation to Adam (peace be upon him). He lived four hundred and sixty-four years, and between him and Thamud there were one hundred years. The dwellings of ʿAd extended from ʿUman to Hadramawt, the most fertile of lands, but God turned them into deserts and sands. He first commanded them with what Noah had commanded his people, then he reproached them for their evil deeds together with their disbelief, saying: ﴿Do you build on every high place?﴾

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The *rīʿ* is the top of the alley." Mujahid said: "It is a narrow pass between two mountains." ʿAta' said: "It is springs in which there is water." Ibn Bahr said: "It is a mountain." It was also said: "It is a small elevation."

The majority (al-Jumhur, the main body of readers) read *rīʿ* with a kasra on the *rāʾ*, while Ibn Abi ʿAbla read it with a fatha on it.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: *(āyatan)* means "a landmark." Mujahid said: "Dovecotes." Al-Naqqash and others said: "Tall palaces." It was also said: "A house of ʿishār (a kind of pregnant she-camel)." It was also said: "A meeting place for boasting." It was also said: "Tall markers by which they would guide themselves on their journeys; they played with them because they used to guide themselves by the stars." It was also said: "A sign to which whoever wishes to play gathers to annoy those passing along the road."

In His saying, there is a denunciation of building in the form of play, as the affluent do in this world.

*Al-maṣāniʿ* is the plural of *maṣnaʿa*. It was said: "It is building over water." It was said: "It is lofty, firmly constructed palaces." It was said: "It is fortresses." Qatada said: "It is water reservoirs." It was said: "It is dovecotes." It was said: "It is dwellings."

*Ittakhadha* here has the meaning of *ʿamila* (to make/do), i.e., *wa-yaʿmalūna maṣāniʿa* ("and they make cisterns"), that is, you build. Labid said:

In the reading of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud): *kay takhludūn* ("in order that you may live forever"). Or the meaning is: your situation resembles the situation of one who lives forever, so for that reason you have built and taken.

Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is interrogative, in the manner of reproach and mockery toward them, i.e., "Are you going to live forever?" The Kufan school holds that *laʿalla* can be interrogative.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: the meaning is "as if you were eternal." In the codex of Ubayy: *kaʾannakum takhludūn* ("as if you were living forever"). It was also read: *kaʾannakum khālidūn* ("as if you were eternal").

Ubayy, ʿAlqama, and Abu al-ʿAliya read it in the passive voice with shadda (*mukhallad*), as the poet said:

*"Will anyone enjoy (life) except a happy one made eternal, / little in cares, who does not pass the night in trouble?"* (p-33)

﴿And when you seize:﴾ i.e., when you intend to seize. It is understood as "intend" so that the condition and its answer do not coincide, as in His saying (the poet):

*"Whenever you rouse her, you rouse her blameworthy."*

i.e., whenever you intend to rouse her.

Al-Hasan said: "They hastened to torment people without deliberation or consideration of the consequences." It was also said: the meaning is that you are angry tyrants, possessing excessive violence and sudden fury. So the building of high edifices indicates love of height, the taking of fortresses in hope of eternity indicates permanence, and tyranny indicates singularity in height; these are attributes of divinity, which cannot be attained by a servant. He was their brother by lineage, and he was a handsome merchant, the most resembling of creation to Adam (peace be upon him). He lived four hundred and sixty-four years, and between him and Thamud there were one hundred years. It was also said: "A meeting place for boasting." It was also said: "Tall markers by which they would guide themselves on their journeys; they played with them because they used to guide themselves by the stars." It was also said: "A sign to which whoever wishes to play gathers to annoy those passing along the road."

In His saying, there is a denunciation of building in the form of play, as the affluent do in this world.

*Al-maṣāniʿ* is the plural of *maṣnaʿa*. It was said: "It is building over water." It was said: "It is lofty, firmly constructed palaces." It was said: "It is fortresses." Qatada said: "It is water reservoirs." It was said: "It is dovecotes." It was said: "It is dwellings."

*Ittakhadha* here has the meaning of *ʿamila* (to make/do), i.e., *wa-yaʿmalūna maṣāniʿa* ("and they make cisterns"), that is, you build. Labid said:

﴿So that perhaps you will live forever.﴾ The apparent meaning is that *laʿalla* retains its original sense of hope, and it seems to be a justification for the building and the taking (of fortresses): i.e., what moves you to do that is the hope of eternity, but there is no eternity. In the reading of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud): *kay takhludūn* ("in order that you may live forever"). Or the meaning is: your situation resembles the situation of one who lives forever, so for that reason you have built and taken.

Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is interrogative, in the manner of reproach and mockery toward them, i.e., "Are you going to live forever?" The Kufan school holds that *laʿalla* can be interrogative.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: the meaning is "as if you were eternal." In the codex of Ubayy: *kaʾannakum takhludūn* ("as if you were living forever"). It was also read: *kaʾannakum khālidūn* ("as if you were eternal").

Ubayy, ʿAlqama, and Abu al-ʿAliya read it in the passive voice with shadda (*mukhallad*), as the poet said:

i.e., whenever you intend to rouse her.

Al-Hasan said: "They hastened to torment people without deliberation or consideration of the consequences." It was also said: the meaning is that you are angry tyrants, possessing excessive violence and sudden fury. Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.﴾ ﴿And indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful.﴾

He was their brother by lineage, and he was a handsome merchant, the most resembling of creation to Adam (peace be upon him). He lived four hundred and sixty-four years, and between him and Thamud there were one hundred years. The dwellings of ʿAd extended from ʿUman to Hadramawt, the most fertile of lands, but God turned them into deserts and sands. He first commanded them with what Noah had commanded his people, then he reproached them for their evil deeds together with their disbelief, saying: ﴿Do you build on every high place?﴾

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The *rīʿ* is the top of the alley." Mujahid said: "It is a narrow pass between two mountains." ʿAta' said: "It is springs in which there is water." Ibn Bahr said: "It is a mountain." It was also said: "It is a small elevation."

The majority (al-Jumhur, the main body of readers) read *rīʿ* with a kasra on the *rāʾ*, while Ibn Abi ʿAbla read it with a fatha on it.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: *(āyatan)* means "a landmark." Mujahid said: "Dovecotes." Al-Naqqash and others said: "Tall palaces." It was also said: "A house of ʿishār (a kind of pregnant she-camel)." It was also said: "A meeting place for boasting." It was also said: "Tall markers by which they would guide themselves on their journeys; they played with them because they used to guide themselves by the stars." It was also said: "A sign to which whoever wishes to play gathers to annoy those passing along the road."

In His saying, there is a denunciation of building in the form of play, as the affluent do in this world.

*Al-maṣāniʿ* is the plural of *maṣnaʿa*. It was said: "It is building over water." It was said: "It is lofty, firmly constructed palaces." It was said: "It is fortresses." Qatada said: "It is water reservoirs." It was said: "It is dovecotes." It was said: "It is dwellings."

*Ittakhadha* here has the meaning of *ʿamila* (to make/do), i.e., *wa-yaʿmalūna maṣāniʿa* ("and they make cisterns"), that is, you build. Labid said:

*"And mountains will remain after us, and cisterns."*

﴿So that perhaps you will live forever.﴾ The apparent meaning is that *laʿalla* retains its original sense of hope, and it seems to be a justification for the building and the taking (of fortresses): i.e., what moves you to do that is the hope of eternity, but there is no eternity. In the reading of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud): *kay takhludūn* ("in order that you may live forever"). Or the meaning is: your situation resembles the situation of one who lives forever, so for that reason you have built and taken.

Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is interrogative, in the manner of reproach and mockery toward them, i.e., "Are you going to live forever?" The Kufan school holds that *laʿalla* can be interrogative.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: the meaning is "as if you were eternal." In the codex of Ubayy: *kaʾannakum takhludūn* ("as if you were living forever"). It was also read: *kaʾannakum khālidūn* ("as if you were eternal").

Ubayy, ʿAlqama, and Abu al-ʿAliya read it in the passive voice with shadda (*mukhallad*), as the poet said:

*"Will anyone enjoy (life) except a happy one made eternal, / little in cares, who does not pass the night in trouble?"* (p-33)

﴿And when you seize:﴾ i.e., when you intend to seize. It is understood as "intend" so that the condition and its answer do not coincide, as in His saying (the poet):

*"Whenever you rouse her, you rouse her blameworthy."*

i.e., whenever you intend to rouse her.

Al-Hasan said: "They hastened to torment people without deliberation or consideration of the consequences." It was also said: the meaning is that you are angry tyrants, possessing excessive violence and sudden fury. So the building of high edifices indicates love of height, the taking of fortresses in hope of eternity indicates permanence, and tyranny indicates singularity in height; these are attributes of divinity, which cannot be attained by a servant. This indicates that love of the world has taken hold of them to the extent that they have exceeded the limits of servitude, and love of the world is the root of every sin.

When He had warned them and rebuked them for their vile deeds, He commanded them a second time to fear God and obey His prophet. Then He commanded them a third time to fear God, to alert them to His goodness toward them and the abundance of His blessing upon them. He mentioned the relative clause (*alladhī*) connected to their knowledge, to alert them and to urge them toward obedience and piety, since thanking the benefactor is obligatory and obeying him is required; and to indicate to them that whoever supplied them with goodness is capable of withdrawing it and of punishing whoever does not fear Him, since this supply does not come from you but is from His bounty, so that He has followed His goodness to you one thing after another.

When He had mentioned what He supplied them with in general terms, referring to their knowledge, He then mentioned it in detail. He began with livestock, which is what establishes leadership in this world and strength against those who oppose them; wealth is the reason for the acquisition of offspring in most cases. Strength is also attained through sons, which is why He joined them with livestock, and because they help in guarding the livestock and tending to it. He followed that with gardens and flowing waters, since supplying them with these is part of perfecting the blessing.

*(Wa-bi-anʿāmin)*: Some grammarians held that it is a *badal* (substitute/apposition) of His saying *(bi-mā taʿlamūna)*, and the governing word was repeated, as in His saying: ﴿Follow the messengers. Follow one who does not ask you for a wage.﴾ [Yasin: 20]. Most grammarians do not consider such a thing a *badal*; rather, in their view it is a repetition of clauses, even if the meaning is one, and it is called *tatbīʿ* (a follow-up repetition). According to them, the governing word may be repeated only when it is a preposition (*ḥarf jarr*) and not the thing it governs, as in: *marartu bi-Zaydin bi-akhīka* ("I passed by Zayd, by your brother").

Then He warned them of the punishment of God, and presented that in the form of fear, not as a definite judgment, since he hoped for their faith. So their reply was: ﴿It is all the same to us,﴾ whether your admonition or its absence. They regarded his words as admonition, since they did not believe in the truth of what he brought, and that he was lying in what he claimed. Their saying this was in the manner of belittling and not caring about what he frightened them with.

Nevertheless, such things have come in the Qur'an by the transmission of reliable authorities, so their acceptance is obligatory, even though other readings are more eloquent and more regular.

He was their brother by lineage, and he was a handsome merchant, the most resembling of creation to Adam (peace be upon him). He lived four hundred and sixty-four years, and between him and Thamud there were one hundred years. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The *rīʿ* is the top of the alley." Mujahid said: "It is a narrow pass between two mountains." ʿAta' said: "It is springs in which there is water." Ibn Bahr said: "It is a mountain." It was also said: "It is a small elevation."

The majority (al-Jumhur, the main body of readers) read *rīʿ* with a kasra on the *rāʾ*, while Ibn Abi ʿAbla read it with a fatha on it.

It was also said: "A meeting place for boasting." It was also said: "Tall markers by which they would guide themselves on their journeys; they played with them because they used to guide themselves by the stars." It was also said: "A sign to which whoever wishes to play gathers to annoy those passing along the road."

In His saying, there is a denunciation of building in the form of play, as the affluent do in this world.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: *(āyatan)* means "a landmark." Mujahid said: "Dovecotes." Al-Naqqash and others said: "Tall palaces." It was also said: "A house of ʿishār (a kind of pregnant she-camel)." It was also said: "A meeting place for boasting." It was also said: "Tall markers by which they would guide themselves on their journeys; they played with them because they used to guide themselves by the stars." It was also said: "A sign to which whoever wishes to play gathers to annoy those passing along the road."

In His saying, there is a denunciation of building in the form of play, as the affluent do in this world.

*Al-maṣāniʿ* is the plural of *maṣnaʿa*. It was said: "It is building over water." It was said: "It is lofty, firmly constructed palaces." It was said: "It is fortresses." Qatada said: "It is water reservoirs." It was said: "It is dovecotes." It was said: "It is dwellings."

*Ittakhadha* here has the meaning of *ʿamila* (to make/do), i.e., *wa-yaʿmalūna maṣāniʿa* ("and they make cisterns"), that is, you build. Labid said:

*"And mountains will remain after us, and cisterns."*

﴿So that perhaps you will live forever.﴾ The apparent meaning is that *laʿalla* retains its original sense of hope, and it seems to be a justification for the building and the taking (of fortresses): i.e., what moves you to do that is the hope of eternity, but there is no eternity. In the reading of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud): *kay takhludūn* ("in order that you may live forever"). Or the meaning is: your situation resembles the situation of one who lives forever, so for that reason you have built and taken.

Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is interrogative, in the manner of reproach and mockery toward them, i.e., "Are you going to live forever?" The Kufan school holds that *laʿalla* can be interrogative.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: the meaning is "as if you were eternal." In the codex of Ubayy: *kaʾannakum takhludūn* ("as if you were living forever"). It was also read: *kaʾannakum khālidūn* ("as if you were eternal").

Ubayy, ʿAlqama, and Abu al-ʿAliya read it in the passive voice with shadda (*mukhallad*), as the poet said:

*"Will anyone enjoy (life) except a happy one made eternal, / little in cares, who does not pass the night in trouble?"* (p-33)

﴿And when you seize:﴾ i.e., when you intend to seize. It is understood as "intend" so that the condition and its answer do not coincide, as in His saying (the poet):

*"Whenever you rouse her, you rouse her blameworthy."*

i.e., whenever you intend to rouse her.

Al-Hasan said: "They hastened to torment people without deliberation or consideration of the consequences." It was also said: the meaning is that you are angry tyrants, possessing excessive violence and sudden fury. So the building of high edifices indicates love of height, the taking of fortresses in hope of eternity indicates permanence, and tyranny indicates singularity in height; these are attributes of divinity, which cannot be attained by a servant. This indicates that love of the world has taken hold of them to the extent that they have exceeded the limits of servitude, and love of the world is the root of every sin.

When He had warned them and rebuked them for their vile deeds, He commanded them a second time to fear God and obey His prophet. Then He commanded them a third time to fear God, to alert them to His goodness toward them and the abundance of His blessing upon them. He mentioned the relative clause (*alladhī*) connected to their knowledge, to alert them and to urge them toward obedience and piety, since thanking the benefactor is obligatory and obeying him is required; and to indicate to them that whoever supplied them with goodness is capable of withdrawing it and of punishing whoever does not fear Him, since this supply does not come from you but is from His bounty, so that He has followed His goodness to you one thing after another.

When He had mentioned what He supplied them with in general terms, referring to their knowledge, He then mentioned it in detail. He began with livestock, which is what establishes leadership in this world and strength against those who oppose them; wealth is the reason for the acquisition of offspring in most cases. Strength is also attained through sons, which is why He joined them with livestock, and because they help in guarding the livestock and tending to it. He followed that with gardens and flowing waters, since supplying them with these is part of perfecting the blessing.

*(Wa-bi-anʿāmin)*: Some grammarians held that it is a *badal* (substitute/apposition) of His saying *(bi-mā taʿlamūna)*, and the governing word was repeated, as in His saying: ﴿Follow the messengers. Follow one who does not ask you for a wage.﴾ [Yasin: 20]. Most grammarians do not consider such a thing a *badal*; rather, in their view it is a repetition of clauses, even if the meaning is one, and it is called *tatbīʿ* (a follow-up repetition). According to them, the governing word may be repeated only when it is a preposition (*ḥarf jarr*) and not the thing it governs, as in: *marartu bi-Zaydin bi-akhīka* ("I passed by Zayd, by your brother").

Then He warned them of the punishment of God, and presented that in the form of fear, not as a definite judgment, since he hoped for their faith. So their reply was: ﴿It is all the same to us,﴾ whether your admonition or its absence. They regarded his words as admonition, since they did not believe in the truth of what he brought, and that he was lying in what he claimed. Their saying this was in the manner of belittling and not caring about what he frightened them with.

The majority read *waʿaẓta* with the *ẓāʾ* clearly pronounced. It is related from Abu ʿAmr, al-Kisaʾi, and ʿAsim that the *ẓāʾ* is assimilated into the *tāʾ* (*idgham*, assimilation). With assimilation, Ibn Muhaysin and al-Aʿmash read it, except that al-Aʿmash added the object pronoun and read: *awaʿaẓtanā* ("did you admonish us?"). It should be a case of *ikhfāʾ* (partial concealment), because the *ẓāʾ* is voiced and emphatic, while the *tāʾ* is voiceless and open; the *ẓāʾ* is stronger than the *tāʾ*. Assimilation is only good between identical sounds or between close sounds when the first is weaker than the second. As for assimilating the stronger into the weaker, it is not good. Nevertheless, such things have come in the Qur'an by the transmission of reliable authorities, so their acceptance is obligatory, even though other readings are more eloquent and more regular.

The phrase ﴿Did you admonish﴾ is balanced (*ʿādala*) by His saying: ﴿or were not among the admonishers﴾, although it could have been balanced by *am lam taʿiẓ* ("or did you not admonish"). As He said: ﴿It is all the same to us whether we grieve or are patient﴾ [Ibrahim: 21], for the sake of the verse-ending (*fāṣila*), just as it balanced in His saying: ﴿It is all the same to you whether you call them or you are silent﴾ [al-Araf: 193], and the construction "am samattum" (or you are silent) did not come. Often, with verse-endings, something is good that would not be good without them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: there is a difference between them, meaning between what came in the verse, namely *am lam takun min al-wāʿiẓīn*, and *am lam taʿiẓ*. He said: because the intended meaning is "It is all the same to us whether you did this act which is admonition, or you were not at all of its people nor engaged in it." So it is more emphatic in showing their lack of regard for his admonition than your saying "or you did not admonish."

When they did not care about what he commanded them, and what he reminded them of of the blessings of God and his warning them of God's vengeance upon them, they answered him by saying: ﴿This is only the custom of the ancients.﴾

ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud), ʿAlqama, al-Hasan, Abu Jaʿfar, Abu ʿAmr, Ibn Kathir, and al-Kisaʾi read *khalquu* with a fatha on the *khāʾ* and sukun on the *lām* (*khalq*). This may mean: what you say and claim is only the fabrication (*ikhtilāq*) of the ancients among the liars before you, so you are upon their paths. ʿAlqama related from ʿAbd Allah: ﴿This is only the fabrication of the ancients.﴾ It may also mean: this structure in which we are is only the structure upon which the ancients were: life and death, with no resurrection and no punishment.

The remaining seven readers read *khuluqu* with two damma (*khuluq*). Abu Qilaba and al-Asmaʿi, from Nafiʿ, read it with a damma on the *khāʾ* and sukun on the *lām*. This reading admits of the two possible meanings that apply to *khuluqu*.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 26, verses 141–159:

﴿Thamud denied the messengers.﴾ ﴿When their brother Salih said to them, "Will you not be mindful of God?"﴾ ﴿Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger.﴾ ﴿So be mindful of God and obey me.﴾ ﴿I ask you for no wage for it; my wage is only from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿Will you be left secure in what is here,﴾ ﴿among gardens and springs,﴾ ﴿and crops and palm trees whose spathes are soft?﴾ ﴿And you carve out homes from the mountains, skillfully.﴾ ﴿So be mindful of God and obey me.﴾ ﴿And do not obey the command of the extravagant,﴾ ﴿who cause corruption in the land and do not reform.﴾ ﴿They said, "You are only one of the bewitched.﴾ ﴿You are only a human like us, so bring a sign, if you are truthful."﴾ ﴿He said, "This is a she-camel; she has a share of water, and you have a share of water on a known day.﴾ ﴿Do not touch her with harm, lest the punishment of a tremendous day seize you."﴾ ﴿But they hamstrung her, and then they became regretful.﴾ ﴿So the punishment seized them. Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.﴾ ﴿And indeed, your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful.﴾

(Will you be left) — it is possible that this is a denial (inkar) that they would be left, abiding in their bliss, never departing from it; and it is possible that it is a reminder of the blessing in God's leaving them free and in the gardens and the other things they enjoy, together with security and ease. This was said by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is a warning to them, meaning: do you expect, if you are ungrateful for the blessings, that your sins will be overlooked? It was also said: (Will you be left?) is an interrogative in the sense of rebuke, i.e., will your Lord leave you? (In what is here) means: in what you are in this world (secure), not fearing His assault. End of quotation. Here, (ما) is a relative pronoun (mawsula), and (هاهنا, here) is an indication of the present, nearby place, i.e., in that which is settled in this place of yours of bliss. (Among gardens) is a substitute (badal) for (what is here): it first summarized and then detailed, just as Hud, peace be upon him, summarized in his words, ﴿He has provided you with what you know﴾ [al-Shu'ara 132], then detailed in his words, ﴿He has provided you with cattle and sons﴾ [al-Shu'ara 133]. The land of Thamud had many orchards, water and palm trees.

(Hadim, al-Hadim) — Ibn 'Abbas said: it is when it has ripened and reached its full development. al-Zuhri said: it is the fine, soft (spathe) as it first emerges. al-Zajjaj said: it is the one whose dates are without stones. al-Dahhak said: it is the one whose parts are piled upon one another. It was also said: the ripe dates that are tipped with a tail. It was said: the ripe dates that crumble. It was said: the spathe, and it approaches its skin from both sides, from their saying (khasr hadim), a slender waist. It was said: the hanging cluster. It was said: the soft pith of the palm heart.

The words (and palm trees) came after (among gardens), although the word "garden" first includes palm trees, and they use "garden" without meaning anything but palm trees, as the poet said:

"As if my two eyes, in the two sides of a barren and killed (she-camel) of the water-carriers, were watering a garden of tall palm trees."

Here he meant palm trees. (Suhuq) is the plural of (sahuq), which is the one whose trunk has gone up high and grown tall. So (palm trees) is singled out by mention after being included in the term (gardens), to alert to its distinction from the trees of the garden by its excellence. Or he meant by (gardens) trees other than palm trees, since the word allows for this sense; then he joined to it (palm trees). He reminded them, may He be exalted, that He had given them the finest and most ripened palm trees, because the female palms bear dates, and their spathe has fineness in it. (Hadim) means: fine and slender. (Al-Barni) is finer than the spathe of the (lawn) variety. It is possible that the fineness of the spathe is due to the abundance of its load, for whenever it is abundant it becomes fine and so is (hadim); and when the load is little, the dates come out excellent. Since the grounds of the palm trees were good, their watering was abundant, and they were free from blight, the load grew heavy with the fineness of the grain.

The majority read (وتَنْحِتُونَ, and you carve) with a (ت, t) for address and a kasra on the (ح, h). Abu Haywa, 'Isa and al-Hasan read it with a fatha on it, which has been mentioned. From him (al-Hasan) there is also a (alif) after the (ح) for elongation. From 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad, from his father, with a (ي, y) from below and a kasra on the (ح). From Abu Haywa and al-Hasan also, with a (ي) from below and a fatha on the (ح). 'Abd Allah, Ibn 'Abbas, Zayd ibn 'Ali, the Kufans, and Ibn 'Amir read (فارِهِينَ, skillful) with an (alif). The rest of the seven read it without an (alif). Mujahid read (مُتَفَرِّهِينَ, exulting), an active participle from (تَفَرَّهَ). The meaning is: energetic, concerned. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: greedy. Ibn Zayd said: strong. Ibn 'Abbas also said, and Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala': insolent, haughty. 'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad said: meaning (mustafrihin), i.e., exaggerating in making the caves fine so that they might protect their wealth in them. Qatada said: secure. al-Kalbi said: tyrannical. Khusayf said: amazed by themselves. 'Ikrima said: comfortable. al-Dahhak said: clever. Abu Salih said: skilled. Ibn Bahr said: capable. Abu 'Ubayda said: exultant.

The apparent meaning of these verses is that the predominant characteristic of the people of Hud was imaginary pleasures: seeking elevation, permanence, exclusivity and tyranny; and of the people of Salih: sensory pleasures of food, drink and strong, good dwellings.

(And do not obey) is an address by the majority to his people. (The extravagant) are their great ones and leaders in disbelief and misguidance, and they were nine men.

(Who cause corruption in the land) means: in the land of Thamud. It was also said: in the whole land, because by their sins the rain was withheld. Since they "cause corruption," its implication is that of an unrestricted (absolute) statement, so He brought (and do not reform), negating reform from them. This is a negation of absolute reform, which necessarily entails the negation of reform in any form whatsoever, so no reform at all comes from them.

(Musahhar) is one who has been bewitched greatly until his intellect is overcome. It was also said: it derives from (sahr), which is the lung, meaning: you are a human who is not fit for prophethood. This view is weakened by their subsequent words, ﴿You are only a human like us﴾, since this sentence would then be an emphasis of what came before it, whereas the original purpose is to add new information (ta'sis). (Mithlana, like us) means: in eating, drinking and other human attributes, so you have no special status in prophethood.

(So bring a sign) means: a mark confirming the truth of your claim. In the speech there is an ellipsis, its estimate being: he said, "I will bring it." They said, "What is it?" (He said, "This is a she-camel…") It was narrated that they proposed to him a pregnant she-camel that would come out of this rock and give birth to a young camel. So Salih sat contemplating, and Gabriel, peace be upon him, said to him: "Pray two units of prayer and ask your Lord for the she-camel." He did so, and the she-camel came out and knelt before them, and gave birth to a young one like her in size. A portion of the story of Thamud and the she-camel has been mentioned in al-A'raf. (Shirb) is the share of water drunk, similar to a watering. Ibn Abi 'Ablah read (شُرْبٌ) with a damma on the (ش) in both places. The apparent meaning of this punishment is that it was in this world, and so it occurred; and its description as tremendous is due to the punishment's descending upon them in it. Describing the day as tremendous is more emphatic than describing the punishment as such, because when the time becomes tremendous through the punishment, the impact of the punishment is greater in its magnitude. The hamstringing is attributed to all of them, because they were all content with it, to the extent that it was narrated that they sought the consent of the woman in her curtain and of the children, and they all agreed.

(So they became regretful) — not the regret of repentance, but the regret of fear that the punishment would descend upon them quickly, and that occurs upon witnessing the punishment at a time when repentance no longer benefits. They became in the morning with their colours changed, just as Salih, peace be upon him, had told them. The punishment was a cry by which their bodies became still and their hearts split, and they all died to the last one, and stones were poured upon them in the midst of that. It was also said: their regret was over not having slain the young camel, but this is a distant view.

The (ال, al-) in (So the punishment seized them) is for a previously known punishment, the punishment of that tremendous day.

(Will you be left) — it is possible that this is a denial (inkar) that they would be left, abiding in their bliss, never departing from it; and it is possible that it is a reminder of the blessing in God's leaving them free and in the gardens and the other things they enjoy, together with security and ease. This was said by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is a warning to them, meaning: do you expect, if you are ungrateful for the blessings, that your sins will be overlooked? It was also said: (Will you be left?) is an interrogative in the sense of rebuke, i.e., will your Lord leave you? (In what is here) means: in what you are in this world (secure), not fearing His assault. End of quotation. Here, (ما) is a relative pronoun (mawsula), and (هاهنا, here) is an indication of the present, nearby place, i.e., in that which is settled in this place of yours of bliss. (Among gardens) is a substitute (badal) for (what is here): it first summarized and then detailed, just as Hud, peace be upon him, summarized in his words, ﴿He has provided you with what you know﴾ [al-Shu'ara 132], then detailed in his words, ﴿He has provided you with cattle and sons﴾ [al-Shu'ara 133]. The land of Thamud had many orchards, water and palm trees.

(Hadim, al-Hadim) — Ibn 'Abbas said: it is when it has ripened and reached its full development. al-Zuhri said: it is the fine, soft (spathe) as it first emerges. al-Zajjaj said: it is the one whose dates are without stones. al-Dahhak said: it is the one whose parts are piled upon one another. It was also said: the ripe dates that are tipped with a tail. It was said: the ripe dates that crumble. It was said: the spathe, and it approaches its skin from both sides, from their saying (khasr hadim), a slender waist. It was said: the hanging cluster. It was said: the soft pith of the palm heart.

The words (and palm trees) came after (among gardens), although the word "garden" first includes palm trees, and they use "garden" without meaning anything but palm trees, as the poet said:

"As if my two eyes, in the two sides of a barren and killed (she-camel) of the water-carriers, were watering a garden of tall palm trees."

Here he meant palm trees. (Suhuq) is the plural of (sahuq), which is the one whose trunk has gone up high and grown tall. So (palm trees) is singled out by mention after being included in the term (gardens), to alert to its distinction from the trees of the garden by its excellence. Or he meant by (gardens) trees other than palm trees, since the word allows for this sense; then he joined to it (palm trees). He reminded them, may He be exalted, that He had given them the finest and most ripened palm trees, because the female palms bear dates, and their spathe has fineness in it. (Hadim) means: fine and slender. (Al-Barni) is finer than the spathe of the (lawn) variety. It is possible that the fineness of the spathe is due to the abundance of its load, for whenever it is abundant it becomes fine and so is (hadim); and when the load is little, the dates come out excellent. Since the grounds of the palm trees were good, their watering was abundant, and they were free from blight, the load grew heavy with the fineness of the grain.

The majority read (وتَنْحِتُونَ, and you carve) with a (ت, t) for address and a kasra on the (ح, h). Abu Haywa, 'Isa and al-Hasan read it with a fatha on it, which has been mentioned. From him (al-Hasan) there is also a (alif) after the (ح) for elongation. From 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad, from his father, with a (ي, y) from below and a kasra on the (ح). From Abu Haywa and al-Hasan also, with a (ي) from below and a fatha on the (ح). 'Abd Allah, Ibn 'Abbas, Zayd ibn 'Ali, the Kufans, and Ibn 'Amir read (فارِهِينَ, skillful) with an (alif). The rest of the seven read it without an (alif). Mujahid read (مُتَفَرِّهِينَ, exulting), an active participle from (تَفَرَّهَ). The meaning is: energetic, concerned. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: greedy. Ibn Zayd said: strong. Ibn 'Abbas also said, and Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala': insolent, haughty. 'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad said: meaning (mustafrihin), i.e., exaggerating in making the caves fine so that they might protect their wealth in them. Qatada said: secure. al-Kalbi said: tyrannical. Khusayf said: amazed by themselves. 'Ikrima said: comfortable. al-Dahhak said: clever. Abu Salih said: skilled. Ibn Bahr said: capable. Abu 'Ubayda said: exultant.

The apparent meaning of these verses is that the predominant characteristic of the people of Hud was imaginary pleasures: seeking elevation, permanence, exclusivity and tyranny; and of the people of Salih: sensory pleasures of food, drink and strong, good dwellings.

(And do not obey) is an address by the majority to his people. (The extravagant) are their great ones and leaders in disbelief and misguidance, and they were nine men.

(Who cause corruption in the land) means: in the land of Thamud. It was also said: in the whole land, because by their sins the rain was withheld. Since they "cause corruption," its implication is that of an unrestricted (absolute) statement, so He brought (and do not reform), negating reform from them. This is a negation of absolute reform, which necessarily entails the negation of reform in any form whatsoever, so no reform at all comes from them.

(Musahhar) is one who has been bewitched greatly until his intellect is overcome. It was also said: it derives from (sahr), which is the lung, meaning: you are a human who is not fit for prophethood. This view is weakened by their subsequent words, ﴿You are only a human like us﴾, since this sentence would then be an emphasis of what came before it, whereas the original purpose is to add new information (ta'sis). (Mithlana, like us) means: in eating, drinking and other human attributes, so you have no special status in prophethood.

(So bring a sign) means: a mark confirming the truth of your claim. In the speech there is an ellipsis, its estimate being: he said, "I will bring it." They said, "What is it?" (He said, "This is a she-camel…") It was narrated that they proposed to him a pregnant she-camel that would come out of this rock and give birth to a young camel. So Salih sat contemplating, and Gabriel, peace be upon him, said to him: "Pray two units of prayer and ask your Lord for the she-camel." He did so, and the she-camel came out and knelt before them, and gave birth to a young one like her in size. A portion of the story of Thamud and the she-camel has been mentioned in al-A'raf. The hamstringing is attributed to all of them, because they were all content with it, to the extent that it was narrated that they sought the consent of the woman in her curtain and of the children, and they all agreed.

(So they became regretful) — not the regret of repentance, but the regret of fear that the punishment would descend upon them quickly, and that occurs upon witnessing the punishment at a time when repentance no longer benefits. They became in the morning with their colours changed, just as Salih, peace be upon him, had told them. The punishment was a cry by which their bodies became still and their hearts split, and they all died to the last one, and stones were poured upon them in the midst of that. It was also said: their regret was over not having slain the young camel, but this is a distant view.

The (ال, al-) in (So the punishment seized them) is for a previously known punishment, the punishment of that tremendous day.

(Will you be left) — it is possible that this is a denial (inkar) that they would be left, abiding in their bliss, never departing from it; and it is possible that it is a reminder of the blessing in God's leaving them free and in the gardens and the other things they enjoy, together with security and ease. This was said by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is a warning to them, meaning: do you expect, if you are ungrateful for the blessings, that your sins will be overlooked? It was also said: (Will you be left?) is an interrogative in the sense of rebuke, i.e., will your Lord leave you? (In what is here) means: in what you are in this world (secure), not fearing His assault. End of quotation. Here, (ما) is a relative pronoun (mawsula), and (هاهنا, here) is an indication of the present, nearby place, i.e., in that which is settled in this place of yours of bliss. (Among gardens) is a substitute (badal) for (what is here): it first summarized and then detailed, just as Hud, peace be upon him, summarized in his words, ﴿He has provided you with what you know﴾ [al-Shu'ara 132], then detailed in his words, ﴿He has provided you with cattle and sons﴾ [al-Shu'ara 133]. The land of Thamud had many orchards, water and palm trees.

(Hadim, al-Hadim) — Ibn 'Abbas said: it is when it has ripened and reached its full development. al-Zuhri said: it is the fine, soft (spathe) as it first emerges. al-Zajjaj said: it is the one whose dates are without stones. al-Dahhak said: it is the one whose parts are piled upon one another. It was also said: the ripe dates that are tipped with a tail. It was said: the ripe dates that crumble. It was said: the spathe, and it approaches its skin from both sides, from their saying (khasr hadim), a slender waist. It was said: the hanging cluster. It was said: the soft pith of the palm heart.

The words (and palm trees) came after (among gardens), although the word "garden" first includes palm trees, and they use "garden" without meaning anything but palm trees, as the poet said:

"As if my two eyes, in the two sides of a barren and killed (she-camel) of the water-carriers, were watering a garden of tall palm trees."

Here he meant palm trees. (Suhuq) is the plural of (sahuq), which is the one whose trunk has gone up high and grown tall. So (palm trees) is singled out by mention after being included in the term (gardens), to alert to its distinction from the trees of the garden by its excellence. Or he meant by (gardens) trees other than palm trees, since the word allows for this sense; then he joined to it (palm trees). He reminded them, may He be exalted, that He had given them the finest and most ripened palm trees, because the female palms bear dates, and their spathe has fineness in it. (Hadim) means: fine and slender. (Al-Barni) is finer than the spathe of the (lawn) variety. It is possible that the fineness of the spathe is due to the abundance of its load, for whenever it is abundant it becomes fine and so is (hadim); and when the load is little, the dates come out excellent. Since the grounds of the palm trees were good, their watering was abundant, and they were free from blight, the load grew heavy with the fineness of the grain.

The majority read (وتَنْحِتُونَ, and you carve) with a (ت, t) for address and a kasra on the (ح, h). Abu Haywa, 'Isa and al-Hasan read it with a fatha on it, which has been mentioned. From him (al-Hasan) there is also a (alif) after the (ح) for elongation. From 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad, from his father, with a (ي, y) from below and a kasra on the (ح). From Abu Haywa and al-Hasan also, with a (ي) from below and a fatha on the (ح). 'Abd Allah, Ibn 'Abbas, Zayd ibn 'Ali, the Kufans, and Ibn 'Amir read (فارِهِينَ, skillful) with an (alif). The rest of the seven read it without an (alif). Mujahid read (مُتَفَرِّهِينَ, exulting), an active participle from (تَفَرَّهَ). The meaning is: energetic, concerned. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: greedy. Ibn Zayd said: strong. Ibn 'Abbas also said, and Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala': insolent, haughty. 'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad said: meaning (mustafrihin), i.e., exaggerating in making the caves fine so that they might protect their wealth in them. Qatada said: secure. al-Kalbi said: tyrannical. Khusayf said: amazed by themselves. 'Ikrima said: comfortable. al-Dahhak said: clever. Abu Salih said: skilled. Ibn Bahr said: capable. Abu 'Ubayda said: exultant.

The apparent meaning of these verses is that the predominant characteristic of the people of Hud was imaginary pleasures: seeking elevation, permanence, exclusivity and tyranny; and of the people of Salih: sensory pleasures of food, drink and strong, good dwellings.

(And do not obey) is an address by the majority to his people. (The extravagant) are their great ones and leaders in disbelief and misguidance, and they were nine men.

(Who cause corruption in the land) means: in the land of Thamud. It was also said: in the whole land, because by their sins the rain was withheld. Since they "cause corruption," its implication is that of an unrestricted (absolute) statement, so He brought (and do not reform), negating reform from them. This is a negation of absolute reform, which necessarily entails the negation of reform in any form whatsoever, so no reform at all comes from them.

(Musahhar) is one who has been bewitched greatly until his intellect is overcome. It was also said: it derives from (sahr), which is the lung, meaning: you are a human who is not fit for prophethood. This view is weakened by their subsequent words, ﴿You are only a human like us﴾, since this sentence would then be an emphasis of what came before it, whereas the original purpose is to add new information (ta'sis). (Mithlana, like us) means: in eating, drinking and other human attributes, so you have no special status in prophethood.

(So bring a sign) means: a mark confirming the truth of your claim. In the speech there is an ellipsis, its estimate being: he said, "I will bring it." They said, "What is it?" (He said, "This is a she-camel…") It was narrated that they proposed to him a pregnant she-camel that would come out of this rock and give birth to a young camel. So Salih sat contemplating, and Gabriel, peace be upon him, said to him: "Pray two units of prayer and ask your Lord for the she-camel." He did so, and the she-camel came out and knelt before them, and gave birth to a young one like her in size. A portion of the story of Thamud and the she-camel has been mentioned in al-A'raf. The hamstringing is attributed to all of them, because they were all content with it, to the extent that it was narrated that they sought the consent of the woman in her curtain and of the children, and they all agreed.

(So they became regretful) — not the regret of repentance, but the regret of fear that the punishment would descend upon them quickly, and that occurs upon witnessing the punishment at a time when repentance no longer benefits. They became in the morning with their colours changed, just as Salih, peace be upon him, had told them. The punishment was a cry by which their bodies became still and their hearts split, and they all died to the last one, and stones were poured upon them in the midst of that. It was also said: their regret was over not having slain the young camel, but this is a distant view.

The (ال, al-) in (So the punishment seized them) is for a previously known punishment, the punishment of that tremendous day.

(Will you be left) — it is possible that this is a denial (inkar) that they would be left, abiding in their bliss, never departing from it; and it is possible that it is a reminder of the blessing in God's leaving them free and in the gardens and the other things they enjoy, together with security and ease. This was said by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is a warning to them, meaning: do you expect, if you are ungrateful for the blessings, that your sins will be overlooked? It was also said: (Will you be left?) is an interrogative in the sense of rebuke, i.e., will your Lord leave you? (In what is here) means: in what you are in this world (secure), not fearing His assault. End of quotation. Here, (ما) is a relative pronoun (mawsula), and (هاهنا, here) is an indication of the present, nearby place, i.e., in that which is settled in this place of yours of bliss. (Among gardens) is a substitute (badal) for (what is here): it first summarized and then detailed, just as Hud, peace be upon him, summarized in his words, ﴿He has provided you with what you know﴾ [al-Shu'ara 132], then detailed in his words, ﴿He has provided you with cattle and sons﴾ [al-Shu'ara 133]. The land of Thamud had many orchards, water and palm trees.

(Hadim, al-Hadim) — Ibn 'Abbas said: it is when it has ripened and reached its full development. al-Zuhri said: it is the fine, soft (spathe) as it first emerges. al-Zajjaj said: it is the one whose dates are without stones. al-Dahhak said: it is the one whose parts are piled upon one another. It was also said: the ripe dates that are tipped with a tail. It was said: the ripe dates that crumble. It was said: the spathe, and it approaches its skin from both sides, from their saying (khasr hadim), a slender waist. It was said: the hanging cluster. It was said: the soft pith of the palm heart.

The words (and palm trees) came after (among gardens), although the word "garden" first includes palm trees, and they use "garden" without meaning anything but palm trees, as the poet said:

"As if my two eyes, in the two sides of a barren and killed (she-camel) of the water-carriers, were watering a garden of tall palm trees."

Here he meant palm trees. (Suhuq) is the plural of (sahuq), which is the one whose trunk has gone up high and grown tall. So (palm trees) is singled out by mention after being included in the term (gardens), to alert to its distinction from the trees of the garden by its excellence. Or he meant by (gardens) trees other than palm trees, since the word allows for this sense; then he joined to it (palm trees). He reminded them, may He be exalted, that He had given them the finest and most ripened palm trees, because the female palms bear dates, and their spathe has fineness in it. (Hadim) means: fine and slender. (Al-Barni) is finer than the spathe of the (lawn) variety. It is possible that the fineness of the spathe is due to the abundance of its load, for whenever it is abundant it becomes fine and so is (hadim); and when the load is little, the dates come out excellent. Since the grounds of the palm trees were good, their watering was abundant, and they were free from blight, the load grew heavy with the fineness of the grain.

The majority read (وتَنْحِتُونَ, and you carve) with a (ت, t) for address and a kasra on the (ح, h). Abu Haywa, 'Isa and al-Hasan read it with a fatha on it, which has been mentioned. From him (al-Hasan) there is also a (alif) after the (ح) for elongation. From 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad, from his father, with a (ي, y) from below and a kasra on the (ح). From Abu Haywa and al-Hasan also, with a (ي) from below and a fatha on the (ح). 'Abd Allah, Ibn 'Abbas, Zayd ibn 'Ali, the Kufans, and Ibn 'Amir read (فارِهِينَ, skillful) with an (alif). The rest of the seven read it without an (alif). Mujahid read (مُتَفَرِّهِينَ, exulting), an active participle from (تَفَرَّهَ). The meaning is: energetic, concerned. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: greedy. Ibn Zayd said: strong. Ibn 'Abbas also said, and Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala': insolent, haughty. 'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad said: meaning (mustafrihin), i.e., exaggerating in making the caves fine so that they might protect their wealth in them. Qatada said: secure. al-Kalbi said: tyrannical. Khusayf said: amazed by themselves. 'Ikrima said: comfortable. al-Dahhak said: clever. Abu Salih said: skilled. Ibn Bahr said: capable. Abu 'Ubayda said: exultant.

The apparent meaning of these verses is that the predominant characteristic of the people of Hud was imaginary pleasures: seeking elevation, permanence, exclusivity and tyranny; and of the people of Salih: sensory pleasures of food, drink and strong, good dwellings.

(And do not obey) is an address by the majority to his people. (The extravagant) are their great ones and leaders in disbelief and misguidance, and they were nine men.

(Who cause corruption in the land) means: in the land of Thamud. It was also said: in the whole land, because by their sins the rain was withheld. Since they "cause corruption," its implication is that of an unrestricted (absolute) statement, so He brought (and do not reform), negating reform from them. This is a negation of absolute reform, which necessarily entails the negation of reform in any form whatsoever, so no reform at all comes from them.

(Musahhar) is one who has been bewitched greatly until his intellect is overcome. It was also said: it derives from (sahr), which is the lung, meaning: you are a human who is not fit for prophethood. This view is weakened by their subsequent words, ﴿You are only a human like us﴾, since this sentence would then be an emphasis of what came before it, whereas the original purpose is to add new information (ta'sis). (Mithlana, like us) means: in eating, drinking and other human attributes, so you have no special status in prophethood.

(So bring a sign) means: a mark confirming the truth of your claim. In the speech there is an ellipsis, its estimate being: he said, "I will bring it." They said, "What is it?" (He said, "This is a she-camel…") It was narrated that they proposed to him a pregnant she-camel that would come out of this rock and give birth to a young camel. So Salih sat contemplating, and Gabriel, peace be upon him, said to him: "Pray two units of prayer and ask your Lord for the she-camel." He did so, and the she-camel came out and knelt before them, and gave birth to a young one like her in size. A portion of the story of Thamud and the she-camel has been mentioned in al-A'raf. The hamstringing is attributed to all of them, because they were all content with it, to the extent that it was narrated that they sought the consent of the woman in her curtain and of the children, and they all agreed.

(So they became regretful) — not the regret of repentance, but the regret of fear that the punishment would descend upon them quickly, and that occurs upon witnessing the punishment at a time when repentance no longer benefits. They became in the morning with their colours changed, just as Salih, peace be upon him, had told them. The punishment was a cry by which their bodies became still and their hearts split, and they all died to the last one, and stones were poured upon them in the midst of that. It was also said: their regret was over not having slain the young camel, but this is a distant view.

The (ال, al-) in (So the punishment seized them) is for a previously known punishment, the punishment of that tremendous day.

(Will you be left) — it is possible that this is a denial (inkar) that they would be left, abiding in their bliss, never departing from it; and it is possible that it is a reminder of the blessing in God's leaving them free and in the gardens and the other things they enjoy, together with security and ease. This was said by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is a warning to them, meaning: do you expect, if you are ungrateful for the blessings, that your sins will be overlooked? It was also said: (Will you be left?) is an interrogative in the sense of rebuke, i.e., will your Lord leave you? (In what is here) means: in what you are in this world (secure), not fearing His assault. End of quotation. Here, (ما) is a relative pronoun (mawsula), and (هاهنا, here) is an indication of the present, nearby place, i.e., in that which is settled in this place of yours of bliss. (Among gardens) is a substitute (badal) for (what is here): it first summarized and then detailed, just as Hud, peace be upon him, summarized in his words, ﴿He has provided you with what you know﴾ [al-Shu'ara 132], then detailed in his words, ﴿He has provided you with cattle and sons﴾ [al-Shu'ara 133]. The land of Thamud had many orchards, water and palm trees.

(Hadim, al-Hadim) — Ibn 'Abbas said: it is when it has ripened and reached its full development. al-Zuhri said: it is the fine, soft (spathe) as it first emerges. al-Zajjaj said: it is the one whose dates are without stones. al-Dahhak said: it is the one whose parts are piled upon one another. It was also said: the ripe dates that are tipped with a tail. It was said: the ripe dates that crumble. It was said: the spathe, and it approaches its skin from both sides, from their saying (khasr hadim), a slender waist. It was said: the hanging cluster. It was said: the soft pith of the palm heart.

The words (and palm trees) came after (among gardens), although the word "garden" first includes palm trees, and they use "garden" without meaning anything but palm trees, as the poet said:

"As if my two eyes, in the two sides of a barren and killed (she-camel) of the water-carriers, were watering a garden of tall palm trees."

Here he meant palm trees. (Suhuq) is the plural of (sahuq), which is the one whose trunk has gone up high and grown tall. So (palm trees) is singled out by mention after being included in the term (gardens), to alert to its distinction from the trees of the garden by its excellence. Or he meant by (gardens) trees other than palm trees, since the word allows for this sense; then he joined to it (palm trees). He reminded them, may He be exalted, that He had given them the finest and most ripened palm trees, because the female palms bear dates, and their spathe has fineness in it. (Hadim) means: fine and slender. (Al-Barni) is finer than the spathe of the (lawn) variety. It is possible that the fineness of the spathe is due to the abundance of its load, for whenever it is abundant it becomes fine and so is (hadim); and when the load is little, the dates come out excellent. Since the grounds of the palm trees were good, their watering was abundant, and they were free from blight, the load grew heavy with the fineness of the grain.

The majority read (وتَنْحِتُونَ, and you carve) with a (ت, t) for address and a kasra on the (ح, h). Abu Haywa, 'Isa and al-Hasan read it with a fatha on it, which has been mentioned. From him (al-Hasan) there is also a (alif) after the (ح) for elongation. From 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad, from his father, with a (ي, y) from below and a kasra on the (ح). From Abu Haywa and al-Hasan also, with a (ي) from below and a fatha on the (ح). 'Abd Allah, Ibn 'Abbas, Zayd ibn 'Ali, the Kufans, and Ibn 'Amir read (فارِهِينَ, skillful) with an (alif). The rest of the seven read it without an (alif). Mujahid read (مُتَفَرِّهِينَ, exulting), an active participle from (تَفَرَّهَ). The meaning is: energetic, concerned. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: greedy. Ibn Zayd said: strong. Ibn 'Abbas also said, and Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala': insolent, haughty. 'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad said: meaning (mustafrihin), i.e., exaggerating in making the caves fine so that they might protect their wealth in them. Qatada said: secure. al-Kalbi said: tyrannical. Khusayf said: amazed by themselves. 'Ikrima said: comfortable. al-Dahhak said: clever. Abu Salih said: skilled. Ibn Bahr said: capable. Abu 'Ubayda said: exultant.

The apparent meaning of these verses is that the predominant characteristic of the people of Hud was imaginary pleasures: seeking elevation, permanence, exclusivity and tyranny; and of the people of Salih: sensory pleasures of food, drink and strong, good dwellings.

(And do not obey) is an address by the majority to his people. (The extravagant) are their great ones and leaders in disbelief and misguidance, and they were nine men.

(Who cause corruption in the land) means: in the land of Thamud. It was also said: in the whole land, because by their sins the rain was withheld. Since they "cause corruption," its implication is that of an unrestricted (absolute) statement, so He brought (and do not reform), negating reform from them. This is a negation of absolute reform, which necessarily entails the negation of reform in any form whatsoever, so no reform at all comes from them.

(Musahhar) is one who has been bewitched greatly until his intellect is overcome. It was also said: it derives from (sahr), which is the lung, meaning: you are a human who is not fit for prophethood. This view is weakened by their subsequent words, ﴿You are only a human like us﴾, since this sentence would then be an emphasis of what came before it, whereas the original purpose is to add new information (ta'sis). (Mithlana, like us) means: in eating, drinking and other human attributes, so you have no special status in prophethood.

(So bring a sign) means: a mark confirming the truth of your claim. In the speech there is an ellipsis, its estimate being: he said, "I will bring it." They said, "What is it?" (He said, "This is a she-camel…") It was narrated that they proposed to him a pregnant she-camel that would come out of this rock and give birth to a young camel. So Salih sat contemplating, and Gabriel, peace be upon him, said to him: "Pray two units of prayer and ask your Lord for the she-camel." He did so, and the she-camel came out and knelt before them, and gave birth to a young one like her in size. A portion of the story of Thamud and the she-camel has been mentioned in al-A'raf. The hamstringing is attributed to all of them, because they were all content with it, to the extent that it was narrated that they sought the consent of the woman in her curtain and of the children, and they all agreed.

(So they became regretful) — not the regret of repentance, but the regret of fear that the punishment would descend upon them quickly, and that occurs upon witnessing the punishment at a time when repentance no longer benefits. They became in the morning with their colours changed, just as Salih, peace be upon him, had told them. The punishment was a cry by which their bodies became still and their hearts split, and they all died to the last one, and stones were poured upon them in the midst of that. It was also said: their regret was over not having slain the young camel, but this is a distant view.

The (ال, al-) in (So the punishment seized them) is for a previously known punishment, the punishment of that tremendous day.
