(Will you be left) — it is possible that this is a denial (inkar) that they would be left, abiding in their bliss, never departing from it; and it is possible that it is a reminder of the blessing in God's leaving them free and in the gardens and the other things they enjoy, together with security and ease. This was said by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is a warning to them, meaning: do you expect, if you are ungrateful for the blessings, that your sins will be overlooked? It was also said: (Will you be left?) is an interrogative in the sense of rebuke, i.e., will your Lord leave you? (In what is here) means: in what you are in this world (secure), not fearing His assault. End of quotation. Here, (ما) is a relative pronoun (mawsula), and (هاهنا, here) is an indication of the present, nearby place, i.e., in that which is settled in this place of yours of bliss. (Among gardens) is a substitute (badal) for (what is here): it first summarized and then detailed, just as Hud, peace be upon him, summarized in his words, ﴿He has provided you with what you know﴾ [al-Shu'ara 132], then detailed in his words, ﴿He has provided you with cattle and sons﴾ [al-Shu'ara 133]. The land of Thamud had many orchards, water and palm trees.

(Hadim, al-Hadim) — Ibn 'Abbas said: it is when it has ripened and reached its full development. al-Zuhri said: it is the fine, soft (spathe) as it first emerges. al-Zajjaj said: it is the one whose dates are without stones. al-Dahhak said: it is the one whose parts are piled upon one another. It was also said: the ripe dates that are tipped with a tail. It was said: the ripe dates that crumble. It was said: the spathe, and it approaches its skin from both sides, from their saying (khasr hadim), a slender waist. It was said: the hanging cluster. It was said: the soft pith of the palm heart.

The words (and palm trees) came after (among gardens), although the word "garden" first includes palm trees, and they use "garden" without meaning anything but palm trees, as the poet said:

"As if my two eyes, in the two sides of a barren and killed (she-camel) of the water-carriers, were watering a garden of tall palm trees."

Here he meant palm trees. (Suhuq) is the plural of (sahuq), which is the one whose trunk has gone up high and grown tall. So (palm trees) is singled out by mention after being included in the term (gardens), to alert to its distinction from the trees of the garden by its excellence. Or he meant by (gardens) trees other than palm trees, since the word allows for this sense; then he joined to it (palm trees). He reminded them, may He be exalted, that He had given them the finest and most ripened palm trees, because the female palms bear dates, and their spathe has fineness in it. (Hadim) means: fine and slender. (Al-Barni) is finer than the spathe of the (lawn) variety. It is possible that the fineness of the spathe is due to the abundance of its load, for whenever it is abundant it becomes fine and so is (hadim); and when the load is little, the dates come out excellent. Since the grounds of the palm trees were good, their watering was abundant, and they were free from blight, the load grew heavy with the fineness of the grain.

The majority read (وتَنْحِتُونَ, and you carve) with a (ت, t) for address and a kasra on the (ح, h). Abu Haywa, 'Isa and al-Hasan read it with a fatha on it, which has been mentioned. From him (al-Hasan) there is also a (alif) after the (ح) for elongation. From 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad, from his father, with a (ي, y) from below and a kasra on the (ح). From Abu Haywa and al-Hasan also, with a (ي) from below and a fatha on the (ح). 'Abd Allah, Ibn 'Abbas, Zayd ibn 'Ali, the Kufans, and Ibn 'Amir read (فارِهِينَ, skillful) with an (alif). The rest of the seven read it without an (alif). Mujahid read (مُتَفَرِّهِينَ, exulting), an active participle from (تَفَرَّهَ). The meaning is: energetic, concerned. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: greedy. Ibn Zayd said: strong. Ibn 'Abbas also said, and Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala': insolent, haughty. 'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad said: meaning (mustafrihin), i.e., exaggerating in making the caves fine so that they might protect their wealth in them. Qatada said: secure. al-Kalbi said: tyrannical. Khusayf said: amazed by themselves. 'Ikrima said: comfortable. al-Dahhak said: clever. Abu Salih said: skilled. Ibn Bahr said: capable. Abu 'Ubayda said: exultant.

The apparent meaning of these verses is that the predominant characteristic of the people of Hud was imaginary pleasures: seeking elevation, permanence, exclusivity and tyranny; and of the people of Salih: sensory pleasures of food, drink and strong, good dwellings.

(And do not obey) is an address by the majority to his people. (The extravagant) are their great ones and leaders in disbelief and misguidance, and they were nine men.

(Who cause corruption in the land) means: in the land of Thamud. It was also said: in the whole land, because by their sins the rain was withheld. Since they "cause corruption," its implication is that of an unrestricted (absolute) statement, so He brought (and do not reform), negating reform from them. This is a negation of absolute reform, which necessarily entails the negation of reform in any form whatsoever, so no reform at all comes from them.

(Musahhar) is one who has been bewitched greatly until his intellect is overcome. It was also said: it derives from (sahr), which is the lung, meaning: you are a human who is not fit for prophethood. This view is weakened by their subsequent words, ﴿You are only a human like us﴾, since this sentence would then be an emphasis of what came before it, whereas the original purpose is to add new information (ta'sis). (Mithlana, like us) means: in eating, drinking and other human attributes, so you have no special status in prophethood.

(So bring a sign) means: a mark confirming the truth of your claim. In the speech there is an ellipsis, its estimate being: he said, "I will bring it." They said, "What is it?" (He said, "This is a she-camel…") It was narrated that they proposed to him a pregnant she-camel that would come out of this rock and give birth to a young camel. So Salih sat contemplating, and Gabriel, peace be upon him, said to him: "Pray two units of prayer and ask your Lord for the she-camel." He did so, and the she-camel came out and knelt before them, and gave birth to a young one like her in size. A portion of the story of Thamud and the she-camel has been mentioned in al-A'raf. The hamstringing is attributed to all of them, because they were all content with it, to the extent that it was narrated that they sought the consent of the woman in her curtain and of the children, and they all agreed.

(So they became regretful) — not the regret of repentance, but the regret of fear that the punishment would descend upon them quickly, and that occurs upon witnessing the punishment at a time when repentance no longer benefits. They became in the morning with their colours changed, just as Salih, peace be upon him, had told them. The punishment was a cry by which their bodies became still and their hearts split, and they all died to the last one, and stones were poured upon them in the midst of that. It was also said: their regret was over not having slain the young camel, but this is a distant view.

The (ال, al-) in (So the punishment seized them) is for a previously known punishment, the punishment of that tremendous day.

﴿Thamud denied the messengers.﴾ ﴿When their brother Salih said to them, "Will you not be mindful of God?"﴾ ﴿Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger.﴾ ﴿So be mindful of God and obey me.﴾ ﴿I ask you for no wage for it; my wage is only from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿Will you be left secure in what is here,﴾ ﴿among gardens and springs,﴾ ﴿and crops and palm trees whose spathes are soft?﴾ ﴿And you carve out homes from the mountains, skillfully.﴾ ﴿So be mindful of God and obey me.﴾ ﴿And do not obey the command of the extravagant,﴾ ﴿who cause corruption in the land and do not reform.﴾ ﴿They said, "You are only one of the bewitched.﴾ ﴿You are only a human like us, so bring a sign, if you are truthful."﴾ ﴿He said, "This is a she-camel; she has a share of water, and you have a share of water on a known day.﴾ ﴿Do not touch her with harm, lest the punishment of a tremendous day seize you."﴾ ﴿But they hamstrung her, and then they became regretful.﴾ ﴿So the punishment seized them. Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.﴾ ﴿And indeed, your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful.﴾

(Will you be left) — it is possible that this is a denial (inkar) that they would be left, abiding in their bliss, never departing from it; and it is possible that it is a reminder of the blessing in God's leaving them free and in the gardens and the other things they enjoy, together with security and ease. This was said by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is a warning to them, meaning: do you expect, if you are ungrateful for the blessings, that your sins will be overlooked? It was also said: (Will you be left?) is an interrogative in the sense of rebuke, i.e., will your Lord leave you? (In what is here) means: in what you are in this world (secure), not fearing His assault. End of quotation. Here, (ما) is a relative pronoun (mawsula), and (هاهنا, here) is an indication of the present, nearby place, i.e., in that which is settled in this place of yours of bliss. (Among gardens) is a substitute (badal) for (what is here): it first summarized and then detailed, just as Hud, peace be upon him, summarized in his words, ﴿He has provided you with what you know﴾ [al-Shu'ara 132], then detailed in his words, ﴿He has provided you with cattle and sons﴾ [al-Shu'ara 133]. The land of Thamud had many orchards, water and palm trees.

(Hadim, al-Hadim) — Ibn 'Abbas said: it is when it has ripened and reached its full development. al-Zuhri said: it is the fine, soft (spathe) as it first emerges. al-Zajjaj said: it is the one whose dates are without stones. al-Dahhak said: it is the one whose parts are piled upon one another. It was also said: the ripe dates that are tipped with a tail. It was said: the ripe dates that crumble. It was said: the spathe, and it approaches its skin from both sides, from their saying (khasr hadim), a slender waist. It was said: the hanging cluster. It was said: the soft pith of the palm heart.

The words (and palm trees) came after (among gardens), although the word "garden" first includes palm trees, and they use "garden" without meaning anything but palm trees, as the poet said:

"As if my two eyes, in the two sides of a barren and killed (she-camel) of the water-carriers, were watering a garden of tall palm trees."

Here he meant palm trees. (Suhuq) is the plural of (sahuq), which is the one whose trunk has gone up high and grown tall. So (palm trees) is singled out by mention after being included in the term (gardens), to alert to its distinction from the trees of the garden by its excellence. Or he meant by (gardens) trees other than palm trees, since the word allows for this sense; then he joined to it (palm trees). He reminded them, may He be exalted, that He had given them the finest and most ripened palm trees, because the female palms bear dates, and their spathe has fineness in it. (Hadim) means: fine and slender. (Al-Barni) is finer than the spathe of the (lawn) variety. It is possible that the fineness of the spathe is due to the abundance of its load, for whenever it is abundant it becomes fine and so is (hadim); and when the load is little, the dates come out excellent. Since the grounds of the palm trees were good, their watering was abundant, and they were free from blight, the load grew heavy with the fineness of the grain.

The majority read (وتَنْحِتُونَ, and you carve) with a (ت, t) for address and a kasra on the (ح, h). Abu Haywa, 'Isa and al-Hasan read it with a fatha on it, which has been mentioned. From him (al-Hasan) there is also a (alif) after the (ح) for elongation. From 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad, from his father, with a (ي, y) from below and a kasra on the (ح). From Abu Haywa and al-Hasan also, with a (ي) from below and a fatha on the (ح). 'Abd Allah, Ibn 'Abbas, Zayd ibn 'Ali, the Kufans, and Ibn 'Amir read (فارِهِينَ, skillful) with an (alif). The rest of the seven read it without an (alif). Mujahid read (مُتَفَرِّهِينَ, exulting), an active participle from (تَفَرَّهَ). The meaning is: energetic, concerned. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: greedy. Ibn Zayd said: strong. Ibn 'Abbas also said, and Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala': insolent, haughty. 'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad said: meaning (mustafrihin), i.e., exaggerating in making the caves fine so that they might protect their wealth in them. Qatada said: secure. al-Kalbi said: tyrannical. Khusayf said: amazed by themselves. 'Ikrima said: comfortable. al-Dahhak said: clever. Abu Salih said: skilled. Ibn Bahr said: capable. Abu 'Ubayda said: exultant.

The apparent meaning of these verses is that the predominant characteristic of the people of Hud was imaginary pleasures: seeking elevation, permanence, exclusivity and tyranny; and of the people of Salih: sensory pleasures of food, drink and strong, good dwellings.

(And do not obey) is an address by the majority to his people. (The extravagant) are their great ones and leaders in disbelief and misguidance, and they were nine men.

(Who cause corruption in the land) means: in the land of Thamud. It was also said: in the whole land, because by their sins the rain was withheld. Since they "cause corruption," its implication is that of an unrestricted (absolute) statement, so He brought (and do not reform), negating reform from them. This is a negation of absolute reform, which necessarily entails the negation of reform in any form whatsoever, so no reform at all comes from them.

(Musahhar) is one who has been bewitched greatly until his intellect is overcome. It was also said: it derives from (sahr), which is the lung, meaning: you are a human who is not fit for prophethood. This view is weakened by their subsequent words, ﴿You are only a human like us﴾, since this sentence would then be an emphasis of what came before it, whereas the original purpose is to add new information (ta'sis). (Mithlana, like us) means: in eating, drinking and other human attributes, so you have no special status in prophethood.

(So bring a sign) means: a mark confirming the truth of your claim. In the speech there is an ellipsis, its estimate being: he said, "I will bring it." They said, "What is it?" (He said, "This is a she-camel…") It was narrated that they proposed to him a pregnant she-camel that would come out of this rock and give birth to a young camel. So Salih sat contemplating, and Gabriel, peace be upon him, said to him: "Pray two units of prayer and ask your Lord for the she-camel." He did so, and the she-camel came out and knelt before them, and gave birth to a young one like her in size. A portion of the story of Thamud and the she-camel has been mentioned in al-A'raf. (Shirb) is the share of water drunk, similar to a watering. Ibn Abi 'Ablah read (شُرْبٌ) with a damma on the (ش) in both places. The apparent meaning of this punishment is that it was in this world, and so it occurred; and its description as tremendous is due to the punishment's descending upon them in it. Describing the day as tremendous is more emphatic than describing the punishment as such, because when the time becomes tremendous through the punishment, the impact of the punishment is greater in its magnitude. The hamstringing is attributed to all of them, because they were all content with it, to the extent that it was narrated that they sought the consent of the woman in her curtain and of the children, and they all agreed.

(So they became regretful) — not the regret of repentance, but the regret of fear that the punishment would descend upon them quickly, and that occurs upon witnessing the punishment at a time when repentance no longer benefits. They became in the morning with their colours changed, just as Salih, peace be upon him, had told them. The punishment was a cry by which their bodies became still and their hearts split, and they all died to the last one, and stones were poured upon them in the midst of that. It was also said: their regret was over not having slain the young camel, but this is a distant view.

The (ال, al-) in (So the punishment seized them) is for a previously known punishment, the punishment of that tremendous day.

(p-36) "Do you come to the males?" (ʾa-taʾtūna): an interrogative of denial, rebuke and reproach. (al-Dhukrān): the plural of *dhakar*, the opposite of *unthā* (female). The verb *al-ityān* (coming to) is a metonymy (kināya) for having intercourse with men. Allah, exalted is He, called it an abomination, saying: ﴿Do you commit an abomination such as no one in the worlds has done before you?﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 80]. The statement is specific to the males of the children of Adam. It has also been said that it is specific to strangers.

﴿And you leave what your Lord has created for you﴾ clearly indicates that they did not approach women, either absolutely or for the most part.

﴿What your Lord has created for you﴾ indicates permissibility, under its conditions.

﴿From your spouses﴾ means from the females. The word *min* (from) may be explanatory (lil-tabyīn), relating to His words ﴿what has been created﴾, or partitive (lil-tabʿīḍ), meaning the organ created for intercourse, which is the vagina. This is by omission of a noun, meaning "you leave the coming to". If "what has been created" does not refer to the organ, then another noun must be supplied, meaning "you leave the coming to the vagina of what has been created."

﴿Rather, you are a people transgressing﴾ means exceeding the limit in wrongdoing. The word *bal* (rather) here is an idrāb (a transition from one matter to another, a shift in topic), not a cancellation of the preceding denunciation of them and the condemnation of their deeds. Their transgression is either within the sins of which this sin is one, or in committing this shameful act itself. The sentence begins with the pronoun of address to magnify the ugliness of their deed and to alert that they alone are specific to it, as you say: "You did such and such," meaning, not anyone else. When he forbade them from this ugly act, they threatened him with expulsion, which is banishment from his land where he grew up, meaning: ﴿If you do not desist﴾ from your claim of prophethood and from denouncing us for what we do with males, ﴿you will surely be among those expelled﴾, as we expelled those who forbade us before you. His words ﴿among those expelled﴾ indicate that there were people who had forbidden them from this before, and they expelled them because of that prohibition. Or it means "among those expelled for a reason other than this reason," as if he opposed them in something, and they expelled him, whether the disagreement concerned this particular act or something else.

﴿He said: Indeed I am, for your deed﴾, meaning for the abomination that you are doing. The phrase *li-ʿamalikum* (for your deed) relates either to *al-qālīn* (those who detest), even though *al-* is attached to it, because prepositional phrases and adverbial expressions permit what other words do not, due to the Arabs' latitude in placing them first, where nothing else may come first. Or it is governed by an omitted verb indicated by *al-qālīn*, its estimated form being "Indeed I am one who detests for your deed." Or the *lam* may be explanatory, meaning "for your deed, I mean, from those who detest." That he is part of "those who detest" indicates that others besides him detest this deed, and that this points out that this deed necessitates hatred, so that people hate it. "Among those who detest" is more emphatic than "one who detests," for the reason we mentioned, that people hate him, and because it implies that he is counted among those who hate it. Do you not see that your saying "Zayd is among the scholars" is more emphatic than "Zayd is a scholar," because that testifies that he is counted in their company? Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Rāzī said: *al-qalyu* is intense hatred, as if he hated and so abhorred the heart and liver. End of quote. *Qalā* does not mean *abghaḍa* (to hate). *Qalā* from cooking and *shayy* (roasting) come from one root with differing structure. So the root *qalā* from roasting is of the *wāw* type, and you say: *qalawtu al-laḥm*, so it is *maqlūw*. The root *qalā* from hatred is of the *yāʾ* type: *qalaytu al-rajul*, so he is *maqlīy*. The poet said:

*"I am not one hated for my qualities, nor one who hates."*

When they threatened him with expulsion, he informed them of the hatred of their deed, then he called upon his Lord, saying: ﴿My Lord, save me and my family from what they do﴾, meaning from the punishment for the sins they commit. It is possible that this was a supplication for his family to be protected from falling into a deed like that of his people. His supplication for his family to be saved indicates that they were believers. Since his wife was included among the family, and the apparent meaning of his supplication was that she was included in the salvation, and since she was an unbeliever, she was excepted in His words: ﴿So We saved him and his family, all of them, except an old woman among those who remained behind﴾. His words "an old woman" indicate that she had persisted in disbelief and remained in it until she became old. "Among those who remained behind" is a qualifier, meaning among those remaining from her contemporaries and the people of her household, as Abū ʿUbayda said. (p-37) Qatāda said: among those who remained behind in the punishment descending upon them. The discussion of *ghabara* has preceded, and that it is used in the sense of "remained" (this is the well-known meaning) and in the sense of "passed away." Peace be upon him, his salvation was that Allah, exalted is He, commanded him to travel by night, and his wife was an unbeliever who helped his people against him, so a stone struck her and she perished among those who perished. Qatāda said: Allah rained down stones from the sky upon the wicked of the people and destroyed them. Qatāda also said: The overturning was followed by a rain of stones. *Sāʾa* is in the sense of *biʾsa* (how wretched), and the object of blame is omitted, meaning "their rain." Muqātil said: Allah caused the earth to swallow the people of Lot, and sent stones upon whoever was outside the town, and there was no believer in it except the house of Lot.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 26, verses 176–182:**

﴿The people of al-Aykah denied the messengers. When Shu'ayb said to them, "Will you not be mindful of God? I am a trustworthy messenger to you. So be mindful of God and obey me. I do not ask you any wage for it; my wage is only from the Lord of the worlds. Give full measure, and do not be among those who cause loss. Weigh with a straight balance. Do not diminish people's goods, and do not commit corruption on the earth, causing mischief. Be mindful of Him who created you and the earlier generations." They said, "You are only one of the bewitched. You are only a human like us, and we think you are surely among the liars. So make pieces of the sky fall upon us, if you are among the truthful." They, and the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, share this, and what he brought is what the messengers before him brought, and this is the custom of the prophets.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: The wording in the call of each of these prophets came out identical, since the faith to which they called is one and the same meaning. Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): Why did He repeat in this surah, at the beginning and end of each story, what He repeated? (I answer): Each story in it is like a revelation in its own right, and in it is the same lesson as in the others. Therefore each one conveys a truth, until it begins with the same words with which its counterpart began, and ends with the same words with which its counterpart ended. Moreover, repetition establishes meanings in souls and fixes them in hearts. And since these stories reached ears that were deaf to listening to the truth, and hearts that were closed to reflecting on it, they were given preference through admonition and reminder, and returned to through repetition and reiteration.

[p. 40]

In this view, the sending down of it in Arabic, which is your tongue and the tongue of your people, is a sending down upon your heart, because you understand it and your people understand it. Had it been in a foreign tongue, it would have descended upon your hearing rather than your heart, because you would hear the chimes of letters whose meanings you do not understand or retain. A man may know several languages, and when he is addressed in the language he was first taught, grew up with, and was accustomed to, his heart goes only to the meanings of those words, which he receives with his heart, and he hardly notices how the words were uttered. But if he is addressed in another language, even if he is skilled in it, his attention goes first to its words and then to their meanings. This is the explanation that it descended upon his heart by its descending in a clear Arabic tongue. End of quote. In it there is some length.

It was also said that the pronoun refers to the Messenger of God ﷺ, meaning that his mention and his mission are in the earlier divine books. This would be an iltifat (a shift of grammatical person), since it moves from the second-person pronoun in "upon your heart, that you may be" to the third-person pronoun. The same was said regarding *an yu'lima-hu* ("that it be made known to him"), meaning that it be made known to Muhammad ﷺ, and the consistency of pronouns referring to one thing is clearer. Al-A'mash recited *la-fi zubri* with a sukun on the *ba'*, while the original is with a *damma*. Then He argued against them that the knowledge of the scholars of the Children of Israel of it should have established its authenticity for them. That is, "Was it not a sign for them that the scholars of the Children of Israel knew it?" Many Arabs had become Jews, and many had become Christians, because of their belief in the truth of those religions. So the verse was revealed about that, and what supports this is that the verse is Meccan. Muqatil said: it is Medinan.

This is because a group of them embraced Islam and pointed out places in the Torah and the Gospel in which the Messenger, peace be upon him, was mentioned. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when it is recited to them they say, "We believe in it; indeed it is the truth from our Lord"﴾ [al-Qasas: 53], and so on. It was said: their scholars are those among them who embraced Islam and those who did not. It was said: their prophets, since they pointed to him and reported his attributes, time, and place. The majority read *awa-lam yakun* ("Was it not") with the yaa' below, and *ayatan* ("a sign") in the accusative. This reading is clear in its grammatical construction: the predicate of *yakun* is placed in the middle, and *an ya'lamahu* ("that they know it") is the subject. Ibn 'Amir and al-Jahdari read *takun* with the taa' above, and *ayatun* in the nominative. Al-Zamakhshari said: *ayatun* was made the subject and *an ya'lamahu* the predicate, and it is not like the first, because an indefinite noun is the subject and a definite noun the predicate. Another analysis has been offered to avoid this: it is said that in *takun* there is the pronoun of the matter (*damir al-qissa*), and "*ayatan an ya'lamahu*" is a clause occupying the place of the predicate; it is also permissible on this view that "*lahum ayatan*" be the clause of the matter, and "*an ya'lamahu*" be a substitute for "*ayatan*." End of quote. Ibn 'Abbas read *takun* with the taa' above and *ayatan* in the accusative, like the reading of one who read: "*thumma lam takun fitnatahum*" ("then their trial was not") [al-An'am: 23] with the accusative, except that they said, "*illa an qalu*." And like the verse of Labid:

*fa-madha wa-qaddamaha wa-kanat 'adatan*
*minhu idha hiya 'arradat aqdamuha*

He went forth and advanced it, and it was his custom
that when it turned aside, he advanced upon it.

This indicates either the feminine of the noun because of the feminine of the predicate, or the interpretation of *an ya'lamahu* as a definite knowing, and the interpretation of *illa an qalu* as "the saying," and the interpretation of *al-iqdam* as "the advance." Al-Jahdari read *an ta'lamahu* with the feminine taa', as the poet said:

*qalat Banu 'Amirin khalu Banu Asadin*
*ya bu'sa lil-jahli darran li-aqwami*

The Banu 'Amir said: "Leave the Banu Asad,
Alas for ignorance, a harm to the people!"

It was written in the Mushaf (the codex) as *'ulamau*, with a waw between the *mim* and the *alif*. It was said: this follows the dialect of those who incline the *alif* of *'ulamau* toward the waw, just as they wrote *al-salawata*, *al-zakawata*, and *al-ribawa* in that dialect. Al-Zamakhshari said: the *a'jami* is the one who is not eloquent and has a barbarism and incoherence in his speech; the *a'jami* is like him, except that the addition of the *ya'* of relation gives it an additional emphasis. Ibn 'Atiyya said: *al-a'jamun* is the plural of *a'jam*, which is one who is not eloquent, even if he is of Arab lineage, and it is said of him *a'jam*. This is also said of animals and inanimate things, and from it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The wound of the dumb animal is unrequited." Al-Tabari transmitted from 'Abdullah ibn Mut'i that when he recited this verse while standing at 'Arafat, he said: "This my camel is a dumb animal; had it been revealed to it, it would not have believed." And the *'ajami* is the one whose lineage is among the non-Arabs, even if he is the most eloquent of people. End of quote. In al-Tahrir: *al-a'jamin* is the plural of *a'jam* with a lightening of the form; were it not for this estimation, it would not be permissible to form the sound masculine plural from it. It was said: the meaning is that if We had sent it down in the language of non-Arabs upon a non-Arab man who then recited it to the Arabs, they would not have believed in it, since they would not have understood it, and they would have disdained following it. It was also said: if We had sent the Qur'an down upon some of the non-Arab animals, and he recited it to them, they would not have believed, because of their obstinacy toward His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And even if We had sent down to them the angels﴾ [al-An'am: 111], and so on. The sound plural was used because it was described by being sent down upon it and by recitation, and these are actions of rational beings. It was also said: if it had been sent down upon some of the beasts, and Muhammad ﷺ recited it to them, the beasts would not have believed, and likewise these people, because they are ﴿like livestock; rather, they are further astray in way﴾ [al-Furqan: 44]. End of quote.

When He had explained by what came before, that this Qur'an is in the books of the ancients and that the scholars of the Children of Israel know it, and that in this there are two proofs of the truth of the prophethood of the Messenger of God ﷺ, He made clear that proofs are of no benefit to these disbelievers. Do you not see that it was sent down upon an Arab man in a clear Arabic tongue, and they heard it and understood it and perceived its inimitability and the confirmation of the earlier books of God for it, and despite all that they denied it, and called him at times a poet and at times a sorcerer? Had it been sent down upon one of the non-Arabs who does not speak Arabic well, they would have disbelieved in it and contrived to deny it. Al-Farra' said: *al-a'jamin* is the plural of *a'jam* or *a'jami*, with the *ya'* of relation omitted, just as they said *al-ash'arin*, and its singular is *ash'ari*. Ibn al-Jahm said: al-Kumayt said:

*wa-law jahhaztu qafiyatan sharudan*
*laqad dakhalat buyuta al-Ash'arina*

Had I equipped a wandering rhyme,
it would have entered the houses of the Ash'arites.

End of quote. Al-Hasan and Ibn Miqsam read *al-a'jamiyyin* with the *ya'* of relation, as the plural of *a'jami*. The pronoun in *salaknahu* ("We caused it to enter") apparently refers to what the pronouns before it referred to. It was said: it is the Qur'an, as al-Rummani said. The meaning: like that insertion, which is the causing to enter, the making firm, and the making understood of its meanings.

*Salaknahu* ("We caused it to enter"): We made it enter and established it in *qulubi al-mujrimin* ("the hearts of the criminals"). The meaning is: what followed from that insertion, namely that they understood it and perceived it, yet it increased them only in obstinacy, denial, and disbelief in it. That is, in this very state and this very attribute of disbelief in it and denial of it, just as We placed it therein. How then could their belief in it be expected? It did not change, and their blindness to it through denial and rejection remained, as He said: ﴿And even if We had sent down to you a book upon parchment﴾ [al-An'am: 7], and so on. Al-Kirmani said: We caused it to enter therein, so they knew its meanings and their inability to produce its like, yet they did not believe in it. Yahya ibn Salam said: the pronoun in *salaknahu* refers to denial, and that is what prevented them from believing. End of quote. This is strengthened by His words: ﴿so he recited it to them, and they were not believers in it﴾. Al-Hasan said: the pronoun refers to the disbelief implied by His words: ﴿they were not believers in it﴾. End of quote. This is close to the view before it. 'Ikrimah said: *salaknahu*, that is, the hardness of heart, and God, exalted is He, is the one to whom the causing to enter is attributed, because He is the one who truly brings things into existence, the Guide, and the Creator of misguidance.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 26, verse 192–204 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): How did he attribute the threading (al-salk) together with the quality of denial to Himself? (I answer): He intended by it to indicate that the denial was firmly established in their hearts with the strongest and most lasting establishment, so He made it like a matter to which they had been created disposed. Do you not see their saying: "He is disposed to stinginess" (majbul 'ala al-shuhh)? They mean that stinginess is firmly rooted in him, because innate matters are more firmly established than acquired ones. The evidence for this is that He attributed the not-believing in it to them directly after it, which is His saying: ﴿they do not believe﴾ in it. End of quote. This is according to the path of the Mu'tazilites, and the comparison between the two threadings (salk) requires a difference in the one upon whom it descends. The meaning: like that threading in the hearts of the Quraysh, We threaded it in the hearts of those who committed crime, because the two share the cause of threading, which is criminality. Ibn 'Atiyya said: He intended by them the criminals of every nation, meaning that this is God's custom with them: they do not believe until they see the punishment, so faith does not benefit them after the punishment has befallen them. This is by way of example for the Quraysh, meaning: these are likewise. The unveiling of the unseen by what this verse includes is on the Day of Badr.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): What is the position of ﴿they do not believe in it﴾ from His saying ﴿We threaded it in the hearts of the criminals﴾? (I answer): Its position relative to it is the position of clarification and summary, because it is brought for its firm establishment, denied and rejected in their hearts, so it is followed by what confirms this meaning, that they will not cease to deny it and reject it until they witness the threat. It may also be a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: We threaded it in them while not believing in it. End of quote. As for their seeing the punishment, it was said: in this world; and it was said: on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Jumhur read ﴿fa-ya'tiyahum﴾ with a yā' (ya), meaning: the punishment. Al-Hasan and 'Isa read it with the feminine tā' (ta), making it feminine in accordance with the meaning of "punishment," because it is the retribution, meaning: so the retribution will come to them on the Day of Resurrection, as in the saying: "It came to him, my book," when he was asked, he said: "Is it not a written document?" Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿fa-ta'tiyahum﴾ with the tā', meaning the Hour. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: He made the punishment feminine because it includes the Hour, so it took on the feminine from it, because they used to ask for the punishment of the Resurrection as a denial of it, so it was made feminine for this reason. The masculine does not take the feminine marker unless it is a genitive attached to it, as in: "the people of al-Yamama gathered," "some of his fingers were cut off," and "the chest of the spear-shaft was split," but this is not the case here. Al-Hasan read "baghtatan" with a fatha on the ghayn, and "fa-ta'tiyahum" with the tā' from above, meaning the Hour.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): What is the meaning of the sequence (ta'qib) in His saying ﴿fa-ta'tiyahum bi-ayatin﴾ [al-An'am: 35]? (I answer): The meaning is not that what is intended by seeing the punishment, its sudden arrival, and their request for a respite is their existence simultaneously, but rather the meaning is their ordering in severity, as if it were said: they do not believe in the Qur'an until their seeing the punishment is something more severe than it, namely its overtaking them suddenly, which is more severe than it, namely their asking for a respite. Similar to this is your saying: "If you do evil, the righteous will despise you, so God will despise you," for you do not intend by this ordering that God's contempt occurs right after the contempt of the righteous, but you intend the ordering of the severity of the matter upon the evildoer, and that there results for him, because of the evil, the contempt of the righteous. What is more severe than their contempt? It is the contempt of God. This is seen, and then this occurs in this style, and it takes its place. End of quote. ﴿They will say﴾, that is, every punished nation: ﴿Will we be given respite?﴾, that is, be delayed. This is by way of their wishing and desiring, where desire is of no benefit. Then the wording of the verse returned to rebuking the Quraysh for their haste in seeking God's punishment, in their request for the fall of the sky in pieces and other things, and their saying to the Messenger: "Where is what you promise us?"

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Is it then Our punishment they seek to hasten?﴾ is a rebuke to them through its denial, and a mockery. Its meaning: how can one who is exposed to a punishment, in which he asks, of the same kind as what he is in today, the respite of a blink of an eye, and is not granted it, seek to hasten the punishment? It may be that this is a narration of rebuke, by which they are rebuked when they seek respite on that day, and they hasten this matter in the manner of a narration of a past state. Another aspect connects it to what follows: their haste for the punishment was either because they believed it would not occur and would not befall them, and that they would enjoy long lives in safety and security. So He, Mighty and Exalted, said: ﴿Is it then Our punishment they seek to hasten?﴾ Out of insolence, arrogance, mockery, and reliance on long hope? Then He said: Suppose the matter is as they believe of their enjoyment and long life; when the threat overtakes them after that, what will the long span of their lives and the goodness of their livelihood avail them then? End of quote. It was said: He followed His saying "so it will come to them suddenly" with what will be from them at that time in the manner of regret.

﴿They will say: Will we be given respite?﴾ as a man cries out for it when salvation is impossible, for they know in the Hereafter that there is no refuge, but they say that seeking relief. It was said: they seek a return when the punishment of the Hour suddenly seizes them, but they are not answered in it.

It was said: this follows the dialect of those who incline the *alif* of *'ulamau* toward the waw, just as they wrote *al-salawata*, *al-zakawata*, and *al-ribawa* in that dialect. Al-Zamakhshari said: the *a'jami* is the one who is not eloquent and has a barbarism and incoherence in his speech; the *a'jami* is like him, except that the addition of the *ya'* of relation gives it an additional emphasis. Ibn 'Atiyya said: *al-a'jamun* is the plural of *a'jam*, which is one who is not eloquent, even if he is of Arab lineage, and it is said of him *a'jam*. This is also said of animals and inanimate things, and from it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The wound of the dumb animal is unrequited." Al-Tabari transmitted from 'Abdullah ibn Mut'i that when he recited this verse while standing at 'Arafat, he said: "This my camel is a dumb animal; had it been revealed to it, it would not have believed." And the *'ajami* is the one whose lineage is among the non-Arabs, even if he is the most eloquent of people. End of quote. In al-Tahrir: *al-a'jamin* is the plural of *a'jam* with a lightening of the form; were it not for this estimation, it would not be permissible to form the sound masculine plural from it. It was said: the meaning is that if We had sent it down in the language of non-Arabs upon a non-Arab man who then recited it to the Arabs, they would not have believed in it, since they would not have understood it, and they would have disdained following it. It was also said: if We had sent the Qur'an down upon some of the non-Arab animals, and he recited it to them, they would not have believed, because of their obstinacy toward His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And even if We had sent down to them the angels﴾ [al-An'am: 111], and so on. End of quote.

When He had explained by what came before, that this Qur'an is in the books of the ancients and that the scholars of the Children of Israel know it, and that in this there are two proofs of the truth of the prophethood of the Messenger of God ﷺ, He made clear that proofs are of no benefit to these disbelievers. Do you not see that it was sent down upon an Arab man in a clear Arabic tongue, and they heard it and understood it and perceived its inimitability and the confirmation of the earlier books of God for it, and despite all that they denied it, and called him at times a poet and at times a sorcerer? Had it been sent down upon one of the non-Arabs who does not speak Arabic well, they would have disbelieved in it and contrived to deny it. *wa-law jahhaztu qafiyatan sharudan*
*laqad dakhalat buyuta al-Ash'arina*

Had I equipped a wandering rhyme,
it would have entered the houses of the Ash'arites.

End of quote. Al-Hasan and Ibn Miqsam read *al-a'jamiyyin* with the *ya'* of relation, as the plural of *a'jami*. *Salaknahu* ("We caused it to enter"): We made it enter and established it in *qulubi al-mujrimin* ("the hearts of the criminals"). The meaning is: what followed from that insertion, namely that they understood it and perceived it, yet it increased them only in obstinacy, denial, and disbelief in it. That is, in this very state and this very attribute of disbelief in it and denial of it, just as We placed it therein. How then could their belief in it be expected? It did not change, and their blindness to it through denial and rejection remained, as He said: ﴿And even if We had sent down to you a book upon parchment﴾ [al-An'am: 7], and so on. Al-Kirmani said: We caused it to enter therein, so they knew its meanings and their inability to produce its like, yet they did not believe in it. Yahya ibn Salam said: the pronoun in *salaknahu* refers to denial, and that is what prevented them from believing. End of quote. This is strengthened by His words: ﴿so he recited it to them, and they were not believers in it﴾. Al-Hasan said: the pronoun refers to the disbelief implied by His words: ﴿they were not believers in it﴾. End of quote. This is close to the view before it. 'Ikrimah said: *salaknahu*, that is, the hardness of heart, and God, exalted is He, is the one to whom the causing to enter is attributed, because He is the one who truly brings things into existence, the Guide, and the Creator of misguidance.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 26, verse 192–204 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): How did he attribute the threading (al-salk) together with the quality of denial to Himself? (I answer): He intended by it to indicate that the denial was firmly established in their hearts with the strongest and most lasting establishment, so He made it like a matter to which they had been created disposed. Do you not see their saying: "He is disposed to stinginess" (majbul 'ala al-shuhh)? They mean that stinginess is firmly rooted in him, because innate matters are more firmly established than acquired ones. The evidence for this is that He attributed the not-believing in it to them directly after it, which is His saying: ﴿they do not believe﴾ in it. End of quote. This is according to the path of the Mu'tazilites, and the comparison between the two threadings (salk) requires a difference in the one upon whom it descends. The meaning: like that threading in the hearts of the Quraysh, We threaded it in the hearts of those who committed crime, because the two share the cause of threading, which is criminality. Ibn 'Atiyya said: He intended by them the criminals of every nation, meaning that this is God's custom with them: they do not believe until they see the punishment, so faith does not benefit them after the punishment has befallen them. This is by way of example for the Quraysh, meaning: these are likewise. The unveiling of the unseen by what this verse includes is on the Day of Badr.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): What is the position of ﴿they do not believe in it﴾ from His saying ﴿We threaded it in the hearts of the criminals﴾? (I answer): Its position relative to it is the position of clarification and summary, because it is brought for its firm establishment, denied and rejected in their hearts, so it is followed by what confirms this meaning, that they will not cease to deny it and reject it until they witness the threat. It may also be a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: We threaded it in them while not believing in it. End of quote. As for their seeing the punishment, it was said: in this world; and it was said: on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Jumhur read ﴿fa-ya'tiyahum﴾ with a yā' (ya), meaning: the punishment. Al-Hasan and 'Isa read it with the feminine tā' (ta), making it feminine in accordance with the meaning of "punishment," because it is the retribution, meaning: so the retribution will come to them on the Day of Resurrection, as in the saying: "It came to him, my book," when he was asked, he said: "Is it not a written document?" Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿fa-ta'tiyahum﴾ with the tā', meaning the Hour. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: He made the punishment feminine because it includes the Hour, so it took on the feminine from it, because they used to ask for the punishment of the Resurrection as a denial of it, so it was made feminine for this reason. The masculine does not take the feminine marker unless it is a genitive attached to it, as in: "the people of al-Yamama gathered," "some of his fingers were cut off," and "the chest of the spear-shaft was split," but this is not the case here. Al-Hasan read "baghtatan" with a fatha on the ghayn, and "fa-ta'tiyahum" with the tā' from above, meaning the Hour.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): What is the meaning of the sequence (ta'qib) in His saying ﴿fa-ta'tiyahum bi-ayatin﴾ [al-An'am: 35]? (I answer): The meaning is not that what is intended by seeing the punishment, its sudden arrival, and their request for a respite is their existence simultaneously, but rather the meaning is their ordering in severity, as if it were said: they do not believe in the Qur'an until their seeing the punishment is something more severe than it, namely its overtaking them suddenly, which is more severe than it, namely their asking for a respite. Similar to this is your saying: "If you do evil, the righteous will despise you, so God will despise you," for you do not intend by this ordering that God's contempt occurs right after the contempt of the righteous, but you intend the ordering of the severity of the matter upon the evildoer, and that there results for him, because of the evil, the contempt of the righteous. What is more severe than their contempt? It is the contempt of God. This is seen, and then this occurs in this style, and it takes its place. End of quote. ﴿They will say﴾, that is, every punished nation: ﴿Will we be given respite?﴾, that is, be delayed. This is by way of their wishing and desiring, where desire is of no benefit. Then the wording of the verse returned to rebuking the Quraysh for their haste in seeking God's punishment, in their request for the fall of the sky in pieces and other things, and their saying to the Messenger: "Where is what you promise us?"

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Is it then Our punishment they seek to hasten?﴾ is a rebuke to them through its denial, and a mockery. Its meaning: how can one who is exposed to a punishment, in which he asks, of the same kind as what he is in today, the respite of a blink of an eye, and is not granted it, seek to hasten the punishment? It may be that this is a narration of rebuke, by which they are rebuked when they seek respite on that day, and they hasten this matter in the manner of a narration of a past state. Another aspect connects it to what follows: their haste for the punishment was either because they believed it would not occur and would not befall them, and that they would enjoy long lives in safety and security. So He, Mighty and Exalted, said: ﴿Is it then Our punishment they seek to hasten?﴾ Out of insolence, arrogance, mockery, and reliance on long hope? Then He said: Suppose the matter is as they believe of their enjoyment and long life; when the threat overtakes them after that, what will the long span of their lives and the goodness of their livelihood avail them then? End of quote. It was said: He followed His saying "so it will come to them suddenly" with what will be from them at that time in the manner of regret.

﴿They will say: Will we be given respite?﴾ as a man cries out for it when salvation is impossible, for they know in the Hereafter that there is no refuge, but they say that seeking relief. It was said: they seek a return when the punishment of the Hour suddenly seizes them, but they are not answered in it.

[p. 40]

The pronoun in "wa-innahu" ("and indeed it") refers to the Qur'an, meaning that it is neither soothsaying nor sorcery but is from God. It seems also to refer back to what the surah opened with, namely the disbelievers' turning away from the reminder that comes to them, so that the beginning and the end of the surah correspond. Ibn 'Amir... no. The two Harams (Ibn Kathir and Nafi') [not transliterated], Abu 'Amr, and Hafs recited *nazala* (he sent down) with light stress, and *al-Ruhu al-Amin* (the Trustworthy Spirit) in the nominative. The rest of the seven readers (qira'at, the canonical recitations) read it with the doubled *zay* (*nazzala*, with emphasis) and the accusative for both. Here *al-Ruh* (the Spirit) means Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him, and the reason he is called "the Spirit" has already been explained in the surah of Maryam. Ibn 'Atiyya said, in the sense of a circumstantial clause (hal), like God's words: ﴿And they entered with disbelief, and they had gone out with it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 61]. End of quote.

The apparent meaning is that *'ala qalbika* ("upon your heart") and *li-takuna* ("that you may be") are connected to *nazala*. He specified the heart, and the meaning is "upon you," because it is the place of understanding and steadfastness, and so that it be known that what is sent down upon his heart, peace be upon him, is preserved and cannot be subject to alteration or change. It is also a cause of the sending down or the descent, and he restricted himself to this, because that is more effective in restraining the listener, even though the Qur'an was sent down for warning and for giving good tidings. The apparent meaning is that *bi-lisanin* ("in a tongue") is connected to *nazala*, so he would hear from Jibril letters in Arabic. Ibn 'Atiyya said, and this is the correct view: the "sound of a bell" (*salsalat al-jaras*) is a description of the intensity of the voice, the overlapping of its letters, the speed of its arrival and its harshness. It is possible to connect it to *li-takuna*, and whoever holds that the Prophet ﷺ sometimes heard something like the sound of a bell, from which the Qur'an was understood, relies on this, but it is rejected. End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari said: *bi-lisanin* either connects to *al-mundhirin* ("the warners"), so the meaning is: "that you may be among those who warned with this tongue," and they were five: Hud, Salih, Shu'ayb, Isma'il, and Muhammad ﷺ, and upon them [be peace]. Or it connects to *nazala*, so the meaning is: He sent it down in the clear Arabic tongue so that you might warn by it, because if He had sent it down in a non-Arabic tongue, they would have turned away from it entirely and said, "What shall we do with what we do not understand?" and the warning by it would have been impossible. In this view, the sending down of it in Arabic, which is your tongue and the tongue of your people, is a sending down upon your heart, because you understand it and your people understand it. Had it been in a foreign tongue, it would have descended upon your hearing rather than your heart, because you would hear the chimes of letters whose meanings you do not understand or retain. A man may know several languages, and when he is addressed in the language he was first taught, grew up with, and was accustomed to, his heart goes only to the meanings of those words, which he receives with his heart, and he hardly notices how the words were uttered. But if he is addressed in another language, even if he is skilled in it, his attention goes first to its words and then to their meanings. This is the explanation that it descended upon his heart by its descending in a clear Arabic tongue. End of quote. In it there is some length.

*Wa-innahu* ("and indeed it"), that is, the Qur'an, *la-fi zuburi al-awwalin* ("is in the scriptures of the ancients"): that is, it is mentioned in the earlier revealed books, indicated and pointed out. It was said that its meanings are in them, and by this Abu Hanifa is cited for permitting recitation in Persian in prayer, on the basis that the Qur'an remains Qur'an even when translated into a language other than Arabic, since it was said, "and indeed it is in the scriptures of the ancients," because its meanings are in them. It was also said that the pronoun refers to the Messenger of God ﷺ, meaning that his mention and his mission are in the earlier divine books. This would be an iltifat (a shift of grammatical person), since it moves from the second-person pronoun in "upon your heart, that you may be" to the third-person pronoun. The same was said regarding *an yu'lima-hu* ("that it be made known to him"), meaning that it be made known to Muhammad ﷺ, and the consistency of pronouns referring to one thing is clearer. Al-A'mash recited *la-fi zubri* with a sukun on the *ba'*, while the original is with a *damma*. Then He argued against them that the knowledge of the scholars of the Children of Israel of it should have established its authenticity for them. Many Arabs had become Jews, and many had become Christians, because of their belief in the truth of those religions. Al-Tha'labi reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the people of Makkah sent to the rabbis of Yathrib asking them about the Prophet ﷺ, and they said, "This is his time," and described his attributes, and they confused matters concerning Muhammad, peace be upon him. So the verse was revealed about that, and what supports this is that the verse is Meccan. Muqatil said: it is Medinan.

This is because a group of them embraced Islam and pointed out places in the Torah and the Gospel in which the Messenger, peace be upon him, was mentioned. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when it is recited to them they say, "We believe in it; indeed it is the truth from our Lord"﴾ [al-Qasas: 53], and so on. This reading is clear in its grammatical construction: the predicate of *yakun* is placed in the middle, and *an ya'lamahu* ("that they know it") is the subject. Ibn 'Amir and al-Jahdari read *takun* with the taa' above, and *ayatun* in the nominative. *fa-madha wa-qaddamaha wa-kanat 'adatan*
*minhu idha hiya 'arradat aqdamuha*

He went forth and advanced it, and it was his custom
that when it turned aside, he advanced upon it.

*qalat Banu 'Amirin khalu Banu Asadin*
*ya bu'sa lil-jahli darran li-aqwami*

The Banu 'Amir said: "Leave the Banu Asad,
Alas for ignorance, a harm to the people!"

End of quote. ﴿They will say﴾, that is, every punished nation: ﴿Will we be given respite?﴾, that is, be delayed. This is by way of their wishing and desiring, where desire is of no benefit. Then the wording of the verse returned to rebuking the Quraysh for their haste in seeking God's punishment, in their request for the fall of the sky in pieces and other things, and their saying to the Messenger: "Where is what you promise us?"

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Is it then Our punishment they seek to hasten?﴾ is a rebuke to them through its denial, and a mockery. Its meaning: how can one who is exposed to a punishment, in which he asks, of the same kind as what he is in today, the respite of a blink of an eye, and is not granted it, seek to hasten the punishment? It may be that this is a narration of rebuke, by which they are rebuked when they seek respite on that day, and they hasten this matter in the manner of a narration of a past state. Another aspect connects it to what follows: their haste for the punishment was either because they believed it would not occur and would not befall them, and that they would enjoy long lives in safety and security. So He, Mighty and Exalted, said: ﴿Is it then Our punishment they seek to hasten?﴾ Out of insolence, arrogance, mockery, and reliance on long hope? Then He said: Suppose the matter is as they believe of their enjoyment and long life; when the threat overtakes them after that, what will the long span of their lives and the goodness of their livelihood avail them then? End of quote. It was said: He followed His saying "so it will come to them suddenly" with what will be from them at that time in the manner of regret.

﴿They will say: Will we be given respite?﴾ as a man cries out for it when salvation is impossible, for they know in the Hereafter that there is no refuge, but they say that seeking relief. It was said: they seek a return when the punishment of the Hour suddenly seizes them, but they are not answered in it.

[p. 40]

End of quote.

In this view, the sending down of it in Arabic, which is your tongue and the tongue of your people, is a sending down upon your heart, because you understand it and your people understand it. Had it been in a foreign tongue, it would have descended upon your hearing rather than your heart, because you would hear the chimes of letters whose meanings you do not understand or retain. A man may know several languages, and when he is addressed in the language he was first taught, grew up with, and was accustomed to, his heart goes only to the meanings of those words, which he receives with his heart, and he hardly notices how the words were uttered. But if he is addressed in another language, even if he is skilled in it, his attention goes first to its words and then to their meanings. This is the explanation that it descended upon his heart by its descending in a clear Arabic tongue. End of quote. In it there is some length.

It was also said that the pronoun refers to the Messenger of God ﷺ, meaning that his mention and his mission are in the earlier divine books. This would be an iltifat (a shift of grammatical person), since it moves from the second-person pronoun in "upon your heart, that you may be" to the third-person pronoun. Al-A'mash recited *la-fi zubri* with a sukun on the *ba'*, while the original is with a *damma*. Then He argued against them that the knowledge of the scholars of the Children of Israel of it should have established its authenticity for them. That is, "Was it not a sign for them that the scholars of the Children of Israel knew it?" Many Arabs had become Jews, and many had become Christians, because of their belief in the truth of those religions. So the verse was revealed about that, and what supports this is that the verse is Meccan. Muqatil said: it is Medinan.

This is because a group of them embraced Islam and pointed out places in the Torah and the Gospel in which the Messenger, peace be upon him, was mentioned. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when it is recited to them they say, "We believe in it; indeed it is the truth from our Lord"﴾ [al-Qasas: 53], and so on. It was said: their scholars are those among them who embraced Islam and those who did not. It was said: their prophets, since they pointed to him and reported his attributes, time, and place. The majority read *awa-lam yakun* ("Was it not") with the yaa' below, and *ayatan* ("a sign") in the accusative. This reading is clear in its grammatical construction: the predicate of *yakun* is placed in the middle, and *an ya'lamahu* ("that they know it") is the subject. Ibn 'Amir and al-Jahdari read *takun* with the taa' above, and *ayatun* in the nominative. Al-Zamakhshari said: *ayatun* was made the subject and *an ya'lamahu* the predicate, and it is not like the first, because an indefinite noun is the subject and a definite noun the predicate. Another analysis has been offered to avoid this: it is said that in *takun* there is the pronoun of the matter (*damir al-qissa*), and "*ayatan an ya'lamahu*" is a clause occupying the place of the predicate; it is also permissible on this view that "*lahum ayatan*" be the clause of the matter, and "*an ya'lamahu*" be a substitute for "*ayatan*." End of quote. Ibn 'Abbas read *takun* with the taa' above and *ayatan* in the accusative, like the reading of one who read: "*thumma lam takun fitnatahum*" ("then their trial was not") [al-An'am: 23] with the accusative, except that they said, "*illa an qalu*." And like the verse of Labid:

*fa-madha wa-qaddamaha wa-kanat 'adatan*
*minhu idha hiya 'arradat aqdamuha*

He went forth and advanced it, and it was his custom
that when it turned aside, he advanced upon it.

This indicates either the feminine of the noun because of the feminine of the predicate, or the interpretation of *an ya'lamahu* as a definite knowing, and the interpretation of *illa an qalu* as "the saying," and the interpretation of *al-iqdam* as "the advance." Al-Jahdari read *an ta'lamahu* with the feminine taa', as the poet said:

*qalat Banu 'Amirin khalu Banu Asadin*
*ya bu'sa lil-jahli darran li-aqwami*

The Banu 'Amir said: "Leave the Banu Asad,
Alas for ignorance, a harm to the people!"

It was written in the Mushaf (the codex) as *'ulamau*, with a waw between the *mim* and the *alif*. It was said: this follows the dialect of those who incline the *alif* of *'ulamau* toward the waw, just as they wrote *al-salawata*, *al-zakawata*, and *al-ribawa* in that dialect. Al-Zamakhshari said: the *a'jami* is the one who is not eloquent and has a barbarism and incoherence in his speech; the *a'jami* is like him, except that the addition of the *ya'* of relation gives it an additional emphasis. Ibn 'Atiyya said: *al-a'jamun* is the plural of *a'jam*, which is one who is not eloquent, even if he is of Arab lineage, and it is said of him *a'jam*. This is also said of animals and inanimate things, and from it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The wound of the dumb animal is unrequited." Al-Tabari transmitted from 'Abdullah ibn Mut'i that when he recited this verse while standing at 'Arafat, he said: "This my camel is a dumb animal; had it been revealed to it, it would not have believed." And the *'ajami* is the one whose lineage is among the non-Arabs, even if he is the most eloquent of people. End of quote. In al-Tahrir: *al-a'jamin* is the plural of *a'jam* with a lightening of the form; were it not for this estimation, it would not be permissible to form the sound masculine plural from it. It was said: the meaning is that if We had sent it down in the language of non-Arabs upon a non-Arab man who then recited it to the Arabs, they would not have believed in it, since they would not have understood it, and they would have disdained following it. It was also said: if We had sent the Qur'an down upon some of the non-Arab animals, and he recited it to them, they would not have believed, because of their obstinacy toward His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And even if We had sent down to them the angels﴾ [al-An'am: 111], and so on. The sound plural was used because it was described by being sent down upon it and by recitation, and these are actions of rational beings. It was also said: if it had been sent down upon some of the beasts, and Muhammad ﷺ recited it to them, the beasts would not have believed, and likewise these people, because they are ﴿like livestock; rather, they are further astray in way﴾ [al-Furqan: 44]. End of quote.

When He had explained by what came before, that this Qur'an is in the books of the ancients and that the scholars of the Children of Israel know it, and that in this there are two proofs of the truth of the prophethood of the Messenger of God ﷺ, He made clear that proofs are of no benefit to these disbelievers. Do you not see that it was sent down upon an Arab man in a clear Arabic tongue, and they heard it and understood it and perceived its inimitability and the confirmation of the earlier books of God for it, and despite all that they denied it, and called him at times a poet and at times a sorcerer? Had it been sent down upon one of the non-Arabs who does not speak Arabic well, they would have disbelieved in it and contrived to deny it. Al-Farra' said: *al-a'jamin* is the plural of *a'jam* or *a'jami*, with the *ya'* of relation omitted, just as they said *al-ash'arin*, and its singular is *ash'ari*. Ibn al-Jahm said: al-Kumayt said:

*wa-law jahhaztu qafiyatan sharudan*
*laqad dakhalat buyuta al-Ash'arina*

Had I equipped a wandering rhyme,
it would have entered the houses of the Ash'arites.

End of quote. Al-Hasan and Ibn Miqsam read *al-a'jamiyyin* with the *ya'* of relation, as the plural of *a'jami*. The pronoun in *salaknahu* ("We caused it to enter") apparently refers to what the pronouns before it referred to. It was said: it is the Qur'an, as al-Rummani said. The meaning: like that insertion, which is the causing to enter, the making firm, and the making understood of its meanings.

*Salaknahu* ("We caused it to enter"): We made it enter and established it in *qulubi al-mujrimin* ("the hearts of the criminals"). The meaning is: what followed from that insertion, namely that they understood it and perceived it, yet it increased them only in obstinacy, denial, and disbelief in it. That is, in this very state and this very attribute of disbelief in it and denial of it, just as We placed it therein. How then could their belief in it be expected? It did not change, and their blindness to it through denial and rejection remained, as He said: ﴿And even if We had sent down to you a book upon parchment﴾ [al-An'am: 7], and so on. Al-Kirmani said: We caused it to enter therein, so they knew its meanings and their inability to produce its like, yet they did not believe in it. Yahya ibn Salam said: the pronoun in *salaknahu* refers to denial, and that is what prevented them from believing. End of quote. This is strengthened by His words: ﴿so he recited it to them, and they were not believers in it﴾. Al-Hasan said: the pronoun refers to the disbelief implied by His words: ﴿they were not believers in it﴾. End of quote. This is close to the view before it. 'Ikrimah said: *salaknahu*, that is, the hardness of heart, and God, exalted is He, is the one to whom the causing to enter is attributed, because He is the one who truly brings things into existence, the Guide, and the Creator of misguidance.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 26, verse 192–204 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): How did he attribute the threading (al-salk) together with the quality of denial to Himself? (I answer): He intended by it to indicate that the denial was firmly established in their hearts with the strongest and most lasting establishment, so He made it like a matter to which they had been created disposed. Do you not see their saying: "He is disposed to stinginess" (majbul 'ala al-shuhh)? They mean that stinginess is firmly rooted in him, because innate matters are more firmly established than acquired ones. The evidence for this is that He attributed the not-believing in it to them directly after it, which is His saying: ﴿they do not believe﴾ in it. End of quote. This is according to the path of the Mu'tazilites, and the comparison between the two threadings (salk) requires a difference in the one upon whom it descends. The meaning: like that threading in the hearts of the Quraysh, We threaded it in the hearts of those who committed crime, because the two share the cause of threading, which is criminality. Ibn 'Atiyya said: He intended by them the criminals of every nation, meaning that this is God's custom with them: they do not believe until they see the punishment, so faith does not benefit them after the punishment has befallen them. This is by way of example for the Quraysh, meaning: these are likewise. The unveiling of the unseen by what this verse includes is on the Day of Badr.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): What is the position of ﴿they do not believe in it﴾ from His saying ﴿We threaded it in the hearts of the criminals﴾? (I answer): Its position relative to it is the position of clarification and summary, because it is brought for its firm establishment, denied and rejected in their hearts, so it is followed by what confirms this meaning, that they will not cease to deny it and reject it until they witness the threat. It may also be a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: We threaded it in them while not believing in it. End of quote. As for their seeing the punishment, it was said: in this world; and it was said: on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Jumhur read ﴿fa-ya'tiyahum﴾ with a yā' (ya), meaning: the punishment. Al-Hasan and 'Isa read it with the feminine tā' (ta), making it feminine in accordance with the meaning of "punishment," because it is the retribution, meaning: so the retribution will come to them on the Day of Resurrection, as in the saying: "It came to him, my book," when he was asked, he said: "Is it not a written document?" Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿fa-ta'tiyahum﴾ with the tā', meaning the Hour. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: He made the punishment feminine because it includes the Hour, so it took on the feminine from it, because they used to ask for the punishment of the Resurrection as a denial of it, so it was made feminine for this reason. The masculine does not take the feminine marker unless it is a genitive attached to it, as in: "the people of al-Yamama gathered," "some of his fingers were cut off," and "the chest of the spear-shaft was split," but this is not the case here. Al-Hasan read "baghtatan" with a fatha on the ghayn, and "fa-ta'tiyahum" with the tā' from above, meaning the Hour.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): What is the meaning of the sequence (ta'qib) in His saying ﴿fa-ta'tiyahum bi-ayatin﴾ [al-An'am: 35]? (I answer): The meaning is not that what is intended by seeing the punishment, its sudden arrival, and their request for a respite is their existence simultaneously, but rather the meaning is their ordering in severity, as if it were said: they do not believe in the Qur'an until their seeing the punishment is something more severe than it, namely its overtaking them suddenly, which is more severe than it, namely their asking for a respite. Similar to this is your saying: "If you do evil, the righteous will despise you, so God will despise you," for you do not intend by this ordering that God's contempt occurs right after the contempt of the righteous, but you intend the ordering of the severity of the matter upon the evildoer, and that there results for him, because of the evil, the contempt of the righteous. What is more severe than their contempt? It is the contempt of God. This is seen, and then this occurs in this style, and it takes its place. End of quote. ﴿They will say﴾, that is, every punished nation: ﴿Will we be given respite?﴾, that is, be delayed. This is by way of their wishing and desiring, where desire is of no benefit. Then the wording of the verse returned to rebuking the Quraysh for their haste in seeking God's punishment, in their request for the fall of the sky in pieces and other things, and their saying to the Messenger: "Where is what you promise us?"

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Is it then Our punishment they seek to hasten?﴾ is a rebuke to them through its denial, and a mockery. Its meaning: how can one who is exposed to a punishment, in which he asks, of the same kind as what he is in today, the respite of a blink of an eye, and is not granted it, seek to hasten the punishment? Then He said: Suppose the matter is as they believe of their enjoyment and long life; when the threat overtakes them after that, what will the long span of their lives and the goodness of their livelihood avail them then? End of quote. It was said: He followed His saying "so it will come to them suddenly" with what will be from them at that time in the manner of regret.

﴿They will say: Will we be given respite?﴾ as a man cries out for it when salvation is impossible, for they know in the Hereafter that there is no refuge, but they say that seeking relief. It was said: they seek a return when the punishment of the Hour suddenly seizes them, but they are not answered in it.

He went forth and advanced it, and it was his custom

The Banu 'Amir said: "Leave the Banu Asad,
Alas for ignorance, a harm to the people!"
