The evidence for this is that He attributed the not-believing in it to them directly after it, which is His saying: ﴿they do not believe﴾ in it. End of quote. This is according to the path of the Mu'tazilites, and the comparison between the two threadings (salk) requires a difference in the one upon whom it descends. The meaning: like that threading in the hearts of the Quraysh, We threaded it in the hearts of those who committed crime, because the two share the cause of threading, which is criminality. Ibn 'Atiyya said: He intended by them the criminals of every nation, meaning that this is God's custom with them: they do not believe until they see the punishment, so faith does not benefit them after the punishment has befallen them. This is by way of example for the Quraysh, meaning: these are likewise. The unveiling of the unseen by what this verse includes is on the Day of Badr.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): What is the position of ﴿they do not believe in it﴾ from His saying ﴿We threaded it in the hearts of the criminals﴾? (I answer): Its position relative to it is the position of clarification and summary, because it is brought for its firm establishment, denied and rejected in their hearts, so it is followed by what confirms this meaning, that they will not cease to deny it and reject it until they witness the threat. It may also be a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: We threaded it in them while not believing in it. End of quote. As for their seeing the punishment, it was said: in this world; and it was said: on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Jumhur read ﴿fa-ya'tiyahum﴾ with a yā' (ya), meaning: the punishment. Al-Hasan and 'Isa read it with the feminine tā' (ta), making it feminine in accordance with the meaning of "punishment," because it is the retribution, meaning: so the retribution will come to them on the Day of Resurrection, as in the saying: "It came to him, my book," when he was asked, he said: "Is it not a written document?" Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿fa-ta'tiyahum﴾ with the tā', meaning the Hour. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: He made the punishment feminine because it includes the Hour, so it took on the feminine from it, because they used to ask for the punishment of the Resurrection as a denial of it, so it was made feminine for this reason. The masculine does not take the feminine marker unless it is a genitive attached to it, as in: "the people of al-Yamama gathered," "some of his fingers were cut off," and "the chest of the spear-shaft was split," but this is not the case here. Al-Hasan read "baghtatan" with a fatha on the ghayn, and "fa-ta'tiyahum" with the tā' from above, meaning the Hour.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): What is the meaning of the sequence (ta'qib) in His saying ﴿fa-ta'tiyahum bi-ayatin﴾ [al-An'am: 35]? (I answer): The meaning is not that what is intended by seeing the punishment, its sudden arrival, and their request for a respite is their existence simultaneously, but rather the meaning is their ordering in severity, as if it were said: they do not believe in the Qur'an until their seeing the punishment is something more severe than it, namely its overtaking them suddenly, which is more severe than it, namely their asking for a respite. Similar to this is your saying: "If you do evil, the righteous will despise you, so God will despise you," for you do not intend by this ordering that God's contempt occurs right after the contempt of the righteous, but you intend the ordering of the severity of the matter upon the evildoer, and that there results for him, because of the evil, the contempt of the righteous. What is more severe than their contempt? It is the contempt of God. This is seen, and then this occurs in this style, and it takes its place. End of quote. ﴿They will say﴾, that is, every punished nation: ﴿Will we be given respite?﴾, that is, be delayed. This is by way of their wishing and desiring, where desire is of no benefit. Then the wording of the verse returned to rebuking the Quraysh for their haste in seeking God's punishment, in their request for the fall of the sky in pieces and other things, and their saying to the Messenger: "Where is what you promise us?"

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Is it then Our punishment they seek to hasten?﴾ is a rebuke to them through its denial, and a mockery. Its meaning: how can one who is exposed to a punishment, in which he asks, of the same kind as what he is in today, the respite of a blink of an eye, and is not granted it, seek to hasten the punishment? It may be that this is a narration of rebuke, by which they are rebuked when they seek respite on that day, and they hasten this matter in the manner of a narration of a past state. Another aspect connects it to what follows: their haste for the punishment was either because they believed it would not occur and would not befall them, and that they would enjoy long lives in safety and security. So He, Mighty and Exalted, said: ﴿Is it then Our punishment they seek to hasten?﴾ Out of insolence, arrogance, mockery, and reliance on long hope? Then He said: Suppose the matter is as they believe of their enjoyment and long life; when the threat overtakes them after that, what will the long span of their lives and the goodness of their livelihood avail them then? End of quote. It was said: He followed His saying "so it will come to them suddenly" with what will be from them at that time in the manner of regret.

﴿They will say: Will we be given respite?﴾ as a man cries out for it when salvation is impossible, for they know in the Hereafter that there is no refuge, but they say that seeking relief. It was said: they seek a return when the punishment of the Hour suddenly seizes them, but they are not answered in it.

[p. 40]

The pronoun in "wa-innahu" ("and indeed it") refers to the Qur'an, meaning that it is neither soothsaying nor sorcery but is from God. It seems also to refer back to what the surah opened with, namely the disbelievers' turning away from the reminder that comes to them, so that the beginning and the end of the surah correspond. Ibn 'Amir... no. The two Harams (Ibn Kathir and Nafi') [not transliterated], Abu 'Amr, and Hafs recited *nazala* (he sent down) with light stress, and *al-Ruhu al-Amin* (the Trustworthy Spirit) in the nominative. The rest of the seven readers (qira'at, the canonical recitations) read it with the doubled *zay* (*nazzala*, with emphasis) and the accusative for both. Here *al-Ruh* (the Spirit) means Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him, and the reason he is called "the Spirit" has already been explained in the surah of Maryam. Ibn 'Atiyya said, in the sense of a circumstantial clause (hal), like God's words: ﴿And they entered with disbelief, and they had gone out with it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 61]. End of quote.

The apparent meaning is that *'ala qalbika* ("upon your heart") and *li-takuna* ("that you may be") are connected to *nazala*. He specified the heart, and the meaning is "upon you," because it is the place of understanding and steadfastness, and so that it be known that what is sent down upon his heart, peace be upon him, is preserved and cannot be subject to alteration or change. It is also a cause of the sending down or the descent, and he restricted himself to this, because that is more effective in restraining the listener, even though the Qur'an was sent down for warning and for giving good tidings. The apparent meaning is that *bi-lisanin* ("in a tongue") is connected to *nazala*, so he would hear from Jibril letters in Arabic. Ibn 'Atiyya said, and this is the correct view: the "sound of a bell" (*salsalat al-jaras*) is a description of the intensity of the voice, the overlapping of its letters, the speed of its arrival and its harshness. It is possible to connect it to *li-takuna*, and whoever holds that the Prophet ﷺ sometimes heard something like the sound of a bell, from which the Qur'an was understood, relies on this, but it is rejected. End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari said: *bi-lisanin* either connects to *al-mundhirin* ("the warners"), so the meaning is: "that you may be among those who warned with this tongue," and they were five: Hud, Salih, Shu'ayb, Isma'il, and Muhammad ﷺ, and upon them [be peace]. Or it connects to *nazala*, so the meaning is: He sent it down in the clear Arabic tongue so that you might warn by it, because if He had sent it down in a non-Arabic tongue, they would have turned away from it entirely and said, "What shall we do with what we do not understand?" and the warning by it would have been impossible. In this view, the sending down of it in Arabic, which is your tongue and the tongue of your people, is a sending down upon your heart, because you understand it and your people understand it. Had it been in a foreign tongue, it would have descended upon your hearing rather than your heart, because you would hear the chimes of letters whose meanings you do not understand or retain. A man may know several languages, and when he is addressed in the language he was first taught, grew up with, and was accustomed to, his heart goes only to the meanings of those words, which he receives with his heart, and he hardly notices how the words were uttered. But if he is addressed in another language, even if he is skilled in it, his attention goes first to its words and then to their meanings. This is the explanation that it descended upon his heart by its descending in a clear Arabic tongue. End of quote. In it there is some length.

*Wa-innahu* ("and indeed it"), that is, the Qur'an, *la-fi zuburi al-awwalin* ("is in the scriptures of the ancients"): that is, it is mentioned in the earlier revealed books, indicated and pointed out. It was said that its meanings are in them, and by this Abu Hanifa is cited for permitting recitation in Persian in prayer, on the basis that the Qur'an remains Qur'an even when translated into a language other than Arabic, since it was said, "and indeed it is in the scriptures of the ancients," because its meanings are in them. It was also said that the pronoun refers to the Messenger of God ﷺ, meaning that his mention and his mission are in the earlier divine books. This would be an iltifat (a shift of grammatical person), since it moves from the second-person pronoun in "upon your heart, that you may be" to the third-person pronoun. The same was said regarding *an yu'lima-hu* ("that it be made known to him"), meaning that it be made known to Muhammad ﷺ, and the consistency of pronouns referring to one thing is clearer. Al-A'mash recited *la-fi zubri* with a sukun on the *ba'*, while the original is with a *damma*. Then He argued against them that the knowledge of the scholars of the Children of Israel of it should have established its authenticity for them. That is, "Was it not a sign for them that the scholars of the Children of Israel knew it?" Because the Quraysh used to refer many transmitted matters to the Children of Israel, asking them about them and saying, "They are the people of the divine books." Many Arabs had become Jews, and many had become Christians, because of their belief in the truth of those religions. Al-Tha'labi reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the people of Makkah sent to the rabbis of Yathrib asking them about the Prophet ﷺ, and they said, "This is his time," and described his attributes, and they confused matters concerning Muhammad, peace be upon him. So the verse was revealed about that, and what supports this is that the verse is Meccan. Muqatil said: it is Medinan.

*'Ulama'u Bani Isra'il* ("the scholars of the Children of Israel") means 'Abdullah ibn Salam and others like him, as said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. This is because a group of them embraced Islam and pointed out places in the Torah and the Gospel in which the Messenger, peace be upon him, was mentioned. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when it is recited to them they say, "We believe in it; indeed it is the truth from our Lord"﴾ [al-Qasas: 53], and so on. It was said: their scholars are those among them who embraced Islam and those who did not. It was said: their prophets, since they pointed to him and reported his attributes, time, and place. The majority read *awa-lam yakun* ("Was it not") with the yaa' below, and *ayatan* ("a sign") in the accusative. This reading is clear in its grammatical construction: the predicate of *yakun* is placed in the middle, and *an ya'lamahu* ("that they know it") is the subject. Ibn 'Amir and al-Jahdari read *takun* with the taa' above, and *ayatun* in the nominative. Al-Zamakhshari said: *ayatun* was made the subject and *an ya'lamahu* the predicate, and it is not like the first, because an indefinite noun is the subject and a definite noun the predicate. Another analysis has been offered to avoid this: it is said that in *takun* there is the pronoun of the matter (*damir al-qissa*), and "*ayatan an ya'lamahu*" is a clause occupying the place of the predicate; it is also permissible on this view that "*lahum ayatan*" be the clause of the matter, and "*an ya'lamahu*" be a substitute for "*ayatan*." End of quote. Ibn 'Abbas read *takun* with the taa' above and *ayatan* in the accusative, like the reading of one who read: "*thumma lam takun fitnatahum*" ("then their trial was not") [al-An'am: 23] with the accusative, except that they said, "*illa an qalu*." And like the verse of Labid:

*fa-madha wa-qaddamaha wa-kanat 'adatan*
*minhu idha hiya 'arradat aqdamuha*

He went forth and advanced it, and it was his custom
that when it turned aside, he advanced upon it.

This indicates either the feminine of the noun because of the feminine of the predicate, or the interpretation of *an ya'lamahu* as a definite knowing, and the interpretation of *illa an qalu* as "the saying," and the interpretation of *al-iqdam* as "the advance." Al-Jahdari read *an ta'lamahu* with the feminine taa', as the poet said:

*qalat Banu 'Amirin khalu Banu Asadin*
*ya bu'sa lil-jahli darran li-aqwami*

The Banu 'Amir said: "Leave the Banu Asad,
Alas for ignorance, a harm to the people!"

It was written in the Mushaf (the codex) as *'ulamau*, with a waw between the *mim* and the *alif*. It was said: this follows the dialect of those who incline the *alif* of *'ulamau* toward the waw, just as they wrote *al-salawata*, *al-zakawata*, and *al-ribawa* in that dialect. Al-Zamakhshari said: the *a'jami* is the one who is not eloquent and has a barbarism and incoherence in his speech; the *a'jami* is like him, except that the addition of the *ya'* of relation gives it an additional emphasis. Ibn 'Atiyya said: *al-a'jamun* is the plural of *a'jam*, which is one who is not eloquent, even if he is of Arab lineage, and it is said of him *a'jam*. This is also said of animals and inanimate things, and from it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The wound of the dumb animal is unrequited." Al-Tabari transmitted from 'Abdullah ibn Mut'i that when he recited this verse while standing at 'Arafat, he said: "This my camel is a dumb animal; had it been revealed to it, it would not have believed." And the *'ajami* is the one whose lineage is among the non-Arabs, even if he is the most eloquent of people. End of quote. In al-Tahrir: *al-a'jamin* is the plural of *a'jam* with a lightening of the form; were it not for this estimation, it would not be permissible to form the sound masculine plural from it. It was said: the meaning is that if We had sent it down in the language of non-Arabs upon a non-Arab man who then recited it to the Arabs, they would not have believed in it, since they would not have understood it, and they would have disdained following it. It was also said: if We had sent the Qur'an down upon some of the non-Arab animals, and he recited it to them, they would not have believed, because of their obstinacy toward His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And even if We had sent down to them the angels﴾ [al-An'am: 111], and so on. The sound plural was used because it was described by being sent down upon it and by recitation, and these are actions of rational beings. It was also said: if it had been sent down upon some of the beasts, and Muhammad ﷺ recited it to them, the beasts would not have believed, and likewise these people, because they are ﴿like livestock; rather, they are further astray in way﴾ [al-Furqan: 44]. End of quote.

When He had explained by what came before, that this Qur'an is in the books of the ancients and that the scholars of the Children of Israel know it, and that in this there are two proofs of the truth of the prophethood of the Messenger of God ﷺ, He made clear that proofs are of no benefit to these disbelievers. Do you not see that it was sent down upon an Arab man in a clear Arabic tongue, and they heard it and understood it and perceived its inimitability and the confirmation of the earlier books of God for it, and despite all that they denied it, and called him at times a poet and at times a sorcerer? Had it been sent down upon one of the non-Arabs who does not speak Arabic well, they would have disbelieved in it and contrived to deny it. Al-Farra' said: *al-a'jamin* is the plural of *a'jam* or *a'jami*, with the *ya'* of relation omitted, just as they said *al-ash'arin*, and its singular is *ash'ari*. Ibn al-Jahm said: al-Kumayt said:

*wa-law jahhaztu qafiyatan sharudan*
*laqad dakhalat buyuta al-Ash'arina*

Had I equipped a wandering rhyme,
it would have entered the houses of the Ash'arites.

End of quote. Al-Hasan and Ibn Miqsam read *al-a'jamiyyin* with the *ya'* of relation, as the plural of *a'jami*. The pronoun in *salaknahu* ("We caused it to enter") apparently refers to what the pronouns before it referred to. It was said: it is the Qur'an, as al-Rummani said. The meaning: like that insertion, which is the causing to enter, the making firm, and the making understood of its meanings.

*Salaknahu* ("We caused it to enter"): We made it enter and established it in *qulubi al-mujrimin* ("the hearts of the criminals"). The meaning is: what followed from that insertion, namely that they understood it and perceived it, yet it increased them only in obstinacy, denial, and disbelief in it. That is, in this very state and this very attribute of disbelief in it and denial of it, just as We placed it therein. How then could their belief in it be expected? It did not change, and their blindness to it through denial and rejection remained, as He said: ﴿And even if We had sent down to you a book upon parchment﴾ [al-An'am: 7], and so on. Al-Kirmani said: We caused it to enter therein, so they knew its meanings and their inability to produce its like, yet they did not believe in it. Yahya ibn Salam said: the pronoun in *salaknahu* refers to denial, and that is what prevented them from believing. End of quote. This is strengthened by His words: ﴿so he recited it to them, and they were not believers in it﴾. Al-Hasan said: the pronoun refers to the disbelief implied by His words: ﴿they were not believers in it﴾. End of quote. This is close to the view before it. 'Ikrimah said: *salaknahu*, that is, the hardness of heart, and God, exalted is He, is the one to whom the causing to enter is attributed, because He is the one who truly brings things into existence, the Guide, and the Creator of misguidance.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 26, verse 192–204 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): How did he attribute the threading (al-salk) together with the quality of denial to Himself? (I answer): He intended by it to indicate that the denial was firmly established in their hearts with the strongest and most lasting establishment, so He made it like a matter to which they had been created disposed. Do you not see their saying: "He is disposed to stinginess" (majbul 'ala al-shuhh)? They mean that stinginess is firmly rooted in him, because innate matters are more firmly established than acquired ones. The evidence for this is that He attributed the not-believing in it to them directly after it, which is His saying: ﴿they do not believe﴾ in it. End of quote. This is according to the path of the Mu'tazilites, and the comparison between the two threadings (salk) requires a difference in the one upon whom it descends. The meaning: like that threading in the hearts of the Quraysh, We threaded it in the hearts of those who committed crime, because the two share the cause of threading, which is criminality. Ibn 'Atiyya said: He intended by them the criminals of every nation, meaning that this is God's custom with them: they do not believe until they see the punishment, so faith does not benefit them after the punishment has befallen them. This is by way of example for the Quraysh, meaning: these are likewise. The unveiling of the unseen by what this verse includes is on the Day of Badr.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): What is the position of ﴿they do not believe in it﴾ from His saying ﴿We threaded it in the hearts of the criminals﴾? (I answer): Its position relative to it is the position of clarification and summary, because it is brought for its firm establishment, denied and rejected in their hearts, so it is followed by what confirms this meaning, that they will not cease to deny it and reject it until they witness the threat. It may also be a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: We threaded it in them while not believing in it. End of quote. As for their seeing the punishment, it was said: in this world; and it was said: on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Jumhur read ﴿fa-ya'tiyahum﴾ with a yā' (ya), meaning: the punishment. Al-Hasan and 'Isa read it with the feminine tā' (ta), making it feminine in accordance with the meaning of "punishment," because it is the retribution, meaning: so the retribution will come to them on the Day of Resurrection, as in the saying: "It came to him, my book," when he was asked, he said: "Is it not a written document?" Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿fa-ta'tiyahum﴾ with the tā', meaning the Hour. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: He made the punishment feminine because it includes the Hour, so it took on the feminine from it, because they used to ask for the punishment of the Resurrection as a denial of it, so it was made feminine for this reason. The masculine does not take the feminine marker unless it is a genitive attached to it, as in: "the people of al-Yamama gathered," "some of his fingers were cut off," and "the chest of the spear-shaft was split," but this is not the case here. Al-Hasan read "baghtatan" with a fatha on the ghayn, and "fa-ta'tiyahum" with the tā' from above, meaning the Hour.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): What is the meaning of the sequence (ta'qib) in His saying ﴿fa-ta'tiyahum bi-ayatin﴾ [al-An'am: 35]? (I answer): The meaning is not that what is intended by seeing the punishment, its sudden arrival, and their request for a respite is their existence simultaneously, but rather the meaning is their ordering in severity, as if it were said: they do not believe in the Qur'an until their seeing the punishment is something more severe than it, namely its overtaking them suddenly, which is more severe than it, namely their asking for a respite. Similar to this is your saying: "If you do evil, the righteous will despise you, so God will despise you," for you do not intend by this ordering that God's contempt occurs right after the contempt of the righteous, but you intend the ordering of the severity of the matter upon the evildoer, and that there results for him, because of the evil, the contempt of the righteous. What is more severe than their contempt? It is the contempt of God. This is seen, and then this occurs in this style, and it takes its place. End of quote. ﴿They will say﴾, that is, every punished nation: ﴿Will we be given respite?﴾, that is, be delayed. This is by way of their wishing and desiring, where desire is of no benefit. Then the wording of the verse returned to rebuking the Quraysh for their haste in seeking God's punishment, in their request for the fall of the sky in pieces and other things, and their saying to the Messenger: "Where is what you promise us?"

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Is it then Our punishment they seek to hasten?﴾ is a rebuke to them through its denial, and a mockery. Its meaning: how can one who is exposed to a punishment, in which he asks, of the same kind as what he is in today, the respite of a blink of an eye, and is not granted it, seek to hasten the punishment? It may be that this is a narration of rebuke, by which they are rebuked when they seek respite on that day, and they hasten this matter in the manner of a narration of a past state. Another aspect connects it to what follows: their haste for the punishment was either because they believed it would not occur and would not befall them, and that they would enjoy long lives in safety and security. So He, Mighty and Exalted, said: ﴿Is it then Our punishment they seek to hasten?﴾ Out of insolence, arrogance, mockery, and reliance on long hope? Then He said: Suppose the matter is as they believe of their enjoyment and long life; when the threat overtakes them after that, what will the long span of their lives and the goodness of their livelihood avail them then? End of quote. It was said: He followed His saying "so it will come to them suddenly" with what will be from them at that time in the manner of regret.

﴿They will say: Will we be given respite?﴾ as a man cries out for it when salvation is impossible, for they know in the Hereafter that there is no refuge, but they say that seeking relief. It was said: they seek a return when the punishment of the Hour suddenly seizes them, but they are not answered in it.

Abu Hayyan's commentary on Surah al-Shu'ara' (26), verses 205–209:

﴿Have you considered: if We let them enjoy [worldly life] for years﴾. This is an address to the Messenger (peace be upon him), establishing the proof against them: the period of respite, delay and reprieve does not benefit them once the punishment descends after it. Ikrimah said: "'Years' means the lifespan of the world." End of quote.

It is established in the science of Arabic grammar (ʿilm al-ʿarabiyyah) that أرَأيْتَ (ara'ayta), when it means "inform me" (akhbirni), takes two objects: the first is in the accusative, and the second is an interrogative clause. Usually the Arabs say: أرَأيْتَ زَيْدًا ما صَنَعَ؟ ("Have you seen Zayd: what did he do?"). Whatever occurs that outwardly contradicts this is interpreted (ta'wil) accordingly, and the discussion of this was fully covered at the beginning of Surat al-An'am.

Here the object of أرَأيْتَ is omitted, because it is in a relation of dependency (tanazuʿ) over ﴿what they were promised﴾, with أرَأيْتَ and جاءَهم both seeking it. If the second verb is given the governing role, then it is the subject, so it is in the nominative with جاءَهم. It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative governed by أرَأيْتَ, with the governing role given to the first verb, and the subject pronoun is implied in جاءَهم. The second object is the clause ﴿what did it avail them﴾, where ما is interrogative: that is, "What benefit to them was their enjoyment in those years they were given enjoyment?" In the sentence there is an omitted element that contains the pronoun referring back to the first object, namely: "What benefit to them was their enjoyment when it came, i.e., what was promised, which is the punishment?" The apparent meaning of what the commentators explained for ما أغنى ("what did it avail") is that ما is negative, and the interrogative may come implying the meaning of negation, as in His saying: ﴿Will any be destroyed except the wrongdoing people?﴾ [al-An'am: 47], after His saying "أرَأيْتَكم" in Surat al-An'am; meaning: none is destroyed except the wrongdoing people. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that ما may be interrogative or negative. It is also read: يُمَتَّعُونَ, with the mim sukun and the ta' lightened.

Then God informs that He never destroyed any town of the towns except that He had sent to it those who warn it of God's punishment, if it disobeyed and did not believe, as He said: ﴿And We would never punish until We have sent a messenger﴾ [al-Isra': 15]. Mundhirun (warners) is plural because (min qaryah) is general over the wrongdoing towns, as if it were said: "We did not destroy the wrongdoing towns." The clause from His saying ﴿for them are warners﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from (qaryah). The i'rab (grammatical parsing) may be that لَها is in the position of a circumstantial phrase, and مُنْذِرُونَ is raised by the preceding prepositional phrase, so the meaning is "except having for it warners", making the circumstantial element a single word rather than a clause. The circumstantial element coming after a negation is eloquent, as in your saying: ما مَرَرْتُ بِأحَدٍ إلّا قائِمًا ("I did not pass by anyone except standing").

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: how was the waw removed from the clause after إلّا, while it was not removed from it in His saying ﴿And We did not destroy any town except that it had a known decree﴾ [al-Hijr: 4]? I say: the original is the removal of the waw, because the clause is a description (sifah) of qaryah; and when the waw is added, it is to emphasize the connection of the description to the described." End of quote.

As for ﴿and their eighth is their dog﴾ [al-Kahf: 22], its discussion has already been covered in its place.

(ذِكْرى, dhikra, "a reminder") is in the accusative as a circumstantial element according to al-Kisa'i, and as an infinitive (masdar) according to al-Zajjaj. As a circumstantial element, it is either that one supposes (yuqaddar) ذَوِي ذِكْرى ("possessors of a reminder") or مُذَكِّرِينَ ("reminding"). As an infinitive, the governing element is مُنْذِرُونَ, because it has the meaning of مُذَكِّرُونَ ذِكْرى, i.e., a reminder. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that ذِكْرى be an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), saying: "on the meaning that they are warned for the sake of admonition and reminding"; and that it be in the nominative as a description in the sense of مُنْذِرُونَ ذَوُو ذِكْرى ("warners possessing a reminder"), or that they are made into a reminder because of their intensity in reminding and their elaboration in it. He and Ibn 'Atiyyah permitted that it be in the nominative as the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject, in the sense of هَذِهِ ذِكْرى ("this is a reminder"), with the clause being parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah). Al-Zamakhshari said: "Another possibility is that ذِكْرى is connected to أهْلَكْنا as an object of purpose, and the meaning is: 'We did not destroy any town being wrongdoers except after We had established the proof against them by sending warners to them, so that it would be a reminder and a lesson for others, so they would not disobey as they disobeyed.'"

﴿And We were not wrongdoers﴾, so that We would destroy a people who were not wrongdoers. This aspect is what is relied upon. End of quote.

This is not something to rely upon, because the position of the majority is that what comes before إلّا does not govern what comes after it, unless it is an exception, or the thing excepted from, or a follower of it not depending on the particle, as in: ما مَرَرْتُ بِأحَدٍ إلّا زِيدٍ خَيْرٍ مِن عَمْرٍو. The object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) is none of these three, so it is not permissible for it to be connected to أهْلَكْنا. The permissibility of this may be derived according to the positions of al-Kisa'i and al-Akhfash, although neither of them explicitly stated the object of purpose specifically.

Abu Hayyan's commentary on Surah al-Shu'ara' (26), verses 205–209:

﴿Have you considered: if We let them enjoy [worldly life] for years﴾. This is an address to the Messenger (peace be upon him), establishing the proof against them: the period of respite, delay and reprieve does not benefit them once the punishment descends after it. Ikrimah said: "'Years' means the lifespan of the world." End of quote.

It is established in the science of Arabic grammar (ʿilm al-ʿarabiyyah) that أرَأيْتَ (ara'ayta), when it means "inform me" (akhbirni), takes two objects: the first is in the accusative, and the second is an interrogative clause. Usually the Arabs say: أرَأيْتَ زَيْدًا ما صَنَعَ؟ ("Have you seen Zayd: what did he do?"). Whatever occurs that outwardly contradicts this is interpreted (ta'wil) accordingly, and the discussion of this was fully covered at the beginning of Surat al-An'am.

Here the object of أرَأيْتَ is omitted, because it is in a relation of dependency (tanazuʿ) over ﴿what they were promised﴾, with أرَأيْتَ and جاءَهم both seeking it. If the second verb is given the governing role, then it is the subject, so it is in the nominative with جاءَهم. It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative governed by أرَأيْتَ, with the governing role given to the first verb, and the subject pronoun is implied in جاءَهم. The second object is the clause ﴿what did it avail them﴾, where ما is interrogative: that is, "What benefit to them was their enjoyment in those years they were given enjoyment?" In the sentence there is an omitted element that contains the pronoun referring back to the first object, namely: "What benefit to them was their enjoyment when it came, i.e., what was promised, which is the punishment?" The apparent meaning of what the commentators explained for ما أغنى ("what did it avail") is that ما is negative, and the interrogative may come implying the meaning of negation, as in His saying: ﴿Will any be destroyed except the wrongdoing people?﴾ [al-An'am: 47], after His saying "أرَأيْتَكم" in Surat al-An'am; meaning: none is destroyed except the wrongdoing people. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that ما may be interrogative or negative. It is also read: يُمَتَّعُونَ, with the mim sukun and the ta' lightened.

Then God informs that He never destroyed any town of the towns except that He had sent to it those who warn it of God's punishment, if it disobeyed and did not believe, as He said: ﴿And We would never punish until We have sent a messenger﴾ [al-Isra': 15]. Mundhirun (warners) is plural because (min qaryah) is general over the wrongdoing towns, as if it were said: "We did not destroy the wrongdoing towns." The clause from His saying ﴿for them are warners﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from (qaryah). The i'rab (grammatical parsing) may be that لَها is in the position of a circumstantial phrase, and مُنْذِرُونَ is raised by the preceding prepositional phrase, so the meaning is "except having for it warners", making the circumstantial element a single word rather than a clause. The circumstantial element coming after a negation is eloquent, as in your saying: ما مَرَرْتُ بِأحَدٍ إلّا قائِمًا ("I did not pass by anyone except standing").

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: how was the waw removed from the clause after إلّا, while it was not removed from it in His saying ﴿And We did not destroy any town except that it had a known decree﴾ [al-Hijr: 4]? I say: the original is the removal of the waw, because the clause is a description (sifah) of qaryah; and when the waw is added, it is to emphasize the connection of the description to the described." End of quote.

If we take لَها مُنْذِرُونَ as a clause, it would not be permissible for it to come as a description after إلّا. The position of the majority (al-jumhur) is that a description does not come after إلّا when it depends on the particle of exception, as in: ما جاءَنِي أحَدٌ إلّا راكِبٌ ("No one came to me except a rider"). When something like this is heard, they interpret it as a substitute (badal), i.e., إلّا رَجُلٌ راكِبٌ ("except a man, a rider"). What supports the soundness of this position is that the Arabs say: ما مَرَرْتُ بِأحَدٍ إلّا قائِمًا, and it is not transmitted from their speech: ما مَرَرْتُ بِأحَدٍ إلّا قائِمٌ. If the clause were in the position of a description of an indefinite noun, the singular form would have come after إلّا as a description of it. If the description does not depend on a particle, it comes after إلّا, as in: ما جاءَنِي أحَدٌ إلّا زَيْدٌ خَيْرٌ مِن عَمْرٍو; the implied sense is: ما جاءَنِي أحَدٌ خَيْرٌ مِن عَمْرٍو إلّا زَيْدٌ ("No one who is better than Amr came to me except Zayd"). As for the waw being added to emphasize the connection of the description to the described, this is not known in the works of the grammarians. If you say: جاءَنِي رَجُلٌ وعاقِلٌ, with وعاقِلٌ as a description of رَجُلٌ, it is not permitted. The waw is added to descriptions optionally only when some of them are conjoined to others and their referents differ, as in: (مَرَرْتُ) بِزَيْدٍ الكَرِيمِ والشُّجاعِ والشّاعِرِ ("I passed by Zayd the generous, the brave and the poet"). As for ﴿and their eighth is their dog﴾ [al-Kahf: 22], its discussion has already been covered in its place.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 26, verses 210–227 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And the devils did not bring it down. It is not befitting for them, nor are they able to do so. Indeed, they are cut off from hearing it.﴾ ﴿So do not invoke another god along with Allah, lest you be among those punished.﴾ ﴿And warn your nearest kinsmen.﴾ ﴿And lower your wing to those among the believers who follow you.﴾ ﴿But if they disobey you, then say: "I am innocent of what you do."﴾ ﴿And rely upon the Mighty, the Merciful,﴾ ﴿who sees you when you stand up,﴾ ﴿and your movements among those who prostrate.﴾ ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend?﴾ ﴿They descend upon every lying sinner,﴾ ﴿who give ear, and most of them are liars.﴾ ﴿And the poets, the misguided follow them.﴾ ﴿Do you not see that they wander in every valley,﴾ ﴿and that they say what they do not do?﴾ ﴿Except those who believe, do righteous deeds, remember Allah often, and defend themselves after they have been wronged. And those who have done wrong will know what a final return they will return to.﴾

The polytheists of Quraysh used to say: "Muhammad has a companion from the jinn who informs him, as soothsayers are informed." So this was revealed. The pronoun in ﴿بِهِ﴾ ("with it") refers to the Qur'an. Rather, ﴿the Trustworthy Spirit brought it down﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 193].

Al-Hasan read ﴿الشَّياطُونَ﴾ (ash-shayatun, with a waw in the nominative), which was discussed in al-Baqarah. Abu Hatim and the readers rejected it. Abu Hatim said: "It is an error on his part, or against him." Al-Nahhas said: "It is an error according to all the grammarians." Al-Mahdawi said: "It is not permissible in Arabic." Al-Farra' said: "The shaykh erred; he thought it was the nun found in the words hajā'in." Then al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: "If it is permissible to cite the verse of al-'Ajjaj and Ru'bah, then why is it not permissible to cite the reading of al-Hasan and his companion, meaning Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa', when we know that both of them recited it only after having heard it?" Yunus ibn Habib said: "I heard a Bedouin say: 'I entered gardens, and behind them were gardens (bastanun)'; so I said: 'How similar this is to the reading of al-Hasan.'" End of quotation.

This reading has been explained as follows: since its final part is like the final part of Yabrin and Filastin, just as the i'rab (case inflection) of these is applied to the nun at times and to what precedes it at other times, so they say: Yabrin and Yabrun, Filastin and Filastun. The same is applied to ash-shayatin, by analogy with them, so they say: ash-shayatin and ash-shayatun. Abu Fayd Mu'arrij al-Sadusi said: "If its derivation is from shaṭa, meaning 'to burn' (yashītu shawṭatan), then there is a basis for both readings." It was said: its basis is that the intensive pattern of it is shayyat, and its plural is ash-shayyatun. They lightened the yā', though it has been narrated from both of them that it was read with the shaddah (doubling), and others recited with it. End of quotation.

Al-A'mash read ﴿الشَّياطُونَ﴾ as well, as al-Hasan and Ibn al-Sumayfa' did. These three are among the transmitters of the Qur'an who read it this way, and it is not possible to say that they erred, because of their standing in knowledge and in the transmission of the Qur'an.

How excellent is the order of these clauses! He first negated the devils' descending with it, and negation usually applies to what is possible, though here it is impossible for the devils to descend with the Qur'an. Then He negated its suitability, meaning that even if it were assumed possible, they would not be fit for it. Then He negated their ability to do so and that it was impossible for them to descend with it. So He ascended from negating possibility, to negating suitability, to negating capacity and ability. This is an escalating emphasis in negating their descent with it. Then He gave the reason why they are excluded from hearing the speech of the people of heaven: they are pelted with meteors.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So do not invoke another god along with Allah﴾. In reality the address is to the listener, since He, exalted is He, knew that this could not be from the Messenger ﷺ. For this reason the exegetes (mufassirun) said: the meaning is, "Say, O Muhammad, to those who disbelieve: do not invoke another god along with Allah." Then He commanded him to warn his clan (ʿashīrah). The ʿashīrah is below the fakhdh (sub-clan) and above the faṣīlah (branch). He singled out the clan, although he was commanded to warn all people, as He said: ﴿to warn the people﴾ [Yunus: 2]. This is because warning them, being his own kin, leaves no room for favoritism or leniency toward them, and because they and other people are one and the same law in threat and warning. If his kin were warned and threatened, despite the compassion a person naturally feels toward them, then others would be even more and more fittingly included. Or it is because the beginning is with those nearest to him, then those after them, as He said: ﴿Fight those of the disbelievers who are near to you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 123]. And when he (ﷺ) entered Makkah he said: "Every usury of the Jahiliyyah is placed under these two feet of mine, and the first usury I place is the usury of al-ʿAbbas." Because the clan is the expected source of obedience, and he can be firmer with them than with others, and they bear more patiently with him.

The Messenger ﷺ carried out what his Lord commanded him, warning his clan. He called the nearest, then the nearest by sub-clan. Hadiths have been narrated from him about this.

﴿And lower your wing to those among the believers who follow you﴾: the discussion of these phrases was given earlier at the end of al-Hijr, and it is a metaphor for humility. One of the poets said:

*"You are renowned for lowering the wing, so do not be, in raising it, a falcon."*

He forbade him from arrogance after humility. The ajdal is the falcon. The phrase ﴿among the believers﴾ is general, covering his clan and others. Since warning results either in obedience or disobedience, the division is made upon both. The meaning is: whoever follows you as a believer, humble yourself to him. Therefore its counterpart came: ﴿But if they disobey you﴾, then disassociate yourself from them and from their deeds. In this there is a truce (muwada'ah) that was abrogated (naskh) by the verse of the sword.

The apparent reference of the pronoun in ﴿عَصَوْكَ﴾ ("they disobey you") is to those who were commanded to be warned, namely the clan, and what he disassociated himself from is their worship of idols and their taking another god. It was also said: the pronoun refers to those among the believers who followed him, meaning: if they disobey you, O Muhammad, in the rulings and branches of Islam, after their affirmation and faith in you, ﴿then say: "I am innocent of what you do"﴾, not "of you," meaning: show your displeasure with their deeds and your rejection of them. Had He commanded him to disassociate himself from them, nothing would remain after this as an intercession for the disobedient. Then Allah, exalted is He, commanded him to rely upon Him.

Nafi', Ibn ʿAmir, Abu Ja'far and Shaybah read ﴿فَتَوَكَّلْ﴾ with fa', and the rest of the seven read it with waw. The description "the Mighty" fits, meaning the One who cannot be overcome, and "the Merciful," meaning the One who has mercy on you. These two attributes are the ones that appear at the ends of the stories in this surah. So reliance upon One who has these two attributes suffices you against the evil of whoever hates you among these people and others. He overcomes your enemies by His might, and gives you victory over them by His mercy. Reliance (tawakkul) is entrusting the matter to the one who owns the matter and has power over it.

Then He was described as the One before whom you are in plain sight, and this is from His mercy to you, that He qualified you to worship Him, and to what you do of tahajjud (night prayer). Most of the exegetes, including Ibn ʿAbbas, held that the meaning is "when you stand up for prayer."

The majority read ﴿وَتَقَلُّبَكَ﴾ as a verbal noun of taqallaba, coordinated with the kaf in ﴿يَراكَ﴾. Jannah ibn Hubaysh read ﴿وَتَقَلَّبُكَ﴾ as the imperfect of qallaba with shaddah, coordinated with ﴿يَراكَ﴾. Mujahid and Qatadah said: ﴿فِي السَّاجِدِينَ﴾ ("among those who prostrate") means among the worshippers who pray. Ibn ʿAbbas said: in the loins of Adam, Noah and Abraham until you came forth. ʿIkrimah said: He sees you standing and prostrating. It was said: the meaning of "stand up" (taqumu) is that you are alone with yourself. Also from Mujahid: what is meant is the turning of his gaze toward those who pray behind him, as he said: "Complete the bowing and prostration, for by Allah I see you from behind me." In Ibn ʿAtiyyah's al-Wajiz: the apparent meaning of the verse is that it refers to standing in prayer, and it may also refer to all his conduct, and this is the interpretation of Mujahid and Qatadah. "Among those who prostrate" means your prayer with those who pray, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrimah and others. Ibn ʿAbbas also said, and Qatadah: it means your turning among the believers, so he referred to them by "those who prostrate." Ibn Jubayr said: it means the prophets, that is, your turning as the other prophets turned. Al-Zamakhshari said: He mentioned what he used to do in the depths of the night, standing for tahajjud, and turning as he examined the states of the worshippers among his companions, so that he could observe them without their noticing, and know their inner states and how they worked for their hereafter. It is related that when the obligation of the night prayer was abrogated, he went around the houses of his companions that night to see what they were doing, out of his eagerness for them and for the acts of obedience and good deeds that were found among them. He found their houses like beehives, because of what he heard of their murmuring with the remembrance of Allah and recitation. The intended meaning of "those who prostrate" is those who pray. It was also said: its meaning is He sees you when you stand up to lead the people in congregational prayer, and your turning among those who prostrate is your movement among them in their standing, bowing, prostrating and sitting when you lead them. It is related from Muqatil that he asked Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him: "Do you find congregational prayer in the Qur'an?" So he recited this verse. It is also possible that your condition is not hidden from Me, whenever you stand and turn among those who prostrate, in the sufficiency of the affairs of religion. End of quotation.

﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing﴾ of what you say, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of what you intend and do. The Rafidah went to the view that the fathers of the Prophet ﷺ were believers, and they took as evidence His saying: ﴿and your turning among those who prostrate﴾. They said: it admits the aspects that were mentioned, and it admits that the meaning is that He moved his soul from one prostrating person to another prostrating person, as we say. When it admits all these aspects, it is necessary to take the verse as covering all of them, because there is no contradiction and no preference among them. They also cited his (ﷺ) saying: "I was never moved from the loins of pure men to the wombs of pure women," and whoever was a disbeliever is impure, based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, the polytheists are impure﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28]. As for His saying: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar﴾ [al-An'am: 74], the word "father" may be applied to an uncle, as the sons of Jacob said to him: ﴿We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac﴾ [al-Baqarah: 133]. They called Ishmael a "father," although he was an uncle to them.

* *

﴿Say: "Shall I inform you?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 60], meaning: say, O Muhammad, "Shall I tell you?" This is an interrogative of confirmation and affirmation. The phrase ﴿upon whom﴾ is connected to ﴿descend﴾ ("tanazzalu"), and the clause containing the sense of the interrogative is in the position of an object for ﴿unabbi'ukum﴾ ("I inform you"), because it is suspended (mu'allaq), since it means "I make you know." If you consider it transitive to two objects, it stands in place of the second object; if you consider it transitive to three, it stands in place of the two. When the interrogative is suspended from the governing verb, it does not remain in its true sense of seeking information, but its meaning reverts to that of a statement. Do you not see that when you say: "I knew whether Zayd was in the house or ʿAmr," the meaning is: "I knew one of them was in the house"? The meaning is not that knowledge proceeded from him, and then he asked the addressee to specify who was in the house, Zayd or ʿAmr. So the meaning here is: "Shall I make you know upon whom the devils descend?" not that he asked the addressees about the person upon whom the devils descend.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) on surah 26, verses 210–227 (part 2 of 2):

Since this is the meaning, the report comes after it with His saying: ﴿The devils descend upon every lying, sinful one.﴾ It is as if, when He said, "Shall I inform you of such-and-such?" it was said to Him, "Inform us," and He said: ﴿They descend upon every lying one﴾, who abounds in *ifk* (lying), which is falsehood. *Athim* (sinful) means one who abounds in sin. *Affak* and *athim* are both intensive forms (*sighatai mubalagha*, forms of emphasis), and the intended referents are the soothsayers (*al-kahana*). The pronoun in ﴿yulqun﴾ (they cast) may refer to the devils, meaning they listen attentively and give ear, in order to snatch something of what the angels say, so that they then bring it down to the soothsayers. Or it may mean ﴿yulqun al-sam'a﴾ (they cast the hearing), that is, what is heard, to those upon whom they descend. (And most of them), that is, most of the devils who cast, ﴿are liars﴾.

So, on the meaning of listening attentively, the clause is a resumptive report (*isti'naf ikhbar*, a new independent statement). On the meaning of casting what is heard to the soothsayers, it may be a resumptive statement, and it may also be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the devils, meaning: "The devils descend upon every lying, sinful one, casting what they have heard." It is also possible that the pronoun in ﴿yulqun﴾ refers back to ﴿every lying, sinful one﴾, and the pronoun is made plural because ﴿every lying one﴾ carries a general sense (*'umum*) and includes individuals beneath it. It was also held that the meaning is: they cast their hearing to the devils, so that the devils may convey to them what they fix in their ears; or that ﴿yulqun al-sam'a﴾ means they cast what is heard from the devils to people. And most of them, that is, most of the soothsayers, are liars. This accords with what is reported: they receive from the devils a single word that was heard from heaven, and they mix with it a hundred lies. When that one word proves true, it becomes a cause of misguidance for whoever hears it.

If the pronoun refers back to ﴿every lying one﴾, then ﴿yulqun﴾ may be a resumptive report about the liars, or it may be a qualifier (*sifa*) of ﴿every lying one﴾. There is no contradiction between His saying ﴿every lying one﴾ and His saying ﴿and most of them are liars﴾, because the *affak* is the one who abounds in lying, and this does not indicate that he speaks only falsehood. So the meaning is: among the liars, whoever tells the truth regarding what he relates from the jinn is, in most cases, deluded.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: ﴿And it is indeed a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 192], and ﴿The devils did not bring it down﴾, and ﴿Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend?﴾ — why did He separate these [from one another] and [why did He separate them] from [their] brothers?" He answered: "The intention is to separate them by verses that are not in their meaning, so that one returns to the coming of them, and the mention of what is in them praises it again and again. Thereby it indicates that the meaning in which they were revealed is among the meanings that ascribed to Allah's aversion toward them. The example is: a man narrates a story, and in his breast there is concern for something in it and special care for it, so you see him repeat its mention and never cease returning to it." End of quotation.

When He mentioned the soothsayers with their great falsehood and their state, which required denying the speech of the Qur'an (since some of the disbelievers had said about the Qur'an that it is poetry, just as they said about the Messenger that he is a soothsayer, and that what he brought is of the category of soothsaying), Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Nor is it the word of a soothsayer﴾ [al-Haqqah: 42], and He said: ﴿Nor is it the word of a poet﴾ [al-Haqqah: 41].

Then He said: ﴿As for the poets, the deviators follow them.﴾ It was said: this was revealed concerning Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt, Abu 'Izzah, Musafi' al-Jumahi, Hubayrah ibn Abi Wahb, Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith, and Ibn al-Zib'ara. Ibn al-Zib'ara and Abu Sufyan embraced Islam. The word *al-shu'ara'* (the poets) is general and includes every poet, and the one blamed is he who satirizes and praises for a forbidden desire, slanders chaste women, speaks falsehood, and says what is not lawful in the Shari'ah.

'Isa read *al-shu'ara'a* with a fatha (accusative), as an *ishtighal* construction (where a verb governs a pronoun referring to the noun that precedes it, so that the noun is put in the accusative). The majority read it with a damma (nominative), as a subject and predicate (*mubtada' wa khabar*). Al-Sulami, al-Hasan (with a variant from him), and Nafi' read *yatba'uhum* with a single *ta'* (lightened), while the rest of the seven read it with the doubled *ta'* (shaddah). Al-Hasan and 'Abd al-Warith, from Abu 'Amr, read the *'ayn* with a sukun. Harun reported the accusative of it from some of them, and this is problematic.

*Al-ghawun* (the deviators): Ibn 'Abbas said: "the transmitters (*al-ruwat*)." He also said: "those who admire their poetry and keep company with them." 'Ikrimah said: "the rabble who follow the poet." Mujahid and Qatadah said: "the devils." 'Ata' said: "the foolish polytheists who follow their poets."

﴿Have you not seen that they wander in every valley?﴾ This is a figurative image of their going off in every path of speech, their recklessness, their lack of concern in exaggerating in speech, and their overstepping the limit of moderation in it, to the point that they prefer the most cowardly of people over 'Antarah, the most miserly over Hatim, slander the innocent, and call the pious a sinner. Ibn 'Abbas said: "It is their making the good ugly and their making the ugly good."

﴿And that they say what they do not do.﴾ This is because of their excess in the varieties of speech and their fondness for eloquence and subtle meanings: they may attribute to themselves what never happened to them. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, dismissed the hadd (prescribed punishment) for wine from al-Nu'man ibn 'Adi, on account of a poem he had composed to his wife, when he argued against him with this verse. He had appointed him over Bisan, then dismissed him and wanted to flog him. And al-Farazdaq, for Sulayman ibn 'Abd al-Malik, said:

*fa-bitna ka-annahunna musarra'at, wa-bittu afuddu aghlaq al-khitam*

(So they spent the night as if they were struck down, and I spent the night breaking open the seals of the wine-jars.)

Sulayman said to him: "The hadd has become binding upon you." He said: "Allah has averted the hadd from me by His saying: ﴿And that they say what they do not do.﴾"

He, the Exalted, informed about the poets with the states that contradict the state of prophethood, since their affair, as He mentioned, is following the deviators, taking up the varieties of speech, praising and blaming things, and attributing to them what did not happen. This is unlike the state of prophethood, for it is one path, followed only by the rightly guided. The call of the prophets is one: calling to the Oneness of Allah and His worship, encouraging the Hereafter, and truthfulness. Moreover, what they brought cannot be brought by anyone else, given the manifestation of the miracle.

Since what preceded was a censure of the poets, He made an exception among them for those who were characterized by faith, righteous deeds, and frequent remembrance of Allah, and that (remembrance) predominated over their poetry. When they composed poetry, it was about the Oneness of Allah, praising Him, praising His Messenger ﷺ and his Companions, admonition, asceticism, good manners, facilitating knowledge, and everything about which speech is lawful in the Shari'ah. So they are not stained in their speech by sin or defect. Poetry is a category of speech: its good is good, and its ugly is ugly.

A man from the 'Alawi family said to 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd: "My chest surges with poetry." He said: "What prevents you from it in what is not harmful?"

It was said: the intended ones excepted are Hassan, 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah, Ka'b ibn Malik, Ka'b ibn Zuhayr, and whoever defended the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Ka'b ibn Malik: "Satirize them, for by Him in whose hand is my soul, it is more painful to them than arrows." And he said to Hassan: "Say, and the Holy Spirit is with you." This is the meaning of His saying ﴿and they defend themselves﴾, that is, with speech against whoever wronged them.

'Ata' ibn Yasar and others said: when He censured the poets with His saying ﴿As for the poets﴾, the verse was grievous to Hassan, Ibn Rawahah, and Ka'b ibn Malik, and they mentioned that to the Messenger, peace be upon him. Then the verse of exception was revealed at Medina. Ibn Zayd restricted His saying ﴿and remember Allah much﴾ and said: that is, in their poetry. Ibn 'Abbas said: it became a disposition and habit for them, as Labid said when he was asked for his poetry: "Allah has replaced poetry for me with the Qur'an, which is better than it."

When He mentioned ﴿and they defend themselves after they have been wronged﴾, He threatened the wrongdoers with this great, terrifying threat that splits the livers, and He left it vague in His saying: ﴿Those who have wronged will know what sort of return they will return to.﴾

When Abu Bakr appointed 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, he recited to him: ﴿Those who have wronged will know what sort of return they will return to,﴾ and the pious predecessors (*al-salaf al-salih*) would admonish one another with it. What is understood from the Shari'ah is that those who wronged are the disbelievers. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Explaining *zulm* (wrong) as disbelief is a specification (*ta'lil*), and he had mentioned earlier that ﴿those who wronged﴾ is unrestricted, and this is from him in the manner of the Mu'tazilah (*i'tizal*)."

Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Arqam, from al-Hasan, read *ayya munfalatin yanfalitun* (with a fa' and two ta's). Its meaning: those who wronged hope to escape from the punishment of Allah, but they will know that there is no way for them to escape, which is salvation. *Wa-sa-ya'lamu* here is suspended (*mu'allaqah*, i.e., the verb of knowing is blocked from governing what follows). *Ayya munqalabin* is an interrogative, and the element governing it is *yanqalibun*, which is a verbal noun (*masdar*). The clause occupies the position of the object of *sa-ya'lamu*.

Abu al-Baqa' said: *ayya munqalabin* is a masdar that is an adjective (*na't*) of a deleted masdar, and the governing element is *yanqalibun inqalaban ayya munqalabin*, and *ya'lamu* does not govern it, because an interrogative is not governed by what precedes it. End of quotation. This is confused, because *ayya*, when it is described by something, is not an interrogative; rather the *ayyu* described is a qualifier (*qasam*) of the *ayya* being asked about, not an oath. *Ayyu* may be conditional, interrogative, relative, or a qualifier according to the opinion of al-Akhfash (where it modifies an indefinite noun, as in: *marartu bi-ayyin mu'jibin laka*, "I passed by someone wonderful to you"), and it may be a form of vocative, connecting to the vocative of what has *al* (the definite article), as in: *ya ayyuha al-rajul* ("O man"). Al-Akhfash claims that the one used in the vocative is a relative. The position of the majority is that it is an independent category (*qasam bi-ra'sihi*), and the qualifier occurs as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of a definite noun. These are the categories of *ayy*. So when you say: "You know what kind of striking you strike," it is interrogative, not a qualifier of a deleted masdar.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 26, verses 210–227 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And the devils did not bring it down. It is not befitting for them, nor are they able to do so. Indeed, they are cut off from hearing it.﴾ ﴿So do not invoke another god along with Allah, lest you be among those punished.﴾ ﴿And warn your nearest kinsmen.﴾ ﴿And lower your wing to those among the believers who follow you.﴾ ﴿But if they disobey you, then say: "I am innocent of what you do."﴾ ﴿And rely upon the Mighty, the Merciful,﴾ ﴿who sees you when you stand up,﴾ ﴿and your movements among those who prostrate.﴾ ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend?﴾ ﴿They descend upon every lying sinner,﴾ ﴿who give ear, and most of them are liars.﴾ ﴿And the poets, the misguided follow them.﴾ ﴿Do you not see that they wander in every valley,﴾ ﴿and that they say what they do not do?﴾ ﴿Except those who believe, do righteous deeds, remember Allah often, and defend themselves after they have been wronged. And those who have done wrong will know what a final return they will return to.﴾

The polytheists of Quraysh used to say: "Muhammad has a companion from the jinn who informs him, as soothsayers are informed." So this was revealed. The pronoun in ﴿بِهِ﴾ ("with it") refers to the Qur'an. Rather, ﴿the Trustworthy Spirit brought it down﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 193].

Al-Hasan read ﴿الشَّياطُونَ﴾ (ash-shayatun, with a waw in the nominative), which was discussed in al-Baqarah. Abu Hatim and the readers rejected it. Abu Hatim said: "It is an error on his part, or against him." Al-Nahhas said: "It is an error according to all the grammarians." Al-Mahdawi said: "It is not permissible in Arabic." Al-Farra' said: "The shaykh erred; he thought it was the nun found in the words hajā'in." Then al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: "If it is permissible to cite the verse of al-'Ajjaj and Ru'bah, then why is it not permissible to cite the reading of al-Hasan and his companion, meaning Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa', when we know that both of them recited it only after having heard it?" Yunus ibn Habib said: "I heard a Bedouin say: 'I entered gardens, and behind them were gardens (bastanun)'; so I said: 'How similar this is to the reading of al-Hasan.'" End of quotation.

This reading has been explained as follows: since its final part is like the final part of Yabrin and Filastin, just as the i'rab (case inflection) of these is applied to the nun at times and to what precedes it at other times, so they say: Yabrin and Yabrun, Filastin and Filastun. The same is applied to ash-shayatin, by analogy with them, so they say: ash-shayatin and ash-shayatun. Abu Fayd Mu'arrij al-Sadusi said: "If its derivation is from shaṭa, meaning 'to burn' (yashītu shawṭatan), then there is a basis for both readings." It was said: its basis is that the intensive pattern of it is shayyat, and its plural is ash-shayyatun. They lightened the yā', though it has been narrated from both of them that it was read with the shaddah (doubling), and others recited with it. End of quotation.

Al-A'mash read ﴿الشَّياطُونَ﴾ as well, as al-Hasan and Ibn al-Sumayfa' did. These three are among the transmitters of the Qur'an who read it this way, and it is not possible to say that they erred, because of their standing in knowledge and in the transmission of the Qur'an.

How excellent is the order of these clauses! He first negated the devils' descending with it, and negation usually applies to what is possible, though here it is impossible for the devils to descend with the Qur'an. Then He negated its suitability, meaning that even if it were assumed possible, they would not be fit for it. Then He negated their ability to do so and that it was impossible for them to descend with it. So He ascended from negating possibility, to negating suitability, to negating capacity and ability. This is an escalating emphasis in negating their descent with it. Then He gave the reason why they are excluded from hearing the speech of the people of heaven: they are pelted with meteors.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So do not invoke another god along with Allah﴾. In reality the address is to the listener, since He, exalted is He, knew that this could not be from the Messenger ﷺ. For this reason the exegetes (mufassirun) said: the meaning is, "Say, O Muhammad, to those who disbelieve: do not invoke another god along with Allah." Then He commanded him to warn his clan (ʿashīrah). The ʿashīrah is below the fakhdh (sub-clan) and above the faṣīlah (branch). He singled out the clan, although he was commanded to warn all people, as He said: ﴿to warn the people﴾ [Yunus: 2]. This is because warning them, being his own kin, leaves no room for favoritism or leniency toward them, and because they and other people are one and the same law in threat and warning. If his kin were warned and threatened, despite the compassion a person naturally feels toward them, then others would be even more and more fittingly included. Or it is because the beginning is with those nearest to him, then those after them, as He said: ﴿Fight those of the disbelievers who are near to you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 123]. And when he (ﷺ) entered Makkah he said: "Every usury of the Jahiliyyah is placed under these two feet of mine, and the first usury I place is the usury of al-ʿAbbas." Because the clan is the expected source of obedience, and he can be firmer with them than with others, and they bear more patiently with him.

The Messenger ﷺ carried out what his Lord commanded him, warning his clan. He called the nearest, then the nearest by sub-clan. Hadiths have been narrated from him about this.

﴿And lower your wing to those among the believers who follow you﴾: the discussion of these phrases was given earlier at the end of al-Hijr, and it is a metaphor for humility. One of the poets said:

*"You are renowned for lowering the wing, so do not be, in raising it, a falcon."*

He forbade him from arrogance after humility. The ajdal is the falcon. The phrase ﴿among the believers﴾ is general, covering his clan and others. Since warning results either in obedience or disobedience, the division is made upon both. The meaning is: whoever follows you as a believer, humble yourself to him. Therefore its counterpart came: ﴿But if they disobey you﴾, then disassociate yourself from them and from their deeds. In this there is a truce (muwada'ah) that was abrogated (naskh) by the verse of the sword.

The apparent reference of the pronoun in ﴿عَصَوْكَ﴾ ("they disobey you") is to those who were commanded to be warned, namely the clan, and what he disassociated himself from is their worship of idols and their taking another god. It was also said: the pronoun refers to those among the believers who followed him, meaning: if they disobey you, O Muhammad, in the rulings and branches of Islam, after their affirmation and faith in you, ﴿then say: "I am innocent of what you do"﴾, not "of you," meaning: show your displeasure with their deeds and your rejection of them. Had He commanded him to disassociate himself from them, nothing would remain after this as an intercession for the disobedient. Then Allah, exalted is He, commanded him to rely upon Him.

Nafi', Ibn ʿAmir, Abu Ja'far and Shaybah read ﴿فَتَوَكَّلْ﴾ with fa', and the rest of the seven read it with waw. The description "the Mighty" fits, meaning the One who cannot be overcome, and "the Merciful," meaning the One who has mercy on you. These two attributes are the ones that appear at the ends of the stories in this surah. So reliance upon One who has these two attributes suffices you against the evil of whoever hates you among these people and others. He overcomes your enemies by His might, and gives you victory over them by His mercy. Reliance (tawakkul) is entrusting the matter to the one who owns the matter and has power over it.

Then He was described as the One before whom you are in plain sight, and this is from His mercy to you, that He qualified you to worship Him, and to what you do of tahajjud (night prayer). Most of the exegetes, including Ibn ʿAbbas, held that the meaning is "when you stand up for prayer."

The majority read ﴿وَتَقَلُّبَكَ﴾ as a verbal noun of taqallaba, coordinated with the kaf in ﴿يَراكَ﴾. Jannah ibn Hubaysh read ﴿وَتَقَلَّبُكَ﴾ as the imperfect of qallaba with shaddah, coordinated with ﴿يَراكَ﴾. Mujahid and Qatadah said: ﴿فِي السَّاجِدِينَ﴾ ("among those who prostrate") means among the worshippers who pray. Ibn ʿAbbas said: in the loins of Adam, Noah and Abraham until you came forth. ʿIkrimah said: He sees you standing and prostrating. It was said: the meaning of "stand up" (taqumu) is that you are alone with yourself. Also from Mujahid: what is meant is the turning of his gaze toward those who pray behind him, as he said: "Complete the bowing and prostration, for by Allah I see you from behind me." In Ibn ʿAtiyyah's al-Wajiz: the apparent meaning of the verse is that it refers to standing in prayer, and it may also refer to all his conduct, and this is the interpretation of Mujahid and Qatadah. "Among those who prostrate" means your prayer with those who pray, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrimah and others. Ibn ʿAbbas also said, and Qatadah: it means your turning among the believers, so he referred to them by "those who prostrate." Ibn Jubayr said: it means the prophets, that is, your turning as the other prophets turned. Al-Zamakhshari said: He mentioned what he used to do in the depths of the night, standing for tahajjud, and turning as he examined the states of the worshippers among his companions, so that he could observe them without their noticing, and know their inner states and how they worked for their hereafter. It is related that when the obligation of the night prayer was abrogated, he went around the houses of his companions that night to see what they were doing, out of his eagerness for them and for the acts of obedience and good deeds that were found among them. He found their houses like beehives, because of what he heard of their murmuring with the remembrance of Allah and recitation. The intended meaning of "those who prostrate" is those who pray. It was also said: its meaning is He sees you when you stand up to lead the people in congregational prayer, and your turning among those who prostrate is your movement among them in their standing, bowing, prostrating and sitting when you lead them. It is related from Muqatil that he asked Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him: "Do you find congregational prayer in the Qur'an?" So he recited this verse. It is also possible that your condition is not hidden from Me, whenever you stand and turn among those who prostrate, in the sufficiency of the affairs of religion. End of quotation.

﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing﴾ of what you say, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of what you intend and do. The Rafidah went to the view that the fathers of the Prophet ﷺ were believers, and they took as evidence His saying: ﴿and your turning among those who prostrate﴾. They said: it admits the aspects that were mentioned, and it admits that the meaning is that He moved his soul from one prostrating person to another prostrating person, as we say. When it admits all these aspects, it is necessary to take the verse as covering all of them, because there is no contradiction and no preference among them. They also cited his (ﷺ) saying: "I was never moved from the loins of pure men to the wombs of pure women," and whoever was a disbeliever is impure, based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, the polytheists are impure﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28]. As for His saying: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar﴾ [al-An'am: 74], the word "father" may be applied to an uncle, as the sons of Jacob said to him: ﴿We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac﴾ [al-Baqarah: 133]. They called Ishmael a "father," although he was an uncle to them.

* *

﴿Say: "Shall I inform you?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 60], meaning: say, O Muhammad, "Shall I tell you?" This is an interrogative of confirmation and affirmation. The phrase ﴿upon whom﴾ is connected to ﴿descend﴾ ("tanazzalu"), and the clause containing the sense of the interrogative is in the position of an object for ﴿unabbi'ukum﴾ ("I inform you"), because it is suspended (mu'allaq), since it means "I make you know." If you consider it transitive to two objects, it stands in place of the second object; if you consider it transitive to three, it stands in place of the two. When the interrogative is suspended from the governing verb, it does not remain in its true sense of seeking information, but its meaning reverts to that of a statement. Do you not see that when you say: "I knew whether Zayd was in the house or ʿAmr," the meaning is: "I knew one of them was in the house"? The meaning is not that knowledge proceeded from him, and then he asked the addressee to specify who was in the house, Zayd or ʿAmr. So the meaning here is: "Shall I make you know upon whom the devils descend?" not that he asked the addressees about the person upon whom the devils descend.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) on surah 26, verses 210–227 (part 2 of 2):

Since this is the meaning, the report comes after it with His saying: ﴿The devils descend upon every lying, sinful one.﴾ It is as if, when He said, "Shall I inform you of such-and-such?" it was said to Him, "Inform us," and He said: ﴿They descend upon every lying one﴾, who abounds in *ifk* (lying), which is falsehood. *Athim* (sinful) means one who abounds in sin. *Affak* and *athim* are both intensive forms (*sighatai mubalagha*, forms of emphasis), and the intended referents are the soothsayers (*al-kahana*). The pronoun in ﴿yulqun﴾ (they cast) may refer to the devils, meaning they listen attentively and give ear, in order to snatch something of what the angels say, so that they then bring it down to the soothsayers. Or it may mean ﴿yulqun al-sam'a﴾ (they cast the hearing), that is, what is heard, to those upon whom they descend. (And most of them), that is, most of the devils who cast, ﴿are liars﴾.

So, on the meaning of listening attentively, the clause is a resumptive report (*isti'naf ikhbar*, a new independent statement). On the meaning of casting what is heard to the soothsayers, it may be a resumptive statement, and it may also be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the devils, meaning: "The devils descend upon every lying, sinful one, casting what they have heard." It is also possible that the pronoun in ﴿yulqun﴾ refers back to ﴿every lying, sinful one﴾, and the pronoun is made plural because ﴿every lying one﴾ carries a general sense (*'umum*) and includes individuals beneath it. It was also held that the meaning is: they cast their hearing to the devils, so that the devils may convey to them what they fix in their ears; or that ﴿yulqun al-sam'a﴾ means they cast what is heard from the devils to people. And most of them, that is, most of the soothsayers, are liars. This accords with what is reported: they receive from the devils a single word that was heard from heaven, and they mix with it a hundred lies. When that one word proves true, it becomes a cause of misguidance for whoever hears it.

If the pronoun refers back to ﴿every lying one﴾, then ﴿yulqun﴾ may be a resumptive report about the liars, or it may be a qualifier (*sifa*) of ﴿every lying one﴾. There is no contradiction between His saying ﴿every lying one﴾ and His saying ﴿and most of them are liars﴾, because the *affak* is the one who abounds in lying, and this does not indicate that he speaks only falsehood. So the meaning is: among the liars, whoever tells the truth regarding what he relates from the jinn is, in most cases, deluded.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: ﴿And it is indeed a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 192], and ﴿The devils did not bring it down﴾, and ﴿Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend?﴾ — why did He separate these [from one another] and [why did He separate them] from [their] brothers?" He answered: "The intention is to separate them by verses that are not in their meaning, so that one returns to the coming of them, and the mention of what is in them praises it again and again. Thereby it indicates that the meaning in which they were revealed is among the meanings that ascribed to Allah's aversion toward them. The example is: a man narrates a story, and in his breast there is concern for something in it and special care for it, so you see him repeat its mention and never cease returning to it." End of quotation.

When He mentioned the soothsayers with their great falsehood and their state, which required denying the speech of the Qur'an (since some of the disbelievers had said about the Qur'an that it is poetry, just as they said about the Messenger that he is a soothsayer, and that what he brought is of the category of soothsaying), Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Nor is it the word of a soothsayer﴾ [al-Haqqah: 42], and He said: ﴿Nor is it the word of a poet﴾ [al-Haqqah: 41].

Then He said: ﴿As for the poets, the deviators follow them.﴾ It was said: this was revealed concerning Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt, Abu 'Izzah, Musafi' al-Jumahi, Hubayrah ibn Abi Wahb, Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith, and Ibn al-Zib'ara. Ibn al-Zib'ara and Abu Sufyan embraced Islam. The word *al-shu'ara'* (the poets) is general and includes every poet, and the one blamed is he who satirizes and praises for a forbidden desire, slanders chaste women, speaks falsehood, and says what is not lawful in the Shari'ah.

'Isa read *al-shu'ara'a* with a fatha (accusative), as an *ishtighal* construction (where a verb governs a pronoun referring to the noun that precedes it, so that the noun is put in the accusative). The majority read it with a damma (nominative), as a subject and predicate (*mubtada' wa khabar*). Al-Sulami, al-Hasan (with a variant from him), and Nafi' read *yatba'uhum* with a single *ta'* (lightened), while the rest of the seven read it with the doubled *ta'* (shaddah).
