Al-Hasan and 'Abd al-Warith, from Abu 'Amr, read the *'ayn* with a sukun. Harun reported the accusative of it from some of them, and this is problematic.

*Al-ghawun* (the deviators): Ibn 'Abbas said: "the transmitters (*al-ruwat*)." He also said: "those who admire their poetry and keep company with them." 'Ikrimah said: "the rabble who follow the poet." Mujahid and Qatadah said: "the devils." 'Ata' said: "the foolish polytheists who follow their poets."

﴿Have you not seen that they wander in every valley?﴾ This is a figurative image of their going off in every path of speech, their recklessness, their lack of concern in exaggerating in speech, and their overstepping the limit of moderation in it, to the point that they prefer the most cowardly of people over 'Antarah, the most miserly over Hatim, slander the innocent, and call the pious a sinner. Ibn 'Abbas said: "It is their making the good ugly and their making the ugly good."

﴿And that they say what they do not do.﴾ This is because of their excess in the varieties of speech and their fondness for eloquence and subtle meanings: they may attribute to themselves what never happened to them. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, dismissed the hadd (prescribed punishment) for wine from al-Nu'man ibn 'Adi, on account of a poem he had composed to his wife, when he argued against him with this verse. He had appointed him over Bisan, then dismissed him and wanted to flog him. And al-Farazdaq, for Sulayman ibn 'Abd al-Malik, said:

*fa-bitna ka-annahunna musarra'at, wa-bittu afuddu aghlaq al-khitam*

(So they spent the night as if they were struck down, and I spent the night breaking open the seals of the wine-jars.)

Sulayman said to him: "The hadd has become binding upon you." He said: "Allah has averted the hadd from me by His saying: ﴿And that they say what they do not do.﴾"

He, the Exalted, informed about the poets with the states that contradict the state of prophethood, since their affair, as He mentioned, is following the deviators, taking up the varieties of speech, praising and blaming things, and attributing to them what did not happen. This is unlike the state of prophethood, for it is one path, followed only by the rightly guided. The call of the prophets is one: calling to the Oneness of Allah and His worship, encouraging the Hereafter, and truthfulness. Moreover, what they brought cannot be brought by anyone else, given the manifestation of the miracle.

Since what preceded was a censure of the poets, He made an exception among them for those who were characterized by faith, righteous deeds, and frequent remembrance of Allah, and that (remembrance) predominated over their poetry. When they composed poetry, it was about the Oneness of Allah, praising Him, praising His Messenger ﷺ and his Companions, admonition, asceticism, good manners, facilitating knowledge, and everything about which speech is lawful in the Shari'ah. So they are not stained in their speech by sin or defect. Poetry is a category of speech: its good is good, and its ugly is ugly.

A man from the 'Alawi family said to 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd: "My chest surges with poetry." He said: "What prevents you from it in what is not harmful?"

It was said: the intended ones excepted are Hassan, 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah, Ka'b ibn Malik, Ka'b ibn Zuhayr, and whoever defended the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Ka'b ibn Malik: "Satirize them, for by Him in whose hand is my soul, it is more painful to them than arrows." And he said to Hassan: "Say, and the Holy Spirit is with you." This is the meaning of His saying ﴿and they defend themselves﴾, that is, with speech against whoever wronged them.

'Ata' ibn Yasar and others said: when He censured the poets with His saying ﴿As for the poets﴾, the verse was grievous to Hassan, Ibn Rawahah, and Ka'b ibn Malik, and they mentioned that to the Messenger, peace be upon him. Then the verse of exception was revealed at Medina. Ibn Zayd restricted His saying ﴿and remember Allah much﴾ and said: that is, in their poetry. Ibn 'Abbas said: it became a disposition and habit for them, as Labid said when he was asked for his poetry: "Allah has replaced poetry for me with the Qur'an, which is better than it."

When He mentioned ﴿and they defend themselves after they have been wronged﴾, He threatened the wrongdoers with this great, terrifying threat that splits the livers, and He left it vague in His saying: ﴿Those who have wronged will know what sort of return they will return to.﴾

When Abu Bakr appointed 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, he recited to him: ﴿Those who have wronged will know what sort of return they will return to,﴾ and the pious predecessors (*al-salaf al-salih*) would admonish one another with it. What is understood from the Shari'ah is that those who wronged are the disbelievers. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Explaining *zulm* (wrong) as disbelief is a specification (*ta'lil*), and he had mentioned earlier that ﴿those who wronged﴾ is unrestricted, and this is from him in the manner of the Mu'tazilah (*i'tizal*)."

Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Arqam, from al-Hasan, read *ayya munfalatin yanfalitun* (with a fa' and two ta's). Its meaning: those who wronged hope to escape from the punishment of Allah, but they will know that there is no way for them to escape, which is salvation. *Wa-sa-ya'lamu* here is suspended (*mu'allaqah*, i.e., the verb of knowing is blocked from governing what follows). *Ayya munqalabin* is an interrogative, and the element governing it is *yanqalibun*, which is a verbal noun (*masdar*). The clause occupies the position of the object of *sa-ya'lamu*.

Abu al-Baqa' said: *ayya munqalabin* is a masdar that is an adjective (*na't*) of a deleted masdar, and the governing element is *yanqalibun inqalaban ayya munqalabin*, and *ya'lamu* does not govern it, because an interrogative is not governed by what precedes it. End of quotation. This is confused, because *ayya*, when it is described by something, is not an interrogative; rather the *ayyu* described is a qualifier (*qasam*) of the *ayya* being asked about, not an oath. *Ayyu* may be conditional, interrogative, relative, or a qualifier according to the opinion of al-Akhfash (where it modifies an indefinite noun, as in: *marartu bi-ayyin mu'jibin laka*, "I passed by someone wonderful to you"), and it may be a form of vocative, connecting to the vocative of what has *al* (the definite article), as in: *ya ayyuha al-rajul* ("O man"). Al-Akhfash claims that the one used in the vocative is a relative. The position of the majority is that it is an independent category (*qasam bi-ra'sihi*), and the qualifier occurs as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of a definite noun. These are the categories of *ayy*. So when you say: "You know what kind of striking you strike," it is interrogative, not a qualifier of a deleted masdar.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 26, verses 210–227 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And the devils did not bring it down. It is not befitting for them, nor are they able to do so. Indeed, they are cut off from hearing it.﴾ ﴿So do not invoke another god along with Allah, lest you be among those punished.﴾ ﴿And warn your nearest kinsmen.﴾ ﴿And lower your wing to those among the believers who follow you.﴾ ﴿But if they disobey you, then say: "I am innocent of what you do."﴾ ﴿And rely upon the Mighty, the Merciful,﴾ ﴿who sees you when you stand up,﴾ ﴿and your movements among those who prostrate.﴾ ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend?﴾ ﴿They descend upon every lying sinner,﴾ ﴿who give ear, and most of them are liars.﴾ ﴿And the poets, the misguided follow them.﴾ ﴿Do you not see that they wander in every valley,﴾ ﴿and that they say what they do not do?﴾ ﴿Except those who believe, do righteous deeds, remember Allah often, and defend themselves after they have been wronged. And those who have done wrong will know what a final return they will return to.﴾

The polytheists of Quraysh used to say: "Muhammad has a companion from the jinn who informs him, as soothsayers are informed." So this was revealed. The pronoun in ﴿بِهِ﴾ ("with it") refers to the Qur'an. Rather, ﴿the Trustworthy Spirit brought it down﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 193].

Al-Hasan read ﴿الشَّياطُونَ﴾ (ash-shayatun, with a waw in the nominative), which was discussed in al-Baqarah. Abu Hatim and the readers rejected it. Abu Hatim said: "It is an error on his part, or against him." Al-Nahhas said: "It is an error according to all the grammarians." Al-Mahdawi said: "It is not permissible in Arabic." Al-Farra' said: "The shaykh erred; he thought it was the nun found in the words hajā'in." Then al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: "If it is permissible to cite the verse of al-'Ajjaj and Ru'bah, then why is it not permissible to cite the reading of al-Hasan and his companion, meaning Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa', when we know that both of them recited it only after having heard it?" Yunus ibn Habib said: "I heard a Bedouin say: 'I entered gardens, and behind them were gardens (bastanun)'; so I said: 'How similar this is to the reading of al-Hasan.'" End of quotation.

This reading has been explained as follows: since its final part is like the final part of Yabrin and Filastin, just as the i'rab (case inflection) of these is applied to the nun at times and to what precedes it at other times, so they say: Yabrin and Yabrun, Filastin and Filastun. The same is applied to ash-shayatin, by analogy with them, so they say: ash-shayatin and ash-shayatun. Abu Fayd Mu'arrij al-Sadusi said: "If its derivation is from shaṭa, meaning 'to burn' (yashītu shawṭatan), then there is a basis for both readings." It was said: its basis is that the intensive pattern of it is shayyat, and its plural is ash-shayyatun. They lightened the yā', though it has been narrated from both of them that it was read with the shaddah (doubling), and others recited with it. End of quotation.

Al-A'mash read ﴿الشَّياطُونَ﴾ as well, as al-Hasan and Ibn al-Sumayfa' did. These three are among the transmitters of the Qur'an who read it this way, and it is not possible to say that they erred, because of their standing in knowledge and in the transmission of the Qur'an.

How excellent is the order of these clauses! He first negated the devils' descending with it, and negation usually applies to what is possible, though here it is impossible for the devils to descend with the Qur'an. Then He negated its suitability, meaning that even if it were assumed possible, they would not be fit for it. Then He negated their ability to do so and that it was impossible for them to descend with it. So He ascended from negating possibility, to negating suitability, to negating capacity and ability. This is an escalating emphasis in negating their descent with it. Then He gave the reason why they are excluded from hearing the speech of the people of heaven: they are pelted with meteors.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So do not invoke another god along with Allah﴾. In reality the address is to the listener, since He, exalted is He, knew that this could not be from the Messenger ﷺ. For this reason the exegetes (mufassirun) said: the meaning is, "Say, O Muhammad, to those who disbelieve: do not invoke another god along with Allah." Then He commanded him to warn his clan (ʿashīrah). The ʿashīrah is below the fakhdh (sub-clan) and above the faṣīlah (branch). He singled out the clan, although he was commanded to warn all people, as He said: ﴿to warn the people﴾ [Yunus: 2]. This is because warning them, being his own kin, leaves no room for favoritism or leniency toward them, and because they and other people are one and the same law in threat and warning. If his kin were warned and threatened, despite the compassion a person naturally feels toward them, then others would be even more and more fittingly included. Or it is because the beginning is with those nearest to him, then those after them, as He said: ﴿Fight those of the disbelievers who are near to you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 123]. And when he (ﷺ) entered Makkah he said: "Every usury of the Jahiliyyah is placed under these two feet of mine, and the first usury I place is the usury of al-ʿAbbas." Because the clan is the expected source of obedience, and he can be firmer with them than with others, and they bear more patiently with him.

The Messenger ﷺ carried out what his Lord commanded him, warning his clan. He called the nearest, then the nearest by sub-clan. Hadiths have been narrated from him about this.

﴿And lower your wing to those among the believers who follow you﴾: the discussion of these phrases was given earlier at the end of al-Hijr, and it is a metaphor for humility. One of the poets said:

*"You are renowned for lowering the wing, so do not be, in raising it, a falcon."*

He forbade him from arrogance after humility. The ajdal is the falcon. The phrase ﴿among the believers﴾ is general, covering his clan and others. Since warning results either in obedience or disobedience, the division is made upon both. The meaning is: whoever follows you as a believer, humble yourself to him. Therefore its counterpart came: ﴿But if they disobey you﴾, then disassociate yourself from them and from their deeds. In this there is a truce (muwada'ah) that was abrogated (naskh) by the verse of the sword.

The apparent reference of the pronoun in ﴿عَصَوْكَ﴾ ("they disobey you") is to those who were commanded to be warned, namely the clan, and what he disassociated himself from is their worship of idols and their taking another god. It was also said: the pronoun refers to those among the believers who followed him, meaning: if they disobey you, O Muhammad, in the rulings and branches of Islam, after their affirmation and faith in you, ﴿then say: "I am innocent of what you do"﴾, not "of you," meaning: show your displeasure with their deeds and your rejection of them. Had He commanded him to disassociate himself from them, nothing would remain after this as an intercession for the disobedient. Then Allah, exalted is He, commanded him to rely upon Him.

Nafi', Ibn ʿAmir, Abu Ja'far and Shaybah read ﴿فَتَوَكَّلْ﴾ with fa', and the rest of the seven read it with waw. The description "the Mighty" fits, meaning the One who cannot be overcome, and "the Merciful," meaning the One who has mercy on you. These two attributes are the ones that appear at the ends of the stories in this surah. So reliance upon One who has these two attributes suffices you against the evil of whoever hates you among these people and others. He overcomes your enemies by His might, and gives you victory over them by His mercy. Reliance (tawakkul) is entrusting the matter to the one who owns the matter and has power over it.

Then He was described as the One before whom you are in plain sight, and this is from His mercy to you, that He qualified you to worship Him, and to what you do of tahajjud (night prayer). Most of the exegetes, including Ibn ʿAbbas, held that the meaning is "when you stand up for prayer."

The majority read ﴿وَتَقَلُّبَكَ﴾ as a verbal noun of taqallaba, coordinated with the kaf in ﴿يَراكَ﴾. Jannah ibn Hubaysh read ﴿وَتَقَلَّبُكَ﴾ as the imperfect of qallaba with shaddah, coordinated with ﴿يَراكَ﴾. Mujahid and Qatadah said: ﴿فِي السَّاجِدِينَ﴾ ("among those who prostrate") means among the worshippers who pray. Ibn ʿAbbas said: in the loins of Adam, Noah and Abraham until you came forth. ʿIkrimah said: He sees you standing and prostrating. It was said: the meaning of "stand up" (taqumu) is that you are alone with yourself. Also from Mujahid: what is meant is the turning of his gaze toward those who pray behind him, as he said: "Complete the bowing and prostration, for by Allah I see you from behind me." In Ibn ʿAtiyyah's al-Wajiz: the apparent meaning of the verse is that it refers to standing in prayer, and it may also refer to all his conduct, and this is the interpretation of Mujahid and Qatadah. "Among those who prostrate" means your prayer with those who pray, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrimah and others. Ibn ʿAbbas also said, and Qatadah: it means your turning among the believers, so he referred to them by "those who prostrate." Ibn Jubayr said: it means the prophets, that is, your turning as the other prophets turned. Al-Zamakhshari said: He mentioned what he used to do in the depths of the night, standing for tahajjud, and turning as he examined the states of the worshippers among his companions, so that he could observe them without their noticing, and know their inner states and how they worked for their hereafter. It is related that when the obligation of the night prayer was abrogated, he went around the houses of his companions that night to see what they were doing, out of his eagerness for them and for the acts of obedience and good deeds that were found among them. He found their houses like beehives, because of what he heard of their murmuring with the remembrance of Allah and recitation. The intended meaning of "those who prostrate" is those who pray. It was also said: its meaning is He sees you when you stand up to lead the people in congregational prayer, and your turning among those who prostrate is your movement among them in their standing, bowing, prostrating and sitting when you lead them. It is related from Muqatil that he asked Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him: "Do you find congregational prayer in the Qur'an?" So he recited this verse. It is also possible that your condition is not hidden from Me, whenever you stand and turn among those who prostrate, in the sufficiency of the affairs of religion. End of quotation.

﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing﴾ of what you say, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of what you intend and do. The Rafidah went to the view that the fathers of the Prophet ﷺ were believers, and they took as evidence His saying: ﴿and your turning among those who prostrate﴾. They said: it admits the aspects that were mentioned, and it admits that the meaning is that He moved his soul from one prostrating person to another prostrating person, as we say. When it admits all these aspects, it is necessary to take the verse as covering all of them, because there is no contradiction and no preference among them. They also cited his (ﷺ) saying: "I was never moved from the loins of pure men to the wombs of pure women," and whoever was a disbeliever is impure, based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, the polytheists are impure﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28]. As for His saying: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar﴾ [al-An'am: 74], the word "father" may be applied to an uncle, as the sons of Jacob said to him: ﴿We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac﴾ [al-Baqarah: 133]. They called Ishmael a "father," although he was an uncle to them.

* *

﴿Say: "Shall I inform you?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 60], meaning: say, O Muhammad, "Shall I tell you?" This is an interrogative of confirmation and affirmation. The phrase ﴿upon whom﴾ is connected to ﴿descend﴾ ("tanazzalu"), and the clause containing the sense of the interrogative is in the position of an object for ﴿unabbi'ukum﴾ ("I inform you"), because it is suspended (mu'allaq), since it means "I make you know." If you consider it transitive to two objects, it stands in place of the second object; if you consider it transitive to three, it stands in place of the two. When the interrogative is suspended from the governing verb, it does not remain in its true sense of seeking information, but its meaning reverts to that of a statement. Do you not see that when you say: "I knew whether Zayd was in the house or ʿAmr," the meaning is: "I knew one of them was in the house"? The meaning is not that knowledge proceeded from him, and then he asked the addressee to specify who was in the house, Zayd or ʿAmr. So the meaning here is: "Shall I make you know upon whom the devils descend?" not that he asked the addressees about the person upon whom the devils descend.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) on surah 26, verses 210–227 (part 2 of 2):

Since this is the meaning, the report comes after it with His saying: ﴿The devils descend upon every lying, sinful one.﴾ It is as if, when He said, "Shall I inform you of such-and-such?" it was said to Him, "Inform us," and He said: ﴿They descend upon every lying one﴾, who abounds in *ifk* (lying), which is falsehood. *Athim* (sinful) means one who abounds in sin. *Affak* and *athim* are both intensive forms (*sighatai mubalagha*, forms of emphasis), and the intended referents are the soothsayers (*al-kahana*). The pronoun in ﴿yulqun﴾ (they cast) may refer to the devils, meaning they listen attentively and give ear, in order to snatch something of what the angels say, so that they then bring it down to the soothsayers. Or it may mean ﴿yulqun al-sam'a﴾ (they cast the hearing), that is, what is heard, to those upon whom they descend. (And most of them), that is, most of the devils who cast, ﴿are liars﴾.

So, on the meaning of listening attentively, the clause is a resumptive report (*isti'naf ikhbar*, a new independent statement). On the meaning of casting what is heard to the soothsayers, it may be a resumptive statement, and it may also be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the devils, meaning: "The devils descend upon every lying, sinful one, casting what they have heard." It is also possible that the pronoun in ﴿yulqun﴾ refers back to ﴿every lying, sinful one﴾, and the pronoun is made plural because ﴿every lying one﴾ carries a general sense (*'umum*) and includes individuals beneath it. It was also held that the meaning is: they cast their hearing to the devils, so that the devils may convey to them what they fix in their ears; or that ﴿yulqun al-sam'a﴾ means they cast what is heard from the devils to people. And most of them, that is, most of the soothsayers, are liars. This accords with what is reported: they receive from the devils a single word that was heard from heaven, and they mix with it a hundred lies. When that one word proves true, it becomes a cause of misguidance for whoever hears it.

If the pronoun refers back to ﴿every lying one﴾, then ﴿yulqun﴾ may be a resumptive report about the liars, or it may be a qualifier (*sifa*) of ﴿every lying one﴾. There is no contradiction between His saying ﴿every lying one﴾ and His saying ﴿and most of them are liars﴾, because the *affak* is the one who abounds in lying, and this does not indicate that he speaks only falsehood. So the meaning is: among the liars, whoever tells the truth regarding what he relates from the jinn is, in most cases, deluded.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: ﴿And it is indeed a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 192], and ﴿The devils did not bring it down﴾, and ﴿Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend?﴾ — why did He separate these [from one another] and [why did He separate them] from [their] brothers?" He answered: "The intention is to separate them by verses that are not in their meaning, so that one returns to the coming of them, and the mention of what is in them praises it again and again. Thereby it indicates that the meaning in which they were revealed is among the meanings that ascribed to Allah's aversion toward them. The example is: a man narrates a story, and in his breast there is concern for something in it and special care for it, so you see him repeat its mention and never cease returning to it." End of quotation.

When He mentioned the soothsayers with their great falsehood and their state, which required denying the speech of the Qur'an (since some of the disbelievers had said about the Qur'an that it is poetry, just as they said about the Messenger that he is a soothsayer, and that what he brought is of the category of soothsaying), Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Nor is it the word of a soothsayer﴾ [al-Haqqah: 42], and He said: ﴿Nor is it the word of a poet﴾ [al-Haqqah: 41].

Then He said: ﴿As for the poets, the deviators follow them.﴾ It was said: this was revealed concerning Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt, Abu 'Izzah, Musafi' al-Jumahi, Hubayrah ibn Abi Wahb, Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith, and Ibn al-Zib'ara. Ibn al-Zib'ara and Abu Sufyan embraced Islam. The word *al-shu'ara'* (the poets) is general and includes every poet, and the one blamed is he who satirizes and praises for a forbidden desire, slanders chaste women, speaks falsehood, and says what is not lawful in the Shari'ah.

'Isa read *al-shu'ara'a* with a fatha (accusative), as an *ishtighal* construction (where a verb governs a pronoun referring to the noun that precedes it, so that the noun is put in the accusative). The majority read it with a damma (nominative), as a subject and predicate (*mubtada' wa khabar*). Al-Sulami, al-Hasan (with a variant from him), and Nafi' read *yatba'uhum* with a single *ta'* (lightened), while the rest of the seven read it with the doubled *ta'* (shaddah). Al-Hasan and 'Abd al-Warith, from Abu 'Amr, read the *'ayn* with a sukun. Harun reported the accusative of it from some of them, and this is problematic.

*Al-ghawun* (the deviators): Ibn 'Abbas said: "the transmitters (*al-ruwat*)." He also said: "those who admire their poetry and keep company with them." 'Ikrimah said: "the rabble who follow the poet." Mujahid and Qatadah said: "the devils." 'Ata' said: "the foolish polytheists who follow their poets."

﴿Have you not seen that they wander in every valley?﴾ This is a figurative image of their going off in every path of speech, their recklessness, their lack of concern in exaggerating in speech, and their overstepping the limit of moderation in it, to the point that they prefer the most cowardly of people over 'Antarah, the most miserly over Hatim, slander the innocent, and call the pious a sinner. Ibn 'Abbas said: "It is their making the good ugly and their making the ugly good."

﴿And that they say what they do not do.﴾ This is because of their excess in the varieties of speech and their fondness for eloquence and subtle meanings: they may attribute to themselves what never happened to them. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, dismissed the hadd (prescribed punishment) for wine from al-Nu'man ibn 'Adi, on account of a poem he had composed to his wife, when he argued against him with this verse. He had appointed him over Bisan, then dismissed him and wanted to flog him. And al-Farazdaq, for Sulayman ibn 'Abd al-Malik, said:

*fa-bitna ka-annahunna musarra'at, wa-bittu afuddu aghlaq al-khitam*

(So they spent the night as if they were struck down, and I spent the night breaking open the seals of the wine-jars.)

Sulayman said to him: "The hadd has become binding upon you." He said: "Allah has averted the hadd from me by His saying: ﴿And that they say what they do not do.﴾"

He, the Exalted, informed about the poets with the states that contradict the state of prophethood, since their affair, as He mentioned, is following the deviators, taking up the varieties of speech, praising and blaming things, and attributing to them what did not happen. This is unlike the state of prophethood, for it is one path, followed only by the rightly guided. The call of the prophets is one: calling to the Oneness of Allah and His worship, encouraging the Hereafter, and truthfulness. Moreover, what they brought cannot be brought by anyone else, given the manifestation of the miracle.

Since what preceded was a censure of the poets, He made an exception among them for those who were characterized by faith, righteous deeds, and frequent remembrance of Allah, and that (remembrance) predominated over their poetry. When they composed poetry, it was about the Oneness of Allah, praising Him, praising His Messenger ﷺ and his Companions, admonition, asceticism, good manners, facilitating knowledge, and everything about which speech is lawful in the Shari'ah. So they are not stained in their speech by sin or defect. Poetry is a category of speech: its good is good, and its ugly is ugly.

A man from the 'Alawi family said to 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd: "My chest surges with poetry." He said: "What prevents you from it in what is not harmful?"

It was said: the intended ones excepted are Hassan, 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah, Ka'b ibn Malik, Ka'b ibn Zuhayr, and whoever defended the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Ka'b ibn Malik: "Satirize them, for by Him in whose hand is my soul, it is more painful to them than arrows." And he said to Hassan: "Say, and the Holy Spirit is with you." This is the meaning of His saying ﴿and they defend themselves﴾, that is, with speech against whoever wronged them.

'Ata' ibn Yasar and others said: when He censured the poets with His saying ﴿As for the poets﴾, the verse was grievous to Hassan, Ibn Rawahah, and Ka'b ibn Malik, and they mentioned that to the Messenger, peace be upon him. Then the verse of exception was revealed at Medina. Ibn Zayd restricted His saying ﴿and remember Allah much﴾ and said: that is, in their poetry. Ibn 'Abbas said: it became a disposition and habit for them, as Labid said when he was asked for his poetry: "Allah has replaced poetry for me with the Qur'an, which is better than it."

When He mentioned ﴿and they defend themselves after they have been wronged﴾, He threatened the wrongdoers with this great, terrifying threat that splits the livers, and He left it vague in His saying: ﴿Those who have wronged will know what sort of return they will return to.﴾

When Abu Bakr appointed 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, he recited to him: ﴿Those who have wronged will know what sort of return they will return to,﴾ and the pious predecessors (*al-salaf al-salih*) would admonish one another with it. What is understood from the Shari'ah is that those who wronged are the disbelievers. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Explaining *zulm* (wrong) as disbelief is a specification (*ta'lil*), and he had mentioned earlier that ﴿those who wronged﴾ is unrestricted, and this is from him in the manner of the Mu'tazilah (*i'tizal*)."

Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Arqam, from al-Hasan, read *ayya munfalatin yanfalitun* (with a fa' and two ta's). Its meaning: those who wronged hope to escape from the punishment of Allah, but they will know that there is no way for them to escape, which is salvation. *Wa-sa-ya'lamu* here is suspended (*mu'allaqah*, i.e., the verb of knowing is blocked from governing what follows). *Ayya munqalabin* is an interrogative, and the element governing it is *yanqalibun*, which is a verbal noun (*masdar*). The clause occupies the position of the object of *sa-ya'lamu*.

Abu al-Baqa' said: *ayya munqalabin* is a masdar that is an adjective (*na't*) of a deleted masdar, and the governing element is *yanqalibun inqalaban ayya munqalabin*, and *ya'lamu* does not govern it, because an interrogative is not governed by what precedes it. End of quotation. This is confused, because *ayya*, when it is described by something, is not an interrogative; rather the *ayyu* described is a qualifier (*qasam*) of the *ayya* being asked about, not an oath. *Ayyu* may be conditional, interrogative, relative, or a qualifier according to the opinion of al-Akhfash (where it modifies an indefinite noun, as in: *marartu bi-ayyin mu'jibin laka*, "I passed by someone wonderful to you"), and it may be a form of vocative, connecting to the vocative of what has *al* (the definite article), as in: *ya ayyuha al-rajul* ("O man"). Al-Akhfash claims that the one used in the vocative is a relative. The position of the majority is that it is an independent category (*qasam bi-ra'sihi*), and the qualifier occurs as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of a definite noun. These are the categories of *ayy*. So when you say: "You know what kind of striking you strike," it is interrogative, not a qualifier of a deleted masdar.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 26, verses 210–227 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And the devils did not bring it down. It is not befitting for them, nor are they able to do so. Indeed, they are cut off from hearing it.﴾ ﴿So do not invoke another god along with Allah, lest you be among those punished.﴾ ﴿And warn your nearest kinsmen.﴾ ﴿And lower your wing to those among the believers who follow you.﴾ ﴿But if they disobey you, then say: "I am innocent of what you do."﴾ ﴿And rely upon the Mighty, the Merciful,﴾ ﴿who sees you when you stand up,﴾ ﴿and your movements among those who prostrate.﴾ ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend?﴾ ﴿They descend upon every lying sinner,﴾ ﴿who give ear, and most of them are liars.﴾ ﴿And the poets, the misguided follow them.﴾ ﴿Do you not see that they wander in every valley,﴾ ﴿and that they say what they do not do?﴾ ﴿Except those who believe, do righteous deeds, remember Allah often, and defend themselves after they have been wronged. And those who have done wrong will know what a final return they will return to.﴾

The polytheists of Quraysh used to say: "Muhammad has a companion from the jinn who informs him, as soothsayers are informed." So this was revealed. The pronoun in ﴿بِهِ﴾ ("with it") refers to the Qur'an. Rather, ﴿the Trustworthy Spirit brought it down﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 193].

Al-Hasan read ﴿الشَّياطُونَ﴾ (ash-shayatun, with a waw in the nominative), which was discussed in al-Baqarah. Abu Hatim and the readers rejected it. Abu Hatim said: "It is an error on his part, or against him." Al-Nahhas said: "It is an error according to all the grammarians." Al-Mahdawi said: "It is not permissible in Arabic." Al-Farra' said: "The shaykh erred; he thought it was the nun found in the words hajā'in." Then al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: "If it is permissible to cite the verse of al-'Ajjaj and Ru'bah, then why is it not permissible to cite the reading of al-Hasan and his companion, meaning Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa', when we know that both of them recited it only after having heard it?" Yunus ibn Habib said: "I heard a Bedouin say: 'I entered gardens, and behind them were gardens (bastanun)'; so I said: 'How similar this is to the reading of al-Hasan.'" End of quotation.

This reading has been explained as follows: since its final part is like the final part of Yabrin and Filastin, just as the i'rab (case inflection) of these is applied to the nun at times and to what precedes it at other times, so they say: Yabrin and Yabrun, Filastin and Filastun. The same is applied to ash-shayatin, by analogy with them, so they say: ash-shayatin and ash-shayatun. Abu Fayd Mu'arrij al-Sadusi said: "If its derivation is from shaṭa, meaning 'to burn' (yashītu shawṭatan), then there is a basis for both readings." It was said: its basis is that the intensive pattern of it is shayyat, and its plural is ash-shayyatun. They lightened the yā', though it has been narrated from both of them that it was read with the shaddah (doubling), and others recited with it. End of quotation.

Al-A'mash read ﴿الشَّياطُونَ﴾ as well, as al-Hasan and Ibn al-Sumayfa' did. These three are among the transmitters of the Qur'an who read it this way, and it is not possible to say that they erred, because of their standing in knowledge and in the transmission of the Qur'an.

How excellent is the order of these clauses! He first negated the devils' descending with it, and negation usually applies to what is possible, though here it is impossible for the devils to descend with the Qur'an. Then He negated its suitability, meaning that even if it were assumed possible, they would not be fit for it. Then He negated their ability to do so and that it was impossible for them to descend with it. So He ascended from negating possibility, to negating suitability, to negating capacity and ability. This is an escalating emphasis in negating their descent with it. Then He gave the reason why they are excluded from hearing the speech of the people of heaven: they are pelted with meteors.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So do not invoke another god along with Allah﴾. In reality the address is to the listener, since He, exalted is He, knew that this could not be from the Messenger ﷺ. For this reason the exegetes (mufassirun) said: the meaning is, "Say, O Muhammad, to those who disbelieve: do not invoke another god along with Allah." Then He commanded him to warn his clan (ʿashīrah). The ʿashīrah is below the fakhdh (sub-clan) and above the faṣīlah (branch). He singled out the clan, although he was commanded to warn all people, as He said: ﴿to warn the people﴾ [Yunus: 2]. This is because warning them, being his own kin, leaves no room for favoritism or leniency toward them, and because they and other people are one and the same law in threat and warning. If his kin were warned and threatened, despite the compassion a person naturally feels toward them, then others would be even more and more fittingly included. Or it is because the beginning is with those nearest to him, then those after them, as He said: ﴿Fight those of the disbelievers who are near to you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 123]. And when he (ﷺ) entered Makkah he said: "Every usury of the Jahiliyyah is placed under these two feet of mine, and the first usury I place is the usury of al-ʿAbbas." Because the clan is the expected source of obedience, and he can be firmer with them than with others, and they bear more patiently with him.

The Messenger ﷺ carried out what his Lord commanded him, warning his clan. He called the nearest, then the nearest by sub-clan. Hadiths have been narrated from him about this.

﴿And lower your wing to those among the believers who follow you﴾: the discussion of these phrases was given earlier at the end of al-Hijr, and it is a metaphor for humility. One of the poets said:

*"You are renowned for lowering the wing, so do not be, in raising it, a falcon."*

He forbade him from arrogance after humility. The ajdal is the falcon. The phrase ﴿among the believers﴾ is general, covering his clan and others. Since warning results either in obedience or disobedience, the division is made upon both. The meaning is: whoever follows you as a believer, humble yourself to him. Therefore its counterpart came: ﴿But if they disobey you﴾, then disassociate yourself from them and from their deeds. In this there is a truce (muwada'ah) that was abrogated (naskh) by the verse of the sword.

The apparent reference of the pronoun in ﴿عَصَوْكَ﴾ ("they disobey you") is to those who were commanded to be warned, namely the clan, and what he disassociated himself from is their worship of idols and their taking another god. It was also said: the pronoun refers to those among the believers who followed him, meaning: if they disobey you, O Muhammad, in the rulings and branches of Islam, after their affirmation and faith in you, ﴿then say: "I am innocent of what you do"﴾, not "of you," meaning: show your displeasure with their deeds and your rejection of them. Had He commanded him to disassociate himself from them, nothing would remain after this as an intercession for the disobedient. Then Allah, exalted is He, commanded him to rely upon Him.

Nafi', Ibn ʿAmir, Abu Ja'far and Shaybah read ﴿فَتَوَكَّلْ﴾ with fa', and the rest of the seven read it with waw. The description "the Mighty" fits, meaning the One who cannot be overcome, and "the Merciful," meaning the One who has mercy on you. These two attributes are the ones that appear at the ends of the stories in this surah. So reliance upon One who has these two attributes suffices you against the evil of whoever hates you among these people and others. He overcomes your enemies by His might, and gives you victory over them by His mercy. Reliance (tawakkul) is entrusting the matter to the one who owns the matter and has power over it.

Then He was described as the One before whom you are in plain sight, and this is from His mercy to you, that He qualified you to worship Him, and to what you do of tahajjud (night prayer). Most of the exegetes, including Ibn ʿAbbas, held that the meaning is "when you stand up for prayer."

The majority read ﴿وَتَقَلُّبَكَ﴾ as a verbal noun of taqallaba, coordinated with the kaf in ﴿يَراكَ﴾. Jannah ibn Hubaysh read ﴿وَتَقَلَّبُكَ﴾ as the imperfect of qallaba with shaddah, coordinated with ﴿يَراكَ﴾. Mujahid and Qatadah said: ﴿فِي السَّاجِدِينَ﴾ ("among those who prostrate") means among the worshippers who pray. Ibn ʿAbbas said: in the loins of Adam, Noah and Abraham until you came forth. ʿIkrimah said: He sees you standing and prostrating. It was said: the meaning of "stand up" (taqumu) is that you are alone with yourself. Also from Mujahid: what is meant is the turning of his gaze toward those who pray behind him, as he said: "Complete the bowing and prostration, for by Allah I see you from behind me." In Ibn ʿAtiyyah's al-Wajiz: the apparent meaning of the verse is that it refers to standing in prayer, and it may also refer to all his conduct, and this is the interpretation of Mujahid and Qatadah. "Among those who prostrate" means your prayer with those who pray, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrimah and others. Ibn ʿAbbas also said, and Qatadah: it means your turning among the believers, so he referred to them by "those who prostrate." Ibn Jubayr said: it means the prophets, that is, your turning as the other prophets turned. Al-Zamakhshari said: He mentioned what he used to do in the depths of the night, standing for tahajjud, and turning as he examined the states of the worshippers among his companions, so that he could observe them without their noticing, and know their inner states and how they worked for their hereafter. It is related that when the obligation of the night prayer was abrogated, he went around the houses of his companions that night to see what they were doing, out of his eagerness for them and for the acts of obedience and good deeds that were found among them. He found their houses like beehives, because of what he heard of their murmuring with the remembrance of Allah and recitation. The intended meaning of "those who prostrate" is those who pray. It was also said: its meaning is He sees you when you stand up to lead the people in congregational prayer, and your turning among those who prostrate is your movement among them in their standing, bowing, prostrating and sitting when you lead them. It is related from Muqatil that he asked Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him: "Do you find congregational prayer in the Qur'an?" So he recited this verse. It is also possible that your condition is not hidden from Me, whenever you stand and turn among those who prostrate, in the sufficiency of the affairs of religion. End of quotation.

﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing﴾ of what you say, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of what you intend and do. The Rafidah went to the view that the fathers of the Prophet ﷺ were believers, and they took as evidence His saying: ﴿and your turning among those who prostrate﴾. They said: it admits the aspects that were mentioned, and it admits that the meaning is that He moved his soul from one prostrating person to another prostrating person, as we say. When it admits all these aspects, it is necessary to take the verse as covering all of them, because there is no contradiction and no preference among them. They also cited his (ﷺ) saying: "I was never moved from the loins of pure men to the wombs of pure women," and whoever was a disbeliever is impure, based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, the polytheists are impure﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28]. As for His saying: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar﴾ [al-An'am: 74], the word "father" may be applied to an uncle, as the sons of Jacob said to him: ﴿We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac﴾ [al-Baqarah: 133]. They called Ishmael a "father," although he was an uncle to them.

* *

﴿Say: "Shall I inform you?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 60], meaning: say, O Muhammad, "Shall I tell you?" This is an interrogative of confirmation and affirmation. The phrase ﴿upon whom﴾ is connected to ﴿descend﴾ ("tanazzalu"), and the clause containing the sense of the interrogative is in the position of an object for ﴿unabbi'ukum﴾ ("I inform you"), because it is suspended (mu'allaq), since it means "I make you know." If you consider it transitive to two objects, it stands in place of the second object; if you consider it transitive to three, it stands in place of the two. When the interrogative is suspended from the governing verb, it does not remain in its true sense of seeking information, but its meaning reverts to that of a statement. Do you not see that when you say: "I knew whether Zayd was in the house or ʿAmr," the meaning is: "I knew one of them was in the house"? The meaning is not that knowledge proceeded from him, and then he asked the addressee to specify who was in the house, Zayd or ʿAmr. So the meaning here is: "Shall I make you know upon whom the devils descend?" not that he asked the addressees about the person upon whom the devils descend.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) on surah 26, verses 210–227 (part 2 of 2):

Since this is the meaning, the report comes after it with His saying: ﴿The devils descend upon every lying, sinful one.﴾ It is as if, when He said, "Shall I inform you of such-and-such?" it was said to Him, "Inform us," and He said: ﴿They descend upon every lying one﴾, who abounds in *ifk* (lying), which is falsehood. *Athim* (sinful) means one who abounds in sin. *Affak* and *athim* are both intensive forms (*sighatai mubalagha*, forms of emphasis), and the intended referents are the soothsayers (*al-kahana*). The pronoun in ﴿yulqun﴾ (they cast) may refer to the devils, meaning they listen attentively and give ear, in order to snatch something of what the angels say, so that they then bring it down to the soothsayers. Or it may mean ﴿yulqun al-sam'a﴾ (they cast the hearing), that is, what is heard, to those upon whom they descend. (And most of them), that is, most of the devils who cast, ﴿are liars﴾.

So, on the meaning of listening attentively, the clause is a resumptive report (*isti'naf ikhbar*, a new independent statement). On the meaning of casting what is heard to the soothsayers, it may be a resumptive statement, and it may also be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the devils, meaning: "The devils descend upon every lying, sinful one, casting what they have heard." It is also possible that the pronoun in ﴿yulqun﴾ refers back to ﴿every lying, sinful one﴾, and the pronoun is made plural because ﴿every lying one﴾ carries a general sense (*'umum*) and includes individuals beneath it. It was also held that the meaning is: they cast their hearing to the devils, so that the devils may convey to them what they fix in their ears; or that ﴿yulqun al-sam'a﴾ means they cast what is heard from the devils to people. And most of them, that is, most of the soothsayers, are liars. This accords with what is reported: they receive from the devils a single word that was heard from heaven, and they mix with it a hundred lies. When that one word proves true, it becomes a cause of misguidance for whoever hears it.

If the pronoun refers back to ﴿every lying one﴾, then ﴿yulqun﴾ may be a resumptive report about the liars, or it may be a qualifier (*sifa*) of ﴿every lying one﴾. There is no contradiction between His saying ﴿every lying one﴾ and His saying ﴿and most of them are liars﴾, because the *affak* is the one who abounds in lying, and this does not indicate that he speaks only falsehood. So the meaning is: among the liars, whoever tells the truth regarding what he relates from the jinn is, in most cases, deluded.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: ﴿And it is indeed a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 192], and ﴿The devils did not bring it down﴾, and ﴿Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend?﴾ — why did He separate these [from one another] and [why did He separate them] from [their] brothers?" He answered: "The intention is to separate them by verses that are not in their meaning, so that one returns to the coming of them, and the mention of what is in them praises it again and again. Thereby it indicates that the meaning in which they were revealed is among the meanings that ascribed to Allah's aversion toward them. The example is: a man narrates a story, and in his breast there is concern for something in it and special care for it, so you see him repeat its mention and never cease returning to it." End of quotation.

When He mentioned the soothsayers with their great falsehood and their state, which required denying the speech of the Qur'an (since some of the disbelievers had said about the Qur'an that it is poetry, just as they said about the Messenger that he is a soothsayer, and that what he brought is of the category of soothsaying), Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Nor is it the word of a soothsayer﴾ [al-Haqqah: 42], and He said: ﴿Nor is it the word of a poet﴾ [al-Haqqah: 41].

Then He said: ﴿As for the poets, the deviators follow them.﴾ It was said: this was revealed concerning Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt, Abu 'Izzah, Musafi' al-Jumahi, Hubayrah ibn Abi Wahb, Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith, and Ibn al-Zib'ara. Ibn al-Zib'ara and Abu Sufyan embraced Islam. The word *al-shu'ara'* (the poets) is general and includes every poet, and the one blamed is he who satirizes and praises for a forbidden desire, slanders chaste women, speaks falsehood, and says what is not lawful in the Shari'ah.

'Isa read *al-shu'ara'a* with a fatha (accusative), as an *ishtighal* construction (where a verb governs a pronoun referring to the noun that precedes it, so that the noun is put in the accusative). The majority read it with a damma (nominative), as a subject and predicate (*mubtada' wa khabar*). Al-Sulami, al-Hasan (with a variant from him), and Nafi' read *yatba'uhum* with a single *ta'* (lightened), while the rest of the seven read it with the doubled *ta'* (shaddah). Al-Hasan and 'Abd al-Warith, from Abu 'Amr, read the *'ayn* with a sukun. Harun reported the accusative of it from some of them, and this is problematic.

*Al-ghawun* (the deviators): Ibn 'Abbas said: "the transmitters (*al-ruwat*)." He also said: "those who admire their poetry and keep company with them." 'Ikrimah said: "the rabble who follow the poet." Mujahid and Qatadah said: "the devils." 'Ata' said: "the foolish polytheists who follow their poets."

﴿Have you not seen that they wander in every valley?﴾ This is a figurative image of their going off in every path of speech, their recklessness, their lack of concern in exaggerating in speech, and their overstepping the limit of moderation in it, to the point that they prefer the most cowardly of people over 'Antarah, the most miserly over Hatim, slander the innocent, and call the pious a sinner. Ibn 'Abbas said: "It is their making the good ugly and their making the ugly good."

﴿And that they say what they do not do.﴾ This is because of their excess in the varieties of speech and their fondness for eloquence and subtle meanings: they may attribute to themselves what never happened to them. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, dismissed the hadd (prescribed punishment) for wine from al-Nu'man ibn 'Adi, on account of a poem he had composed to his wife, when he argued against him with this verse. He had appointed him over Bisan, then dismissed him and wanted to flog him. And al-Farazdaq, for Sulayman ibn 'Abd al-Malik, said:

*fa-bitna ka-annahunna musarra'at, wa-bittu afuddu aghlaq al-khitam*

(So they spent the night as if they were struck down, and I spent the night breaking open the seals of the wine-jars.)

Sulayman said to him: "The hadd has become binding upon you." He said: "Allah has averted the hadd from me by His saying: ﴿And that they say what they do not do.﴾"

He, the Exalted, informed about the poets with the states that contradict the state of prophethood, since their affair, as He mentioned, is following the deviators, taking up the varieties of speech, praising and blaming things, and attributing to them what did not happen. This is unlike the state of prophethood, for it is one path, followed only by the rightly guided. The call of the prophets is one: calling to the Oneness of Allah and His worship, encouraging the Hereafter, and truthfulness. Moreover, what they brought cannot be brought by anyone else, given the manifestation of the miracle.

Since what preceded was a censure of the poets, He made an exception among them for those who were characterized by faith, righteous deeds, and frequent remembrance of Allah, and that (remembrance) predominated over their poetry. When they composed poetry, it was about the Oneness of Allah, praising Him, praising His Messenger ﷺ and his Companions, admonition, asceticism, good manners, facilitating knowledge, and everything about which speech is lawful in the Shari'ah. So they are not stained in their speech by sin or defect. Poetry is a category of speech: its good is good, and its ugly is ugly.

A man from the 'Alawi family said to 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd: "My chest surges with poetry." He said: "What prevents you from it in what is not harmful?"

It was said: the intended ones excepted are Hassan, 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah, Ka'b ibn Malik, Ka'b ibn Zuhayr, and whoever defended the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Ka'b ibn Malik: "Satirize them, for by Him in whose hand is my soul, it is more painful to them than arrows." And he said to Hassan: "Say, and the Holy Spirit is with you." This is the meaning of His saying ﴿and they defend themselves﴾, that is, with speech against whoever wronged them.

'Ata' ibn Yasar and others said: when He censured the poets with His saying ﴿As for the poets﴾, the verse was grievous to Hassan, Ibn Rawahah, and Ka'b ibn Malik, and they mentioned that to the Messenger, peace be upon him. Then the verse of exception was revealed at Medina. Ibn Zayd restricted His saying ﴿and remember Allah much﴾ and said: that is, in their poetry. Ibn 'Abbas said: it became a disposition and habit for them, as Labid said when he was asked for his poetry: "Allah has replaced poetry for me with the Qur'an, which is better than it."

When He mentioned ﴿and they defend themselves after they have been wronged﴾, He threatened the wrongdoers with this great, terrifying threat that splits the livers, and He left it vague in His saying: ﴿Those who have wronged will know what sort of return they will return to.﴾

When Abu Bakr appointed 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, he recited to him: ﴿Those who have wronged will know what sort of return they will return to,﴾ and the pious predecessors (*al-salaf al-salih*) would admonish one another with it. What is understood from the Shari'ah is that those who wronged are the disbelievers. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Explaining *zulm* (wrong) as disbelief is a specification (*ta'lil*), and he had mentioned earlier that ﴿those who wronged﴾ is unrestricted, and this is from him in the manner of the Mu'tazilah (*i'tizal*)."

Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Arqam, from al-Hasan, read *ayya munfalatin yanfalitun* (with a fa' and two ta's). Its meaning: those who wronged hope to escape from the punishment of Allah, but they will know that there is no way for them to escape, which is salvation. *Wa-sa-ya'lamu* here is suspended (*mu'allaqah*, i.e., the verb of knowing is blocked from governing what follows). *Ayya munqalabin* is an interrogative, and the element governing it is *yanqalibun*, which is a verbal noun (*masdar*). The clause occupies the position of the object of *sa-ya'lamu*.

Abu al-Baqa' said: *ayya munqalabin* is a masdar that is an adjective (*na't*) of a deleted masdar, and the governing element is *yanqalibun inqalaban ayya munqalabin*, and *ya'lamu* does not govern it, because an interrogative is not governed by what precedes it. End of quotation. This is confused, because *ayya*, when it is described by something, is not an interrogative; rather the *ayyu* described is a qualifier (*qasam*) of the *ayya* being asked about, not an oath. *Ayyu* may be conditional, interrogative, relative, or a qualifier according to the opinion of al-Akhfash (where it modifies an indefinite noun, as in: *marartu bi-ayyin mu'jibin laka*, "I passed by someone wonderful to you"), and it may be a form of vocative, connecting to the vocative of what has *al* (the definite article), as in: *ya ayyuha al-rajul* ("O man"). Al-Akhfash claims that the one used in the vocative is a relative. The position of the majority is that it is an independent category (*qasam bi-ra'sihi*), and the qualifier occurs as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of a definite noun. These are the categories of *ayy*. So when you say: "You know what kind of striking you strike," it is interrogative, not a qualifier of a deleted masdar.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 26, verses 210–227 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And the devils did not bring it down. It is not befitting for them, nor are they able to do so. Indeed, they are cut off from hearing it.﴾ ﴿So do not invoke another god along with Allah, lest you be among those punished.﴾ ﴿And warn your nearest kinsmen.﴾ ﴿And lower your wing to those among the believers who follow you.﴾ ﴿But if they disobey you, then say: "I am innocent of what you do."﴾ ﴿And rely upon the Mighty, the Merciful,﴾ ﴿who sees you when you stand up,﴾ ﴿and your movements among those who prostrate.﴾ ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend?﴾ ﴿They descend upon every lying sinner,﴾ ﴿who give ear, and most of them are liars.﴾ ﴿And the poets, the misguided follow them.﴾ ﴿Do you not see that they wander in every valley,﴾ ﴿and that they say what they do not do?﴾ ﴿Except those who believe, do righteous deeds, remember Allah often, and defend themselves after they have been wronged. And those who have done wrong will know what a final return they will return to.﴾

The polytheists of Quraysh used to say: "Muhammad has a companion from the jinn who informs him, as soothsayers are informed." So this was revealed. The pronoun in ﴿بِهِ﴾ ("with it") refers to the Qur'an. Rather, ﴿the Trustworthy Spirit brought it down﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 193].

Al-Hasan read ﴿الشَّياطُونَ﴾ (ash-shayatun, with a waw in the nominative), which was discussed in al-Baqarah. Abu Hatim and the readers rejected it. Abu Hatim said: "It is an error on his part, or against him." Al-Nahhas said: "It is an error according to all the grammarians." Al-Mahdawi said: "It is not permissible in Arabic." Al-Farra' said: "The shaykh erred; he thought it was the nun found in the words hajā'in." Then al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: "If it is permissible to cite the verse of al-'Ajjaj and Ru'bah, then why is it not permissible to cite the reading of al-Hasan and his companion, meaning Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa', when we know that both of them recited it only after having heard it?" Yunus ibn Habib said: "I heard a Bedouin say: 'I entered gardens, and behind them were gardens (bastanun)'; so I said: 'How similar this is to the reading of al-Hasan.'" End of quotation.

This reading has been explained as follows: since its final part is like the final part of Yabrin and Filastin, just as the i'rab (case inflection) of these is applied to the nun at times and to what precedes it at other times, so they say: Yabrin and Yabrun, Filastin and Filastun. The same is applied to ash-shayatin, by analogy with them, so they say: ash-shayatin and ash-shayatun. Abu Fayd Mu'arrij al-Sadusi said: "If its derivation is from shaṭa, meaning 'to burn' (yashītu shawṭatan), then there is a basis for both readings." It was said: its basis is that the intensive pattern of it is shayyat, and its plural is ash-shayyatun. They lightened the yā', though it has been narrated from both of them that it was read with the shaddah (doubling), and others recited with it. End of quotation.

Al-A'mash read ﴿الشَّياطُونَ﴾ as well, as al-Hasan and Ibn al-Sumayfa' did. These three are among the transmitters of the Qur'an who read it this way, and it is not possible to say that they erred, because of their standing in knowledge and in the transmission of the Qur'an.

How excellent is the order of these clauses! He first negated the devils' descending with it, and negation usually applies to what is possible, though here it is impossible for the devils to descend with the Qur'an. Then He negated its suitability, meaning that even if it were assumed possible, they would not be fit for it. Then He negated their ability to do so and that it was impossible for them to descend with it. So He ascended from negating possibility, to negating suitability, to negating capacity and ability. This is an escalating emphasis in negating their descent with it. Then He gave the reason why they are excluded from hearing the speech of the people of heaven: they are pelted with meteors.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So do not invoke another god along with Allah﴾. In reality the address is to the listener, since He, exalted is He, knew that this could not be from the Messenger ﷺ. For this reason the exegetes (mufassirun) said: the meaning is, "Say, O Muhammad, to those who disbelieve: do not invoke another god along with Allah." Then He commanded him to warn his clan (ʿashīrah). The ʿashīrah is below the fakhdh (sub-clan) and above the faṣīlah (branch). He singled out the clan, although he was commanded to warn all people, as He said: ﴿to warn the people﴾ [Yunus: 2]. This is because warning them, being his own kin, leaves no room for favoritism or leniency toward them, and because they and other people are one and the same law in threat and warning. If his kin were warned and threatened, despite the compassion a person naturally feels toward them, then others would be even more and more fittingly included. Or it is because the beginning is with those nearest to him, then those after them, as He said: ﴿Fight those of the disbelievers who are near to you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 123]. And when he (ﷺ) entered Makkah he said: "Every usury of the Jahiliyyah is placed under these two feet of mine, and the first usury I place is the usury of al-ʿAbbas." Because the clan is the expected source of obedience, and he can be firmer with them than with others, and they bear more patiently with him.

The Messenger ﷺ carried out what his Lord commanded him, warning his clan. He called the nearest, then the nearest by sub-clan. Hadiths have been narrated from him about this.

﴿And lower your wing to those among the believers who follow you﴾: the discussion of these phrases was given earlier at the end of al-Hijr, and it is a metaphor for humility. One of the poets said:

*"You are renowned for lowering the wing, so do not be, in raising it, a falcon."*

He forbade him from arrogance after humility. The ajdal is the falcon. The phrase ﴿among the believers﴾ is general, covering his clan and others. Since warning results either in obedience or disobedience, the division is made upon both. The meaning is: whoever follows you as a believer, humble yourself to him. Therefore its counterpart came: ﴿But if they disobey you﴾, then disassociate yourself from them and from their deeds. In this there is a truce (muwada'ah) that was abrogated (naskh) by the verse of the sword.

The apparent reference of the pronoun in ﴿عَصَوْكَ﴾ ("they disobey you") is to those who were commanded to be warned, namely the clan, and what he disassociated himself from is their worship of idols and their taking another god. It was also said: the pronoun refers to those among the believers who followed him, meaning: if they disobey you, O Muhammad, in the rulings and branches of Islam, after their affirmation and faith in you, ﴿then say: "I am innocent of what you do"﴾, not "of you," meaning: show your displeasure with their deeds and your rejection of them. Had He commanded him to disassociate himself from them, nothing would remain after this as an intercession for the disobedient. Then Allah, exalted is He, commanded him to rely upon Him.

Nafi', Ibn ʿAmir, Abu Ja'far and Shaybah read ﴿فَتَوَكَّلْ﴾ with fa', and the rest of the seven read it with waw. The description "the Mighty" fits, meaning the One who cannot be overcome, and "the Merciful," meaning the One who has mercy on you. These two attributes are the ones that appear at the ends of the stories in this surah. So reliance upon One who has these two attributes suffices you against the evil of whoever hates you among these people and others. He overcomes your enemies by His might, and gives you victory over them by His mercy. Reliance (tawakkul) is entrusting the matter to the one who owns the matter and has power over it.

Then He was described as the One before whom you are in plain sight, and this is from His mercy to you, that He qualified you to worship Him, and to what you do of tahajjud (night prayer). Most of the exegetes, including Ibn ʿAbbas, held that the meaning is "when you stand up for prayer."

The majority read ﴿وَتَقَلُّبَكَ﴾ as a verbal noun of taqallaba, coordinated with the kaf in ﴿يَراكَ﴾. Jannah ibn Hubaysh read ﴿وَتَقَلَّبُكَ﴾ as the imperfect of qallaba with shaddah, coordinated with ﴿يَراكَ﴾. Mujahid and Qatadah said: ﴿فِي السَّاجِدِينَ﴾ ("among those who prostrate") means among the worshippers who pray. Ibn ʿAbbas said: in the loins of Adam, Noah and Abraham until you came forth. ʿIkrimah said: He sees you standing and prostrating. It was said: the meaning of "stand up" (taqumu) is that you are alone with yourself. Also from Mujahid: what is meant is the turning of his gaze toward those who pray behind him, as he said: "Complete the bowing and prostration, for by Allah I see you from behind me." In Ibn ʿAtiyyah's al-Wajiz: the apparent meaning of the verse is that it refers to standing in prayer, and it may also refer to all his conduct, and this is the interpretation of Mujahid and Qatadah. "Among those who prostrate" means your prayer with those who pray, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrimah and others. Ibn ʿAbbas also said, and Qatadah: it means your turning among the believers, so he referred to them by "those who prostrate." Ibn Jubayr said: it means the prophets, that is, your turning as the other prophets turned. Al-Zamakhshari said: He mentioned what he used to do in the depths of the night, standing for tahajjud, and turning as he examined the states of the worshippers among his companions, so that he could observe them without their noticing, and know their inner states and how they worked for their hereafter. It is related that when the obligation of the night prayer was abrogated, he went around the houses of his companions that night to see what they were doing, out of his eagerness for them and for the acts of obedience and good deeds that were found among them. He found their houses like beehives, because of what he heard of their murmuring with the remembrance of Allah and recitation. The intended meaning of "those who prostrate" is those who pray. It was also said: its meaning is He sees you when you stand up to lead the people in congregational prayer, and your turning among those who prostrate is your movement among them in their standing, bowing, prostrating and sitting when you lead them. It is related from Muqatil that he asked Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him: "Do you find congregational prayer in the Qur'an?" So he recited this verse. It is also possible that your condition is not hidden from Me, whenever you stand and turn among those who prostrate, in the sufficiency of the affairs of religion. End of quotation.

﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing﴾ of what you say, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of what you intend and do. The Rafidah went to the view that the fathers of the Prophet ﷺ were believers, and they took as evidence His saying: ﴿and your turning among those who prostrate﴾. They said: it admits the aspects that were mentioned, and it admits that the meaning is that He moved his soul from one prostrating person to another prostrating person, as we say. When it admits all these aspects, it is necessary to take the verse as covering all of them, because there is no contradiction and no preference among them. They also cited his (ﷺ) saying: "I was never moved from the loins of pure men to the wombs of pure women," and whoever was a disbeliever is impure, based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, the polytheists are impure﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28]. As for His saying: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar﴾ [al-An'am: 74], the word "father" may be applied to an uncle, as the sons of Jacob said to him: ﴿We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac﴾ [al-Baqarah: 133]. They called Ishmael a "father," although he was an uncle to them.

* *

﴿Say: "Shall I inform you?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 60], meaning: say, O Muhammad, "Shall I tell you?" This is an interrogative of confirmation and affirmation. The phrase ﴿upon whom﴾ is connected to ﴿descend﴾ ("tanazzalu"), and the clause containing the sense of the interrogative is in the position of an object for ﴿unabbi'ukum﴾ ("I inform you"), because it is suspended (mu'allaq), since it means "I make you know." If you consider it transitive to two objects, it stands in place of the second object; if you consider it transitive to three, it stands in place of the two. When the interrogative is suspended from the governing verb, it does not remain in its true sense of seeking information, but its meaning reverts to that of a statement. Do you not see that when you say: "I knew whether Zayd was in the house or ʿAmr," the meaning is: "I knew one of them was in the house"? The meaning is not that knowledge proceeded from him, and then he asked the addressee to specify who was in the house, Zayd or ʿAmr. So the meaning here is: "Shall I make you know upon whom the devils descend?" not that he asked the addressees about the person upon whom the devils descend.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) on surah 26, verses 210–227 (part 2 of 2):

Since this is the meaning, the report comes after it with His saying: ﴿The devils descend upon every lying, sinful one.﴾ It is as if, when He said, "Shall I inform you of such-and-such?" it was said to Him, "Inform us," and He said: ﴿They descend upon every lying one﴾, who abounds in *ifk* (lying), which is falsehood. *Athim* (sinful) means one who abounds in sin. *Affak* and *athim* are both intensive forms (*sighatai mubalagha*, forms of emphasis), and the intended referents are the soothsayers (*al-kahana*). The pronoun in ﴿yulqun﴾ (they cast) may refer to the devils, meaning they listen attentively and give ear, in order to snatch something of what the angels say, so that they then bring it down to the soothsayers. Or it may mean ﴿yulqun al-sam'a﴾ (they cast the hearing), that is, what is heard, to those upon whom they descend. (And most of them), that is, most of the devils who cast, ﴿are liars﴾.

So, on the meaning of listening attentively, the clause is a resumptive report (*isti'naf ikhbar*, a new independent statement). On the meaning of casting what is heard to the soothsayers, it may be a resumptive statement, and it may also be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the devils, meaning: "The devils descend upon every lying, sinful one, casting what they have heard." It is also possible that the pronoun in ﴿yulqun﴾ refers back to ﴿every lying, sinful one﴾, and the pronoun is made plural because ﴿every lying one﴾ carries a general sense (*'umum*) and includes individuals beneath it. It was also held that the meaning is: they cast their hearing to the devils, so that the devils may convey to them what they fix in their ears; or that ﴿yulqun al-sam'a﴾ means they cast what is heard from the devils to people. And most of them, that is, most of the soothsayers, are liars. This accords with what is reported: they receive from the devils a single word that was heard from heaven, and they mix with it a hundred lies. When that one word proves true, it becomes a cause of misguidance for whoever hears it.

If the pronoun refers back to ﴿every lying one﴾, then ﴿yulqun﴾ may be a resumptive report about the liars, or it may be a qualifier (*sifa*) of ﴿every lying one﴾. There is no contradiction between His saying ﴿every lying one﴾ and His saying ﴿and most of them are liars﴾, because the *affak* is the one who abounds in lying, and this does not indicate that he speaks only falsehood. So the meaning is: among the liars, whoever tells the truth regarding what he relates from the jinn is, in most cases, deluded.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: ﴿And it is indeed a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 192], and ﴿The devils did not bring it down﴾, and ﴿Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend?﴾ — why did He separate these [from one another] and [why did He separate them] from [their] brothers?" He answered: "The intention is to separate them by verses that are not in their meaning, so that one returns to the coming of them, and the mention of what is in them praises it again and again. Thereby it indicates that the meaning in which they were revealed is among the meanings that ascribed to Allah's aversion toward them. The example is: a man narrates a story, and in his breast there is concern for something in it and special care for it, so you see him repeat its mention and never cease returning to it." End of quotation.

When He mentioned the soothsayers with their great falsehood and their state, which required denying the speech of the Qur'an (since some of the disbelievers had said about the Qur'an that it is poetry, just as they said about the Messenger that he is a soothsayer, and that what he brought is of the category of soothsaying), Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Nor is it the word of a soothsayer﴾ [al-Haqqah: 42], and He said: ﴿Nor is it the word of a poet﴾ [al-Haqqah: 41].

Then He said: ﴿As for the poets, the deviators follow them.﴾ It was said: this was revealed concerning Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt, Abu 'Izzah, Musafi' al-Jumahi, Hubayrah ibn Abi Wahb, Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith, and Ibn al-Zib'ara. Ibn al-Zib'ara and Abu Sufyan embraced Islam. The word *al-shu'ara'* (the poets) is general and includes every poet, and the one blamed is he who satirizes and praises for a forbidden desire, slanders chaste women, speaks falsehood, and says what is not lawful in the Shari'ah.

'Isa read *al-shu'ara'a* with a fatha (accusative), as an *ishtighal* construction (where a verb governs a pronoun referring to the noun that precedes it, so that the noun is put in the accusative). The majority read it with a damma (nominative), as a subject and predicate (*mubtada' wa khabar*). Al-Sulami, al-Hasan (with a variant from him), and Nafi' read *yatba'uhum* with a single *ta'* (lightened), while the rest of the seven read it with the doubled *ta'* (shaddah). Al-Hasan and 'Abd al-Warith, from Abu 'Amr, read the *'ayn* with a sukun. Harun reported the accusative of it from some of them, and this is problematic.

*Al-ghawun* (the deviators): Ibn 'Abbas said: "the transmitters (*al-ruwat*)." He also said: "those who admire their poetry and keep company with them." 'Ikrimah said: "the rabble who follow the poet." Mujahid and Qatadah said: "the devils." 'Ata' said: "the foolish polytheists who follow their poets."

﴿Have you not seen that they wander in every valley?﴾ This is a figurative image of their going off in every path of speech, their recklessness, their lack of concern in exaggerating in speech, and their overstepping the limit of moderation in it, to the point that they prefer the most cowardly of people over 'Antarah, the most miserly over Hatim, slander the innocent, and call the pious a sinner. Ibn 'Abbas said: "It is their making the good ugly and their making the ugly good."

﴿And that they say what they do not do.﴾ This is because of their excess in the varieties of speech and their fondness for eloquence and subtle meanings: they may attribute to themselves what never happened to them. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, dismissed the hadd (prescribed punishment) for wine from al-Nu'man ibn 'Adi, on account of a poem he had composed to his wife, when he argued against him with this verse. He had appointed him over Bisan, then dismissed him and wanted to flog him. And al-Farazdaq, for Sulayman ibn 'Abd al-Malik, said:

*fa-bitna ka-annahunna musarra'at, wa-bittu afuddu aghlaq al-khitam*

(So they spent the night as if they were struck down, and I spent the night breaking open the seals of the wine-jars.)

Sulayman said to him: "The hadd has become binding upon you." He said: "Allah has averted the hadd from me by His saying: ﴿And that they say what they do not do.﴾"

He, the Exalted, informed about the poets with the states that contradict the state of prophethood, since their affair, as He mentioned, is following the deviators, taking up the varieties of speech, praising and blaming things, and attributing to them what did not happen. This is unlike the state of prophethood, for it is one path, followed only by the rightly guided. The call of the prophets is one: calling to the Oneness of Allah and His worship, encouraging the Hereafter, and truthfulness. Moreover, what they brought cannot be brought by anyone else, given the manifestation of the miracle.

Since what preceded was a censure of the poets, He made an exception among them for those who were characterized by faith, righteous deeds, and frequent remembrance of Allah, and that (remembrance) predominated over their poetry. When they composed poetry, it was about the Oneness of Allah, praising Him, praising His Messenger ﷺ and his Companions, admonition, asceticism, good manners, facilitating knowledge, and everything about which speech is lawful in the Shari'ah. So they are not stained in their speech by sin or defect. Poetry is a category of speech: its good is good, and its ugly is ugly.

A man from the 'Alawi family said to 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd: "My chest surges with poetry." He said: "What prevents you from it in what is not harmful?"

It was said: the intended ones excepted are Hassan, 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah, Ka'b ibn Malik, Ka'b ibn Zuhayr, and whoever defended the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Ka'b ibn Malik: "Satirize them, for by Him in whose hand is my soul, it is more painful to them than arrows." And he said to Hassan: "Say, and the Holy Spirit is with you." This is the meaning of His saying ﴿and they defend themselves﴾, that is, with speech against whoever wronged them.

'Ata' ibn Yasar and others said: when He censured the poets with His saying ﴿As for the poets﴾, the verse was grievous to Hassan, Ibn Rawahah, and Ka'b ibn Malik, and they mentioned that to the Messenger, peace be upon him. Then the verse of exception was revealed at Medina. Ibn Zayd restricted His saying ﴿and remember Allah much﴾ and said: that is, in their poetry. Ibn 'Abbas said: it became a disposition and habit for them, as Labid said when he was asked for his poetry: "Allah has replaced poetry for me with the Qur'an, which is better than it."

When He mentioned ﴿and they defend themselves after they have been wronged﴾, He threatened the wrongdoers with this great, terrifying threat that splits the livers, and He left it vague in His saying: ﴿Those who have wronged will know what sort of return they will return to.﴾

When Abu Bakr appointed 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, he recited to him: ﴿Those who have wronged will know what sort of return they will return to,﴾ and the pious predecessors (*al-salaf al-salih*) would admonish one another with it. What is understood from the Shari'ah is that those who wronged are the disbelievers. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Explaining *zulm* (wrong) as disbelief is a specification (*ta'lil*), and he had mentioned earlier that ﴿those who wronged﴾ is unrestricted, and this is from him in the manner of the Mu'tazilah (*i'tizal*)."
